en: The Mahāyāna-uttaratantra-śāstra, Volume One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
First, I pay homage to the Most Victorious Honored One, who has transcended desire and surpassed the three realms of existence.
I also revere the Omniscient One, The subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Deathless Nectar,
And the assembly of the Eightfold Noble Path, The stainless and pure Saṅgha,
The Bhikṣu Pūrṇaśīla, And the various masters of treatises such as Mi-ji.
The assembly of Sarvāstivādins, those who follow the true path like the king of oxen—
toward all such masters of treatises, we pay our respects and accord with them.
Now I shall proceed to explain the *Vyākhyāyukti*, the treatise that reveals and adorns [the meaning].
Those who hear it shall attain fulfillment, and from this all manner of goodness arises.
Regarding what is worthy of refuge and what is not, what is worthy of offering and what is not—
within these, one should explain the distinctions between good and evil.
(1) It is said:
I have heard that in the past, there was a merchant from the kingdom of Gandhāra who traveled to the kingdom of Mathurā.
Having arrived in that country, there was a Buddhist stūpa within it; among the merchants was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who went daily to that stūpa to pay respectful homage.
On the road leading toward the stupa, there were several brahmins who, seeing the upāsakas prostrating before the Buddha’s stupa, all mocked them together.

On another day, when the weather was extremely hot, these brahmins, having finished their meals, wandered about and dispersed; some were on the road, some stood by the gates, some were bathing, some were applying fragrant unguents, and some were walking or sitting.
At that time, the upāsaka prostrated at the stūpa and turned back; when the brahmins saw him, they called out, "Come, upāsaka! Sit here.
They spoke to the upāsaka, saying:
"Why is it that you now do not recognize those such as Maheśvara and Viṣṇu to pay them homage, yet instead worship a Buddhist stūpa? Will this not cause you vexation?"
Then the upāsaka replied to him, saying:
"I know but a small portion of the World-Honored One’s merits; for this reason, I look up to him with reverence and pay him homage.
I do not yet know what virtues or moral power you, a deva, possess that you should wish me to bow in homage toward you."
When the brahmins heard these words, they glared with anger and rebuked him:
"You foolish man!
How can you speak such words, not knowing the divine power possessed by our gods?"
The brahmins then spoke in verse:
“The city of the asuras is lofty and prominent, with three tiers surrounding it;
suspended in mid-air, it is filled entirely with men and women.”
"I, a celestial being, draw my bow and release my arrow from afar, piercing that city wall;
in a single thought, it is utterly consumed by fire, like dry grass being burned.
When the upāsaka heard this verse, he laughed loudly and said:
"Such a thing as this is beneath my dignity and is not something I hold in reverence.
He replied with a verse:
Life is like dew upon a leaf; All that is born must inevitably perish.
"How can one who possesses wisdom inflict injury with bow and arrow?
When the brahmins heard this verse, they all spoke with one voice, rebuking the upāsaka:
"This is a fool! That asura possesses great power and delights in evil deeds; yet our celestial deities have the power to slay him. How can you say he is not wise?"
At that time, having been rebuked, the lay follower sighed deeply and spoke in verse:
"Having clearly observed both the beautiful and the foul, The wise cultivate wholesome deeds;
They are able to obtain great rewards, And thereafter experience happiness."
How can one conceive of merit in what is actually a fault?
When wrong views have increased, one praises evil as being good;
because of such unwholesome karma, one will later reap the retribution of great suffering.
When the brahmins heard these words, they stared with wide eyes, raised their hands, and, trembling with rage and baring their arms, spoke thus:
"You are utterly foolish and inauspicious! If these various devas do not receive our respect, whom then do you respect?"
At that time, the upāsaka, with a calm and composed mind, spoke to him, saying:
"Although I am alone, I value the application of reason; one should not compete in debate by relying on the strength of factions."
Then the lay follower spoke again in verse:
“The objects of your offerings are fierce and fond of violence;
if you serve them and consider it a meritorious deed, [you will surely fall into the same state].”
One should likewise give rise to reverence; for even toward lions, tigers, and wolves,
which cause harm when provoked, or toward evil spirits and rākṣasas,
the foolish give rise to reverence out of fear.
Those who possess wisdom should investigate deeply;
if one does not cause harm, then one may be treated with respect.
Those who possess all virtues never harbor a mind of malice.
Those who practice various evils will inevitably cause ruin and harm;
they are unable to properly distinguish between merit and fault.
They conceive thoughts of malice toward merit, and perceive merit within faults.
Those who cause harm and oppression are revered and followed by the foolish;
yet toward those of virtuous merit, they instead give rise to thoughts of contempt.
The world is entirely inverted, unable to distinguish between those worthy of honor.
"One born in Gandhāra understands and discriminates between good and evil;
therefore, he has faith in the Tathāgata and does not revere Maheśvara.
When the brāhmaṇa heard these words, he immediately spoke as follows:
“Ho, Gandhāra! Of what lineage do you come, and what virtues and moral conduct do you possess that you are called a Buddha?
At that time, the upāsaka replied with a verse:
"Having departed from the palace of the Śākyas, he has perfected all-encompassing wisdom;
all faults have been weeded out, and all virtues are universally complete.
Among all sentient beings, there has never been one whom he has not benefited."
"Having realized the characteristics of all phenomena and understanding them all with complete clarity,
such a Great Sage is therefore titled 'Buddha'.
At that time, the brahmins spoke again in verse:
"You say that the Buddha, the Great Sage, should have committed acts of violence;
yet here in Jambudvīpa are Caṇḍakauśika, Vatsa, Vāsiṣṭha, Tiṣya, and Ajita."
Thus these great seers, whose fame is heard throughout the world,
are able to bind great divine spells that utterly destroy all kingdoms.
You, named the Buddha, the Great Seer, should likewise perform such a spell.
"You Buddha possess great virtue; you ought to perform acts of harassment.
If you do not employ incantations to cause harm, how can you be called a Great Sage?
At that time, the lay follower could not bear to hear those words of slander; he covered his ears with his hands and spoke this verse:
"Alas! Do not utter evil words; do not slander the Buddha by claiming he possesses incantations.
To revile the Most Victorious Honored One will result in the reaping of great suffering in the future.
At that time, the brahmin spoke again in verse:
"If the Buddha possessed no incantations and spells, he would not be called one of great power;
if he were incapable of causing affliction or harm, how could he be called a Great Sage?
I am merely speaking the truth—why do you call it slander?"
Then the brahmins clapped their hands and laughed loudly, saying:
"Therefore, you fool, you have certainly fallen into defeat."
Then the upāsaka said to the brāhmaṇa: "Do not mock!
Your statement that the Tathāgata possesses neither great merit nor great power is false speech."
The Tathāgata truly possesses the power of great merit that has forever severed the root of incantations; he will never again perform acts of affliction or harm.
Listen attentively now!
I shall speak for you.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Because of greed, hatred, and delusion, one performs great evil spells;
when these evil spells are being bound, malevolent spirits seize their words."
Toward sentient beings who commit transgressions, they practice acts of affliction and harm.
The Buddha has severed greed, hatred, and delusion; through his vast compassion, he brings great benefit, forever uprooting the source of evil spells and leaving only manifold deeds of goodness.
Therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is entirely free from affliction or harm;
by the power of his great merit, he delivers beings from immeasurable suffering.
For what reason do you now say that the Buddha lacks great power?
When the brahmins heard these verses, their anger subsided, and they said to the upāsaka, "We wish to ask a few questions now; please do not be angry with us."
"O upāsaka! If the Buddha possessed no malevolent spells, how could he receive the offerings of others?
Since he neither causes harm nor provides benefit, how can he be called a Great Sage?"
The upāsaka said:

“The Tathāgata possesses great compassion; he never employs malevolent incantations to harm or diminish sentient beings, nor does he act for the sake of gain or sustenance. He accepts offerings solely for the purpose of benefiting others.”
And he spoke in verse:
“With great compassion, he takes pity on all living beings, Constantly desiring to uproot their suffering;
Seeing those who undergo affliction, He regards them as more than his own self.”
Why do you cast evil spells and perform acts of harm?
The nature of sentient beings is suffering, oppressed by birth, old age, sickness, and death;
like an abscess smeared with dry ash, why do you inflict further cruelty?
"By means of the Dharma of constant coolness, may all burning afflictions be brought to rest.
When the brahmins heard these words, they immediately lowered their heads and reflected upon them, thinking:
"This is a most excellent matter."
His mind desired to give rise to faith, thinking:
"Gandhāra, you are skilled in discerning superior places; that you are able to have such faith is truly rare!
Therefore, I praise you."
"Gandhara means 'not in vain'; 'Gandha' means 'to hold. Because he holds what is good and discards what is evil, he has received this name.
Then he spoke in verse:
"One who can uphold this earth Is called a virtuous man (satpuruṣa)."
"O supreme among virtuous men, you are truly a Gandhāra.
At that time, the upāsaka thought to himself:
"This brāhmaṇa’s mind is inclined toward faith and understanding; he is fit to be a vessel. I shall now further explain for him in detail the merits of the Buddha."
At that time, the upāsaka’s countenance was bright and joyful as he spoke these words:
“I am greatly delighted to see your faith in the Buddha.
You should now listen briefly to my words; you ought to examine both their merits and their faults.”
And he spoke in verse:
"Observing the Buddha’s virtues, one is fully satisfied by a single sight;
In precepts, learning, concentration, and wisdom, none are equal to the Buddha."
Among all mountains, Sumeru is supreme; among all streams, the ocean is first.
Among the world’s gods and humans, none can equal the Buddha.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he is able to undergo every form of suffering.
I shall surely cause them to attain liberation, never abandoning or forsaking them.
Who among those who have taken refuge in the Buddha fails to obtain benefit?
Who among those who have taken refuge in the Buddha does not attain liberation?
Who follows the Buddha’s teaching Yet does not sever their afflictions?
With his power of supernatural mastery, The Buddha subdues all non-Buddhists;
His fame is heard far and wide, Pervading the lands of the ten directions.
Only the Buddha’s lion’s roar proclaims that all conditioned phenomena are without self;
his teaching always abides in the middle, unattached to the two extremes.
Among gods and humans alike, he speaks thus.
Unable to skillfully discern the karmic retributions of the fetters and outflows,
after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, various kingdoms constructed stupas and temples that adorned the world like the stars in the sky.
"Therefore, you should know that the Buddha is the most supreme and honored one.
When the brahmins heard these words, some conceived faith, some left the household life, and some attained the Way.
(2) One should carefully contemplate what is appropriate according to the Dharma; if one can so contemplate, one will understand its meaning.

I have heard that in the past there was a brahmin named Kauśika, who was well-versed in the Sāṃkhya treatises, the Vaiśeṣika treatises, and the Nyāya treatises, and who thoroughly understood and analyzed such treatises as these.
That brahmin resided in the city of Pāṭaliputra. Outside the city, there was a village.
On account of some minor business, that brahmin went to that village and arrived at the home of a relative.
At that time, his friend was away on some business, so the Brahmin Kauśika spoke to his family members:
"Does your household have any sacred scriptures?"
"I wish to read both while waiting for him to return.
At that time, his wife, who was close to him, took the books for him; by chance, she obtained the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* and gave it to him.
Having obtained the sutra, he went to a secluded place among the forest trees and read it. He heard: "Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations;

conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is grasping; conditioned by grasping is becoming; conditioned by becoming is birth; and conditioned by birth arise old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair—this is called the Truth of Origination."

With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—the entire mass of suffering—cease.
Upon reading it for the first time, he did not yet understand; however, by the second reading, he immediately realized the doctrine of non-self (*anātman*).
The teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are attached to two views:

the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Having deeply understood that all phenomena (*dharma*) are subject to arising and ceasing and possess no permanence, he thought to himself:
"All external treatises are entirely devoid of the Dharma for transcending birth and death; only within this sutra is found the Dharma for transcending birth and death and attaining liberation.
With a heart full of joy, he immediately raised both hands and spoke these words:
"Now, for the first time, I have obtained the true treatise! Now, for the first time, I have obtained the true treatise!"
Sitting upright in meditation, he contemplated and deeply understood its meaning; his countenance became radiant and joyful like a flower in full bloom, and he spoke again:

"Only now do I truly know the bonds of birth and death and understand the Dharma that transcends the world; I have realized that the various treatises taught by the non-Buddhists are utterly deceptive and do not lead one beyond birth and death."
He sighed and said:
"The Buddha-dharma is most true and most real; it teaches that there is cause and effect, such that when the cause ceases, the effect ceases.
The teachings of the non-Buddhists are utterly false; they claim there is an effect while denying its cause. They do not understand cause and effect, nor do they know liberation."
Reflecting upon myself in the past, I felt deep astonishment and laughter at how I could have sought to cross the river of birth and death through the teachings of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

In the past, while seeking liberation from birth and death among the non-Buddhists, it was as if a person were drowning amidst the waves of the Ganges; fearing for his life, he grasped whatever he encountered, yet failed to escape the calamity and perished submerged in the water.

I am also like this: when I encounter those non-Buddhists seeking deliverance from birth and death, their doctrines entirely lack the methods for liberation and transcendence of the world; consequently, they sink into the river of birth and death, lose their virtuous bodies and lives, and fall into the three evil realms.
Now that you have seen this treatise, you should practice in accordance with it to attain liberation from birth and death.

The scriptures and treatises of non-Buddhists are like the delirious speech of the foolish and mad; all ninety-six types of paths are entirely false and deceptive. Only the Buddha-way is supremely true and perfectly correct.
The followers of the six teachers and other wise men all claim for themselves to be omniscient, yet these are all false words.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is omniscient; he is truthful and not deceptive.
Then Kauśika spoke in verse:
"What is performed by the non-Buddhists Is false and not real;
It is like the play of small children, Piling up earth to make cities and walls."
"A drunken elephant tramples it, Scattering and destroying it until nothing remains;
The Buddha’s refutation of all non-Buddhist doctrines Is likewise of this nature.

At that time, the Brahmin Kauśika conceived a heart of deep faith and reverence for the Buddha-dharma. He abandoned the teachings of the non-Buddhists, eliminated his false views, and constantly recited the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* day and night.
At that time, his kinsman, who was returning home with several Brahmins, asked his wife:
"I have heard that Kauśika has arrived here; where is he now?"
The wife said to her husband:
"That brahmin just now borrowed some scriptures; I took them and gave them to him, though I did not know which sūtras they were.
However, once he received them, he opened and turned them over repeatedly, snapping his fingers in praise with a joyfulness unlike anything I have ever seen."
Upon hearing these words, he went to that place and saw Kauśika sitting upright in contemplation;
he then asked him, "What are you contemplating right now?"
Then Kauśika replied with a verse:
“Foolish and devoid of wisdom, They wander through the three realms of existence, Like the wheel of a potter; They revolve without end.”
"I contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination as the locus for liberation.
At that time, his friend said to him:

"You have conceived such a sense of wonder toward this sutra! I obtained this sutra from a member of the Śākya clan, intending to wash away its characters so that I might write upon them the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra."
Having heard these words, the brahmin Kauśika rebuked his friend:
"You foolish man!
How can you wish to wash this sutra with water?"
"This sublime Dharma should be transcribed using pure gold and enshrined within a precious casket, to be honored with various offerings.
He then spoke in verse:
"If I possessed wealth and treasures, I would construct a stūpa out of pure gold."
Inlaid with the seven precious gems, with jeweled tables and exquisite cloth covers—
adorned with the utmost refinement and used for making offerings—
even performing such deeds as these still does not satisfy my mind.
When his friend heard these words, he was filled with great indignation and said:
"What profound, subtle, and unprecedented matters are there in this sutra?"
"Why must you surpass the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* by desiring to make offerings with pure gold and various precious jewels?
When Kauśika heard these words, his expression turned somber, and he spoke thus:
"For what reason do you now hold the Buddha’s sūtras in such contempt?"
The Vaiśeṣika treatise is fraught with extreme faults; how can it be compared to the Buddha’s word?

Like the Vaiśeṣika treatise, it fails to understand the characteristics of phenomena and confuses cause and effect; regarding even shallow and mundane matters such as the causes and effects of a jar, it lacks the wisdom and discernment to comprehend them, let alone understand the meaning of the causes and effects of the human body, the sense faculties, and awakening wisdom.
At that time, his friend said to Kauśika:
"For what reason do you now say that the Vaiśeṣika treatise does not understand cause and effect?
That treatise states that broken shards are the cause of a jar; how then can you say it does not understand cause and effect?"
Kauśika said: "Your Vaiśeṣika treatise indeed contains such words, yet they lack logical consistency. Consider this for a moment:

just as threads serve as the warp and woof before there is a cloth, so it is with a jar; because the jar exists first, there are subsequently shards. If the jar did not exist beforehand, how could there be shards?"
Furthermore, a broken tile is useless whereas a jar or a pitcher is useful; therefore, a broken tile cannot serve as a cause.

We observe that a potter takes clay to produce a jar and does not use a broken tile; moreover, we see that broken tiles exist only after a jar has been destroyed. If the jar has not yet been destroyed, how could there be broken pieces?
Then his friend said:
"If you believe that the Vaiśeṣika treatise is entirely devoid of reason, then why should we labor in vain and bring hardship upon ourselves?"
When his friends, companions, and fellow brahmins heard these words, they were filled with grief and distress, thinking:
"If it is as he says, then the Vaiśeṣika treatise can no longer be trusted from this day forward?"
Kauśika said:
"The Vaiśeṣika treatises are not only untrustworthy now; they have long been untrustworthy even to those who have observed them well since ancient times."

Why is this so? Formerly, before the Buddha endowed with the ten powers had appeared in the world, all sentient beings were shrouded by ignorance; being blind and sightless, they conceived the notion of clarity regarding the Vaiśeṣika treatises.
Once the Sun of the Buddha has risen and the light of wisdom shines clearly, the Vaiśeṣika treatises have nothing further to offer and should be entirely abandoned.
They are like the owl, which can roam about with power and efficacy at night, yet hides away during the day, lacking all such power and efficacy.
The Vaiśeṣika treatise is likewise so; now that the Sun of the Buddha has risen, that treatise is of no use.
His friend spoke again:
“If it is as you say, that the Vaiśeṣika treatise is not equal to the Buddha’s sūtras, then might these sūtras of the Buddha perhaps be compared to the Sāṃkhya treatise?”
Kauśika said: "As stated in the Sāṃkhya scriptures, there are five members by which a formal argument reaches its conclusion:
first, the proposition (*pratijñā*); second, the reason (*hetu*); third, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); fourth, the application (*upanaya*); and fifth, the conclusion (*nigamana*)."

In your Sāṃkhya scriptures, there is no analogy that can clearly illustrate [the nature of things] as clearly as the example of a bull; how much less could one clarify the characteristics of dharmas through debate? Why is this so?
In your Sāṃkhya scriptures, it is said that *pradhāna* is unproduced and eternal, pervading all places and yet moving to every location.
As stated in the Sāṃkhya scriptures, *pradhāna* is not produced from another, its essence is eternal, it can produce all things, and it pervades everywhere, reaching every place.
To speak in such a manner involves many faults and errors. Why is this?
Within the three realms of existence, there is not a single phenomenon that can produce something by itself without arising from another; therefore, there is error.
Furthermore, the claim that it can reach every place by being already omnipresent is also flawed. Why?
If it were already omnipresent beforehand, where would there be anything left for it to reach?
If it goes to [the other parts], then that which is already pervaded would not be pervaded;
these two principles being contradictory, their meaning is self-contradictory.
If this were the case, then it would be impermanent.
"If it is as you say— that [the self] does not arise from another yet can produce things, and goes everywhere to reach every place—
then these words are false.
Having heard these words, the brahmin friend said to Kauśika:
"You have formed an alliance with the Śākyas, and thus you speak in this manner.

However, the Buddhist scriptures also contain great errors; they claim that there is no beginning to birth and death, and furthermore, they state that within all phenomena (*dharma*) there is no self (*ātman*) whatsoever."
Then Kauśika said to his friend:
"I have seen that in the Buddha-dharma, birth and death are boundless and all things are without self; therefore, my present devotion and faith are profound."

If a person clings to the notion of a self, they will ultimately be unable to attain the path to liberation; if one knows there is no self, then there is no craving, and because there is no craving, one attains liberation.
If one calculates that there is a self, then there will be craving and attachment; since craving and attachment pervade the cycle of birth and death, how can one attain the path to liberation?
Furthermore, if it is said that birth and death have a beginning, then as for this first body, does it arise from wholesome or unwholesome karma?
Does it arise spontaneously, independent of good and evil?
If this body were obtained through good and evil, then one could not say that there was an initial beginning of the body.
If this body were obtained without depending on good and evil, then how could these dharmas of good and evil exist?
If it were so, your doctrine would entail that half arises from causes and half does not arise from causes; to speak in such a manner involves a great fault.
In my Buddha-dharma, there is no beginning, and therefore there is no error.
Then a friend said to Kauśika:
"Where there is bondage, there is liberation. You say that there is no self, and thus there is no bondage; if there is no bondage, who is it that attains liberation?"
Kauśika said: "Although there is no self, there is still bondage and liberation. Why is this?"
"Because they are shrouded by afflictions, one is bound; if one cuts off the afflictions, one attains liberation. Therefore, although there is no self, there still exist bondage and liberation.
The Brahmins spoke again:
"If there is no self, who goes to the next world?"
Then Kauśika addressed the people, saying: "Listen well!

From past afflictions and various karmas, one obtains the present body and its faculties; from now, by again creating various karmas in the present, through these causes and conditions, one obtains the future body and its faculties."
I shall now delight in providing an analogy to clarify this meaning. It is like a grain seed:

through the convergence of various conditions, a sprout is produced; yet this seed does not truly produce the sprout. Because the seed ceases, the sprout grows; because the seed ceases, there is no permanence; and because the sprout arises, there is no annihilation.
The Buddha’s teaching on receiving a body is likewise: although there is no self, the retribution of karma is not lost.
The brahmins said:
"We have heard you teach the Dharma of non-self, which has washed away the defilements of our minds; yet we still have some slight doubts and now wish to inquire further."
"If there is no self, how is it that one remembers and does not forget the deeds performed in the past?
He replied:
"Because there is mindfulness and awareness associated with the mind, one is able to recollect events of the three periods of time without forgetting them."
He asked again:
"If there is no self, then the past has already ceased and the present mind arises; since arising and ceasing are distinct, how can one remember and not forget?"

He replied: "In all instances of rebirth, consciousness acts as the seed that enters the field of the mother's womb; moistened by the water of craving, the tree of the body comes into being. Just as a peach seed grows according to its kind, so too do these aggregates (skandhas) perform karma that can induce subsequent aggregates. Yet, these preceding aggregates do not produce the subsequent aggregates; rather, through the causal conditions of karma, one receives the subsequent aggregates. Although birth and cessation differ, the continuity remains unbroken."
It is like a nursing mother giving medicine to her infant; when the child’s illness is cured, although the mother is not the child, the power and efficacy of the medicine reaches the child.
The *skandhas* (aggregates) are likewise: because of the power of karma, one receives subsequent *skandhas* and remembers them without forgetting.
The brahmins spoke again, saying:
"In the scriptures you have studied, it is only taught that there is no self; do you now understand this and feel joy?"
Then Kauśika recited for him the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* and said to him:
“Ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness, and so on, up to birth conditioning aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair.”
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; continuing thus until, with the cessation of old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction cease.
Because these arise from a multitude of conditions and lack a sovereign master, one thereby realizes non-self within them; it is not merely that the sūtras speak of non-self.

Furthermore, because there is a body, there is a mind; because there are the body and mind, the sense faculties have their functions, and consciousness performs discernment and discrimination. Having realized this matter, I understand that there is no self.
He asked again:
"If it is as you say—that the succession of bodies received through birth and death continues without interruption—what fault would there be in possessing the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi)?
He replied:

"Because of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one performs various karmas and undergoes the forms of good and evil within the five destinies; when one obtains an evil form, one experiences various sufferings and afflictions.

If one severs the view of a self-body, one does not give rise to karmas; because one does not give rise to karmas, one does not receive a body; because one does not receive a body, all afflictions are forever stilled, and one attains nirvāṇa."
Why do you say that the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is not a fault?

Furthermore, if the view of a self were not a fault, there would be no birth and death; one would not undergo the suffering of birth and death within the three realms of existence. Therefore, it is indeed a fault.

At that time, the brahmin examined the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination both forward and backward; he developed deep faith and understanding, and with a heart full of joy, briefly praised the Buddha’s Dharma, speaking in verse:
"When the Tathāgata was in the world, He preached the Dharma to subdue all disputants.
The Buddha-sun shines upon the world, And all the various heretics are eclipsed."
Now that I have encountered the bequeathed Dharma, I am as if in the presence of the World-Honored One.
Among the Śākyas, he is most excellent and sublime; he has profoundly penetrated the characteristics of all phenomena.
That which is called the Tathāgata is true and not false.
Contemplating all phenomena in both their forward and reverse orders, his fame spread everywhere.
Facing the direction of the Buddha’s nirvana, he joined his palms in reverence and paid homage, exclaiming:
"The World-Honored Buddha truly possesses a heart of great compassion."
"Most excellent among all sages, peerless in the world,
I now take refuge in him who possesses incomparable morality, concentration,
and wisdom. Kauśika said:
“How is it that you now understand the Buddha’s merits so profoundly?

His friend replied, “Having heard this Dharma, I therefore know the immeasurable merits of the Buddha. It is like agarwood, which is black, heavy, and oily; for these reasons, when it is burned, it is exceedingly fragrant and its scent is perceived both near and far.”
Thus, because I have seen the Tathāgata’s body of concentration and wisdom, I know that the World-Honored One possesses great merit.

Although I do not behold the Buddha at this moment, seeing the holy traces of the Buddha, I know him to be most supreme. It is just as when someone, seeing the footprints of an elephant beside a flower pond, knows it to be a large one; likewise, although one does not see the Buddha while reading the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra*, one knows that the merit of the Buddha’s holy traces is greatest.
Seeing that his friends had developed deep faith and understanding, he marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and said:

"In the past, you have read and recited many non-Buddhist scriptures; yet now, upon hearing the Buddha’s sutras for but a brief moment, you have understood their meaning and completely abandoned those external texts—this is truly most rare."
He then spoke in verse:
"Having cast aside erroneous views and discourses, One who has faith and understanding in the true and correct Dharma— Such a person is difficult to find; Therefore, I praise this as rare."
We do not merely praise you; we also praise the various external treatises because their principles are base and shallow, and for that reason, we have completely abandoned them.

"Because those treatises possess faults and defects, they have caused us to develop a sense of weary detachment and a mind of faith and understanding. The Buddha is truly a Great Man with no equal; his fame is universally heard throughout the lands of the ten directions."

The various heterodox doctrines of outsiders are fraught with internal contradictions from beginning to end; they are like deceitful speech that cannot be clearly discerned. Because of their inherent flaws, I have abandoned them and gained entry into the Buddha-dharma. It is just as when people suffer from the heat of the sun during the spring and summer and all wish to escape it, yet once winter’s cold arrives, everyone longs for its return.

The treatises of the non-Buddhists are likewise; they should truly be abandoned like the summer sun, yet one should also reflect that it is through these very treatises that faith is born, just as one longs for the sun during the cold season.
At that time, his friends asked Kauśika,
"What should we do now? Kauśika replied:
"Now it is fitting that we abandon all heterodox doctrines and leave the household life to study the Way within the Buddha-dharma. Why is this?

Just as when a great torch is lit in the darkness of night, all the pigeons and birds fall down; so too, once the lamp of the Buddha’s wisdom has appeared in the world, all followers of external paths must surely fall. For this reason, we now wish to leave the household life to study the Way."
Thereupon, Kauśika departed from the house of his kinsmen and went straight to the monastery to seek ordination; having been ordained, he attained arhatship.
For what reason and by what causes was this matter spoken?
Because various non-Buddhists are constantly deluded by their own false doctrines, the sūtras and śāstras on the twelve links of dependent origination are taught to analyze and refute them.
(3) Furthermore, when selecting a field of merit, one should take its virtue as the standard; one should not discriminate based on whether it is young or old, robust or decrepit.

I have heard that in the past, there was a donor who sent a spiritual friend, a practitioner of the Way, to a saṃghārāma to invite the assembly of monks, specifically requesting only those who were elderly and not those who were young.
Later, when a knowledgeable lay devotee invited the assembly of monks, it was the turn of the śrāmaṇeras; however, they were not permitted [to eat].
The śrāmaṇeras said:
"For what reason are we śrāmaṇeras not permitted [to eat]?"
He replied, "The donor does not need it; it is not mine.
The monk who was exhorting and converting him then spoke this verse:
"The elders possess long-standing virtue; their hair is white and their faces are wrinkled.
Their eyebrows are prominent and their teeth have fallen out; their backs are bent and their limbs are slack.
The donor delights in such as these, and does not rejoice at seeing the young."

At that time, there were several śrāmaṇeras in the monastery, all of whom were arhats. It was as if someone had provoked a lion by touching its vital parts at the waist, causing it to become enraged; the śrāmaṇeras all spoke thus:
"That donor is foolish and lacks wisdom; he does not delight in those with virtue, but only craves the elderly."
Then the śrāmaṇeras spoke in verse:
"One who is called an elder Is not necessarily one with white hair, wrinkled face, and missing teeth;
if he is foolish and lacks wisdom, he is not truly an elder."
What is truly noble is the ability to cultivate merit, to eliminate all evils, and to purely practice the holy life; such a person is called an elder.
Regarding praise or blame, we do not give rise to thoughts of increase or decrease.
We must ensure that those donors do not incur transgressions,
nor allow them to slander the Sangha— the field of merit— by harboring views of increase or decrease.
We should go to them quickly and inspire them.
Lest they fall into the evil realms,
he immediately employed his supernormal powers to manifest the form of an old man,
with white hair and wrinkled face, bushy eyebrows and fallen teeth.
Hunchbacked and leaning on a staff, he went to the house of that donor.
Once the donor had seen him, his heart was filled with great joy;
he burned incense, scattered famous flowers, and quickly invited him to take his seat.
Having arrived, in a mere moment, he returned to the form of a śrāmaṇera.
The donor was struck with amazement; such was his miraculous transformation!
Having drunk the celestial nectar, his countenance suddenly became radiant and changed.
At that time, the śrāmaṇera spoke these words:

"I am neither a yakṣa nor a rākṣasa. Previously, seeing that you, donor, had selected the elderly and conceived thoughts of high and low regarding the Sangha—the field of merit—I thereby destroyed your roots of goodness; therefore, I manifested this transformation to cause you to repent and reform."
He then spoke in verse:
"Just as a mosquito's proboscis Wishes to exhaust the depths of the great ocean,
so too is it impossible for anyone in the world To fathom the merit of the Saṃgha."
"All are powerless to calculate the virtues of the Saṃgha;
how much less can you, all alone, seek to measure them?
The śrāmaṇera spoke again:

"You should not now compare the elders and the juniors among the Saṃgha based on their physical appearance. One who seeks the Dharma does not observe physical appearance, but focuses solely on wisdom.

Though one’s body may be young, if they have severed all fetters and outflows and attained the Noble Path, they are so; though one is old, if they are negligent, they are called 'young' [in spirit]. What you have done is most improper."

If one were to attempt to exhaust the depths of the ocean with one's fingernails, such a thing is impossible; so it is with you: to seek to measure the field of merit with your own intelligence in order to know its high and low points—this too is impossible.
Have you not heard the *Sūtra of the Four Not-Looking-Down*, spoken by the Tathāgata?
A prince, a snake, fire, and a śrāmaṇera—all these must never be treated with contempt.

As the World-Honored One taught in the parable of the mango fruit: some are ripe within but unripe without, while others are ripe without but unripe within. Do not recklessly judge the merits or shortcomings of others; even in a single thought-moment, one may attain the Way.

"You have now committed a most grievous transgression. If you have any doubts, you may ask about them all now; from this day forward, never again give rise to such discriminatory thoughts regarding the Sangha, the field of merit."
He then spoke in verse:
“The ocean of the Sangha’s merit Is beyond anyone’s capacity to measure;
Even the Buddha gave rise to joy and reverence, Praising it himself with a hundred verses.”
How much more so for all other people?
Who would not praise this vast and excellent field of merit, where planting even a little yields great benefit?
The harmonious Saṃgha of Śākyamuni is called the Third Jewel.
Amidst the great assembly, do not judge a person by their appearance.
One must not, based on lineage, dignified demeanor, or eloquent speech,
venerate someone for their outward form before having fathomed their inner virtue.
Observing his form, though it appears young and frail, he possesses wisdom and high virtue;
yet, not knowing the conduct of his inner mind, one might further give rise to contempt.
It is like a great forest where *campaka* flowers are interspersed with *eranda* weeds.
Though the various trees differ in height, their groves are no different;
though the Sangha has elders and juniors, one should not give rise to discrimination.
When Kāśyapa wished to leave the home life, he cast off his body’s most exquisite garments.
Taking even the lowest garment from the storehouse, it was still worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
Such is the nature of the Sangha as a field of merit:
by making offerings to even the most lowly member, one obtains a reward for a hundred thousand lifetimes.
Just as the waters of the great ocean do not harbor a corpse,
so too the ocean of the Sangha does not tolerate those who violate the precepts.
Among the ranks of ordinary monks, even one who maintains the fewest precepts is held in the highest regard.
By revering and making offerings with devotion, one can obtain a great karmic reward.
Therefore, toward the Sangha— whether they be elders or the young—
one should offer sustenance with an impartial mind and not give rise to discrimination.
At that time, having heard these words, the donor’s hair stood on end; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he sought mercy and repented:
“Ordinary, foolish people have many faults and transgressions. I pray that you will accept my repentance and, out of compassion, explain all my doubts.”
Then he spoke in verse:
“You possess great wisdom, Having severed the net of all doubts;
If I were not to consult you, I would not be a wise person.”
At that time, the śrāmaṇera said to him:
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you.
The donor asked:
“Venerable Sir!
Between reverence for the Buddha and reverence for the Saṅgha, which is superior?
The śrāmaṇera replied:
"Do you not know that there are the Three Jewels?
The donor replied,
"Although I now indeed know that there are the Three Jewels, could there not be one most supreme among them?"
The śrāmaṇera replied,
"I see no increase or decrease in the Buddha or the Saṃgha.
He then spoke this verse:
“There was a brahmin of great lineage, named Tulaśa;
whether in praise or blame, he made no distinction regarding the Buddha, and offered food to the Tathāgata.
Since the Tathāgata did not accept it, none within the three realms could consume it.”
Casting it into the water, smoke and flames arose simultaneously.
Gopikā offered the robe, and the Buddha commanded that it be given to the community of monks;
by this causal connection, the Three Jewels are equal and without distinction.
At that time, having heard these words, the donor immediately said:
"If the Buddha and the Sangha are equal and no different, for what reason did you place the food in the water instead of giving it to the assembly of monks?"
The śrāmaṇera replied, “The Tathāgata has no stinginess regarding food at all; he did this only because he wished to manifest the power of the virtues of the Saṃgha.”

Why was this so? Because when the Buddha observed this food, he saw that within the three realms there was no one capable of digesting it; if it were placed in water, the water would immediately boil with flames.
Nevertheless, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī still offered her robes to the Buddha, who returned them to the Saṃgha; once the assembly of monks had accepted them, they underwent no change.
"Therefore, you should know that the Saṃgha possesses great virtue; the Buddha and the Saṃgha are not different, and it has attained great renown.
At that time, the donor spoke these words:
"From this day forward, toward the assembly of monks, whether they be old or young, I shall honor them with an impartial mind and no longer give rise to discrimination."
The śrāmaṇera replied,
"If you act thus, you shall before long attain the Way of seeing the Truth.
He then spoke this verse:
"Much learning and the observance of precepts, Meditative concentration and wisdom—
For those who proceed toward the three vehicles, They attain both the fruits and the paths.
Just as the river Sindhu Flows and pours into the great ocean,"
All these worthy sages and saints have entered the great ocean of the Saṃgha.
Just as within the Snowy Mountains all manner of wondrous medicines abound,
and just as a fertile field causes seeds to grow, so it is with them.
"All wise and virtuous people emerge from within the Saṅgha.
Having spoken this verse, he said:
"O Dānapati!"
Have you not heard that in the sutras, these three sons of noble family—Aniruddha, Nandi, and Kambila—were addressed by the great general of spirits named Gava, who said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!..."
In all worlds—whether among devas, humans, māras, or brahmās—anyone who can bring these three sons of noble family to mind will be able to cause them to obtain benefit, peace, and happiness.
"If even three people within the Saṃgha can still bring about benefit, how much more so the great assembly?
He then spoke in verse:
"Even three people do not constitute a formal Saṃgha, Yet by mindfulness, they obtain benefit."
As that ghost leader said: "Even one who has not yet attained the name 'one who recollects the Saṅgha' still obtains such great benefit;
how much more so for one who truly recollects the Saṅgha?
Therefore, you should know that all meritorious and virtuous deeds [arise from this]."
All emerge from within the Saṃgha.
Just as only the great ocean can withstand and receive the rain of a mighty dragon, so too is the assembly of monks: they are able to receive the great rain of the Dharma.
Therefore, you should single-mindedly keep the Sangha in mind.
This assembly of the virtuous, this great multitude of those who have attained liberation—
the Sangha is like a valiant army, capable of crushing the enemy forces of Māra.
Such is the Sangha: a grove of supreme wisdom, wherein all virtuous deeds are gathered and assembled;
it is the great and victorious fellowship that leads to liberation through the three vehicles.
At that time, after the śrāmaṇera had finished praising with these verses, the donor’s retinue was filled with great joy, and they all attained the fruit of srotāpanna.
The Mahāvyūha-śāstra Sūtra, Volume One.
The Mahāvyūha-śāstra Sūtra, Volume Two.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin Dynasty.
(4) Furthermore, for one who listens to the Dharma, there is great benefit: it expands and broadens wisdom, and enables the mind and its faculties to become entirely disciplined and compliant.

I have heard that in the past, in the various kingdoms of Siṃhala, there was a man who obtained a maṇi jewel as large as a person’s knee; this gem was so exquisite and rare in the world that he offered it to the king.
Having obtained the pearl, the king gazed intently at it and spoke this verse:
"The kings of antiquity, Accumulating treasures to seek renown,
Gathered together their guests And displayed their jewels with self-conceit."
At the moment of death when one leaves this state, one abandons all treasures and departs alone;
only wholesome and unwholesome karma follows the body, never leaving it behind.
It is like a bee making honey: others may obtain it, but the bee itself gains nothing.
Wealth and treasures are likewise: they benefit others but do not follow oneself.
In the past, various kings were deceived by their treasures;
though they accumulated them for the sake of others, not a single one followed them when they departed.
I shall now act for myself, ensuring that my treasures follow me;
within the field of merit that is the Buddha alone, I shall cultivate all manner of virtues,
so that they may accompany me into future lives as an imperishable reward of goodness.
When the time of death approaches, one must abandon everything:
the palace, the chambers, and all loved ones;
the ministers and the mighty generals will follow the deceased with sorrowful longing, but upon reaching the cemetery, they shall return home.
Elephants, horses, precious litters and carriages, rare treasures and storehouses,
the people and all the city-states, gardens and delightful groves—
he has cast them all away with effortless ease and departed alone, with no one to follow him.

Having spoken these verses, the king went at once to the site of the stupa and placed this precious jewel upon its pinnacle. It shone with such brilliance as a great star; when it illuminated the royal palace, its radiance reflecting back, it was twice as bright as usual.
The radiance of the jewel was always thus day after day; yet for one day, it suddenly lost its luster. The king, marveling at this, immediately dispatched men to investigate.

Upon arriving there, they did not see the precious jewel, but only saw blood flowing beneath the pillar, staining the ground. Following the trail of blood, they reached the Kāṭhala forest, and before they had even entered the forest, they saw the thief who had stolen the jewel crouching and hiding among the trees.
When the man who had stolen the pearls was taking them, he fell against a thorn and broke his thigh, which is why there was this blood; they then seized him and brought him before the king.
When the king first saw him, he felt great indignation, but seeing his injuries, he gave rise to compassion and looked upon him with a loving heart, saying to him: "Alas, O man!"
"You are exceedingly foolish; having stolen the Buddha’s precious jewel, you will surely fall into the evil realms in a future life.
He then spoke a verse:
"How strange! How utterly foolish, To commit such great evil through lack of wisdom!"
Just as one who fears the blow of a staff Instead receives the infliction of execution;
So too, fearing the suffering of poverty, One gives rise to this deranged and foolish intent:
Unable to endure even slight deprivation, One suffers endless calamities for a long time.
At that time, having heard these verses, one minister immediately addressed the king, saying:
"What Your Majesty has spoken is true and not false.
He then spoke in verse:
“The stupa is a treasure among men; if a fool should steal it, that person for immeasurable kalpas will not encounter the Triple Gem.
Long ago there was a man who, out of faith and joy,”
One who offers *sumana* flowers upon their ears to a stūpa of the Buddha will experience supreme great happiness for ten billion kalpas among humans and devas. Yet,
one who steals jewels from the stūpa of the World-Honored One, the One of Ten Powers, to provide for themselves...
"Because of these karmic conditions, he has sunk into hell.
Another minister, harboring resentment, said:
"The guilt of such a fool is already manifest; why is it necessary to rebuke him?"
"You ought to be subjected to execution.
The king said to his ministers,
"Do not utter such words!"
"Since that person is already dead, why must you kill him again?
It is as when a person has fallen to the ground; one ought to help them up.
At that time, the king spoke this verse:
"This person has already violated his conduct; you should quickly rescue him.
I shall bestow wealth and treasures upon him, so that he may repent and cultivate merit, enabling him to escape and be free from the great sufferings and hardships of the future."
I shall provide him with wealth so that he may make offerings to the Buddha;
if he does not turn toward the Buddha, his transgressions will never be extinguished.
Just as a person who has stumbled on the ground can still be helped up by supporting them, [so too is the power of the Buddha's grace].
"Because of the Buddha, one incurs transgressions and offenses; yet because of the Buddha, they are also extinguished.
At that time, the king immediately bestowed great wealth upon him, instructing him to perform various meritorious deeds for the sake of the Buddha.
At that time, the thief thought to himself:
"Now, O Great King!
Had I not been one who has been disciplined and harmonized within the Buddha-dharma, I would surely have been executed for my transgression."
"This king is truly capable of forbearance; he is indeed a great man who pardons my grave offense.
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni is most extraordinary, for he is able to transform and guide a king of such wrong views as to perform such an act."

Having spoken these words, he returned to the site of the stūpa and crawled toward the monastery. Joining his palms in reverent devotion, he made this declaration: "The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One is the true savior of the world;

though he has entered parinirvāṇa, he is still able to bestow life upon me as a gift. The world universally calls him the 'True Savior,' and his fame is heard throughout all worlds. Since he has now saved my life, the title 'True Savior' is not established in vain."
He then spoke in verse:
“The world calls you the True Savior; this name is indeed not in vain.
Having now received your rescue, I understand the true meaning of being a Savior.”
The world is entirely ablaze, filled with many stifling torments;
the cool moon of compassion shines forth to dispel the suffering of feverish affliction.
When the Tathāgata was in the world, at the abode of the wilderness spirits,
To rescue the Elder Śreṣṭhin was not difficult;
but after my parinirvāṇa, to deliver others from peril through the bequeathed Dharma and enable me [and them] to escape suffering and affliction— this is truly most difficult.
How is it that the worldly artisans, with such marvelous skill, have conformed to the Sage’s mind?
In their image, he raises his right hand, displaying a gesture of consolation;
when those who are terrified behold it, they are even able to cast off their fear.
How much more so when the Buddha was in the world, for those he rescued were exceedingly numerous;
now that we have encountered this great suffering and calamity, it is the image that has saved us.
(5) Furthermore, as for one who has few desires, although they possess wealth and goods, their mind does not cling to them; thus they may still be called one who has few desires.
I have heard that in the past there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*). At that time, he had a close friend who placed his faith in the Brahminical dharma.

This friend, a devout believer in the Brahmins, wore tattered clothing, practiced austerities, scorched himself with the five fires, constantly ate coarse food, and slept amidst filth and excrement. He then called out to the lay follower, saying:
"You should come here and observe these Brahmins. Have you ever seen a person of such high conduct, who purifies their body through self-mortification, possessing such few desires and contentment?"
The upāsaka said,
"Such high conduct could indeed deceive you.
He then went with his friends to question the brāhmaṇa:
"What do you seek through these ascetic practices now?
The brahmin replied,
"I now practice asceticism desiring to become a king."
Then the upāsaka said to his friend:

"This man is now seeking the treasures and jewels of the great earth's treasuries; he slaughters [beings] at will, indulges in delicious flavors, and delights in the beauty of women as palace attendants, amusing himself with all kinds of music."

Although he serves as a minister or a householder possessing various treasures, these do not satisfy his desires; rather, he seeks all the people, lands, and precious gems of the entire earth—how, then, can he be called one of few desires?

"You merely see that his bodily conduct consists of ascetic practices and thus claim he has few desires; you do not know that this man’s seeking is insatiable, yet you call him one who has few desires.
He then spoke in verse:
"What is called 'having few desires' Does not necessarily mean loathing food and clothing."
To have no means of livelihood and thus claim to have few desires—
such a person today has a mind like a great river or ocean;
how can one who craves insatiably be called one with few desires?
Now, practicing these ascetic austerities for the sake of craving and thirsting after the five desires,
this person is truly hypocritical; falsely manifesting the appearance of fewness of wishes,
he inflicts suffering upon himself out of greed, yet in reality, he is not one who possesses few desires.
Having spoken these verses, the upāsaka further said:
"This man now possesses all manner of greed, anger, and delusion; he does not possess even a fraction of what is practiced by sages and saints."
Therefore, you should know that one who has few desires does not consist of possessing much wealth or many precious objects.
How is this known?
For example, King Bimbisāra possessed a kingdom, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures, yet he was still called one who had few desires.

Why is this so? Although they possess wealth and treasures, their minds do not cling to them, as they delight in the Noble Path. For this reason, even though they may be rich with an abundance of the seven precious gems overflowing [their homes], their minds harbor no longing; this is called having few desires.
"Though one lacks wealth and treasures yet remains insatiable in their longing, they cannot be said to have 'few desires and contentment.
Thus he spoke in verse:
'If it were because of lacking food and clothing, Then those such as the naked Nirgranthas [would be considered so].'"
Those who undergo various arduous labors and practice asceticism,
as well as hungry ghosts, animals, and those afflicted by poverty and all manner of distress—
those in such states of hardship should also be called practitioners of asceticism.
That person is just like this: they merely exhaust themselves in vain;
though their body performs ascetic practices, their mind harbors greed and attachment.
Seeking without satiety, they cannot be called one of few desires.
Though one may possess many things, if the mind has no attachment,
and one practices with delight in the Noble Path, this is called having few desires.
It is like farmers who sow seeds in the fields.
To greedily gather many fruits and rewards is not called having few desires.
One’s body is like a malignant ulcer; it requires various implements for its maintenance.
Because the mind seeks the Path, one is called a person of few desires.
To treat the malignant ulcer of evil, one accepts few requisites for life;
with a mind that does not crave future existence, this is truly called having few desires.
With a mind free from flattery and crookedness, one likewise seeks neither fame nor profit.
"Though one possesses the means of livelihood,
fame, and genuine virtue, yet can maintain such conduct— this indeed is true fewness of desires.
(6) Furthermore, though one may observe the precepts for the sake of the pleasures of humans and devas, this is called breaking the precepts.

I have heard that in the past, there was a śramaṇa who, together with a brāhmaṇa, observed the summer retreat (varṣā) in a forest. At that time, the śramaṇa went back and forth to the brāhmaṇa’s place frequently; he engaged in activities with him, maintaining neither intimacy nor distance, but remaining impartial between them.
Why is this so? If one associates with them too intimately, they may give rise to arrogance; if one distances oneself from them, they will think one harbors hatred.
Thus, he spoke in verse:
"If one places a staff in the midday sun, it casts no shadow whether held upright or laid flat;
yet when the staff is held leaning at an angle, its shadow becomes long and extended.
So it is with that person: they should maintain a middle way toward both kin and strangers."
Once they have become gradually relaxed and at ease, I shall then preach the Dharma to them.

"This brahmin lacks wisdom; he cannot distinguish between the worthy and the foolish, and his service is exceedingly burdensome. Therefore, it is not appropriate for me now to be overly intimate with him, nor should I remain distant."
Why is this? Serving fools is suffering; not understanding how to serve them is likewise called suffering.
Through various skillful means, they gradually associate with one another, come to trust each other, and are able to converse.
At that time, the bhikṣu asked the brāhmaṇa:

"For what reason do you now raise your hands toward the sun, lie upon ashes and dust, go naked and eat grass, and stand on one foot day and night without lying down? For what purpose do you practice such austerities?"
The brāhmaṇa replied,
“I seek a king. Shortly thereafter,
this brāhmaṇa fell ill and went to consult a physician for a method to treat his disease.
The physician replied,
"It is necessary that you eat meat.
Thereupon, the brahmin spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"You should go to the house of my donor for me and beg for a little meat to cure my illness.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"Now is the very moment for me to transform him."
Having had this thought, he transformed himself into a sheep and tied it beside him.
The brahmin asked the bhikṣu, "You were seeking meat; where is it now?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“The sheep is itself the meat.
The brāhmaṇa became greatly incensed and spoke these words:
"Would I rather kill a sheep and eat its flesh?
Thereupon, the bhikṣu answered with a verse:
"If you now feel compassion for a single sheep, you still do not wish to kill it."
Later, if you become a king, you will slaughter cattle,
sheep, pigs, chickens, dogs, and wild beasts in measureless numbers;
while you sit upon your royal throne, the cooks shall provide you with food.
When you are filled with anger, you should say, "I shall cut off his head," or "I shall sever his hands and feet," and at other times,
"I shall gouge out his eyes. Yet now, out of pity for a single sheep, you wish to slaughter many.
If you truly possess a compassionate heart, you should abandon the intent to seek the throne.
It is like a man facing execution who drinks much wine out of fear of suffering;
or like a flowering grove in full bloom when a fierce fire is about to consume it.
Furthermore, just as wearing a golden chain, though beautiful, can act as a fetter, so too is the position of a king:
it is constantly accompanied by a heart of fear.
Though surrounded by powerful attendants and adorned with precious jewels, [it remains a source of anxiety].
Failing to see future calamities, the ordinary person greedily craves and seeks.
Having obtained [what they desire], they commit various evils and fall into the three evil realms;
like a moth greedy for the color of fire, it throws itself into the flame and is consumed by its own destruction.
Though one possesses the pleasures of the five desires, And one's fame is widely known, One constantly harbors much fear;
The affliction of sorrow and suffering is extremely deep.
It is like grasping a venomous snake, Or holding a torch against the wind.
The arrival of danger and harm cannot be avoided, just like the suffering at the moment of death.
When the king goes forth on his excursion, he wears a celestial crown upon his head,
adorned with necklaces of various jewels and robes of the most exquisite beauty.
Mounted upon fine horses and chariots of many jewels, he went out on inspection;
his retinue numbered hundreds of thousands, and his majestic power was most magnificent.
Whenever there were enemies or invaders, his precious armor would spontaneously adorn his body.
Victory brings much slaughter; defeat costs one’s life and limb.
With exquisite perfumes smeared upon the body, and fine garments scented with fragrance, one indulges the palate with various delicacies and a hundred flavors.
Whatever was required was granted according to his wishes, with no one ever opposing him;
yet whether walking, coming, sitting, or lying down, all his movements were met with suspicion and fear.
Even his close friends did not trust him, for though they were indeed his kinsmen and friends, [they remained wary].
Constantly possessing a mind of peril and fear, how can it be called happiness?
It is like a fish swallowing a hook and bait, or like a sharp blade smeared with honey;
it is also like a net or a snare, for fish and beasts greedily crave its flavor.
Failing to see future suffering and affliction, even those of noble wealth and status are likewise;
in the end, they undergo the torments of hell.
Within that hell, the walls, enclosures, houses, and ground are all ablaze, and the sinners dwell therein.
Fire issues from the burning of the body, and the suffering experienced is immeasurable.
You should reflect for yourself: since the pleasure obtained is so slight, while the various sufferings and afflictions are so many, you ought therefore to contemplate suffering.
"Do not seek noble sovereignty; abandon your heart that seeks such things.
Seek only liberation, and all sufferings will be completely eliminated.
Having heard this verse, the brāhmaṇa remained silent and did not answer; he joined his palms toward the bhikṣu and said:
"Venerable One!
Your eloquence has awakened my mind; even if I were to become the king of those thirty-two heavens, I would find no pleasure therein.
He then spoke this verse:
"With benevolent intent and skillful means, with clear wisdom capable of discernment, you have removed my evil aspirations and shown me the path of true correctness.
A good friend should be thus; such is what is praised by the world."
One should always associate with such friends, who are free from the affliction of strife;
they rightly guide my mind, turning me away from the crooked and leading me into the right path,
showing me the signs of good and evil, and enabling me to attain liberation.

(7) Furthermore, those who rely on wrong paths encounter manifold sufferings and afflictions, whereas those who cultivate the right path increase in faith and renown; therefore, a person of wisdom should discern between the wrong and the right.

I have heard that in the past there was a man who practiced a minor form of asceticism by the side of a road; when people were present, he would lie upon thorns, but when no one was around, he would dwell elsewhere.
Someone, having seen this, said to him:
"You might as well lie down slowly upon the thorns; why must you cast your body down so as to cause such great injury?
Upon hearing this, the man gave rise to deep resentment and anger, threw himself down, casting his body onto the thorns, suffering even more intensely than before.
At that time, a lay follower (upāsaka) was standing beside him; upon seeing this, the ascetic shook himself, and his suffering became even more intense.
The lay follower then said to him:
"Previously you used only a small thorn, but now you use the thorns of anger to pierce yourself."
The thorns previously mentioned cause only slight injury and destruction; the thorns of greed and hatred, however, are deep and sharp.

One who lies upon thorny brambles suffers pain for only a single lifetime, whereas the suffering from the thorns of greed and hatred extends to immeasurable lifetimes. A wound inflicted by a physical thorn is easily healed, but the wound caused by the thorns of greed and hatred does not subside for kalpas. Therefore, one should swiftly remove these deeply poisonous thorns.
Then he spoke in verse:
"You should now diligently pull out The deep, poisonous thorns within your heart;
With the sharp sword of wisdom, You ought to sever the brambles of greed and hatred."
Those deeply attached to greed and hatred cannot dispel them life after life;
the ignorant and those with various false views do not recognize the true and authentic Path.
They torment their bodies by lying upon thorns, seeking to leave suffering through further suffering.
When people see one lying upon thorns, there are none who do not flee from them at a distance;
yet you alone, amidst such suffering, embrace it and will not let go.
Seeing this matter, I then know what is heterodox and what is orthodox.
Therefore, I take refuge once more in the World-Honored One of Ten Powers,
who with great compassion uproots the sufferings of the multitude and reveals the Right Path;
for those multitudes who have traversed deviant ways, he guides them by means of the Eightfold Noble Path.
Those of external paths and wrong views, deceived by suffering, are excessively attached to it;
thus they wander through saṃsāra without end.
Those possessed of wisdom, seeing this, increase their faith all the more.
The non-Buddhists are deeply deluded; [only] through the exhaustion of suffering does one attain liberation.
Thus the Great Sage who has transcended the world has taught:
when all requisites are fully provided, one attains the cultivation of the Eightfold Noble Path; by cultivating the path, one attains liberation.
For this reason, you should know that one attains liberation through peace and happiness;
it is not as you non-Buddhists claim, that one attains nirvāṇa by undergoing suffering.
It is based on the mind that one performs various karmas, such as those that are wholesome or unwholesome.
You should subdue your mind; why do you pointlessly torment your body?
The body is the locus of all fetters and afflictions, yet you falsely practice various forms of austerity.
If this were the path of practicing the Way, then hell would surely be that path.
Yet within these hells, one undergoes the full brunt of manifold agonies—
being hacked and severed, immersed in excrement, and scorched by blazing fires.
Although they endure such sufferings, these cannot be called ascetic practices.
Wisdom dispels the three karmas, and all defilements are eliminated.
The teaching of Śākyamuni instructs all people:
they should seek the nectar of the heavens, and he further proclaims the practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, adorning one's wisdom—this is called true asceticism.
Why exhaust the body in vain, creating useless suffering?
This suffering is exceedingly long-lasting, deep and vast, without limit or bound.
"Just as there may be a wicked son who fails to provide filial support,
but instead commits various sinful acts, thereby undergoing manifold sufferings.
At that time, those non-Buddhists spoke these words:
"The various sages practiced austerities, And likewise attained birth in the heavens.
The upāsaka spoke a verse in reply to him, saying:
"The sages were born in the heavens Not because they lay upon thorns."
Through generosity, morality, and truthful speech, one is born in the heavens;
though you have performed ascetic practices, they yield no benefit at all.
It is like a farmer in spring who does not sow any seeds.
When autumn arrives, there are no fruits, yet one might expect a harvest.
You all are likewise: if you do not plant the seeds of roots of goodness but merely practice various ascetic penances, in the end you shall gain nothing at all.
Now, those who wish to cultivate the Path should rely upon this body;
by providing it with delicious food and drink, they shall satisfy its life-force.
Once its strength and vigor are fully replenished, it will be able to cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Through extreme fasting, one suffers from intense hunger and thirst; body and mind are both agitated and distressed.
If the mind cannot be made single-pointed and concentrated, how can one attain the fruits of holiness?
Even when consuming delicacies and fine foods, one does not crave their exquisite flavors.
Yet for the sake of precepts and truthful speech, through generosity, patience, and meditative concentration—
these serve as seeds capable of yielding virtuous fruits.
Though the body suffers from hunger and thirst, the mind still longs for exquisite flavors.
If one is not yet satisfied even with the cause, how much less could one obtain its beautiful fruit?
If one harbors a harmful mind, causing others to give rise to fear;
if one eliminates that harmful mind and is able to bestow fearlessness upon others—
This is what is called practicing the Dharma;
if one instead gives rise to harmful intent, it is called non-Dharma.
One should never harbor the thought of harming others; because of this mind of non-harming, [one attains peace].
There is no harm done to others; even if one arouses a heart of great compassion, one will obtain a great fruit of goodness.
Although you practice self-starvation and sleep while hungry and thirsty, it is likewise a matter of no benefit.
The non-Buddhists spoke thus:
"Just as you have given rise to a mind of loving-kindness, it may not necessarily bring benefit, yet it will yield a great karmic fruit."
"Even if one sleeps while fasting, the result is likewise;
though it may not benefit others, one still attains a favorable karmic retribution.
The upāsaka replied:
“Loving-kindness eliminates hatred and harm; because it eliminates hatred and harm, one can obtain a wholesome retribution.
Your practice of asceticism increases hatred;
since it gives rise to evil in body and speech, how could you obtain a wholesome fruit?”
The mind of loving-kindness is not like that; when the mind of loving-kindness arises, it can eliminate hatred and harm.
Because hatred and harm are absent, one gives rise to wholesome conduct of body and speech.
To practice asceticism that is fruitless—how could this be comparable to benevolent compassion?
Just as when a lion roars, no other beasts can stand before him;
so it is with this matter: all those of the various non-Buddhist paths [cannot withstand it].
None dared to oppose him.
When he preached the Dharma to refute the non-Buddhists, they remained silent, unable to offer a reply.
(8) Furthermore, physical and verbal actions cannot be autonomous; they necessarily depend upon the mind.

I have heard that in the past, there was a bhikṣuṇī who went to the country of Śākala. In that country, there was a brahmin who performed the ascetic practice of "scorching with five fires. From his forehead flowed water; sweat poured from his chest, armpits, and bosom; his throat was parched and his lips and tongue were scorched until he had no saliva left.

Fire is placed on all four sides, like molten gold, or like yellow hair, blazing with a crimson glow; scorched by the intense heat of summer upon its surface, it tosses and turns, unable to find any place of refuge, its body parched and rotting like a pancake on a griddle.
This brahmin constantly wore coarse woolen garments and scorched his body with five fires;
thus, people of the time called him "Coarse-Woolen-Scorcher. When a bhikṣuṇī saw this, she said to him:
"That which ought to be scorched you do not scorch, yet that which ought not to be scorched you do scorch."
At that time, having heard these words, Sūcīloma became extremely incensed and spoke thus:
"You evil shaveling!
What is there to roast?"
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"If you wish to know where one should apply heat, you need only apply heat to your own mind of anger and resentment; if you can apply heat to the mind, that is called true heating."

It is like a cart drawn by an ox: if the cart does not move, one must urge the ox rather than beat the cart. The body is like the cart and the mind is like that ox; for this reason, you should roast the mind—why would you instead torment the body?
Furthermore, this body is like a forest or a wall; even if it were burned and scorched, what benefit would that bring?
He then spoke in verse:
"The mind is the lord of the city; If the lord of the city is full of anger, One may as well seek the city itself."
There is nothing added to it.
It is like a lion, whom someone might strike or shoot with arrows, bows, tiles, or stones.
Yet that lion pursued that man. It was like a foolish dog:
when someone throws a clod or a stone at it, it chases after the clod or stone instead of seeking out its origin.
The term "lion" is a metaphor for the wise person, who is able to seek out the root and extinguish afflictions.
The term "deluded dog" refers to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), who scorch their bodies with the five heats yet fail to recognize the root of the mind.
The brahmin asked, "What is meant by 'roasting the heart'?
The bhikṣuṇī replied:
“The wisdom of the Four Truths is like four masses of fire, and the cultivation of the path is like the sun.
Now, as for wisdom: using the fires of the Four Truths and the pure sun of the cultivated path, one heats the mind with these five dharmas.”
Yet this body is not subject to one's own will; for what reason do you torment it?
If you wish to cause suffering, you should direct it toward that which is the root of the body’s capacity to suffer.
Coming, going, sitting, and lying down are not performed by the body; they are merely driven by the mind.
If these are not actions of the body, yet the fault lies with the mind, why then do you torment the body?
If the mind departs from the body, the body is like wood or stone.
Therefore, the wise person should discipline the mind and should not torment the body.
Furthermore, if you attain the Way by means of these five heats with which you scorch your body as an ascetic practice,
then the sentient beings in hell— who undergo immeasurable suffering and various forms of torment—
should also attain the Way.
The brahmin said: "To engage in ascetic practices with the intention of creating [merit] is called 'cultivating the path.
However, the beings in hell are oppressed by suffering; therefore, one should not say that they are cultivating the path."
The bhikṣuṇī said:
“If one could obtain merit simply by generating the thought [of giving], then even a small child holding a torch should likewise obtain merit; yet in reality, this is not the case.”
"Inferring from this, that which you have performed— the practice of scorching the body with the five fires—
is likewise devoid of merit.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"The infant and the young child possess no wisdom; therefore, they have no merit.
I possess wisdom and have performed such deeds as this—tormenting my body with the five heats—and for that reason, I have merit."
The bhikṣuṇī said:
“If one who possesses wisdom and practices asceticism thereby gains merit,
then a pearl diver who pierces his own body to draw blood so that pearls may be obtained should likewise possess merit.”
The brahmin said: "Because of a greedy mind, even though one sheds blood, it is not called merit.
