The bhikṣuṇī said:
"If you practice asceticism out of a craving for heavenly pleasures, it too would be without merit.
If there were no karmic fruit through such craving and seeking, then hunters should not receive their rewards."
If you cannot obtain [the reward], then for this practice of yours, even the fruit of asceticism—
the blissful retribution of the heavens— should not be obtained.
Why now do you turn your body and mind about, wishing to obtain celestial bliss through asceticism?
Within my Buddha-dharma, there is no such thing as obtaining the bliss of those heavens by practicing asceticism such as scorching the body with the five fires.
By cultivating truthful speech and other such virtuous merits, one attains the bliss of rebirth in heaven even while driven by greed or fear.
It is like taking medicine: whether out of desire or dread, once it has been ingested, its medicinal power will inevitably take effect.
"If those who abide in truthful speech possess such virtues, then whether out of greed or fear, they will surely attain celestial bliss.
At that time, the brahmin, his words exhausted and his logic defeated,
was unable to offer a rebuttal and remained silent.
At that time, those around him conceived pure faith within the Buddha-dharma and took deep delight in the True Dharma.
They said to one another:
"Excellent is the Buddha-dharma! It possesses great power of wisdom, profound and difficult to fathom."
The wisdom of the non-Buddhists is extremely shallow and superficial.
It is like a sudden flare of fire; if it touches a person's body, there is no one who does not fear it.
The blazing fire of the Buddha-dharma is likewise; when it touches the Brahmins, it causes them to tremble with fear.
We who have now heard the Buddha-dharma, this most excellent discourse, should all turn toward it in devotion;
we shall pay respectful homage at the place where the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
Homage to the World-Honored One, whose voice is gentle and soft as he expounds the Dharma.
Though women’s wisdom is shallow, having drunk the Buddha’s ambrosia, they are now able to preach the Dharma among the great assembly without fear.
Who would not show reverence for the Buddha’s words?
This bhikṣuṇī, though her wisdom is slight and shallow, is able to employ the words of the Muni, the World-Honored One, to extinguish the fetters.
Thus, he was still able to cause this brāhmaṇa to remain silent and unable to offer a retort.
(9) Furthermore, desire is like a lump of meat that various birds compete to seize; a person of wisdom, deeply understanding the peril of wealth, does not crave or cling to it.

I have heard that in the past, in the kingdom of Śūrpāraka, there was a bhikṣu who discovered a hidden treasure within a ruined wall. Inside was a large copper jar filled with gold coins. He took a poor upāsaka and showed him the place, saying to him:
"You may take this treasure to provide for your livelihood."
Then the upāsaka asked the bhikṣu,
"When did you see this?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I have only seen it today," the upāsaka said.
"I have not only seen this treasure today; I have seen it for a long time, yet I did not use it."
Listen well now!
I shall explain the faults inherent in these jewels.
If one takes these jewels and it becomes known to the king, one may face death, or be punished, or even be imprisoned; such sufferings as these are beyond counting.
Then he spoke in verse:
"I have seen this jewel arrive after a period of many, long years;
this jewel is poisonous and harmful, more virulent than that black venomous snake."
Therefore, regarding these treasures, one should have no mind of greed at all;
viewing them as poisonous snakes, one should not conceive the thought of them as wealth.
One may be bound, imprisoned, or punished, and at times even face death.
All manner of calamities arise from these jewels;
they can summon all kinds of suffering and their harm is truly terrifying.
Therefore, regarding these jewels, I do not give rise to thoughts of greed or attachment.
Beings are deluded and attached to jewels, calling them precious playthings;
yet these jewels are things of peril, and they falsely conceive thoughts of peace and goodness.
Since such faults and afflictions exist, what use is there for these jewels?
Thus this body, defiled by pus, is pursued merely for the sake of its own limbs and life;
since it must eventually be abandoned, decayed, and destroyed, what use is there for precious jewels?
It is like throwing fire upon wood; there is never a time when one is satisfied.
The human mind is likewise: its longing knows no satiety.
If you have compassion for me, teach me the Dharma of few desires;
why do you speak of showing me wealth and treasures?
Indeed, few desires and contentment can give rise to great benefit and happiness;
whereas for those with many desires, the faculties are perpetually distracted,
they greedily seek without satiety, and their hopes only increase their suffering.
Yet this person of many desires constantly gives rise to thoughts of desire;
their greed for profit knows no limit, like the mouth of a makara fish.
But that person of few desires, because they lack the suffering of greedy seeking, [remains at peace].
Their hearts were constantly filled with joy, celebrating together as if at a festival.
At that time, the lay follower praised the Dharma of having few desires and being content; the bhikṣu conceived a sense of wonder and praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
Truly a man of integrity!

Although he has not yet donned the dharma robes, his mind has already renounced the world; he is able to follow the Buddha’s words and understand the dharma of few desires, and this state of few desires is praised by all Buddhas.
The bhikṣu said:
"To summarize what you have said, it is deeply censurable and makes me feel ashamed.

While you currently live at home with a wife, children, relatives, servants, and laborers, you ought to be greedily seeking wealth to provide for yourself; yet you can follow the Buddha’s words and praise having few desires."
Suppose there were someone with an iron tongue; no one could possibly reproach one who is content with few desires.

Although I have now shaved my hair and beard and wear the dharma-robes, thus appearing outwardly like a śramaṇa, in truth I do not know the dharma of a śramaṇa. Yet I am currently teaching you matters of great desire, unable to describe the dharma of few desires praised by the Dharma King—the source of all virtues—which the Buddha’s sūtras also declare to be the very foundation of a śramaṇa.
In the past, when the Tathāgata had finished his almsround, if there were any remaining food, he would sometimes give it to the bhikṣus or place it in water to provide for the insects.
At that time, two bhikṣus who had not received enough almsfood entered from outside with expressions of hunger. Having seen them, the Buddha said to them:
"There is some leftover food here; would you be able to eat it?"
A certain bhikṣu said:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has taught that there is great merit in having few desires; how could I now greedily crave and eat this food?"
A certain bhikṣu said:
"The remaining food of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is difficult to encounter; even the celestial kings Brahmā and Śakra all bear it upon their heads with reverence."
"If I were to eat now, it would increase my physical appearance, strength, well-being, and eloquence.
Such food is extremely difficult to encounter; why should I not eat?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised those who did not eat:
"Excellent, Bhikṣu!
You are able to practice the Buddha's teachings by observing the dharma of few desires.
Although this bhikṣu followed the Buddha’s words, the Buddha did not praise him for eating the food left over from the Buddha.
"Therefore, you should know that the practice of few desires is the teaching and the foundation of the precepts approved by the Buddha.
He then spoke these verses:
"Those who wish to obtain the benefit of the Dharma Should understand the principle of few desires."
Such is the dharma of few desires, the noble ornament and necklace.
In this life, one casts off the heavy burden; free from sorrow, one finds joy.
This is indeed Great Nirvana, the primary gateway to its dwelling place.
He restrains the hosts of Māra’s armies at the narrow passes that must be guarded;
having crossed the realm of Māra, he is sealed with the supreme seal.
His observance of the precepts is like the vast ocean; his fewness of desires is like the tide.
It can serve as a dense canopy for all meritorious deeds;
for those exhausted by craving and seeking, it is a place to rest their carriage and find relief.
To draw near those with few desires is like milking a cow.
From it, curd, butter, and the finest clarified butter (*sarpis*) are obtained;
likewise, through fewness of desire, all virtues are produced.
Those who can extend their hands in giving—these hands are called "exalted and magnificent."
If the recipient can withdraw their hand, the merit of that restraint exceeds even the former.
If one says, "I shall give," the value of these words is difficult to measure;
yet if the recipient says, "I have enough," that immeasurable merit exceeds even the former.
If you wish to attain the Dharma, you should associate with those of few desires;
the One of Ten Powers has declared that fewness of desire is itself the quality of the noble lineage.
Having few desires and no material possessions, one increases virtue, learning, and wisdom.
Such is the dharma of few desires, the sustenance of those who have gone forth.
Though there be thirst and craving, they can never cause disturbance;
setting aside the happiness of future lives, one attains peace and security in the present.

"Furthermore, (10) those who are content, though poor, are called wealthy; those who lack contentment, though wealthy, are poor. Only when one is filled with noble wisdom is one called truly great in wealth."

I have heard that in the past there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) whom some people reviled as being the most impoverished. However, this lay follower delighted in the Dharma of contentment praised by the Buddha; thus, in accordance with the characteristics of the Dharma, he spoke these verses:
"Freedom from illness is the supreme benefit; Contentment is the supreme wealth;
A virtuous friend is the supreme kin; Nirvāṇa is the supreme bliss."
When the upāsaka had finished speaking these verses, he said to that man:
"As the Buddha has taught, one who is content is wealthy; why do you now call me poor?"
He further spoke in verse:
"Though one possesses various treasures and an abundance of the necessities of life,
one who does not have faith in the Triple Gem is said to be the most impoverished."
Though one lacks various precious jewels and the necessities of life,
one who can have faith in the Triple Gem is called the foremost wealthy person.
I now revere the Triple Gem, taking faith as my treasure.
For what reason do you say that I am poor?
Although Śakra and Vaiśravaṇa possess an abundance of precious jewels,
when it comes to the time of giving, they cannot relinquish them all.
My heart loves contentment; regarding all wealth and treasures, I have no mind of greedy attachment and am able to relinquish them all.
Even the treasuries of the wealthy and noble contain many rare and precious jewels.
Water, fire, and thieves can all plunder and seize;
when one suffers such loss, great anguish arises,
which neither skilled physicians nor wondrous medicines can cure.
"I take faith as my treasure, which no one can plunder;
my mind is serene and joyful, free from all anxiety, affliction, and suffering.
Having spoken this verse, he further said:

"Therefore, you should know that although one may possess treasuries, elephants, horses, the seven treasures, and the necessities of life, one who lacks contentment is still called poor; for this reason, the Buddha taught that contentment is the greatest wealth."
When the multitude heard these words, they all exclaimed, "Excellent! This is truly the correct teaching; he possesses great wisdom and is called a Great Man.
They said to one another, "From this day forward, even if he has no wealth or treasures, as long as he possesses faith, we shall regard him as a wealthy man."

One amasses wealth through suffering solely for the sake of pleasure; it is intended to provide for one's household and kin so that they lack nothing. Such pleasure, however, pertains only to the present life.
The treasure of faith serves one throughout successive lifetimes, allowing for the free enjoyment of wealth among humans and devas; therefore, know that faith is the foremost of treasures.
Possessing such wealth of faith within the cycle of birth and death, one experiences supreme happiness and is free from all suffering and affliction.

Gold, silver, and precious jewels can give rise to calamities and afflictions; day and night one dwells in anxiety and fear of being plundered by others. Yet there are eight perils, and because of greedy attachment, one undergoes suffering for many lifetimes.

Because one possesses faith, one is able to obtain the wealth of precepts, the wealth of generosity, the wealth of concentration, and the wealth of wisdom; if one lacks faith, how could such forms of wealth be obtained?
Therefore, the wealth of faith is the foremost.
"Because I possess these riches, I declare myself to be very wealthy before others; because I accumulated deep roots of wholesome karma in the past, I am now able to have faith and be content."
And he spoke in verse:
"Because one possesses faith, One does not commit any evil;
All virtues and merits Take faith as their messenger."
Faith is like an arrow shot from a river;
its swift current is exceedingly rapid, able to cause the mind and consciousness to reach the wholesome Dharma with great speed.
Who possesses such abundant wealth and treasures as one who can surpass the great riches of faith?
Though one may possess great wealth, when that wealth is lost, one becomes poor;
yet at the time of death, one must abandon it all and depart alone.
Nothing follows one into the next world, except for the wealth of faith, which can never be lost.
It constantly follows one from birth to birth, bringing joy for many eons.
While worldly people amass wealth and treasures, which only give rise to greed, the treasure of faith is not like this; seeing it brings forth true delight.
Among all forms of wealth, the wealth of faith is supreme;
he who reveals this meaning is the Sage’s teaching.
Therefore, I am not poor, for the wealth of faith is most excellent.
The rest are not called wealth; faith alone is true wealth.
For one who gives with faith, their material possessions will increase;
for one who gives to others without faith, the karmic fruit will be exceedingly meager.
The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra, Fascicle Two.
The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra, Fascicle Three.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
11. Furthermore, if there is a disciple who is able to firmly uphold the precepts and is revered by others, all people of the world will also respect their teacher.
I have heard that in the past, there were certain bhikṣus traveling through a wilderness who were plundered by bandits and stripped of their robes.
At that time, these bandits, fearing that the bhikṣus would go and report them to the village, intended to kill them all.
One among the bandits had previously been a monk;
he said to his companions, "Why do you wish to slaughter them all now?

According to the dharma of a bhikṣu, one must not harm even a blade of grass. If we bind the bhikṣus with grass now, they will be so afraid of harming it that they will ultimately be unable to run in the four directions to raise the alarm."
The bandits immediately bound him with grass and abandoned him, departing.

Once the bhikṣus were thus bound by the grass, fearing they would violate their prohibitions, they did not dare to pull it off. Having no clothes upon their bodies, they were scorched by the sun; they were tormented by mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas. Bound from morning until midday, the time passed until sunset and the onset of deep, pitch-black darkness. Nocturnal birds and beasts ran about crosswise, while wild foxes howled in packs and owls shrieked; their evil cries and wailing were most terrifying.
An elderly bhikṣu said to the young monks: "Listen well!
Human life is brief, like the swift current of a river; even if one dwells in heaven, it will soon perish—how much more so can human life be preserved?"
Since life is not long-lasting, why would one destroy the prohibitions and precepts for the sake of life?
You people should know! A human body is difficult to obtain;

the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter; the sense faculties are difficult to possess; and faith is difficult to give rise to. Each of these matters is difficult to meet, like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log.

The Buddha’s true path is not like those ninety-five kinds of heterodox views and delusions which lack any karmic fruit; one who practices the Buddha-way will certainly attain the correct fruition. Why, then, would you begrudge such a precarious, fragile, and unstable life by destroying the holy teaching of the Buddha?
If one protects the Buddha’s words, one will possess renown and merit in the present life and experience happiness in the future.
As the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If there is one who possesses wisdom, And is able to firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts..."
Seeking the realms of humans and devas, as well as nirvāṇa, one shall obtain them according to one's wishes.
One’s fame will be widely known, and all shall offer one worship;
one will surely attain the bliss of humans and devas, and also achieve the fruit of liberation.
The Naga King Elāpattra, because he violated the precepts by plucking and injuring the leaves of trees,
fell into the state of a naga at the end of his life;
none of the Buddhas predicted that he would ever escape from being a naga.
To be able to steadfastly uphold the prohibitive precepts is an exceedingly difficult matter;
the characteristics of the precepts are extremely numerous, and it is difficult to discern and understand them clearly.
Like standing amidst a grove of swords or a thicket of thorns, one is frequently wounded and destroyed while dwelling therein.

"Fools and inferior beings are incapable of upholding such precepts. Thus, those bhikṣus, oppressed by suffering, were unable to bend, stretch, or move; fearing that they might break the grass and thereby violate their prohibitions, they said to one another:

"Our practice is just like that scale: we must keep our position perfectly level, allowing neither increase nor decrease. Now, in this place of terror and peril, we maintain our resolve without fail—this is what it means to be truly steadfast. With these lowly lives, we shall trade for the noble Dharma, the bliss of humans and devas, and the bliss of Nirvāṇa. We have nowhere else to go now; we shall simply protect our precepts until death and never transgress them."
Then he spoke in verse:
"In the past, we have committed various evil deeds;
though we may have attained birth in the human realm, we have engaged in theft and adultery with the wives of others."
Under the laws of kings, they undergo execution and punishment beyond all calculation;
Furthermore, they endure the sufferings of the hells, which are likewise difficult to reckon;
Or they take the bodies of animals—oxen, sheep, chickens, and dogs.
Deer, wild animals, birds, and beasts are slaughtered by others;
they lose their lives without limit, yet have never gained even the slightest benefit.
We, at this present time, for the sake of guarding the noble precepts, [shall likewise sacrifice ourselves].
By relinquishing this fragile life, one will surely obtain great benefit.
We are now in peril; we shall certainly sacrifice our lives, so that after our deaths, we may be reborn in heaven and enjoy happiness.
If one violates the prohibitive precepts, one will incur an evil reputation in the present life, be held in contempt by others, and fall into the evil realms at the end of life.
Now we shall together establish a solemn covenant: from now until the end of our lives, [we shall not do so].
Even if this sunlight were to scorch my body and life until they were dry,
I would maintain the Buddha’s precepts and never violate them midway.
Even if various evil beasts were to tear at and rend my hands and feet, [I would not break the precepts].
"I shall never dare to violate or transgress the prohibitions and precepts of the Lion of the Śākyas.
I would rather die upholding the precepts than live having broken them.

When the bhikṣus heard this verse spoken by the elder bhikṣu, they each straightened their bodies, remaining unmoving and unshaking, like a great tree whose branches and leaves do not stir when there is no wind.
At that time, the king happened to go out on a hunt; as he traveled along, he gradually arrived at the place where the bhikṣus were bound.
Seeing them from afar, doubt arose in his mind, and he thought to himself:
"Are those naked ones Nirgranthas?"
"Are these śramaṇas?

Having had this thought, he sent people to investigate; the bhikṣus, feeling deep shame and embarrassment, covered their bodies, so that the messengers could clearly recognize them as the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākya.
"How do you know this?
Because his right shoulder is black.
The messenger then returned and reported this.
“Great King!
He is a śramaṇa, not a Nirgrantha.
Then he spoke in verse:
“O King, you should now know that he has been plundered by bandits;
Ashamed, he is bound with grass, Like a great elephant restrained by a hook.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King was filled with deep suspicion and wonder, and silently thought to himself:
"I should now go to where that bhikṣu is.
Having thought this, he immediately spoke in verse:
"With hands bound by green grass, Like the wings of a parrot,"
Furthermore, like a sacrificial sheep, Neither moving nor shaking;
though knowing it is in peril, It remains silent and does not harm the grass.
Like a forest consumed by fire, Or a yak dying for the sake of its tail.
Having spoken this verse, he went to where [the man] was and asked him in verse:
"Your body is exceedingly robust, Free from illness and seemingly full of strength.
By what cause and condition Are you bound by grass and unable to move?"
Do you not know that your own bodies possess strength?
Are you deluded by incantations, or is this a form of asceticism,
or do you loathe your own bodies?
"I pray that you will quickly explain its meaning.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu replied in verse:
"This grass is exceedingly fragile; it would not be difficult to snap it all at once."
However, because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is bound by the adamantine precepts and maintains the prohibitions of all dharmas,
he did not dare to pull it out and sever it abruptly.
The Buddha taught that all grasses and trees are entirely villages of spirits and deities.
We dare not disobey, and for this reason we cannot sever [the ties].
It is like drawing a boundary around a snake within a charmed circle;
by the power of the divine incantation, the venomous serpent cannot cross over.
The World-Honored Muni has delineated the boundaries; we dare not transgress them.
Although our lives must eventually come to an end in extinction, we vow to die upholding the precepts, never to live having violated them.
Both the virtuous and the non-virtuous alike relinquish their physical life;
yet the virtuous preserve their wisdom-life and further possess renown,
while the non-virtuous lose their wisdom-life and likewise forfeit their reputation.
We śramaṇas take the observance of the precepts as our strength;
the observance of the precepts is a fertile field from which all merits can arise,
serving as the stairway for rebirth in heaven and the seed of a good reputation.
"Having attained the bridge and ferry to the noble state, the foremost among all benefits—what person of wisdom would wish to break this vessel of virtuous precepts?
At that time, the king’s heart was filled with great joy; he immediately untied the grass bonds of the bhikṣu and spoke these verses:
“Excellent is this steadfast persistence in that which was taught by the Lion of the Śākyas;
rather than abandoning one’s own body or life, one protects the Dharma without transgression.
I now likewise take refuge in you who thus manifest the Great Dharma.”
I take refuge in the Muni, the Honored One of Liberation, who has transcended all feverish affliction and firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts; to him I now also pay homage.

(12) Furthermore, if a person’s inner mind is virtuous and good, they will bring much peace and benefit to all; therefore, the wise should cultivate their minds, constantly keeping them virtuous and good.
I have heard that in the past, there were certain bhikṣus who entered the sea with merchants to gather treasures. Once they reached the open sea, their ship was wrecked.

At that time, a young bhikṣu held onto a single plank, while an elder bhikṣu, failing to obtain a plank, was about to sink into the water. Terrified and trembling, fearing he would be swept away by the waves, the elder spoke to the youth:
"Do you not remember the precepts established by the Buddha—that one must respect one's elders?"
"You should give the plank you have obtained to me.
At that time, the youth reflected:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has indeed spoken these words: 'Whatever brings benefit and happiness should first be offered to the senior monks.'"
He further thought to himself:
"If I give this plank to the Elder, I will surely sink into the swirling waves and currents; the perils of the great ocean are exceedingly deep and vast, and my life will likely not be preserved.

Furthermore, I am young and have only recently left the household life, having not yet attained the fruits of the Path; I am troubled by this. Now is the very time for me to sacrifice my body to save the Elder."
Having formed this thought, he spoke these verses:
"For my own complete deliverance, and to follow the supreme word of the Buddha,
I shall become a mass of immeasurable merit, my fame pervading the ten directions."
My body and life are most base and lowly; how could I ever transgress the holy teaching?
Having now received the Buddha’s precepts, I shall surely uphold them firmly until death.
To remain in accord with the Buddha’s words, I offer these wooden boards and sacrifice my very life.
If one does not perform difficult deeds, one will never attain difficult fruits.
If I hold onto this plank, I shall surely cross the perils of the great ocean;
if I do not comply with the Sage’s intent, I shall sink into the sea of birth and death.
I shall now drown and die; though I die, I shall still be called victorious.
If I were to abandon the Buddha’s teaching, I would lose the benefits of human and celestial realms, as well as Great Nirvana and the unsurpassed, supreme bliss.
Having spoken this verse, he immediately cast the board away and offered it to the Elder.
Once the Elder had accepted the board, the sea deity, moved by his sincere devotion, immediately took up the young bhikṣu and placed him upon the shore.

The Sea God joined his palms and said to the bhikṣu, "I now take refuge in you who firmly uphold the precepts; that you, having encountered such a perilous situation, are still able to maintain the Buddha's precepts."
The Sea God spoke this verse in praise of the bhikṣu:
"You are truly a bhikṣu, You are indeed an ascetic;
I name you a śramaṇa, For you truly deserve that title."
By the power of your virtue, you and your companions, along with your wealth and treasures, have escaped this great peril; all have emerged in safety.
Your vow is firm and steadfast, as you respectfully follow what the Buddha has taught.
You are a most eminent person, capable of removing all calamities and hardships.
How could I now fail to provide you with protection?
To see the Truth and maintain the precepts—this is not yet difficult.
That an ordinary person does not violate the prohibitions is indeed called rare.
For a bhikṣu to dwell in peace and security, pure and self-restrained,
such that he is able not to violate the precepts— this is not yet difficult.
Not yet having attained the fruit of the Path, they dwell amidst great terror;
yet, relinquishing their own cherished lives, they uphold the precepts of the Buddha’s teaching.
To be able to do what is difficult to do—this is most rare.

13 (13) Furthermore, if one does not perceive the path, even though one may be widely learned, one cannot uproot the suffering of birth and death; therefore, the wise person should seek the vision of the Truths.
I have heard that in the past, two brothers both left the household life together; the elder brother attained arhatship, while the younger brother recited the Tripiṭaka.
At that time, the arhat said to the one who knew the Tripiṭaka:
"You should practice dhyāna."
The Tripitaka Master replied,
“I shall practice dhyāna.
The arhat bhikṣu spoke to him again, saying:
“Have you not heard what the Buddha has taught: that one who practices the Path should act as if their head or clothes were on fire?
Then he spoke this verse:
“If one commits such deeds today, It may not even last until tomorrow.”
Human life cannot be guaranteed; one should swiftly cultivate wholesome deeds.
When the great army of death arrives, there is no place for seeking or pleading.
At the moment of passing away, one does not know by which path one will go.
In the dark, one follows the conditions of karma, Knowing not whether the path is far or near.
Life is like a lamp in the wind; One knows not the moment it will be extinguished.
Your words that you shall act clearly tomorrow— Such speech is utterly false and vain.
A dead tiger is extremely violent and impetuous; it shows no mercy or indulgence at all.
Once it suddenly arrives, it will not wait until tomorrow.
The King of Death is full of cruelty and harm; you should give rise to fear.
One should know that the body is precarious and fragile, and life is swift and difficult to preserve.
One ought to diligently contemplate the internal body, abandon the pursuit of mere erudition,
seek liberation from the world, and uproot the source of birth and death.
When death suddenly arrives, remorseful heat reaches no remedy;
if you now perceive the traces of the Path, later there will be no affliction of remorseful heat.
Within the Buddha-dharma, that which is firm and substantial is what is called attaining the traces of the Path.
If one's learning is accompanied by hypocrisy, one should abandon it and not cherish it;
though one may be widely learned and erudite, if one does not attain the traces of the Path, it is like a blind man holding a lamp: he illuminates others but cannot see for himself.
If one desires to seek self-benefit, one must perceive the path of the sages;
dwelling among the assembly, one roars the lion’s roar, with eloquent and skillful speech,
expounding the characteristics of all phenomena, analyzing and resolving doubts and difficulties.
He is able to cause the assembly listening to the Dharma to all give rise to a heart of joy,
and further causes all people to attain complete tranquility and compliance.
Yet, despite such deeds, at the moment of death his mind becomes confused and deranged.
Falling into the evil realms, one is ridiculed by the wise.
The Dharma you have taught is replete with words and phrases;
you explain cause and effect in proper sequence, its exquisite flavor delighting the mind.
Sweet as sugarcane juice;
yet unable to discipline oneself, and having not severed the three evil destinies,
what is the use of seeking liberation for oneself in vain?
Ordinary worldlings are not to be trusted; you should quickly seek the vision of the Truth.
You possess great renown, and all say that you preach the Dharma well;
yet though you have empty fame, what benefit will it bring you?
One should observe the internal body, silently practicing meditative concentration.
Of those who have long been learned in the scriptures, their number was once very great;
yet they have all passed away through impermanence, and those remaining are exceedingly few.
Through diligent toil one seeks renown, yet even when attained, it is lost again;
the Buddha taught that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely impermanent.
The Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, accomplished the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividya*).
Having eliminated the three obstructions and contemplated the three periods of time in a single thought-moment,
these World-Honored Ones, whose fame filled the ten directions,
have all now entered parinirvāṇa; even their names have followed them into extinction.
"Therefore, you should now diligently cultivate vigor,
renounce fame and reputation, and single-mindedly seek liberation.
The Tripitaka Master replied:
"I shall do exactly as you say.
Before long, his body was stricken with a grave illness; fearing that his life was about to end, he felt deep remorse and spoke this verse:
"How strange! On this very day, Within the noble Dharma of the Buddha..."
Though one may be fully endowed with precepts and learning, yet fail to perceive the Truths,
if I were to die now, I would be no different from a dog;
submerged in the whirlpool of birth and death, like the wheel of a potter.
I am now worthy of compassion; though I have not yet realized the path, may my teacher show me mercy and pity, and exhort me to practice meditative reflection.
Yet I did not follow his Dharma teachings and did not practice even a small portion of them.
Therefore, at this time, one cannot perceive the True Reality.
Though I am Śākyamuni, the great lamp of the Dharma,
yet as the foremost of the ignorant, I am unable to illuminate myself.
"Because they cannot illuminate [the truth], they shall forever sink into the suffering of birth and death.
When his fellow students heard of his illness, they all came to visit him; seeing his terror, they were all struck with amazement and each said:
"Have you not heard what the Buddha has taught?"
"A person of great learning possesses the power of wisdom and is able to understand impermanence; therefore, you should not now feel sorrow or fear.
At that time, the sick bhikṣu immediately spoke a verse in response to his fellow student, saying:
"I have previously received your instruction, And I shall practice the method of seated meditation."
From today until tomorrow, one is indolent and deceives oneself;
thus, throughout this single lifetime, one passes in vain with nothing gained.
This body is like a mass of foam, yet I have not deeply contemplated it.
Perversely calculating it to be solid and real, one fails to perceive that death has suddenly arrived;
becoming single-mindedly attached to the Dharma of much learning, one gives rise to the notion of being supreme,
only to be suddenly swallowed by the python of death— then regret and remorse will be of no avail.
As stated in the Sūtras: "One should practice seated meditation with single-minded diligence and without weariness;
this is what was taught for the destruction of the fetters.
Though the Buddha has given such instruction, those who are unable to act in accordance with it—
Burned by the fire of the heat of remorse, my mind is parched with distress.
Now I am extremely dark and weak, like an infant or a fool;
among those six realms of existence, I do not know which path to take.
I do not know whether in future lives I shall hear the Buddha’s words;
wandering through the three realms of existence, what kind of person shall I encounter?
Nor do I know what deeds I shall perform in the future.
Some may lose their original mind, giving rise to the three poisons;
they do not cultivate various wholesome deeds, but only commit manifold evils.
Alas, what great suffering! I have deceived and deluded myself.
"Having already escaped all calamities, you ought to attain the supramundane path.
Why, out of delusion and error, do you indulge in negligence and self-indulgence?
When his fellow students heard these verses, they comforted him again, saying:
“You are both widely learned and firm in the observance of the precepts; you ought to be at ease. Why do you suffer such anxiety and fear?
The sick bhikṣu replied, “I am now afflicted by illness and in great distress; seeing that all my virtuous friends have abandoned me, my death is certain.”
Weeping and shedding tears, he said to his elder brother:
"I pray you, draw near to me; because of my foolishness and delusion, I failed to follow your instructions. Now that my illness is grave, I shall surely pass away to the next world."
"I pray that you, my elder brother, will look upon me with compassion and deliver me, so that I may be freed from this great suffering.
He then spoke these verses:
"Dwelling together within the Buddha-dharma, You are called a Jewel among Śramaṇas; [May you likewise deliver me from this great suffering. "
Repeatedly he instructed and admonished me, yet I, foolish and inferior, did not obey.
Because of this matter, my remorse and feverish distress have redoubled;
like the stifling heat of midsummer, they burn with fierce, blazing flames.
For having betrayed your teachings of gratitude, my remorse and feverish distress exceed even that;
now having nothing else to rely upon, I shall take refuge in you alone.
When I receive a future body, please look upon me and do not forget me.
May I, in a future life, encounter the Buddha-dharma and once again attain the way of renunciation.
May my wearing of the dharma-robes not be in vain; may I surely attain the fruits of the Path.
As for all other pursuits such as worldly learning and occupations, may I abandon them and never engage in them again.
Dedicated solely to seeking liberation, he has no other aspiration or pursuit.
Even if, in future lives, he seeks the realization of the Truth,
his skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and veins may all wither and dry away.
Masterful over body, life, and destiny, he shall never forsake liberation.
Furthermore, may his future bodies always diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas,
practicing with vigor throughout the six periods of day and night, never for a moment ceasing.
When the sick bhikṣu had spoken this verse, his heart was filled with trepidation. Seeing this, his elder brother felt great compassion and said:
"Excellent, excellent!"

That you are now able to give rise to deep regret and form a vow is well; however, previously I instructed you not to follow my words, yet when you were later struck with alarm and remorse, what could have been done?
And he spoke in verse:
"Afflicted by a grave and terminal illness, the great life-force is not far off;
my limbs and joints all grow slack, as the 'sword-wind' dissolves my form."
When medicine can no longer cure him, the physician abandons him and departs;
those around him all cry out, "Alas! His death is certain!
His kinsmen and women stand before him, weeping in grief.
At the moment of death, there is great terror; the fear and dread are beyond comparison.
If one were in a state of health and vigor, and knew that death brings such suffering, who would not resolve to seek the Way and strive to attain the fruit of liberation?
In the prime of life, when free from affliction, one is indolent and lacks diligence;
occupied only with worldly affairs, one does not cultivate generosity, precepts, or meditation.
Later, when struck by a grave illness, the sense-faculties burn like fire.
"When one is on the verge of being swallowed by death, only then does one regret not having sought to cultivate goodness.
That sick bhikṣu then passed away and was reborn among human beings.
At that time, the arhat, observing with his divine eye, knew the place of his rebirth and went to his house several times.

As this child gradually grew, his wet nurse carried him to a monastery to visit an Arhat. While holding the child, she did not grasp him firmly; her hand slipped, and he fell to the ground, striking his head against a stone. The child became greatly enraged, and upon the end of his life, he fell into hell.
At that time, the Arhat again observed with his divine eye and saw that [the being] had been born in the hells, a place of suffering and hardship. He then spoke this verse:
"Alas, what a great ruin! Born in a place so difficult to rescue, Even the Buddha’s power finds it hard to pull one out; How much less can I provide salvation?"
Focusing the mind on wisdom that is free from outflows cannot be cultivated through suffering;
within the torments of hell, there is not even a moment of a joyful heart.
Since there is not even a moment of a joyful heart, how could one possibly maintain focused mindfulness?
Because they lack focused mindfulness, they do not attain wisdom free from outflows.
In such a perilous state, how can they be rescued?
They undergo great suffering in hell, which cannot be described by any analogy.
Even if one were to force an analogy, death among humans is suffering for which a slight comparison might be found; yet that [other] suffering constantly exceeds this.
Like fire set upon dry fuel, there is no time when it is even momentarily cool.
The suffering of the hells is likewise; there is no moment of rest.
The intermediate state bodies within the hells are all like masses of molten iron;
the agony of burning with feverish torment is beyond all calculation.
One should eliminate indolence, Without resting day or night,
Diligently cultivating the Noble Path, To surely reach the end of suffering.
Therefore, first cultivate the Path, And you shall attain the fruit of liberation.
Thereafter, through extensive learning, one fashions a wondrous necklace.
(14) Furthermore, having seen this matter, one should give rise to alarm and awakening: noble status and honorable rank are not permanent.
I have heard that in the past, when King Candana-Kaṇiṭṭha was about to depart for the city of Kaṇiṭṭha, he encountered five hundred beggars along the way who cried out with one voice,
"Give to us as you do to me!"
Upon hearing these words, the king attained awakening and immediately thought to himself: "He has awakened me;
in days past I myself experienced poverty and suffering. If I do not practice giving now, I shall likewise become like him hereafter."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Because in a previous life, Though possessing abundant wealth and treasures,
He said there was nothing to give away, He has now obtained this poverty and low status."
"If I were to say 'no' now, later I would be the same as them.
At that time, there was a minister named Devadharma who dismounted from his horse, joined his palms, and addressed the king, saying:
"All these beggars say they are just like me."
The king replied to the minister, saying:
"I have heard his words, yet my understanding of them differs from yours.
Your understanding takes it to mean begging for money and various material goods."
"What I have understood, I shall explain for you; listen well now!
He then spoke in verse:
"These beggars have come on purpose to awaken me."
By means of this poor and lowly form, you have shown yourself so that I may see you.
You say that you received this body because of stinginess and a failure to practice generosity;
deceived by heedlessness, you have come to receive this form of suffering.
To these wretched beggars, he revealed such a meaning as this:
"I myself was once a king, like the moon among the stars;
a precious canopy covered my head, and hosts of courtesans stood at my left and right."
The attendants were all magnificently adorned, and all who heard of them cleared the way;
yet despite such various and wondrous things,
because of a failure to practice giving, one now suffers the misery of poverty and low status.
Happiness and pleasure delude your mind, so you do not perceive that suffering will follow.
O Lord of Men, you should know this: I am now in extreme agony;
you ought to practice giving, lest you become like me in the future.
Having heard this verse, the celestial minister Dharmasena was filled with profound joy; he joined his palms and said to the king:
"As the Buddha has said:
'When seeing others suffer, one should examine oneself.'"
"The King now truly accords with the Buddha’s intention; by seeing that beggar, he has been awakened.
Excellent, Great King!
Your mind is so subtle that you are able to awaken to this matter and skillfully understand and discern the meaning of what the Buddha has taught."
"Great King, you truly deserve the name 'Upholder of the Great Earth,' for you are indeed a lord of the earth without falsehood.

Why is this? Because you are able to skillfully discern the profound meanings of the Buddha-dharma and possess keen wisdom and clear understanding; therefore, you are called the Lord of the Great Earth."
Then he spoke in verse:
"The Lord of the Earth should always be thus; this intention is unsurpassed.
This intention is difficult to maintain constantly, and it is likewise difficult to achieve self-benefit thereby."
A human body is extremely difficult to obtain; faith is likewise difficult to give rise to;
wealth and treasures are hard to find in abundance; and a field of merit is even more difficult to encounter.
Such individual matters as these are exceedingly rare to assemble together.
Just as a blind turtle in the great ocean might encounter a floating yoke with a single hole,
such a rare occurrence as this, O Great King, you possess in its entirety;
therefore, at this time, you ought not to indulge your own mind and will.
The human body is like a flash of lightning; it flashes briefly and does not remain long.
Though one has obtained a human body, it is fragile and cannot be relied upon.
At the moment of death, both shoulders droop and all the joints become slack.
Though he possesses the four dignified postures, his movements are no longer free.
With eyes gazing upward, he is as if seized by the poison of death;
though his relatives stand by his side, they all weep in sorrow upon seeing him.
Touching his body with her hand, she comforted him, saying, "Do not fear.
Having seen her and been thus consoled, his grief increased all the more.
He knew for certain that he had already departed, having entered upon the long road of death.
Though one possesses abundant wealth and goods, they cannot serve as provisions for the journey.
When all the channels are severed and the complexion undergoes total transformation,
life comes to summon one away, like a lamp extinguished when the oil is exhausted.
At such a time as this, who would be able to practice generosity,
uphold the precepts, and cultivate patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom?
Before such a time arrives, one should apply oneself with diligent effort.
"Furthermore, (15) it is impossible for one to carry wealth and treasures into the next world at the time of death, except through the practice of giving and the performance of meritorious deeds;
if one fears poverty in the next world, one should cultivate the virtue of generosity."
I have heard that in the past there was a king named Nanda. At that time, this king accumulated precious treasures with the intention of taking them into the next world, and he thought to himself:
"I shall now collect all the treasures of the kingdom so that none remain outside."
Out of greed for wealth, he placed his own daughter upon the floor of a brothel and commanded his attendants, saying:
"If anyone brings jewels to seek this girl, bring that person along with the jewels to me."
In this manner, he collected all the money and treasures of the kingdom until they were entirely exhausted and gathered in the royal treasury.

At that time, there was a widow who had an only son whom she cherished with great affection. This son, seeing that the princess’s appearance was magnificent and her countenance extraordinary, became deeply infatuated with her. Since his family possessed no wealth with which to make his advances, he eventually fell ill; his body grew emaciated and his breath grew faint.
The mother asked her son,
"What ailment is so severe?
The son then related the circumstances in detail to his mother.
"If I am not able to associate with him, I shall certainly die; of this there is no doubt.
The mother said to her son:
"All the money and treasures within the kingdom have been exhausted without exception; where could one obtain such wealth?"
He further reflected:
"When your father died, there was a gold coin in his mouth; if you open the grave, you may obtain that coin and use it to identify yourself."
He immediately followed his mother’s words, went to open his father’s grave, and took the money from within.
Having obtained the money, he went to the king’s daughter.
At that time, the king’s daughter sent this man along with the money she had given him to show it to the king. When the king saw them, he said to the man:
"The gold and treasures within the kingdom have all been exhausted, with the exception of my own treasury; from where did you obtain this money?
You must have discovered a hidden treasure."
After being subjected to various forms of torture and interrogation until he was forced to reveal where the money was obtained,
the man said to the king:
"I truly did not find any hidden treasure in the earth."
"My mother showed me that when my deceased father died, he placed money in his mouth; I opened the grave and took it out, which is why I obtained this money.

At that time, the king sent men to investigate the truth of the matter. When the messengers arrived, they indeed saw the place where the money had been in the mouth of the deceased father, and only then did they believe him.
Having heard this, the king reflected to himself:
"I previously gathered all manner of treasures, hoping to take these riches with me into the next world;
yet that father could not even carry away a single coin, let alone many more."
He then spoke in verse:
"I previously labored to gather All manner of rare treasures,
Hoping to carry money and goods With me into the next world."
"Now I observe those who open graves, yet they take back the gold coins;
they do not even follow after a single coin, let alone many precious treasures.
He further reflected thus:
"What skillful means should be employed so that these precious treasures may follow me into the next world?
In the past, King Māndhātṛ, together with his armies and hosts,
as well as his elephants, horses, and the seven treasures, all arrived in the heavens."
Rāma constructed a bridge of grass and was able to reach the city of Laṅkā;
I now wish to ascend to heaven, yet there are no ladders or steps;
I wish to go to the city of Laṅkā, yet there are likewise no ferries or bridges.
"I now have no expedient means to carry these treasures into future lives.
At that time, there was a minister who was wise and perceptive; having already understood the king's intention, he spoke these words:

"What Your Majesty has said is precisely the truth. If one must possess wealth and treasures when receiving a future body, yet these current jewels, as well as elephants and horses, cannot be carried into future lives."
Why is this? Your Majesty, this present body of yours cannot even reach the next life, let alone these treasures, elephants, and horses!
What means should be employed so that these precious things may reach the future existence?
"Only by giving to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, and beggars will the reward of merit benefit a person and surely reach the next world.
He then spoke these verses:
"One who adorns their face Sees its excellence reflected in the water; But one who adorns themselves with generosity Will see it reflected in the world beyond."
Beauty and ugliness follow the face; their reflections appear entirely within the water.
If it is adorned, the reflection is beautiful; if it is defiled, the reflection is ugly.
The present body is like the face, and the form received hereafter is like the reflection.
Adorning one's form with precepts and wisdom, one later obtains desirable fruits;
if one performs evil deeds, one later undergoes extremely bitter retribution.
With a mind of faith, one uses wealth and goods to make offerings to parents and teachers.
The śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are poor and in distress are like the water at the back; within it, one sees a reflected image,
and the shadows of the deeds of giving, morality, and wisdom likewise appear therein.
The king has a multitude of attendants, palace women and handmaidens,
ministers and officials, as well as musicians and performers;
yet when his life comes to an end, they follow him with sorrowful longing to the cemetery.
Having arrived, he immediately returned home, with not a single follower in attendance.
The ladies of the inner palace on duty, the storehouses of various treasures,
the elephants, horses, precious litters and carriages, and all articles of entertainment— [he abandoned them all].
The people of the kingdoms and cities, the gardens and pleasure groves for recreation—
all these he abandons and departs alone, with no one following after him.
Only his own good and evil karma follows him closely, never letting him go.

"If a person is at the point of death, their breathing becomes labored and coarse; their throat and tongue become parched and dry so that they cannot swallow water or speak clearly; their gaze is no longer steady and their tendons and sinews snap; the 'sword-wind' (kṣurapra-vāyu) dismembers the body as the joints and limbs loosen; the bodily mechanisms cease and fail so that movement is impossible; and the entire body is racked with pain as if pierced by needles."

At the time when life comes to an end, one sees great darkness as if falling into a deep pit; wandering alone in the vast wilderness without companions, only the cultivation of merit serves as a kinsman to protect one.
"If you act for the sake of future lives, you should quickly cultivate merit.
He then spoke in verse:
"When a person's life comes to an end, They go alone, without companions or followers."
One must inevitably abandon all beloved relatives and friends;
wandering alone in the midst of darkness, through places of dread and terror,
one is separated from all those held dear, solitary and friendless.
"Therefore, one should adorn oneself with the provisions of wholesome dharmas.
To fulfill this meaning, Pārluṣi praised the king with six verses, speaking them as follows:
"Though one may possess various precious jewels, Accumulated like the Snowy Mountains,"
Elephants, horses, and various precious chariots, counselors and incantations—
when the time of death arrives, one cannot escape it through these means;
one should cultivate all wholesome deeds to secure benefit and happiness for oneself.
Those with eyes like blue lotuses should diligently practice precepts and generosity;
death is a great terror, and all who hear of it are struck with fear.
Throughout all the worlds, there is none who does not eventually perish.
For this reason, Great King, you ought to contemplate the suffering of death.
One whose eyes are like blue lotuses should cultivate wholesome deeds;
for the sake of one’s own benefit and happiness, one should diligently practice morality and generosity.
When a person’s life comes to an end, wealth and treasures do not follow;
their vigor, beauty, and prime youth shall never return again.
Those with eyes like blue lotuses should cultivate wholesome deeds.
To secure benefit and happiness for oneself,
one should diligently practice ethical discipline and generosity.
Mṛgāra, King Jayadeva, Tuṇḍuruka, and Sāgaradatta—
The haughty and powerful lords, those who have crossed over the waves of many lifetimes—
such as these supreme among men, the great kings, their armies,
and their officials— all have utterly perished and vanished.
Joy and sorrow arise in succession; thoughts emerge one after another.
O you whose eyes are like blue lotuses, you should cultivate wholesome deeds so that you may experience happiness for yourself;
you ought to diligently practice the precepts and generosity.
Wealth, treasures, and noble status—these things are difficult to encounter;
fortune and rank do not endure, and physical strength waxes and wanes.
Nothing possesses a fixed nature, and even the lord of the earth is not eternal.
Such a most difficult task has now been fully accomplished.
O you whose eyes are like blue lotuses, you should cultivate all manner of virtues so that you may experience happiness for yourself;
you ought to diligently practice the precepts and generosity.
One who is strong, brave, and powerful may be able to leap across the great ocean;
a man of resolute mindfulness may be able to cross over all mountains.
To perform such deeds as these is not yet to be called difficult.
"To be able to benefit future generations—this matter is indeed difficult.

(16) Furthermore, this body is not firm; therefore, the wise person should distinguish themselves by making offerings to their elders and superiors. This is called exchanging the non-firm dharma for the firm dharma.

I have heard that in the past there was a king among the Śākya clan named Aśoka, who had faith and joy in the Triple Gem; whenever he saw a disciple of the Buddha in a quiet place, regardless of whether they were senior or junior, he would invariably dismount from his horse, touch their feet, and pay them homage.

At that time, the king had a great minister named Yaśas, who held wrong views and lacked faith. Seeing the king pay homage to the bhikṣus and others, he conceived a deep sense of slander and spoke to the king, saying:
"These śramaṇas are all of mixed caste who have gone forth; they are not of the kṣatriya or brāhmaṇa castes, but are likewise of mixed vaiśya and śūdra origins."

Furthermore, there are those who work with hides and those who weave; there are also skilled potters, tile-makers, and barbers, as well as low-caste Caṇḍālas and others. Great King, for what reason do you pay homage to them?
Upon hearing these words, the king remained silent and gave no reply.
At another time, he assembled his various ministers and commanded them, saying:
"I now require heads of various kinds; however, you must not carry out executions. I rely upon you to obtain them from those who have died naturally."
He then said to his ministers:
"Now, so-and-so has obtained this head; furthermore, so-and-so has obtained that head.
In this manner, he issued successive commands to all the ministers, ensuring they each obtained different heads and were not permitted to share them.
He addressed Yaśas separately, saying:
"Now, once again, I rely on you to fetch the heads of those who have died, and have each of them sold in the marketplace.
While other such heads were all sold, only the human heads were loathed and despised by those who saw them; people avoided them from afar and none were willing to buy.
When the multitude saw this, they all reviled and insulted him, saying:
"Are you not a caṇḍāla, a yakṣa, or a rākṣasa? Why do you carry about the head of a dead man?"
Having been thus reviled, he returned to the king’s side and said to him:
“I was unable to sell a human head; instead, I was subjected to scolding and abuse.”
The king spoke again, saying,
"If you cannot obtain a price, simply give it away for nothing.
At that time, Yaśas followed the king's instruction and went into the market, proclaiming that he wished to give it away for nothing.
When the citizens saw him, they further reviled and insulted him, and none were willing to take [the head].
Yaśas, filled with shame, returned to the king's presence, joined his palms toward the king, and spoke this verse:
"The heads of oxen, donkeys, elephants, horses, Pigs, sheep, and all other livestock..."
All other heads fetch a price, And people vie with one another to buy them.
Yet all heads have their uses, Except for the human head, which is foul and vile;
There is not a single thing of use in it, So people give it away in vain and refuse to take it.
"And yet I am instead reviled and scolded; how much less likely is there to be a buyer?
The King asked Yajña, "You sell human heads;
for what reason have they not been sold?"
Yaśas said to the king:
"It is something people detest and despise; no one is willing to buy it.
The king asked again:
"Is this one head alone loathsome,
or are all human heads loathsome?
Yaśas replied to the king:
"All human heads are equally loathsome and base; it is not only this one.
The king asked again:
"In that case, is my own head likewise loathed by others?"
Having heard this, Yaśas was terrified and did not dare to respond; he remained silent.
The king spoke again:
"I grant you fearlessness now. Speak the truth: is this head of mine also loathsome?"
Yaśas replied,
"The king's head is likewise.
The king spoke again, saying:
"Is this indeed so? Yaśas replied,
"It is indeed so."
"Great King!
The king said to Yaśas:

"If the heads of all people—whether noble or base—are equally loathsome, why do you now rely on your own noble lineage, physical beauty, and wisdom to boast so highly of yourself, and seek to prevent me from paying homage to the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas?"
Then he spoke in verse:
"Only this human head— All who see it revile and scold it;
There is no value for which it could be sold, It is empty and foul, and one should not draw near it."
Seeing it from afar, all gave rise to anger, saying: "This is inauspicious, vulgar, and evil;
this head is defiled by pus and blood, base and utterly loathsome.
With this lowly head, trade for a head of merit.
"Though one may bend and stretch toward it, not even a hair's breadth is diminished.
The King said to Yaśas:
"Born of mixed lineage and lowly, you cannot perceive its inner essence."
Truly there is moral conduct.
Yet with deluded and confused minds, they reckon themselves to be Brahmins alone possessing the portion of liberation, while regarding all other castes as inferior.
There is no one who attains liberation through them.
If one desires to enter into marriage,
one should seek a partner based on lineage.
If one seeks the wholesome Dharma, what use is there for lineage?
One should not regard one's caste; though born into a noble family, if one commits extremely evil deeds, all people will censure them.
This is what is called lowly and base;
yet if one possesses the practice of the true path within, one will be honored and revered by others—
this is what is called noble and honorable.
When one's virtuous conduct is thus fulfilled, how could one not pay them reverence?
A noble mind makes the body honorable; when a śramaṇa cultivates all forms of goodness—endowed with faith, precepts, generosity, and learning—he is therefore worthy of honor and esteem.
You ought to feel deep reverence.
Why do you not now hear the Dharma taught by the one of the Śākya clan,
who possesses great compassion, the Bull-like Leader on the True Path?
By means of three fragile and precarious things, I shall trade for three firm and enduring things;
the Buddha never speaks with duplicity, therefore I dare not disobey him.
Should I violate the World-Honored One’s instruction, I could no longer be called a true friend.
Just as sugarcane is pressed, Taking the juice and discarding the pulp,
so too is the human body, pressed down by death.
The corpse lies cast upon the ground, incapable of moving forward or stopping.
One should cultivate all manner of virtues through offerings and reverence; therefore, one ought to know this.
With this perishable body, one should trade for the enduring Dharma, just as a wise person, when their house is burning, carries out their wealth and goods.
Just as one would swiftly extract treasure from beneath submerged waters, so too should one quickly retrieve the jewels from this body that will ultimately perish;
it is fitting to exchange this for the enduring Dharma.
The foolish do not discern between the enduring and the non-enduring dharmas.
When the soldiers of Death arrive, it is like entering the mouth of a makara;
at such a time, there will be great terror and profound fear.
It is like extracting fresh butter from curd, or even the finest clarified butter (ghṛta).
Having taken [the cream], the milk-pot is broken, yet no great suffering arises.
This body is also like this: having extracted its firm and essential goodness, when life eventually comes to an end, one will never give rise to regret.
Failing to cultivate various wholesome deeds, one becomes arrogant and heedless;
when the law of death suddenly arrives, it shatters the vessel of the body,
and the mind is left in extreme torment as if scorched by fire.
The knot of sorrow is like fire; the jar of curd is like the body.
You should not obstruct me as I cultivate goodness and grasp the firm Dharma.
Those shrouded in the darkness of ignorance claim for themselves, "I am noble."
I take refuge in the Honored One of Ten Powers,
the lamp of speech who illuminates and examines that which is within one's own body:
the thirty-six kinds of substances, such as skin, flesh, sinews, and bones, in which there is no distinction between the noble and the base.
Noble and lowly are entirely equal; what marks of distinction can there be?
Though there are differences in famous garments and fine robes, as well as in various possessions, the wise should diligently apply themselves to perform acts of reverence and prostration.
When a servant performs various wholesome deeds, this is called grasping at the firm dharma. Why is this said?
Because this body is as swift as lightning, like foam, a bubble, or a heap of sand; it is as unsubstantial as a plantain tree.
This fragile body, though it may endure for a hundred kalpas through the cultivation of merit,
is not as firm as Mount Sumeru or the great earth.
Thus should the wise person trade this [body] for the dharma that is solid and enduring.

*The Mahāyāna-alaṃkāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Three, composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin Dynasty. (17) Furthermore, if those engaged in dispute hear the name of "severing the fetters," the matter of their dispute will be resolved. If one wishes to obtain offerings and respect, one should sever all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

I have heard that in the past, there was an elderly woman who entered a forest to gather leaves from the *pāla* tree to sell for her livelihood; as she traveled along a road by a checkpoint, the guards at the post levied a tax upon her.
At that time, the old woman did not wish to pay the tax, so she said to him:
"If you can take me to the presence of the king, then the tax may be paid; if you do not do so, I will never give it to you."
Thereupon, the patrolmen became agitated and went together to the king's presence. The king asked the old woman:
"For what reason do you now fail to pay the customs duty?
The old woman replied to the king:
“Does Your Majesty recognize that certain bhikṣu?
The king replied, “I do recognize him; he is a great arhat.”
He asked again:
"Does Your Majesty also recognize the second bhikṣu?
The King replied:
"I recognize him; he too is an Arhat.
He asked again, "Do you also recognize the third bhikṣu, the King?"
The king replied, "I know him; he too is an Arhat.
The old woman raised her voice and addressed the king, saying:

"These three arhats are all my sons; when these sons receive the king's offerings, they enable the Great King to receive immeasurable merit, which is precisely what is called 'paying the king’s tax.'"
"How can you wish to further tax and seize from me?
Having heard this, the king marveled at what he had never before experienced:
"Excellent, old mother!"
"I truly did not know that he could produce a noble son;
had I known that this Arhat was your son, I would have offered him even greater offerings and reverence than to you.
Thereupon, the old mother spoke these verses:
"I have raised three sons, valiant and transcending the three realms;
they have all realized arhatship and serve as fields of merit for the world.
O King, when you make offerings to them, you shall obtain blessings equivalent to the tax on goods."
"By what means and stratagem do you seek to tax and seize that which belongs to me?
Upon hearing this verse, the king’s body hair stood on end; he conceived a heart of faith and reverence toward the Triple Gem and, shedding tears, said:
"If even such an old mother as this should be honored with offerings, how much more so her property? It shall not be taxed."
The King spoke in verse:
"From this day forward, like this old mother,
may those who give birth to sons who cross over the three realms of existence become vessels capable of receiving offerings."
Do not permit the taxation of their wealth; all should show them increased respect.
Even if they have companions—whether camels, donkeys, or carriages—laden with many precious treasures, it is for the sake of this old mother.
One should not levy a tax upon him;
he sells tree leaves alone, possessing no other wealth or goods—
how could there be a tax to seize?
In the place where one walks for meditation and cultivates the path,
where practitioners extinguish fetters and sever all outflows— one should revere such a place,
honoring and making offerings to it.
"How much more so for this old mother, who was able to give birth to a noble son—how could one not practice reverence toward her?

(18) It is heard that there was once a son of a great merchant leader named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa. He went to sea to gather treasures, and having returned, he stayed overnight apart from his companions. Losing his way and filled with terror, he was oppressed by hunger and thirst.
From afar he saw a city and thought there was water; he went to the edge of the city, intending to seek water to drink.

However, this city was a city of hungry ghosts (preta). Upon reaching that city, at a crossroads where crowds gather, he saw nothing at all; oppressed by hunger and thirst, he cried out, "Water! Water!"
Upon hearing the sound of this water, the various hungry ghosts all gathered like clouds.
"Who is compassionate enough to give us water?
these hungry ghosts, whose bodies were like scorched pillars and who wrapped themselves in their own hair, all came together with palms joined and spoke thus:
"I beg you for water," said Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
"I am oppressed by thirst, and that is why I have come to seek water."

At that time, when the hungry ghosts heard that Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, being tormented by thirst, was seeking water for himself, their hopes were completely extinguished; they all sighed deeply and spoke these words:
"Do you not know this city of hungry ghosts? Why do you seek water here?"
Then he spoke in verse:
"While we have dwelt in this city for hundreds of thousands of millions of years,
we have not even heard the name of water, much less have we been able to drink it."
Just as a grove of tāla trees is consumed by a blazing fire, so too are we; every limb and joint is ablaze.
Our hair is all disheveled and matted, and our bodies are utterly shattered.
Day and night they think only of food and drink, Trembling with fear, they run in the ten directions.
Driven by hunger and thirst, they gape open their mouths And rush about in search of sustenance.
Someone follows them, brandishing a staff, Chasing after them and inflicting beatings.
My ears constantly hear evil sounds, Never have there been kind words;
How much less has even a single drop of water Moistened my throat and tongue?
If, amidst the mountain valleys, Heavenly dragons were to descend with ambrosia, [I would not receive it.]
All turn into boiling fire, which pours down upon my body.
If I see various channels and rivers, they all turn into flowing fire;
the ponds, marshes, and springs are all seen to be parched and dried up.
Or it turns into thick blood, foul and utterly loathsome.
Should one wish to run toward it, yakṣas seize iron mallets and strike,
so that one cannot approach.
We undergo this suffering; how could we obtain water to bestow as a gift upon you?
In our previous lives, we were miserly, greedy, and exceedingly jealous;
we never gave water or food to a single person.
Not giving one's own goods to others, and suppressing them so that they do not practice generosity—because of such heavy karma, one now undergoes this suffering.
Giving yields great retribution; it is like sowing in spring and harvesting the fruit in autumn.
We did not plant the seeds [of virtue], and so today we suffer this pain.
Through negligence, stinginess, and greed, we undergo this endless suffering;
among all seeds of suffering, none surpasses craving and envy.
One should diligently apply skillful means to eliminate such afflictions.
Giving is the seed of virtue; it can produce all manner of benefit and happiness.
Therefore, one should practice giving, lest one suffer as I do.
Being equal among humans, their physical forms are without distinction;
yet since the karma they create differs, the retribution they receive is likewise diverse.
To one who is wealthy, noble, and possesses abundant treasures, a poor person comes to make a request.
The various devas eat from the same vessel, yet the color of their rice differs.
If one falls among the animals, their karmic retributions likewise differ:
some receive blessings and happiness, while others undergo suffering and affliction.
Because of this poison of greed, humans, devas, and animals are agitated by stinginess and envy;
wherever they go, they suffer diminution.
For the hungry ghosts, there is the burning agony of smoke and flames rising from their limbs and joints.
Like a red flower upon a tree, which a drunken elephant flings far into the air with its trunk, the falling flower leaves its body stained red;
thus the Noble Ones have said: greed and envy are the most painful of vessels.
When seeing those who beg, one’s mind becomes afflicted and turbid;
in that single moment of affliction and turbidity, one is capable of committing base and leaking deeds.
Through foolishness and stinginess in not giving, one plants the very root of poverty.
Accumulating through a greedy mind leads one to fall into the evil realms;
such a person of stingy greed is the very root of all suffering and affliction.
Therefore, the wise should sever this stingy greed.
Whoever desires personal pleasure, fame, honor, and the like,
yet abandons the true path to follow crooked and evil ways,
shall suffer affliction in this life and likewise in the world to come.
The fetters and karma of the world can obstruct the reward of pure giving;
namely, this stinginess and greed, which is the greatest among all enemies.
This body is a massive swelling, [relying on] food, clothing, and medicinal decoctions.
All instruments of pleasure are obstructed and cut off by greed and envy.
Greed and envy are extremely subtle; entering with such subtlety, they are difficult to restrain.
One should therefore use the gate of generosity to make the house of the mind secure and dense.
Do not listen to that greed and envy, lest you enter therein;
for if greed and envy should enter the mind, they can obstruct even the channels, rivers, and great oceans so that one cannot drink from them.
Thus, having encountered these faults and evils, he immediately grew weary of birth and death and returned home to seek renunciation.
Once he had attained renunciation, he diligently cultivated meditative concentration and wisdom, until he realized the fruit of Arhatship.
19. Furthermore, if one who is without fault reproaches another, they may be censured; however, if one who has faults themselves reproaches others, they will instead be mocked by them in return.
I have heard that in the past, a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) was traveling along the same road as some śramaṇas.
There was a young bhikṣu who laughed at that naked ascetic for his lack of shame and modesty.
At that time, among the group of naked ascetics, there was a Brahmin who had some slight understanding of the Buddha-dharma.
He said to the bhikṣu, "Venerable sir!

You must not use your monastic insignia to treat others with contempt or deceive them; nor can you sever the afflictions merely by your monastic appearance. If you have not yet severed the cycle of birth and death and have no prospect of liberation, and if you have not escaped the state of nakedness in your future lives, for what reason do you mock us?"
At this moment, amidst the cycle of birth and death, you are like a tuft of tūla-cotton, drifting east and west with the wind without any fixed time; you should laugh at yourself, not at others.
I know what path you will follow in the future;
like fire covered by ashes, with the fetters still within your heart, you cannot yet be considered secure.
Do not now presume upon your own sense of shame and remorse, for observing your conduct, you have not yet escaped the net of various views.
Now, as for shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*), one certainly does not enter the net of various views; if one does not give rise to unwholesome thoughts, this is called shame and remorse.
Since you yourself have not entered the ranks of those who possess certainty, why do you laugh at others?
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard the naked brahmin speak according to the Dharma, remained silent and gave no reply.
Other bhikṣus, having heard this, praised him, saying:

"One who is able to sever the fetters is called 'possessed of shame and dread of blame. If one who does not sever the fetters were called a bhikṣu, then a performer who shaves his hair should be a bhikṣu; yet, although performers shave their hair, they are not called bhikṣus. One should know that only those who have attained the vision of the Four Noble Truths are true śramaṇas."
Why is this? As it is said in the Sūtra:

"If one does not see the Four Truths, then what is false and what is correct will be indeterminate; because of this indeterminacy between the false and the correct, what is perceived will be erroneous."
"Therefore, one should diligently cultivate the Four Noble Truths; for those who perceive the truths see correctly and will forever leave behind the wrong paths.

(20) Furthermore, one who observes well sees that beautiful forms possess no inherent desire and gives rise to much revulsion; when seeing beautiful forms, they do not give rise to attachment or aversion.
I have heard that in the past there was a monastery with many bhikṣus. Among them was a Dharma Master who possessed the three types of clear knowledge and the six supernormal powers;

his speech was elegant and he was endowed with perfect eloquence. He understood both his own and others' treatises and was skilled in debate and response. Teaching the Dharma according to the capacities of his listeners, he delighted the hearts of the multitude. He was able to kindle the lamp of the Dharma to illuminate and dispel the darkness of ignorance, causing all the people within and outside the city to come daily to hear the Dharma. Having heard and received it, even the youths were no longer heedless.
At that time, there was an elderly courtesan in the city who sighed and spoke these words:
"Now that no one comes or goes among us, how long must we endure such suffering?"
