That courtesan was in the prime of her youth and possessed extraordinary beauty; she was exceptionally intelligent and well-versed in worldly discourse, being fully proficient in all sixty-four arts mastered by women.
Seeing her mother’s distress and sorrow, she immediately asked her mother,
"For what reason are you now so afflicted with grief and suffering?
Her mother replied to the daughter:

"Now all the people within this city delight in listening to the Dharma; none come to my side anymore. My resources are exhausted and I have no means to obtain them; it is for this reason that I am sorrowful."
Having heard this, the girl, relying on her own beauty, said to her mother:
"I shall now adorn myself and go to that assembly; I will be able to cause all the people in that assembly to follow me there."

Having spoken these words, she immediately bathed herself and anointed her body with various fragrances. She adorned herself with necklaces, fine garments, and wore a floral wreath upon her head. Her feet were clad in sandals embellished with many jewels, and she held a staff in her right hand. As she walked with a seductive gait, she moved with graceful, languid gestures, arraying herself in all manner of ornaments like a flowering tree; she was like a celestial being, leading her attendants, whose floral wreaths, necklaces, and fine garments were likewise exquisite.
These attendants—some holding golden vases, some bearing whisks and fans, and some grasping fragrant flowers—waited upon the young woman.

Surrounded by various female entertainers, they spoke and laughed together; some raised their right hands to point out the way. Furthermore, there was an old man with flowers tucked behind his ears, his body painted in black, yellow, crimson, and purple. He laughed and joked with all manner of clever sarcasm, also raising his hand to point forward and backward. Amidst the path, which was filled with the scent of incense and the sounds of drums, music, and singing, they proceeded to a vacant room within the monastery to await the gathering of the assembly.
The time for preaching the Dharma had arrived, and thousands upon thousands of people gathered together.

At that time, the Dharma Master’s hair was extremely white and his elegant eyebrows covered his eyes; he had well-disciplined his sense faculties and his mind was fearless like a lion king. He then ascended the high seat and spoke these verses:
“I observe that those of shallow wisdom Have no means to ascend this seat.”
Timid as a jackal, trembling with fear and finding no peace;
I now ascend this seat, dwelling among the assembly without any dread,
like the king of beasts, roaring to crush heterodox arguments.
At that time, the Dharma Master preached the Dharma in sequence for the great assembly.

Then, that courtesan, wishing to disturb the minds of those gathered, manifested her body at the gate; her attendants scattered among the people, each pointing to the courtesan and saying to the crowd:
"This woman is elegant and her appearance is lovely; you should look at her—what use is there in listening to the Dharma?"
When those people heard these words, they looked around at one another, their minds becoming uneasy.
At that time, the Dharma Master did not understand their intent; wondering at the cause of their behavior, he immediately asked the crowd:
"For what reason have your gazes changed from the usual and your minds become so disordered?"
"Do you not realize that death approaches as swiftly as a galloping horse? Therefore, you ought to diligently cultivate all virtuous deeds.
He then spoke in verse:
"The great torch of the Ten Powers' Dharma Shines universally upon the world;
While the light of wisdom has not yet vanished, you should swiftly cultivate wholesome deeds.
With firm resolve, gather virtuous actions day and night without weariness;
for the lamp of the All-Knowing One’s words will soon be extinguished.
"If he should pass into disappearance, all sentient beings would be plunged into darkness;
even if the light of the sun were present, it would still be called a great gloom.
At that time, having heard these verses, the assembled multitude reverently received the Dharma teachings and focused their minds to listen to the Dharma.

At that time, seeing that the assembly had gathered their minds and composed their intentions, the courtesan again assumed seductive postures; upon witnessing this, the hearts of the congregation once more became distracted.
Then the Dharma Master spoke these verses:
“That woman assumes seductive postures, Causing the assembly to give rise to craving.”
Dragged by the passions of desire, they have robbed me of my single-minded concentration.
Out of reverence for my teaching, I shall restrain them and cause them to desist;
how could those demonic apparitions delude the eyes of the multitude?
"Just as a garland of blue lotuses, tossed and driven by the movement of the waves, so too is the mind of the multitude; it flickers and does not rest for a moment.
At that time, the people were already infatuated and deluded; beholding this wondrous form, they lost their sense of shame and modesty, pointing at one another and speaking these verses:
"This woman is of beautiful form; her arrival today is most auspicious.
Like the crescent moon newly risen, though fallen upon the earth, her countenance transcends all of her time, and her pure eyes are exceedingly exquisite."
"Could this not be the woman Lambā, sent by Śakra?
Or perhaps it is Puṇyavatī; yet her hands do not hold flowers.
Then another person spoke in verse:
"Alas for this woman! Her appearance is most marvelous;
her eyes are like blue lotuses, her nose is prominent and her brows are like painted lines.
Both her cheeks are full and rounded, and her lips are crimson with teeth that are even and closely set."
Her skin was firm yet exceedingly supple; her dignified beauty was most extraordinary.
Her majestic features were delightful to behold, radiant like a mountain of gold.
At that time, the upāsakas, captivated by her appearance, had their minds thrown into confusion.
At that time, the courtesan’s attendants, having witnessed this event, were filled with deep personal joy and exclaimed:
"What we have done today is most excellent; we have been able to capture the attention of this entire assembly to such an extent."

At that time, the Dharma Master marveled at how the fourfold assembly was agitated and had departed from their usual composure. He raised his hand to brush back his brows and looked out over the gathering; he saw that this courtesan was of exquisite countenance, and her attendants were all magnificently adorned. Standing in their midst, the courtesan shone like a brilliant star, stealing the hearts of the ignorant and causing them to lose their right mindfulness.
At that time, the Dharma Master observed the woman’s intentions, wondering for what purpose she had come there;
he then silently entered meditative concentration and perceived that she was driven by delusion and had not come to listen to the Dharma.
However, although this Dharma Master had severed all ill-will, he manifested an expression of anger and raised his voice to shout to the courtesan:

"You are like an anthill, yet you wish to compare your height with that of Sumeru, the King of Mountains! Have you not heard how, when the Buddha was in the world, the sixth Heavenly King, failing to measure his own strength, dared to act with harassment in the presence of the Buddha? By the World-Honored One’s supernatural power, a corpse was fastened around his neck; he was filled with shame and humiliation, becoming a laughingstock for gods and men alike?"
Do you then think that the teachings of the Buddha-Dharma are intended for extinction?
Could there be no arhats who are single-mindedly diligent?
Have all those supreme beings utterly perished?
"If you act thus, you should firmly maintain yourself.

At that time, the Dharma Master used his supernormal powers to transform this courtesan so that her flesh and skin fell away, leaving only white bones, with all the internal organs fully exposed. He then called out to the courtesan before the assembly:
"Just now you gave rise to an evil mind, daring to contend and dispute with the Buddha-Dharma."
At that time, this courtesan stood before the assembly with her skeletal body.
Then the Dharma Master spoke these verses:
“You who once possessed a wondrous countenance and complexion, Stood out as the object of everyone’s gaze;”
Now the flesh has entirely transformed, leaving only empty bones and skeletons.
What you previously delighted in as pure white, you now finally perceive as its true nature:
the skull bone resembles white jade, and its form and color are like the root of a lotus.
The sockets of the eyes are sunken and the temples are hollow; both cheeks resemble deep ravines.
All the joints and mechanisms have fallen apart, and the sinews and veins are merely coarsely stitched together.
The various internal organs within hang suspended in mid-air, laid bare.
Even those who follow him will feel revulsion upon seeing him;
how much more so the rest of the great multitude—
who could possibly take pleasure in seeing him?

At that time, having transformed his form for the sake of the Dharma Master, the skeletal man was exhausted both in body and mind and could not move himself; he then joined his bony hands in reverence and turned toward the Dharma Master.
At that time, the Dharma Master addressed the skeleton, saying:

"Your complexion, your necklaces, and your various bodily ornaments serve only to delude ordinary people, causing them to become deeply attached and sink into the pool of the three realms of existence."
If you can now set aside your graceful gestures and discard your ornaments, I shall show you my tranquil and pure sublime body, so that you may come to know the marketplace of impurity.

This body is covered with thin flesh over a core overflowing with filth; externally, it is falsely adorned with unguents and powders to deceive the eyes of the ignorant. Ordinary people, mired in delusion and blinded by desire, give rise to defiled attachment.
"What wise person, having observed this with discernment, would cherish or delight in it?
At that time, those gathered there, having witnessed this event, all gave rise to a sense of weary revulsion and said to one another:

"What the World-Honored One has spoken is true and not false; all phenomena are like illusions, like transformations, like bubbles on water, or like gold-plated coins—they merely deceive and delude people."

The woman who previously possessed such beautiful features and graceful deportment is now suddenly seen as nothing but a heap of bones; her upright form and various gestures were like those of a sorceress—where has all this gone now?
There was a lay follower who rested his cheek upon his finger and gazed intently at this woman, speaking in verse:
“The Muni has said that sentient beings Are blinded by the craving of desire;
Because they are blind and lack the eye of wisdom, They cannot proceed toward Nirvāṇa.”
Just as a renu-leaf, smeared with honey, is sucked by insects who,
deluded by greed, do not let go even unto death; so too,
those who are heedful observe the true nature of the body with clear insight.
"And yet he does not give rise to thoughts of desire;
he is like the king of white cranes who always dwells in a clear pond, finding no pleasure among the graves.
Furthermore, another upāsaka spoke these words:
"Upon seeing this form, a thought of desire arises; by contemplating those white bones, it is immediately extinguished.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Contemplating that heap of skeletal remains Can give rise to fear in people."
Like a mechanical puppet made of *vīṭar̤a* wood,
The foolish take it to be real and give rise to a mind of attachment and delight.
It is like a deep pit on a path, Covered over with grass upon its surface.
"This body is also like this; one should contemplate it in this way.
Having understood this with true discernment, who would give rise to thoughts of desire?
At that time, those deluded, ignorant, and witless people, having heard these verses, lowered their heads and avoided them, ultimately taking no pleasure in hearing them.
At that time, the woman, seeing herself as an object of reproach to others, prostrated herself with her five limbs touching the ground and spoke this verse:
"I was formerly foolish and ignorant, Failing to measure my own strength.
I pray you turn back and listen to the assembly of Dharma-seekers; Let us all return home together."
Now I finally know that the son of the Śākyas possesses most extraordinary power;
he has transformed my exquisite features so that all who behold me feel revulsion.
Like a foolish infant, I have acted with extreme frivolity.
"To dare to compare the water of an ox's footprint to the great ocean—may you deign to show compassion and pity, and grant me leave to offer this sincere confession.

At that time, the great assembly saw that the woman’s various bones were propped against one another like a reed hut; they were filled with great wonder and astonishment, asking how she could speak such words from within that heap of bones.

Furthermore, he saw all five viscera exposed, like the five viscera suspended on a butcher’s rack, wriggling and quivering like dog meat; the foul stench of the various organs was worse than that of a latrine.
"How is it that we have come to see this?
They then spoke in verse:
"Now we observe the woman’s body, Which is but sinews connecting withered bones."
One sees only a heap of empty bones, yet from their combination, the sounds of speech emerge.
Is there bone within the woman?
Or is there a woman within the bone?
For example, in a vast marsh, a thicket of reeds,
stirred together by the wind, produces a great sound. Just so,
through these dependent and provisional phenomena, the self-substance of a woman is not perceived.
If there is no intrinsic nature, where can the female form abide?
Though one searches exhaustively through all phenomena, it has never existed from the beginning.
When I contemplate the characteristics of the body—its coming and going, its advancing and halting—[I find nothing].
Bending and extending, looking up and down, glancing around and speaking—all these movements depend upon the mutual support of the various joints. The ribs are exceedingly sparse;
sinews wind together to form the mechanisms, which, by means of them, enable motion and turning.
Thus, within each and every one of these, there is no sovereign lord at all;
yet as for this phenomenon, is it existent or non-existent?
Am I deluded by madness and folly, or is my vision disordered by a cataract?
How is it that within such a state, one falsely conceives the appearance of a woman?
It is like binding reeds to create a mechanical device, employing many threads and cords;
it is like molten pure gold, which emits a sound when water is poured upon it.
At that time, the Dharma Master, knowing that the fourfold assembly had all conceived feelings of revulsion, addressed the courtesan, saying:
"What do you intend to do now?
The woman replied to the Dharma Master:
"Would you be willing to give up this dwelling?
He then spoke in verse:
"Great-Head Seer, will you give it up?"
You transformed the celestial maiden Lambā, making her into a mare for a full twelve years;
will you now build a house for me?
Will you make for me a dwelling such as has never been seen before in this world—a dwelling located within a tomb?
"O Virtuous One, Sovereign of Goodness, have compassion for me and grant that this be removed.
At that time, the Dharma Master smiled and spoke these verses:
"Virtuous woman, simply rise; I harbor no heart of anger."
Having shaved one's head and donned the kāṣāya, one should never abandon the Dharma.
If one has desire and attachment for those things, it will cause suffering and affliction to arise.
Those who engage in both good and evil deeds are able to give rise to hatred and anger.
Do you take up resentment as your dwelling?
I have extinguished the fetter of resentment and severed ignorance; my essential nature is free from fetters.
Since I desire to rescue sentient beings, how could I not take up [this burden] as my dwelling?
Birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth— how could a person of wisdom not provide shelter for all these suffering sentient beings?
Like a malignant, poisonous sore, further smeared with harsh and foul ashes,
covered by a thin skin over its internal mechanisms— fools give rise to love and delusion for it;
by the power of my supernormal faculties, I shall open this casket of impurity for you.
Having spoken these verses, he withdrew his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), and the woman returned to her original form.
At that time, the Dharma Master addressed the assembled multitude, saying:
"You all should diligently cultivate virtue."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Inverted thoughts and desires arise like dust stirred up by the wind;
Right contemplation turns away from the face of desire, Washing clean the dust and grime of craving."
There are those with desire and those free from desire; the place where one dwells is not fixed.
By observing well, one attains liberation; through craving and delusion, desire increases.
Therefore, one should constantly practice, single-mindedly cultivating the perception of freedom from desire.
Free from desire, the assembly attained sublime tranquility and achieved the various joys of dhyāna.
At that time, among those in the audience listening to the Dharma, some attained the contemplation of impurity,
while others attained the stage of Srotāpanna as they cultivated the perception of detachment.
Some attain the stage of Anāgāmin; Furthermore, there are those who have left the household life, Who practice with diligence and without indolence, And reach the state of Arhatship.

(21) Furthermore, one who has no mind of attachment can give everything away; such a person gains great renown and receives rewards in the present life. Therefore, one should practice giving and not be stingy or attached.

I have heard that in the past, there was a painter in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī named Kana. Having come to the kingdom of Śaila for some reason, he visited various stūpas and temples; by painting a vihāra there, he received thirty *liang* of gold.

Returning to his own country, he encountered people performing a *pañcavārṣika* festival; conceiving a heart of faith and reverence, he asked the administrative bhikṣu, "Who will prepare the food and drink tomorrow?"
He replied, "There is no agent.
He asked again:
“How much wealth does that bhikṣu require for a single day’s meal?
He replied,
“He requires thirty taels of gold.”
Then the painter gave thirty *tolas* of gold to the administrative monk (*karmadāna*).
Having given him the gold, he returned home, where his wife asked him:
"What have you earned from your labor today?"
The husband replied to his wife, "I have obtained thirty ounces of gold and used it for a meritorious assembly.

Upon hearing this, his wife became extremely indignant and spoke of her husband's faults to her relatives, saying, "All the gold he acquired was spent entirely on a religious assembly; there is nothing left over to maintain the household."
At that time, his kinsmen took the man to the place of legal judgment and said to him:
"The wealth you acquired through the labor of your own strength was not used to maintain your household or your kinsmen, but was spent entirely to provide for various meritorious assemblies."
When the judge heard these words, he asked that man,
"Is it truly so? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
When the judge heard these words, he was struck with a sense of wonder and immediately praised him, saying:
"Excellent, O noble man!"
He divested himself of his own garments, along with his various necklaces and the horse with its saddle, giving them all to that person, and spoke this verse:
"Having long dwelt in the suffering of poverty, One earns wealth through hired labor;
Yet, without using it for one's livelihood, To give it away is truly most difficult."
Though one may possess wealth and resources that are exceedingly abundant,
if one does not examine things well, one cannot give quickly.
By observing the future life from afar, one knows that giving has its fruit and retribution.
"Brave and able to renounce wealth, free from the dust and defilement of stinginess—such is the practitioner of the Dharma who maintains generosity so that it does not perish.
When the painter heard this verse, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; putting on his robes and mounting his saddled horse, he returned to his home.

At that time, the family members saw him arrive at the gate dressed in magnificent attire and riding a horse; thinking he was a person of high status, they were filled with fear and closed their doors to hide away.
The painter said to them:
"I am no other, but your husband."
His wife said to him, "You are a poor man;
from where did you obtain such saddled horses and carriages?
At that time, her husband answered her in verse:
"Listen now, virtuous lady, as I shall speak according to the truth:
although you have now offered this gift to the Saṅgha, it has not yet been consumed.
It is like a seed that has not yet been sown, yet the sprouts and stalks have already begun to grow."
The field of merit is most excellent and beautiful; its fruit and retribution lie ahead.
This monk is a pure field of merit—who would not sow within it?
Just as the intention is to plant the seed, the sprout has already grown for all to see.
When the wife heard this, she attained pure faith and immediately spoke in verse:
"As the Buddha has taught, Giving to the Saṃgha yields great fruit;
The gift bestowed just now Truly reaches its intended destination."
Giving even a small amount of water with a reverent heart yields a retribution greater than the great ocean;
among all assemblies, the Buddha and the Sangha are the most supreme.
When one opens their mind and is about to give, the flowers should already be before them.
"22. Furthermore, one who practices giving does so with supreme faith; the fruit of a gift of even two coins is immeasurable.
I have heard that in the past, a certain woman went to Mount Divāndhakāra and saw a great multitude of people performing a *pañcavārṣika* festival there."
At that time, the woman was begging for alms at the assembly; upon seeing the monks, her heart was filled with joy, and she praised them, saying:
"Excellent, O Noble Sangha!
You are like the great ocean, a dwelling place for all manner of treasures, whom all people honor."
"I alone am poor and have nothing to give.
Having said this, he searched his entire body but found nothing at all. He then thought to himself:
"Previously, I found two copper coins in some excrement."
She then took this money and offered it as a gift to the community of monks.

At that time, the Elder of the Sangha had attained the fruit of Arhatship and possessed the power of knowing others' minds; moreover, he was one who always held himself in high esteem. Seeing that the woman possessed deep faith, and desiring to increase her merit, he did not wait for the Karmadāna, but rose up personally with great earnestness to offer a blessing. Raising his right hand, he cried out in a loud voice:
"May the virtuous Sangha listen!..."
He then spoke in verse:
“The great earth and the vast ocean, and all the treasures they contain—
a maiden such as this can give them all as an offering to the Sangha.”
"Be heedful and observe well; practice the Path to cultivate merit, so that you may attain the Way of Liberation and leave behind the thorns of poverty.

At that time, the young girl gave rise to a most sublime resolve, thinking: "As the Teacher has said, I shall perform what is difficult to do. She then renounced all her wealth, treasures, and possessions without exception. With a heart mingled with sorrow and joy, she prostrated herself on the ground before the Sangha, placed the two coins before the Elder, and weeping uncontrollably, spoke this verse:
"May I, throughout birth and death, forever be free from poverty;
may joy and celebration always gather around me, and may I never be separated from my kinsmen.
I now offer these fruits to the Saṃgha; only the Buddha can discern their fruit."
"By virtue of these merits, may the fruits of my aspirations be swiftly realized;
may this subtle mind of planted goodness cause my physical faculties to emerge quickly.
At that time, having emerged from the mountain, the woman sat beneath a tree; the shade of the tree did not shift, and above her was a canopy of clouds.

At that time, the king of that country had recently lost his queen and was wandering abroad when he saw that cloud-canopy; he went beneath the tree and, upon seeing this young girl, felt a sense of passionate attachment toward her. He brought her back to his palace and appointed her as his foremost and greatest queen.
He then thought to himself:
"The vow I previously made has now been fulfilled according to my heart's desire.
He then addressed the king:

"Taking with him a great quantity of precious objects and prepared offerings, he went to Mount Divākara to make offerings to the assembly of monks, presenting various treasures, pearls, necklaces, and manifold wealth as gifts."
At that time, the Elder did not offer a blessing.
Then the great assembly, wondering at the reason for this, spoke thus:
"Previously, when he was poor and lowly and gave two coins as an offering, he rose to offer a blessing; [why does he not do so now?]"
"Now that she has become the King's consort, why do you not offer blessings for her as she gives away precious jewels, necklaces, and various kinds of wealth?
At that time, the Elder addressed the assembly of monks, saying:
"When I previously offered blessings for her, it was not for the sake of material wealth; rather, I offered blessings because I feared the young girl’s mind might become distracted."
He then spoke these verses:
"Great karmic fruit is not obtained through abundant wealth;
only by means of a supreme and virtuous mind does one attain great karmic fruit."
When she first practiced giving, she relinquished everything;
the Buddha’s wisdom can discern this, which is beyond my ability to know.
Though her wealth and treasures are now great, they do not equal the state of mind she possessed at that time.
One part in sixteen.
Just as merchants, though possessing few goods,
set their hearts on a great reward.
The intention was supreme and vast; for this reason, in the future, the retribution obtained shall also be immeasurable.
With a pure mind, he offered land as a gift, just like that of the city of Śrāvastī.
A woman of the lowest station gave a meal of rice-gruel to Kāśyapa;
by giving earth she obtained the great earth, and by giving rice-gruel she attained preeminence among the gods.
Though the gift was small, her mind was pure and vast; thus the reward she received was likewise immense.
Just as when a drop of oil falls upon a clean white cloth, the grease and grime increase accordingly; it is like a drop of oil on water.
Though the drop of oil is minute, it spreads across the surface of the pond.
For this reason, you should know that because the mind is supreme, the retribution is great.
*Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, Scroll Four;
*Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, Scroll Five.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin Dynasty.

(23) [Discourse 23] Furthermore, if a person associates with a wise and virtuous friend who can cause both the internal and external aspects of their body and mind to be pure, such a person is called a true and virtuous man (*satpuruṣa*).
I have heard that in the past, there was a bhikṣu who, while begging for alms in sequence, arrived at the house of a great brāhmaṇa.
At that time, upon encountering the bhikṣu, the rafter of the house collapsed and smashed a water jar, and a cow broke its halter and bolted in all directions.
Then the brahmin spoke these words:
"How inauspicious is this!
An ill-omened person has entered my home, and thus this strange portent has occurred."
Having heard this, the bhikṣu immediately replied to him, saying:
"Have you perhaps seen the young children within your house, their limbs emaciated, their bellies distended, and their faces swollen?"
The brāhmaṇa said,
"I saw him before.
The bhikṣu spoke again:

"In your house there dwells a yakṣa ghost who resides within your home and sucks away the vital essence of people; this is why the young children in your household have contracted these ailments. Now that this yakṣa, terrified of me, has fled in fear, it is for this reason that your beam has broken, your jar has shattered, and the heifer has snapped its halter."
The brahmin asked,
"What power do you possess?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I possess this power because I have drawn near to the teachings of the Tathāgata; therefore, I cause the yakṣas to fear me in such a manner.
The brāhmaṇa spoke again:
"What is meant by 'the teachings of the Tathāgata'?"

Thereupon, the bhikṣu sequentially expounded the teachings and admonitions of the Buddha’s Dharma; having heard them, the brahmin couple attained realization in their minds and hearts, and both achieved the fruit of srotāpanna.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa spoke these verses:
“Excellent, O one of supreme virtue! You have well expounded the true Dharma.
The Buddha’s teaching, heard through my ears, Has entered the dwelling of my heart.”
May you bring peace and security to my home and act as my protection.
I pray that you will now briefly listen to what I have to say:
tear down the house of my mind and break the beam of my ignorance.
Please skillfully drive away the yakṣa that sucks up merit,
and eliminate the rākṣasas of various views; the jar of delusory theft was filled to the brim with the water of the view of self-identity, but it has now been shattered.
The foolish cow runs wild, pulling at the traces of ignorance until they snap;
all that has been seen before now gathers within my own body.
All forms are like a mirror, with their reflections appearing therein.
Within the beginningless cycle of birth and death, I have never before seen such a thing;
it is because of you that I have now first beheld the Four Noble Truths.
Having now encountered a true spiritual friend, we have met through the convergence of conditions.
It removes the affliction of greed from my heart and drives away the demons within my home.
This has been transmitted in the world for a long time, as taught in the four Vedas:
one should perform the great sacrifice, adorning it with various kinds of objects.
Having fully prepared the sacrificial ground, one bathes in great rivers such as the Ganges to wash away transgressions;
thus one may swiftly attain rebirth in heaven.
Although I have practiced in this way since ancient times, I have never yet obtained the fruit of my labor.
Yet I was unable to know, whether it would certainly be attained or not;
performing sacrifices and ritual ablutions is not equal to drawing near to a virtuous friend.
Now that I have drawn near to a virtuous friend, I have already attained the realization of its fruit.
Neither born nor dying, one attains liberation and proceeds toward nirvāṇa;
forever free from the realm of fear, this is not sought through wealth or treasures.
Even by relying on the power and authority of a king, one might cast oneself from a cliff or enter a blazing fire.
In the severity of the cold winter months, he wraps his body in frozen ice;
in the stifling heat of midsummer, he scorches his body with the five fires.
He lies down to sleep upon rafters of woven wood and upon thorny brambles.
Crossing mountains and traversing the great ocean, performing fire sacrifices and reciting incantations—
through such ascetic practices as these, one cannot attain Nirvāṇa. Only by cultivating meditative wisdom,
along with ethical discipline, learning, and single-minded diligence, can it be attained.
"Such Dharma practices as these—how are they obtained?
They must depend upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), and only then can they be fully attained.
(24) Furthermore, if a person commits evil and ought to fall into hell, by encountering a spiritual friend they can extinguish their offenses and attain birth among humans or devas.
I have heard that in the past, a man from the country of Vāgali came to Central India, and the King of India at that time appointed him as the head of a village.

At that time, there were many Brahmins in that village, and one who was close to him explained the *Rāmāyaṇa* to the village head, as well as the *Bhārata*, saying that those who die in battle are reborn in heaven after death, and those who cast themselves into fire are likewise reborn in the heavens. He further described the various pleasures of the heavens with such skillful rhetoric that he moved the village head’s mind, leading him to believe that these things must certainly be true.

He immediately prepared a fire pit, piled up fragrant wood, and held a Brahmin assembly; when the people had gathered like clouds at the venue, the village headman was about to throw himself into the fire.
This village headman had previously been acquainted with a Śākya bhikṣu. At that time, the bhikṣu came to his house and saw the village headman adorning it in various ways;
the bhikṣu asked, "What do you intend to do?"
The village headman said,
"I wish to be reborn in heaven.
The bhikṣu asked:
"How did you go?
he asked. He immediately replied, "I threw myself into a fire pit and thereby attained rebirth in heaven."
The bhikṣu asked,
"Do you perhaps know the path to the heavens?
He replied:
“I do not know.
The bhikṣu asked,
“If you do not know, how did you manage to go?”
When you travel now, from one village to another, you still require a guide to know the way; how much more so for those celestial paths which are so vast and distant?
The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* above here; without a guide, by what means could one possibly reach that celestial realm?

If it is the pleasures of heaven that you seek, why would that elder Brahmin—who is already advanced in years and destitute of wealth, and whose wife is likewise aged and of ugly countenance—find anything there to love or delight in?
"Why do you not take me along to go to the heavens?
When the village headman heard these words, he thought to himself:
"If one can be born in heaven by throwing oneself into a pit of fire, then that brahmin should go with me."
Why is this? That brahmin is impoverished and afflicted by suffering, having nothing to love or cherish; he ought to abandon his misery and seek the bliss of that heavenly realm.
If he does not depart, he will merely act out deception, seeking to kill me.
Having formed this thought, he immediately stepped forward and seized the hand of the senior brahmin, wishing to leap into the fire together with him toward the heavens.
At that time, the brahmin pushed him away and refused to go.
Why is this? The brahmins and others had come to the assembly solely for the sake of wealth.
At that time, seeing that the brahmins were unwilling to enter the fire, the village headman spoke this verse:
"As for the heavens as they have been heard of, their manifold pleasures are beyond reckoning;
yet upon encountering objects, one gives rise to craving and attachment, looking toward the east while forgetting the west.
Even if one were to calculate all the possessions of one's household and every instrument of pleasure—"
Compared to the heavens, it is like a mustard seed compared to Mount Sumeru;
if you are truly one who has few desires and is free from greedy attachment, then I now observe you.
With the fierce fire of greed blazing,
he watches over his ugly, aged wife; having come to this assembly,
he seeks wealth for the sake of providing for his household.
If you love your son and do not wish for him to be born in heaven,
consider that his power to be born there would be more than sufficient to protect him.
If you do not know the path to heaven, why did you send me there?
If you truly knew the Way of Heaven, why do you not depart?
Why do you delight in instructing others, wishing to make me throw myself into fire?
Is it because you covet my wealth and property, desiring to share in its use?
How can there be such a lack of compassion, so cruel and harsh?
Perhaps it is an enemy from a previous life, surely a great deceiver,
who acts as a companion to death and urges me to be born in heaven.
They exhorted me to die, forcibly compelled me to enter the fire,
and taught people to leave their homes and dwell afar, practicing the dharma of asceticism.
They threw themselves into abysses and rushed into flames, starving themselves to demonstrate the renunciation of food.
Observing the intent of their teachings, I see they wish to sever the lineage of their clan.
These brahmins delight in acts of slaughter;
therefore, I have abandoned them and shall enter the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha-dharma is great compassion; it never harms living beings.
When a great fire consumes the mountains and wilds, the deer all flee and hide.
Because they cherish their own lives, they seek out places of cool relief.
"I, too, should now act likewise; I take refuge with sincerity to seek your protection.
At that time, the bhikṣu, seeing that Bakula’s mind was already weary of the various brāhmaṇas and had developed deep faith and reverence for the Triple Gem, praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Āyuṣmat! It is only now that you have truly entered the path of the gods.
He then spoke this verse:
“The Buddha’s words reach the heavenly realms, And likewise the path of liberation;
these words are certain to arrive, Without ever erring in the interim.
The Omniscient One speaks the Path, Distinguishing its extensive and abbreviated aspects.”
Harmlessness, truthful speech, and the like, as well as generosity and the subduing of the sense faculties—
this is the path to the heavenly realms;
it cannot be attained through such ascetic practices as throwing oneself into deep waters or leaping into fire.
This may serve as a cause for death, but it is not the cause of liberation from the heavens.
In ages past, the human lifespan was long, and the lifespans of the sages were likewise long.
Because they grew weary of this body, they did not wish to dwell long in the world.
Having first practiced the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and severed the fetters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
one knows for oneself that upon casting off this body, one will surely be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
There is no means by which one could lose one's life, even by leaping into a deep abyss or rushing into fire.
Because of losing one's life through this, one attains birth within the Brahma Heaven.
Because meditative concentration severs the fetters, one attains birth in the Brahma Heaven;
it is not by throwing oneself from cliffs or into fire that one attains birth in the heavens.
He had a companion, a seer, who observed with his divine eye:
"Where has this man been reborn after death?
He saw that he was born among the Brahmā gods; first seeing him cast into the abyss and die, he concluded that it was by this means he had attained birth in heaven.
Others, being foolish, do not see this; they claim that by throwing oneself into a deep pool or fire, one will be reborn in the Brahma Heaven, and thus give rise to perverted views.
All other brahmins are likewise ignorant and devoid of wisdom.
They do not contemplate or cultivate meditative concentration to sever the various fetters and afflictions;
they merely observe those who cast themselves into abysses or fires, claiming that such acts lead to rebirth in the heavens.
Because of these inverted delusions, they have consequently produced various sutras and treatises.
The foolish all believe and accept [falsehoods], casting themselves into abysses and rushing into fire.
The wise observe with skill; they abandon such things and do not act upon them.
They practice all wholesome dharmas, taking them as the cause for the heavenly realms.
Throwing oneself into deep waters or leaping into fire and the like are not practices for cultivating goodness that can provide the conditions for escaping death,
nor are they causes for rebirth in heaven; rather,
when body and mind rely upon the Buddha-dharma, this is called the path of quiescent extinction.
"What is the use of these non-Buddhists?
They suffer in vain without fruit, like one who drills water seeking clarified butter; though they toil, it will never be obtained.

(25) Furthermore, those who practice giving should distance themselves from the eight perils. If one accumulates wealth and treasures, perils and difficulties are exceedingly many; for the wise person, practicing giving is what constitutes true stability.
I have heard that in the past, there was a king who punished a merchant and said to him, "List all the wealth you possess.

When the merchant returned home, he reflected upon all the things he had previously given away: the single meal he had given to beggars, and even the grain and grass he had given to birds and beasts; he listed them all for the king.
Having seen this, the king asked,
"For what reason has such a thing come so late?
The merchant replied:
"The King previously commanded that all my wealth be recorded and shown to me; those items recorded in the inventory are what belongs to me.
He then spoke in verse:
"What was shared among the five families, Is now all within this house."
What I have now recorded, none can plunder or seize.
Such a record as this cannot be violated by kings, thieves, water, or fire.
Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans may all be completely melted away,
yet the objects thus offered cannot burn even a single hair.
Wealth entrusted to parents, brothers, and sisters—
All kinsmen and friends will inevitably suffer loss and separation;
only the things one has given away can never be diminished or decayed.
Generosity is a treasury of practice that follows one through every lifetime.
Generosity is the most intimate friend; there is nothing that can destroy it.
The great ocean of poverty is most terrifying, yet generosity is its sturdy ship;
only those who practice giving possess it.
One is able to cross to the other shore.
I know the fruit of giving; therefore, I speak without fear:
that which is recorded as my wealth, the treasures within the household, are shared by the five families.
"Therefore, I did not dare to claim it, saying, 'This is my own possession.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was filled with joy, and he praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
"You are a person of superior merit; I have no need now for anything you possess.
As you have said, this gift is your property, but all other wealth shall be shared together."
At that time, the king spoke these verses:
"If one practices giving, Handing it over with one's own hands,
One should give rise to a joyful mind And not harbor thoughts of regret."
Therefore, in future lives, humans and devas will experience happiness.
Regarding all material wealth and possessions— seeing one's own treasures being divided and belonging to various households—
if one cannot give them away swiftly, [one will suffer].
There is no one who can seize it away;
yet in the end, it will be taken by others. In this life, one’s ill repute is heard afar, and in future lives, one suffers great poverty. This is the height of folly.
Seeing the houses and dwellings of others, as well as their vast wealth and treasures,
which after death are enjoyed by many families, yet not a single hair’s breadth follows one;
witnessing such matters with one's own eyes, one is still unable to feel revulsion.
Swiftly relinquish wealth and possessions; wealth is not shared with the five families, for only through the practice of giving does it endure.
Nothing follows one after death; one must certainly and inevitably leave it all behind.
Yet one does not receive the reward for giving.
The wise person must surely practice giving; since both [the giver and the recipient] are termed "giving," one should personally bestow gifts.
The fragrance of their refined excellence flows constantly;
such wise donors are filled with merit and benefit, and are praised by the people of the world.
Those who possess abundant wealth yet are stingy and do not give are ridiculed by the world.
Even if one possesses wealth and money, yet turns one's back upon a beggar upon seeing them,
though they may abound in riches and treasures, they are called poor and afflicted by decline.
One who gives, though they be impoverished, is always said to possess wealth.
Though a miser possesses great wealth, he is not freed from the affliction of poverty and decline.
When a donor gives the gift of water, it washes away the defilement of mental greed.
Avarice yields no reward of wholesome joy; it leads one onto the path of death.
One will surely fall into a deep pit or trap.
When the spirit departs and the breath ceases, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep—all are entirely abandoned;
at the moment of death, one gives rise to suffering and distress.
Because of this, one gives rise to attachment, fearing great heat and affliction.
One who practices generosity at the time of death experiences joy and has no regrets.
The stingy and envious are reviled by the wise; as for the generous, whether poor or rich, [they are praised].
They constantly experience happiness.
All people avoid and distance themselves from them; though those who are stingy and greedy remain alive, they are in reality no different from hungry ghosts.
Admired by all and beloved by the wise,
one is reborn in the heavens at the end of life.
Since there are those who cherish you, why do you not practice generosity?
Generosity is a virtuous and excellent companion,
a sublime provision; it requires no chariots or horses,
nor any retinue of attendants.
A bridge for future generations; through giving, one leaves behind all hardships, and the five families cannot encroach.
How could there be anyone who loves themselves and yet would not practice giving?
If one obtains even a small amount in a future life, one should still practice giving;
how much more so when practicing even a little generosity yields such great rewards of merit?
Therefore, the wise person should practice giving.
26. Furthermore, if one hears the correct teaching, one is able to be released from bondage.

I have heard that in the past, in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, a criminal was confined within a monastery. During the night, while the community of monks was preaching the Dharma, the man who had been imprisoned came into the midst of the assembly and sat down in order to listen to the Dharma.
There was a bhikṣu who preached a sūtra concerning the forward and reverse order of birth and death, saying:
"The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

'Ordinary, foolish people who have not heard the Dharma do not know form, do not know the origin of form, do not know the gratification of form, do not know the peril of form, do not know the escape from form, and do not know weariness with form; all sentient beings do not truly know such perils as these.'"
If one is bound by form, this is called true bondage.
What is meant by being bound by form?
To perceive and behold that which is upright and handsome is called being bound by form.
Those bound by form are internally and completely fettered.

Yet regarding this form within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they do not know its root; there is no place of crossing in the great river of birth and death, and they do not know the essential means for escaping birth and death. Thus, they are subjected to various fetters within birth and death, from this present body-bondage unto future bodies.
At that time, the one who had been imprisoned heard this Dharma being taught; he contemplated its meaning, memorized it without forgetting, and recited it until he had mastered it.
Then the king sent men to release his bonds, and his close friends, acquaintances, and kinsmen, rejoicing at his liberation, all came to inquire after him.
At that time, the one who had been bound spoke these verses:
“You see my bonds released, And comfort me with joy;
yet those who are ordinary and deluded Are constantly bound and never liberated.”
Form binds the ordinary person; the five aggregates all enchain them.
Birth can bind beings, and death binds them as well.
From this life to future worlds, there has never been a time when they are not bound.
Amidst the fetters of saṃsāra, one undergoes birth and death again and again.
From that teacher, I heard these words spoken;
these words I have heard with my own ears, as taught by the One of All-Knowledge.
All the fetters and latent tendencies bind my mind,
as if bound by a yoke for oxen.
Since I am not yet liberated from them, how can you [be so]?
"I speak of being liberated from my bonds.
If you truly love and care for me, you should petition the King on my behalf so that I may be permitted to go forth into the homeless life."
The far shore of quiescent extinction— if one attains such a state,
only then can it be called liberation.
If one succeeds in leaving the household life, one is then freed from bondage and truly attains liberation.
At that time, having heard these words, his kinsmen petitioned the king, and he was permitted to leave the household life.
Once he had gone forth,
he practiced the Path with diligence and attained arhatship.
Even those sinners who were imprisoned in a monastic dwelling attained liberation for the sake of hearing the Dharma; how much more so for one who intentionally comes to hear it!
Therefore, a practitioner should go to a stupa or monastery to listen to the Dharma.

27 (27) Furthermore, when the suffering of illness becomes severe, one's instructions can no longer be carried out; therefore, while appearing healthy, one should perform whatever tasks are to be done with all possible speed.
I have heard that in the past, King Aśoka, having suffered from a grave illness, took all his wealth and gave it entirely as alms to the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, he requested various treasures from his ministers, but the ministers were unwilling to grant them again. Having obtained only half of an *āmra* fruit which he wished to offer to the Saṃgha, he assembled his ministers and counselors and addressed them, saying:
"Who is the king this very day?"
"Whose verbal teachings and conduct are followed?
The ministers replied, "Only those commanded by the majesty of Your Majesty; throughout Jambudvīpa, your verbal teachings are put into practice."
The King spoke in verse:
"Because you address me as 'King,' and because my commands are carried out,
and because you act in accordance with my will, you have spoken thus."
The words you have spoken are all false;
my teaching has already been destroyed, and none possess autonomy.
Only this half-fruit remains, within which one may attain mastery.
Wealth and nobility are vulgar and base; alas, they are to be censured.
Like a river at the mountain peak, its torrent flows swiftly without a moment's pause;
though I was once the sovereign of men, poverty has suddenly come upon me.
“Poverty is feared by the world; come quickly to my presence.
Having spoken this verse, he further praised the truth and non-falsity of what the World-Honored One had said, and spoke another verse:
“Though wealth and nobility may flourish intensely, they will inevitably meet with decline and extinction.”
The wealthy and noble rarely find joy; when they decline and perish, the world hates them.
These words are not false; they are what Gautama has taught.
Whatever teachings I may have given in days past, [they are all in accord with this].
He speaks with intentional mindfulness, and his words never fail;
spirits and deities receive and uphold his commands throughout the four seas.
All who hear them accept and put them into practice, and none ever oppose them.
Like a river striking a great mountain, its surging waters are turned back and flow in eddies;
decay is like that great mountain, blocking me so that I cannot proceed.
In the past, when I spoke my instructions, none dared to oppose them.
Never has there been such wickedness, nor have invaders ever dared to resist or oppose;
it covers the great earth, and none can go against it.
Whether man or woman, great or small, none dare not show reverence and obedience.
Should there be those who violate the teachings, I am able to subdue them all.
To all those who suffer hardships, I offer consolation and rescue;
for the suffering of illness and the misery of poverty, there is none whom I do not treat and heal.
My merit is now exhausted, and poverty has suddenly arrived;
my distress is indeed such as this.
I am King Aśoka; how is it that I encounter such suffering?
"Having cut the root so that it is severed, the flowers, leaves, branches, and stems—all shall wither and dry up; I am now just like this.
Wealth and nobility are illusory transformations that cannot endure for long."
Looking back at the physicians by his side, he spoke these words: "Alas!

This loathsome and base wealth and honor is but temporary, like a flash of lightning; it vanishes as swiftly as a flame, flickering and unstable like the flapping ears of an elephant, incessantly quivering like the tongue of a snake, and drying up at the sight of the sun like morning dew."
I once heard from another the following verse:
"Riches and status are difficult to restrain; Impulsiveness does not pause for even a moment.
The wise should understand this well; Do not succumb to arrogance or negligence."
In this life and in future worlds, one ought to seek one's own benefit.
Even if one attains wealth and status, though one guards it with stinginess through a hundred means, it will ultimately be destroyed;
for wealth and status follow only the course of action.
Like a snake’s crawl, life is not straight.
One who observes this well should, while still in the prime of health, swiftly cultivate merit.
Furthermore, even when beset by the suffering of illness, one should constantly cultivate merit in the mind.
It does not depend on the physical form.
If one knows that death is certain, then even though one possesses wealth and property,
one cannot freely bestow them as gifts.
When one has acquired wealth and encounters a field of merit, one should promptly bestow gifts.
Whether in a state of physical vigor or when suffering from illness, one should constantly practice giving; there is no difference between these two states.
Yet these various material goods possess nothing but faults and afflictions.
When the time of death approaches, though one’s kinsmen, wife,
and children may possess these very riches, if one wishes to bestow them as gifts, [they will not permit it].
"Rakṣa will not grant it; my life is perilously frail and hangs by a thread, and my wishes are no longer my own.

At that time, King Aśoka’s time for shaving his hair had passed; he wore soiled and greasy garments that were disheveled and untidy. Emaciated, trembling, and gasping with heavy breaths, he turned toward the place where the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa. With all his strength he joined his palms, recollected the virtues of the Buddha, and with tears streaming down his face, spoke these verses:
"Now, with palms joined toward the Buddha, this is my final moment;
the Buddha has taught the three things that are not firm, so as to trade them for the firm Dharma.
I now join my fingers and palms to exchange [them] for the enduring Dharma."
Just as one seeks pure gold from a mountain of molten rock,
Amidst transient wealth and possessions, I have day and night extracted the enduring Dharma;
Whatever remaining merit I now possess, I offer it all to the Most Supreme One.
Now, by this meritorious karma of mine, I do not seek the station of Śakra, nor the retribution of Brahmā,
much less the kingship of Jambudvīpa. By the fruit of this giving,
and through my respectful faith and devotion, [may I attain enlightenment].
"May I attain mastery over the mind, such that none may cut or divide it;
may I attain the noble, pure, and stainless state, forever free from all suffering and affliction.
King Aśoka, having offered half of an *āmra* fruit to the community of monks, called one of his attendants and said to him:
"Do you perhaps remember that I once kept you? Accept my final instruction now:

take this half-fruit and offer it to the community of monks at the Kukkutārāma Monastery. Recite my name and say: 'King Aśoka, who once held sovereignty over Jambudvīpa, has seen his karmic rewards decay and lost his power of mastery;

he now possesses mastery only over this half-fruit. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, accept this final offering of half a fruit from me, so that I may obtain vast retribution in future lives. I pray that others may not, like me, lose their mastery at the time of their end.'"

At that time, the attendant immediately obeyed the king’s command; carrying this half-fruit, he went to the monastery, assembled all the monks, prostrated at their feet, and with palms joined, addressed the community of monks, saying:
“King Aśoka pays homage at the feet of the assembly of monks.”
Having spoken these words, his eyes filled with tears and he was choked with sobs; holding up this half-fruit to show the assembly of monks, he immediately spoke this verse:
"One canopy covers heaven and earth, And its teachings are practiced throughout the land.
It is like the time of midday, When it thoroughly scorches the great earth."
When meritorious karma has been exhausted, collapse suddenly arrives;
deceived and toyed with by one's own actions, one is ruined and loses honor and nobility,
like the sun approaching its setting.
"Furthermore, with this half-fruit, I offer it to the assembly of monks to manifest the mark of impermanence and to show that even the noble and powerful are subject to change and transience.
At that time, having heard these verses, the elders were moved with sorrow and distress; they felt compassion and accepted the half-fruit to show it to the great assembly, saying:
"We should now give rise to a mind of weary detachment.
For the Buddha, the Bhagavān, has spoken thus in the sūtras:
'Upon seeing the decline and suffering of others, one should give rise to a deep sense of weary detachment in one's heart.'"
"When those with hearts behold such a matter as this, who would not feel compassion and give rise to a sense of weary revulsion?
He then spoke in verse:
"The one who is courageous and capable of giving is the most excellent among all kings."
The great elephant of Mūli, named Aśoka,
once possessed all of Jambudvīpa and was entirely free;
yet now, for the sake of his ministers, he is restrained and no longer acts according to his own will.
All things were strictly forbidden, except for half an *āmala* fruit;
over this alone he attained mastery, which he used to bestow upon the Saṃgha.
His wealth was exceedingly vast, and he attained mastery over all things.
Born from a mind of self-exaltation, where is it now?
The foolish and ignorant should observe this and swiftly transform their minds;
all wealth and profit have utterly perished, leaving only this half-fruit.
"Let all the bhikṣu-saṃgha give rise to a mind of weary detachment.
Then the Elder of the Saṃgha said,
"Grind this half-fruit and put it into the saṃgha’s soup."
He then spoke these words:
"Great donor, King Aśoka, this is your final offering; why do you say that all wealth and possessions are entirely impermanent?"
For this reason, the Buddha, the Blessed One, said:
"One should exchange non-durable wealth for durable wealth, exchange a non-durable body for a durable body, and exchange a non-durable life for a durable life."
"O donor! You should give rise to joy; for with impermanent wealth that follows one into future lives, you ought to constantly practice giving so that it never ceases."

28. Furthermore, if foolish people should disparage or revile such a noble person, that noble person will never give rise to anger; even when subjected to the abuse and insults of others, they respond with words of compliance.

I have heard that in the past, there was a man who hosted a gathering in his home and prepared many flower garlands to give to the assembly; when the people received the garlands, they all placed them upon their heads.

There was a certain wise man who was extremely poor and destitute; having gone to a gathering of guests, he received a flower garland in his turn, but instead of placing it upon his head, he set it aside.
Everyone said, "This man is so impoverished that he wishes to sell this garland; that is why he does not wear it."
When the upāsaka heard these words, he replied,
“It is indeed so.
If I sell it, I shall give it to you only after obtaining a very high price.”
He then spoke in verse:
"Just as in the past, Sumana, Who once sold a single flower,
For ninety-one kalpas, He enjoyed happiness in the heavens."
Today, in this final body, I have attained the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Like a cowherd’s daughter who sells foul-smelling weeds and flowers—
things that no one else delights in— that woman sold these flowers.
I attained birth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Now I wish to go to the Buddha, and I also wish to sell these flowers;
that one can give rise to such a mind is rare and extremely difficult to encounter.
"Such a flower-seller as this is peerless within the three realms.
At that time, the people asked the upāsaka,
"Who can obtain great karmic rewards by giving even a small gift?"
Then the lay follower said to the assembly:
"I shall now explain for you the Dharma of firm goodness.
Just as one discards a flower garland once it has withered and dried, the Buddha abandoned his royal throne as if casting away a withered flower."
Then he spoke in verse:
"The Buddha has renounced the station of a wheel-turning monarch, As if casting away a withered garland of flowers;
The seven factors of enlightenment adorn his mind, Pure and free from all defilement."
The adornments are all already complete; what use is there for these flowers?
Yet with a single-minded heart, I offer this garland to the Buddha’s stupa.
Now I sell them to the Buddha, who is peerless in the world.
Such a merchant of the Dharma will never know poverty.
This sale is the most excellent; its fame brings merit.
Now, holding these flowers, I wish to make an offering to the Stūpa.
29 (29) Furthermore, it is like a magician who uses this aggregate-body to perform various feats, enabling those of wisdom to see them and thereby attain understanding.
I have heard that in the past there was a magician who, with a heart of faith and devotion, went to Mount Zhòu'àn (Dayan) to provide a meal for the Saṃgha.

Having completed the offering, he fashioned a woman from śītavana wood—exceedingly beautiful and extraordinary—and before the great assembly, he embraced this woman and kissed her, engaging in sexual acts with her.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they were all filled with resentment and indignation, saying:
"The conduct of this shameless man is vulgar and indecent.
Knowing him to be thus, they did not accept his offerings.

At that time, after the illusionist had finished his act of lust, he heard the bhikṣus criticizing, reviling, and reproaching him; he immediately took a knife and stabbed the woman, dismembering her limbs, gouging out her eyes, cutting off her nose, and killed her with various forms of bitter torment.
When the bhikṣus saw this matter, their resentment and indignation redoubled:
"If we had known you were such as this, we would rather drink poison than accept your offerings."
Then that illusionist spoke these words:
"When you monks see me engaging in sensual desire, you become angry; when you see me severing my desire by killing this woman, you again find it reprehensible.
How then am I to serve the Sangha?"
When the bhikṣus saw this, they were greatly agitated and disturbed, speaking of it in confusion.
At that time, the illusionist immediately took up a śītavana-wood staff and showed it to the assembly of monks, joining his palms and saying:
"That which I created earlier was precisely this wood; what desire to kill could there have been within that wood?"

"I have prepared these foods and drinks in order to bring peace to the bodies of the Sangha, and I have created this illusion in order to bring peace to the minds of the Sangha; may the bhikṣus listen to what I say."
How could you not have heard it?
In the sūtras, the Buddha taught that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations; it is for the purpose of fulfilling those words that I now manifest this illusion.
Such an illusory body has neither lifespan nor life-force;

it is the illusionist of consciousness that operates the mechanical contrivance, causing it to blink its eyes, look up and down, cast glances around, walk, stop, speak, or laugh. For this reason, one deeply understands that this body is truly without a self.
He then spoke in verse:
"First one observes their appearance, and through mental construction, inverted delusions arise;
one perversely gives rise to thoughts of passion for a woman, and enters the snare of the net of desire."
One who observes with deep reality knows that the body is entirely without self;
it is like a skilled illusionist who uses wood to create a woman.
When the mind operates in perversion, the deluded call it a "sentient being."
Within this illusion and deception, one falsely conceives the notions of male and female.
The wise observe well that the aggregates, elements,
and sense bases are dependently and conventionally formed as sentient beings, each part being distinct and separate.
Because they are composed of the aggregation of parts, they are able to perform various karmas;
yet all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are devoid of male or female, and likewise lack a life-span.
They consist of form, desire, and tactile sensations, as well as deportment and location.
These four kinds of desire Turn the minds of the infantile and ignorant.
The Omniscient One has also declared That they are illusory deceptions that delude the world;
Just as within a net of illusions, Various forms and images are conjured.
The net of birth and death is likewise; it manifests the distinctions of the five realms, along with sorrow and joy, hatred and anger, grief and affliction, as well as strife and contention.
Just as those various disturbances are like a ghost pervading the entire body, so too does this net ensnare all beings.
The mind gives rise to all actions, no different from those ghosts.
From the mind arises wind; because of the wind, actions are performed.
Sentient beings see these performed actions as various forms and appearances.
Within these karmic activities, one gives rise to deportment and physical form;
failing to understand the nature of such gestures, one falsely conceives the notion of a "self.
This body is merely a mechanical device, composed of fat, marrow, skin, flesh, and hair.
The thirty-six constituents and so forth, combined together, form the body.
The fool conceives of a "sentient being," yet in reality there is no sovereign master;
it is merely by the power of the winds that one looks up and down, bends and stretches.
Because it relies upon the mind, the five consciousnesses are able to arise;
yet this mental consciousness perishes and shifts with every thought-moment.
Fools give rise to deluded perceptions, reckoning that there is a self within this body.
The various kinds of vocal karma, and likewise bodily karma—
whether speech, laughter, or deportment— are all like the products of illusion;
herein there is no self, for it is devoid of a governing master.
Yet these deceptive phenomena lack life and lack cognition;
they arise from false conceptualization and cause all ordinary beings to sink into ruin.

Just as the magician’s words were true and not otherwise, when the bhikṣus heard this teaching, they all attained the vision of the Truths (dṛṣṭasatya). Therefore, one should know that all phenomena are like illusions; those who can understand this are able to sever the source of all conditioned formations (saṃskāra).
30. Furthermore, the matters of giving and morality are shallow and mundane; those whose roots of goodness have matured are able to delight in the profound Dharma.

I have heard that in the past, King Aśoka first attained faith and frequently invited the Saṃgha into his palace to provide offerings and listen to the Dharma daily. He set up curtains to screen off the women so that they might listen to the Dharma.
At that time, because the women were deeply attached to worldly pleasures, the bhikṣu who was preaching the Dharma spoke only of the merits of giving and morality.

There was a courtesan whose roots of virtue had long since matured; disregarding the king’s law and accepting her share of the punishment, she immediately pushed aside the curtain, approached the bhikṣu, and said to him:
"Is what the Buddha has taught limited only to giving and morality?"
"Is there anything further?
The bhikṣu replied, "Sisters!"
It was not with the intention that there might be such a person of sharp faculties that I made this statement.
If you wish to listen, I shall further explain for you the various profound dharmas.
He said to the woman,
"The Buddha has preached the Dharma never before heard by any in the world, namely the Four Noble Truths.
He then explained them in detail for the woman, and upon hearing them, she attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
At that time, the woman spoke these words:
"Though I have contravened the king's law, I have attained great benefit.
She then spoke this verse:
"Having heard the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, my Dharma-eye has become pure and stainless;
with this fragile and precarious life, I have traded for the firm life of the Buddha-Dharma.
Even if it were a human king who has now come to harm me,"
"Since I have attained the life of wisdom, I shall never again harbor a heart of regret or resentment.
At that time, the palace attendants saw this courtesan violate the royal law; their hearts were filled with trepidation and fear that they might share her guilt.

At that time, having witnessed these events, the courtesan took a knife in her own hand and went before the king; prostrating herself with her five limbs touching the ground, she confessed her crime and begged for death.
She further spoke in verse:
"The king’s laws are most severe and stern, and none dare to transgress them."
For the sake of hearing the Dharma, I have risked offense and accepted death.
Now, parched with thirst for the Dharma, I have boldly approached the assembly of monks;
like a cow in the spring heat, parched with thirst, seeking water and heedless of the staff.
He plunged into the clear stream, drank his fill, and then returned home.
Great King, you should know that the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter;
it is like the udumbara flower, which is rarely met.
The Great True Savior of the three realms has proclaimed all these wondrous Dharmas;
having heard this teaching, how could I not rejoice?
That which he has spoken is truly a lamp and a torch.
The sound of the great drum that extinguishes the fetters, The bridge and ferry for gods and humans;
Again, the sound of the bell of liberation, A joyful and delightful melody.
In days of yore, the Bodhisattva Practiced austerities and diligently sought the Dharma.
By casting oneself from cliffs and cutting off one's own flesh, one seeks the unsurpassed Way.
Having attained it, to be able to explain it to others is something extremely difficult to encounter;
since I have encountered this Dharma, how could I not listen to and accept it?
This body is like a mass of foam, a plantain tree, or a bubble on a flame;
it is entangled by the serpents of the four great elements.
Since it is so difficult to encounter and hear [the Dharma], why begrudge this base and impure body?
Why then would one not listen to the Dharma?
Even when advancing or halting, observing all postures—
whether coming or going, sitting or reclining, looking, gesturing, or speaking— [one should remain mindful].
In truth they are not sentient beings, yet one forms the perception of them as such;
all their various modes of conduct are entirely like illusions,
soon to be dispersed and destroyed, abandoned amidst the burial mounds.
"The corpse is like wood or stone, devoured by crows and birds;
soaked by rain until it rots, it is like a clay figure being destroyed.
When the king heard this verse, he spoke to him, saying:
“You have listened to such a Dharma with a focused mind; what have you realized now?
The courtesan then spoke in verse:
“This is no time for concealment; I ought to speak the truth.”
Having already realized the stage of *srotāpanna*,
you should give rise to a heart of joy and listen well with a sincere mind.
Never following the faith of others, let there be no net of doubt in your heart.
The three evil destinies have been closed; I have reached the limit of birth and death.
I have left the prison of existence;
my firm bonds are now released. Before long, I shall be far removed from them.
I am heading toward the city of ambrosia.
I perceive the aggregates, elements, and sense bases exactly in this way:
I view the body as a basket containing snakes, and the aggregates as thieves with drawn swords.
Desire is like a deceitful enemy feigning friendship; The sense-faculties are like an empty village;
The six objects are thieves who plunder the settlement; And one sinks into the river of craving.
Having awakened to these matters, One seeks that state of peace and security.
Having heard this, the king conceived a redoubled sense of reverence for the Buddha’s Dharma and spoke these words:
“O, the Buddha’s Dharma!
The Greatly Powerful World-Honored One has grown weary of the path of birth and death. O, the Buddha’s Dharma!”
Those who possess faith and aspiration shall all attain liberation.
How do we know this?

Even those of shallow wisdom, such as women, are able to achieve awakening, surpassing the six teachers. Therefore, I now direct my mind toward the abode of the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men and give rise to a heart of refuge: *Namo* to the Greatly Compassionate One who saves all sentient beings! He opens the Dharma of Ambrosia, which men and women, old and young alike, may practice together.
He then spoke in verse:
"If one were to say that women's understanding is called shallow and superficial,
then those other people of profound wisdom must be revered and esteemed before they can truly awaken."
Such profound meaning, revered by the wise,
was spoken by the Honored Muni, the most supreme and perfect guide.
This wondrous Dharma that he taught brings extreme joy to those who hear it.
With single-minded recollection and a concentrated mind, one is able to remain heedful.
What is spoken is not for the sake of debate, nor for the purpose of refutation;
the various discourses and treatises of the non-Buddhists shall all be destroyed by themselves.
Never having praised oneself, yet one's fame pervades the world;
though one speaks of actual merits, this is not called self-praise.
Though one’s majestic power is blazing, one remains profoundly tranquil and possesses quiescence.
Having attained all-encompassing wisdom, he does not rely on it to become arrogant.
Though his deeds are courageous and vigorous, he remains well-disciplined and compliant.
He is liberated from all forms of self-importance, yet he does not become base or inferior.
The teaching has long been widely disseminated, and none are able to criticize or revile it.
What is spoken by the Harmless One contains manifold distinctions;
yet among all people, none are able to speak of its faults.
Though his verbal teachings are abundant and vast, there is no one who grows weary of them;
though what he speaks accords with worldly convention, its principle transcends the world.
These are the words of the Sugata, whose characters are disseminated throughout the world.
Yet it is ever unprecedented; its transformative deliverance is constantly fresh and wondrous.
To such sublime discourse, who would not join their palms in reverence?
Who would not praise the World-Honored One, the Great Lion of Skillful Discourse?
Just as during the spring and summer seasons, both cloudy and sunny days benefit all things;
so too is the Buddha’s word: it brings manifold benefits to sentient beings, can dispel the doubts of the multitude, and provides effective remedies through its skillful exposition.
It can cause one to leave the three realms of existence and reveal the place of peace and security;
it can also cause sentient beings to feel joy or to be struck with awe and fear.
It can cause them to feel contentment, and it can also move them to deep compassion.
He is also able to bring benefit and joy, teaching the Dharma that extinguishes the fetters.
This is a true miraculous power: he speaks what ought to be said, never sparing his own feelings;
though what he says may be harsh and coarse, it is for the sake of truth.
Yet it does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena;
like the waters of the great ocean, from the beginning, through the middle, to the very limit,
they are all equal in their single flavor.
The Buddha-dharma is likewise: good in the beginning, middle, and end; hearing it brings total purity.
One of clear wisdom hears these words with a courageous and satisfied mind;
having heard this teaching, they take no pleasure in external treatises.
His speech is fully perfected, his eloquence most exquisite;
he is neither conceited nor arrogant, and what he says is never timid.
He is the most supreme among all, manifesting the complete fulfillment of meaning.
In truth, he is omniscient; the non-Buddhists possess but little of the essence of meaning.
Though their speech is adorned with wisdom and their words are exceedingly beautiful, they lack true flavor, being but deceitful, false, and sycophantic talk.
In this world of great ignorance and darkness, you hold aloft the torch of Dharma;
entering the realm of ultimate truth is like returning to one’s own home.
O disciples of the Sugata, may I receive your protection.
The great disciples have well subdued their faculties;
regarding those disciples whom they have described,
I now declare with deep faith before this great assembly, proclaiming these words.
From this day forward, I permit all the sons of the Śākyas to enter my palace at any time;
from this day forth, they shall be received with trust.
I grant the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, full liberty to enter the palace.
One can satisfy the female mind with the nectar-like Dharma;
once the female mind is thus stilled, it proceeds toward the state of liberation.
Therefore, one should always listen to the profound meaning of the Four Noble Truths.
The Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra (Treatise on the Great Ornament), Scroll Five;
The Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra (Treatise on the Great Ornament), Scroll Six.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
31. Furthermore, one who possesses actual merit is worthy of receiving offerings, whereas one who lacks actual merit is unworthy of receiving the offerings of others' faith.

I have heard that in the past, among the Kuru clan there was a king named Candanakaṇṭha. Having subdued Eastern India and established his authority, his majesty resounded far and wide and his merit was complete; he then returned toward his own kingdom.
