On the way, at a level and broad spot, he halted to stay the night.

At that time, the king’s heart was filled with devotion, and he took only the Buddha-dharma as his ornament. While at his resting place, he saw a stūpa in the distance and, taking it to be a Buddhist stūpa, led a thousand attendants toward its location. Not far from the stūpa, he dismounted and proceeded on foot; having adorned his head with a precious celestial crown, he arrived at the site of the stūpa, took refuge, prostrated himself, and spoke these verses:
“Free from desire and all fetters and hindrances, Possessing all-encompassing wisdom, Among all sages and saints, He is supreme and without equal.”
Able to act as an uninvited friend to all sentient beings, His fame is heard everywhere in the world;
He is revered throughout the three realms.
Having renounced the three spheres of existence, He has expounded the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.
"Supreme among all treatises, Destroyer of all heterodox doctrines— I now take refuge and pay homage To the true Arhat.

At that time, because the king was mindful of the Tathāgata’s merits, he bowed his head in reverent salutation. As he was performing this prostration, the stūpa immediately crumbled and collapsed, as if scattered by a violent windstorm.
At that time, when the king saw this occurrence, he was greatly alarmed and filled with doubt, saying:
"Now, since no one has touched or approached this stūpa, how is it that it has suddenly collapsed and fallen into ruin without cause?"
"Such a transformation must surely have its causes and conditions.
He then spoke in verse:
"The Lord Śakra, of long life among the gods— one so highly revered—"
With palms joined, he paid homage to the Buddha-stūpa; there was no difference whatsoever in his demeanor.
Toward the One of Ten Powers and Great Majesty, the Honored and Exalted Being, even when Mahābrahmā came to pay his respects, the Buddha likewise showed no change in his countenance.
"My body is lighter than that; it should not be destroyed by me.
This must be the power of a mantra, produced by one who seeks to obstruct the Path.
Having spoken this verse, the king’s heart remained terrified even as the stūpa was being shattered, and he said these words:
"I pray that this transformation may not become a calamity, but rather a source of auspiciousness, so that all sentient beings may attain peace and security.

Since ancient times, I have prostrated myself with my five limbs touching the ground before hundreds of thousands of stupas, never allowing even a single grain of dust to fall or be lost; why is it that today it has transformed in such a manner?"
"I have never before seen such a sign.
He then spoke in verse:
"Are the devas and asuras Engaging in a great battle?"
Is this kingdom about to perish, that my life shall not reach its end?
Is it not that some enemy intends to destroy my country?
Is it not due to the scarcity of grain or the threat of war, or perhaps the onset of pestilence?
"Is it not the case that all the world is beset by calamities?
This is an extremely evil omen; will not the Dharma and desire soon perish?
At that time, the villagers near the stupa, seeing the king’s perplexity and wonder, immediately addressed him with these words:
"Great King!
You should know that this is not a Buddhist stūpa.
He then spoke a verse:
“The Nirgranthas are utterly foolish, their minds scorched by false views;
this is that very stūpa of theirs.
This stūpa possesses little power of merit, and furthermore, it contains no śarīra.”
"Unable to endure the King's veneration, it has therefore been shattered and destroyed.
King Kaniṣka conceived even greater faith and reverence for the Buddha’s Dharma; his body hair stood on end, and with tears falling like rain from both sorrow and joy, he spoke this verse:
"This matter truly ought to be so; I have paid homage to it with the thought that it is the Buddha."
This stūpa will surely crumble; the heavy burden borne by a dragon-elephant cannot be sustained by a donkey.
One ought to erect a temple for the Honored One, the Bull-King Śākyamuni.
One should indeed build a stūpa for him;
one should not accept such offerings. These impure Nirgranthas do not deserve my prostration.
When this stūpa collapsed, it emitted a great sound, like that of the Bahuputra Stūpa.
The Buddha went to where Kāśyapa was, and Kāśyapa prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
"He is my Blessed One; he is my Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If anyone who is not an Arhat were to receive your prostration, their head would shatter into seven pieces."
"By means of this stūpa, I shall now verify that the Buddha’s words are true.
Thus, although wood and stone possess no consciousness, they serve as clear evidence for the Nirgranthas, proving that [the Buddha] is not omniscient.
Having seen this, the king leaped for joy before the great assembly; his faith redoubled and his countenance became serene and pleasant as he spoke these words: "Namo Bhagavate!"
The Honored One of All, the Teacher of Liberation, Śākyamuni Buddha, uttered this lion’s roar:
"Outside of this Dharma, there are no other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
The Buddha’s words are true and without error.

Among all sentient beings—whether they have one foot, two feet, no feet, or many feet; whether they possess form or are formless; whether they possess perception, lack perception, or are neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata alone is the most honored and supreme within this assembly.
To state the essentials: all that the Buddha has taught is manifest today; all non-Buddhist paths are not worth a blade of grass, let alone the teachers Nirgrantha and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
He then spoke in verse:
"I am the king among men; even he is unworthy of receiving my prostration, let alone the Wheel-Turning Kings or the Asura Kings!"
This stūpa today, as if by the power of the tusks and feet of a great elephant king, has been shattered and destroyed.
Because his body was bound by the four types of fetters, he was named Nigaṇṭha.
Just as one who can remove the heat during a great scorching time is called a *nidāgha*, so too the Tathāgata,
the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who can sever all fetters, is truly a *nidāgha*.
For this reason, at this very time, the various disciples of the Nirgranthas,
as well as all other devas and humans, should all make offerings to the Buddha.
The wisdom of the Buddha’s lineage and his fame are exceedingly vast.
When devas, humans, and asuras pay homage to such a stūpa, it shows no sign of being shaken;
it is like using the wings of a mosquito to fan Mount Sumeru.
"Though they exhaust all their power, they cannot cause it to waver.
Therefore, if anyone wishes to obtain merit, they should duly prostrate before the stupas and temples of the Buddha.

32. Furthermore, if a person pursues learning, even though they may violate their conduct, they will soon attain the Path through the power of that learning; for this reason, one should diligently pursue learning.
I have heard that in the past there was a learned bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya. At that time, a widow frequented this bhikṣu’s place repeatedly to listen to his preaching of the Dharma.

At that time, a learned bhikṣu conceived a defiled attachment toward this widow; because of that attachment, all his wholesome dharmas gradually weakened, and being driven by the fetters of an ordinary person's mind, he entered into a verbal agreement with this woman.
The woman said,
"If you can now cease your religious practice and return to secular life, I shall follow you.
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately ceased his religious practice.

Having already renounced the path, he could not endure the sufferings of the world; his body was emaciated and he did not understand worldly occupations. Not knowing how to achieve great wealth from little effort, he reflected to himself:
"By what means can I now sustain my life?"
He further thought to himself:
"Only a hired hand slaughters sheep; the labor required is extremely light, yet the profit gained is great.
Having had this thought, he sought out such a place; because the mind of an ordinary person is easily corrupted, he committed this deed and subsequently became close friends with the butcher.

While he was selling meat, a certain acquaintance—a mendicant monk—chanced upon him on the road. Upon seeing him, the monk recognized him; his hair was disheveled, he wore blue garments, and there was blood upon his body, making him look like a *yama-rākṣasa*. The scales he held for weighing the meat were entirely stained with blood.
Seeing him weighing meat to sell to others, the bhikṣu, having seen this, sighed deeply and reflected:
"The Buddha’s words are true!
The minds of ordinary people are fickle and unstable, extremely easy to turn back."
"Previously I saw this man diligently applying himself to study and upholding the prohibitive precepts; for what reason has he suddenly committed such an act today?
Having had this thought, he immediately spoke in verse:
"If you do not tame the horse, You will be heedless and commit manifold evils."
How is it that one is devoid of shame and remorse, having abandoned the Dharma of self-restraint?
Yet their deportment and every movement are such that they are pleasing for others to behold;
even birds and wild beasts, upon seeing them, feel no alarm or fear.
"Even when walking, he fears harming an ant;
with compassion and pity for all sentient beings—where has such a heart of sorrowful mercy gone now?
Ordinary people have minds that are not settled; they may merely be counted among the ranks of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and for this reason, the Tathāgata does not speak of their outward marks.
If one attains the vision of the reality of the Truths, such a person is called a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"Arrogantly proclaiming themselves, they claim to be true śramaṇas."
"Because of this undisciplined mind, he has suddenly committed such a great evil.
Having spoken these verses, he immediately reflected:
"By what means may I now cause him to attain awakening?"
As the Buddha said:

"When instructing others, one should first cause them to give rise to pure faith in the four objects of unbreakable confidence; these four objects of unbreakable confidence enable sentient beings to perceive the Four Noble Truths."
"I shall now explain for you the root of the performance of karma.
Having formed this thought, he spoke to him, saying:
"At this moment, you have weighed the matter most excellently."
At that time, the meat-seller thought to himself:
"Since this bhikṣu is not buying meat, why does he tell me to weigh it so carefully?
Having had this thought, he immediately spoke a verse:
"This one must surely possess compassion, coming here to rescue and deliver me!
Such a bhikṣu has long been free from the ways of worldly trade;
seeing that I am engaged in evil deeds, he has come wishing to save me."
"These are truly worthy sages who have brought me benefit!

Having spoken this verse, he immediately recalled the various practices he had performed when he was formerly a bhikṣu, and remembered the sūtra he had previously recited, titled "The Aggregate of Suffering, the Transcendence of Desire, and the Taste of Desire."
Having reflected thus, he immediately weighed the flesh and cast it far to the ground; feeling deep revulsion for the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), he said to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir! Venerable sir!"
And he spoke in verse:
"The flavor of desire and the faults of desire— which of these is the greater?
I shall weigh them with the yoke of shame and modesty, holding fast to the scale of wisdom."
Reflecting upon these matters, my mind has attained full penetration;
I see no benefit therein, but perceive only the decline and suffering of desire.
For this reason, I should now abandon desire.
I went to the monastic quarters and once again sought to leave the household life.
Now that I have become so wretchedly lowly through bodily suffering,
though this is still my present body, it is as if I have already fallen into the evil realms.
When I formerly left the household life, I filtered my water before drinking;
out of compassion and pity, I protected the lives of others and harbored no intent to harm.
Today, like a malevolent spirit, I consume the vital essence and blood of men.
I now delight in killing and harming; though I practice it, I cannot abandon it.
Excellent are the words spoken by the Buddha: those who indulge in sensual desires will do no evil that they will not commit.
I have now been driven by my own desires to such a state of decline and suffering.
Since I have not yet realized the Four Noble Truths, from this day forward,
I shall never again be negligent.
Having been heedless in the past, one later ceases and does not act so again;
like the moon freed from clouds, it shines brightly upon the world.
Therefore, I shall now single-mindedly uphold the prohibitive precepts.
Even if fire burns upon my head and my clothes are consumed by flame,
I shall remain firm in my diligence and practice the Dharma of discipline and harmony;
I will sever the difficult-to-subdue fetters and afflictions, and surely attain nirvana.
Even if my sinews and veins were torn asunder, and my physical form were completely withered and dried up,
I would never rest until I had seen the Four Truths;
first I shall extinguish the enemies that are the fetters and defilements, and then I shall obtain the supreme reward for the grace bestowed upon me.
At that time, the bhikṣu, knowing his thoughts and seeing that the fire of wisdom was just about to ignite, spoke this verse:
"If you now go forth from home, You shall surely attain liberation.
Kāli, Saṃgharakṣita, And Citta as well—"
Bhikṣus such as these all returned to secular life seven times,
yet later they again went forth and attained arhatship.
You likewise have not violated the precepts of the World-Honored One of Ten Powers.
You have not given rise to wrong views; you possess the wisdom of much learning.
Having developed the excellence of disenchantment, you cultivate the bliss of tranquility.
You possess the lamp of much learning, which has been extinguished by the wind of the fetters.
Return to the cultivation of extensive learning, and you will surely reach the realm of fearlessness.
Driven by the bonds of defilement, you should rely on the cultivation of meditative concentration;
through the cultivation of concentration, you shall attain superior power and clearly perceive the fetters and latent tendencies.
Because you have constantly practiced and accumulated [virtue], you delight in the Dharma of going forth;
with a mind close to wholesome merit, though it may be damaged by the fetters (*saṃyojana*),
you cultivate and accumulate the Noble Path— this mind grasps the fetters.
"Like an elephant that has snapped its tethering ropes, he goes wherever he pleases at his own will.
At that time, the monk who had left the monastic order immediately abandoned his evil deeds; he returned to the homeless life, practiced with diligence, and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
33. Furthermore, if one wishes to adorn oneself with faultless wholesome karma, one should therefore diligently cultivate all forms of goodness.
I have heard that in the past, there was a farmer who was intelligent and wise; he came into the city together with his companions.

At that time, he saw a man whose appearance was upright and dignified, dressed in magnificent garments and adorned with various necklaces and ornaments; his carriage was likewise splendidly decorated, and he was accompanied by many attendants, all of whom were exquisitely adorned and most impressive to behold.
That wise one said to his traveling companions:
"It is not good; it is not good.
His companions said:
"Such a person possesses majestic virtue and upright appearance; he is deeply worthy of love and respect—what is not good about him?

The wise man replied, "It is not that I find him unattractive, nor do I consider him unworthy of respect. Rather, it is because I failed to cultivate merit in my previous lives that I have now received this lowly body, lacking in majesty and power, and thus am not respected by others."

"If I had previously cultivated merit, how could I have failed to reach the level of such a person? Therefore, I must now diligently cultivate goodness, ensuring that in the future I shall surely surpass him."
He then spoke these verses:
"He has abandoned negligence, Cultivating goodness to obtain benefit and merit;
But because of my negligence, I have not cultivated meritorious deeds."
Therefore, now poor and lowly, lacking dignity and power,
I now reproach myself and thus declare that I am not good.
As I observe myself now, my wretchedness and poverty are most pitiable.
Deceived by the fetters and afflictions, and ruined by negligence,
from this day forward I shall diligently cultivate generosity, morality, and concentration,
so that in future births I may surely obtain a noble lineage and excellent kinsmen.
Handsome and possessed of majestic virtue, with abundant wealth and many attendants,
his every affair beyond reproach, he was revered by the world;
yet now, with this body of today, he regrets it in vain, for nothing can be done.
An evil mind is my enemy; it deceives me into poverty and lowliness.
If one can reproach oneself and repent, by cultivating goodness one attains happiness.
When one commits an evil deed, no wholesome qualities arise at all.
Those who restrain their minds and cultivate goodness possess every form of honor and joy.
The words of the world are not false; there is a distinct differentiation between the retributions of good and evil.
The Buddha has taught the Eightfold Noble Path, by which one can reach Nirvana.
If the mind is attached to wealth and profit,
to nobility, riches, and glory, and seeks further existence, one cannot escape the affliction of aging and decay. Therefore,
I shall apply myself with diligent and focused effort, proceeding toward the direction of fearlessness.
Just as a drunken painter, having painted various forms,
recognizes their flaws upon waking and erases them to create something superior; so too,
due to the folly of past lives, one fashions this present evil body.
"Now I shall extinguish evil karma, And seek superior retribution in the future.
Having seen the retribution of evil, The wise person deeply reproaches themselves.

(34) Furthermore, if one hears well-spoken teachings, one should reflect upon them, for they will surely yield benefit. Therefore, the wise person should always listen to and receive the sublime Dharma.
I have heard that in the past, while the Buddha and Ānanda were traveling through a wilderness in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, they saw a hidden treasure at the edge of a field.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"This is a great venomous snake."
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“It is a venomous snake.
At that time, there was a plowman in the field who, hearing the Buddha and Ānanda speak of the venomous snake, thought to himself:
"I shall go and see for myself what it is that this śramaṇa considers to be a venomous serpent.
He went to that place and saw a heap of pure gold, whereupon he said:
"That which the śramaṇa calls a venomous serpent is actually fine gold."
He immediately took this gold and returned it to his home.

Previously, that man had been poor and lacked sufficient food and clothing; because he obtained the gold, he became increasingly wealthy and prosperous, enjoying food and clothing to his heart's content.

The royal officials investigated his sudden wealth and arrested him, casting him into prison; though the gold he had previously acquired was already exhausted, he could not yet escape, and was about to be executed.
That person cried out:
"A poisonous snake! Ānanda!"
"A venomous serpent, World-Honored One!
Hearing this, the bystanders reported the matter to the king. The king summoned that man and questioned him, saying:
"Why do you cry out,
'A poisonous snake!'? Ānanda!"
"A venomous snake,
World-Honored One!
the man said to the king.
"In days past, while I was plowing my fields, I heard the Buddha and Ānanda speak of poisonous snakes as being evil and venomous.
It is only now that I have truly understood and realized they are indeed poisonous snakes."
He then spoke in verse:
“The words of all Buddhas are non-dual; They have spoken of it as a great venomous snake.
Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One: ‘In truth, it is indeed a wicked venomous snake.’”
The power of the venomous snake, I have now for the first time realized;
toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, my heart of faith and reverence has doubled.
Now that I am facing this peril, I therefore invoke the words of the Buddha.
When bitten by a venomous snake, the affliction falls upon the body alone;
neither relatives nor wife and children,
nor slaves and servants, shall share in that suffering.
Wealth and treasures are like venomous snakes; they bring destruction to oneself and all one’s kinsmen.
Now, regarding wealth and treasures, as well as my relatives and kin, I view them as if they were fierce, poisonous serpents when their wrath is provoked.
The wise should quickly depart, as if abandoning a venomous snake;
they should swiftly seek to leave the household life and go to dwell in the mountain forests.
Who that possesses wisdom, having seen or heard of such matters, would remain?
"And yet you would still cling to wealth and treasures, sealing your mind in delusion?
I thought I had gained great benefit, but instead I have obtained only decline and distress.
Having heard this verse, the king realized that this man had developed a heart of faith and understanding toward the Buddha’s words, and he immediately spoke in verse:
"Since you are now able to believe and revere the Great Seer of Compassion,
whose spoken words are true and never twice-told,
the treasures previously hidden shall all be returned to you."
Furthermore, with wealth and treasures, I shall make offerings to you.
Because you, the Tamer, are worthy of reverence and faith, and because the Sugata speaks the truth,
you are trusted by Great Brahmā and by the asura Bali.
The Heavenly Kings and Śakra, ourselves and all the kings,
the noble clans within the city, the brahmins and kṣatriyas—
those of exalted wisdom and vision— all have no lack of faith and reverence.
"Because you are able to share my faith, you have already obtained the 'flower-retribution' in this life;
now that you believe in the place of supreme faith, you shall surely attain the first fruit.

(35) Furthermore, those who seek profit may or may not obtain it. One who possesses a truly virtuous mind obtains the reality of benefit without seeking it, whereas one who lacks a truly virtuous mind acts out of greed for profit. Therefore, one should cultivate a truly virtuous mind.

I have heard that in the past there was a king. At that time, the son of a chief minister had lost his father early; the son was still young and unable to succeed to the office. His wealth was exhausted, and as no one could introduce him to the king, he lived in poverty and hardship.

He gradually grew up and possessed the talent of a high minister; he was thoroughly skilled in governing the people and adjudicating affairs. As he reached the prime of his youth, his physique was robust and large, and he was endowed with bravery, great strength, and all manner of arts and skills.
He then reflected: "I am currently impoverished; what should I do?"
Furthermore, I am unable to perform any menial labor.
Now, being devoid of merit, my skills and arts cannot be put into practice; yet I was not born into a lowly family. Moreover, I have heard others recite this verse:
"Karma comes and transforms me, That my destitution has reached such a state."
The family business of my parents now has no place for me to employ it.
The work performed by those of low station is not suitable for me to do;
had I lacked meritorious karma, I would have been born into a lowly household.
Though my birthplace is noble, my suffering is thus;
My lowly occupation is easily known, yet it is one I cannot bear.
I shall engage in secret work, So that no one at all may know of it.
While currently engaged in the act of robbing, he conceals it so that others do not perceive it.
With two quivers fastened at his waist and carrying a sharp steel sword,
his legs bound and hands grasping a bow, he adorns himself in various ways.
"Just like a lion cub, he has no fear whatsoever.
Having spoken this verse, he thought to himself:
"Even if I were to rob other places or cause others to become poor, I shall instead rob the king."

Having formed this thought, he went to the royal palace and approached the king’s bedchamber; fearing that the king might wake and suspect him of being a thief, he did not dare speak, but took the king’s garments along with his various necklaces and set them aside in one place.

At that time, by the king’s head was a vessel of water, and beside it was some ash. Pressed by hunger and thirst, he thought the ash was flour and drank the mixture with the water; having drunk and become full, he then realized it was ash.
He then reflected to himself:
"If even ashes can be eaten, how much more so other things?
I would rather eat grass; why should I commit robbery?"
"Since my father's time, this profession has not been practiced by our family.
He then cast aside all his belongings and returned home.
Seeing him emerge empty-handed, the king sighed in admiration and said, "Excellent!"
He immediately summoned that person and said to him:
"For what reason have you now taken this object, placed it back on the ground, and departed empty-handed?
The man replied:
"Great King!
Listen to what I have to say.
He then spoke in verse:
"Why do you commit what is unreasonable?
It is because of hunger and thirst; yet ash-water can quench hunger and thirst, and thus it would pacify the mind of a thief.
Now that you know this hunger and thirst, it is easy to bring them to rest."
Having drunk the water of ashes, I cast the vessel upon the ground;
filled with shame and remorse, I shall never again commit evil.
Great King, you should know that I am no ordinary person.
He was indeed the son of a high minister;
because his family was impoverished, he came to the royal palace and committed an unlawful act.
From this day forward, he shall constantly drink only water mixed with ashes.
I shall subsist by eating grass and live my life, never engaging in the act of theft.
My ancestors of old possessed their own family rites and teachings;
I would rather let my own body perish than destroy these ancient laws and instructions.

When the king saw this, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and praised the son of noble lineage as truly and unfalsely so; for despite his faults, he was able to repent and reform immediately. He then spoke this verse:
“Poverty destroys one’s resolve and endurance, And causes one to cast aside shame and modesty;
A vulgar, base, and wicked person Swiftly commits evil deeds.”
With the hook of your own family dharma, you are able to restrain the signs of what is not the Dharma;
since you can restrain your own mind and do not violate the teachings of your family,
possessing such noble conduct, you shall succeed to the station of your father.
"Now that you have cast aside your deluded mind and are able to perform such a difficult task, I am filled with supreme joy and appoint you as my minister.
There is no need for further deliberation; I have already witnessed your conduct."
His mind is firm and his will is courageous and strong; furthermore, he possesses wisdom and skill.
I have now personally witnessed and known that such a reality is truly rare;
his talent and achievements surpass his father’s twofold, because his heart is truly virtuous.
Therefore, the wise person should act with sincerity and not with hypocrisy.

36 (36) Furthermore, although the active fetters (*saṃyojana*) may not currently arise, if they have not been abandoned, the possession (*prāpti*) of those fetters still persists, just as cold water is cast into hot broth.
I have heard that in the past, there was a teacher and a disciple who, during winter, were in a warm room and saw a mass of fire without smoke or flames.
The teacher said to the disciple:
"Do you see this fire without smoke or flames?
The disciple replied:
“I see it.
The master said to his disciple:
“Place dry firewood on the fire; smoke will arise immediately.”
He spoke again:
"If one blows with the mouth, flames will emerge.
As a teacher for his disciple, he then uttered this verse:
“Just as fire without smoke and flame, so too with the impurity-contemplation of a mind of loving-kindness:
present fetters do not arise, like fire without smoke and flame.
Just as when dry fuel is obtained, smoke and flame arise simultaneously,”
When the fire of the mind encounters causes and conditions, and meets with evil associates,
the smoke of anger and hatred immediately arises; when it beholds beautiful forms,
the fire of greed blazes forth.
Having achieved the possession of the three knowledges, one should diligently cultivate vigor in order to sever greed, hatred, and delusion.
So that the weeds of the fetters do not grow, it is like a path constantly traveled.
None of the various flowers will emerge;
they do not sprout when conditions have not yet met. Because the root has not been severed, they will sprout again once conditions are encountered.
The concentration manifests definitively on the fourth day; however, during the third or second days, it may recede again upon encountering conditions.
Furthermore, it resembles mundane concentration: though suppressed and bound so as not to arise, it is entirely devoid of any signs of affliction.
Desire is like the root of a poisonous tree; if not uprooted, the sprouts will grow back.
It is like a person who, ashamed of their white hair, shaves off all the black as well;
yet before long, the white hair grows back again.
Not permanently severing the fetters and latent tendencies is likewise in this regard:
the fetter of desire and ill-will constrain the mechanism of virtuous conduct;
though their antidotes are present, they do not arise.
One then conceives the thought that it is rare to encounter such [teachings], yet the fetters and afflictions arise again later, leading one to violate the precepts.
Greedily attached to the five desires, one is like a snake hidden in its hole; when it emerges, it stings people.

37 (37) Furthermore, giving is for the sake of liberation and not for the sake of wealth; if it is for the sake of wealth, it is not called "giving. If it is for the sake of liberation, one attains non-arising and the bliss of nirvāṇa. Therefore, the wise person should practice giving for the sake of liberation.
I have heard that in the past, there was a donor who visited a monastic residence to host a gathering.
A practitioner who was a personal acquaintance of the donor said to the senior monk, "Today the donor’s food and drink are exquisite; please preach the Dharma with patience for the donor's sake."

At that time, the Elder, having attained the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, and being skilled in knowing the minds of others, investigated deeply why this assembly had been convened; he then realized that this assembly was for the sake of material gain.
At that time, the Elder spoke to this donor concerning the sufferings of the three evil realms, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

Donor, the offerings you have now prepared are most timely; they are fully endowed with color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor, and are exceedingly pure, so that nothing shall be lacking within the three evil realms."
Then a spiritual friend said to the elder:
"For what purpose do you offer prayers for others that they may lack nothing even within the three evil realms?
At that time, the elder of the Sangha spoke to that son of a practitioner:

"Although I am old and have spoken erroneously, this donor has not practiced the precepts and is driven by the fetters (saṃyojana). Observing his mind, I made this statement: 'This donor is devoted to the pleasures of the five desires, to wealth, and to cattle.'"
Then he spoke these verses:
“In whatever place a donor is reborn, their wealth and treasures will be exceedingly vast;
yet by relying upon those riches and treasures, they are able to give rise to arrogance.”
Arrogance transgresses the bounds of the Dharma; the blind, ignorant, and foolish worldling, by transgressing these bounds, falls into the three evil destinies.
Dwelling within those three evil paths, they regard them as if they were their own home.
If one is born among humans or devas, it is like being a temporary guest.
Therefore, with precepts and generosity as companions, one attains nirvana together;
precepts enable birth in the heavens, while generosity provides all necessary requisites.
One who acts for the sake of liberation will surely reach the end of suffering.
It is like planting a lotus root; when the flowers and leaves are fully developed, its root may also be eaten.
Draw near to the forest of liberation; its flowers and leaves are like happiness, and its roots are like liberation.
Therefore, cultivate precepts and generosity for the sake of liberation alone; they should not be practiced for worldly gain.
38. Furthermore, it is difficult to be free from all calamities, and it is difficult to obtain a human body; having obtained freedom from all calamities, one should always be diligent.
I have heard that in the past, there was a young boy who heard it said in a sutra:
"It is extremely difficult for a blind turtle to encounter the hole of a floating log.

At that time, the boy intentionally bored a hole in a wooden board large enough for his head, cast it into a pond, and entered the water himself. He lowered and raised his head, hoping to enter the hole, but because the water drifted the board away, he could not find it.
He then reflected to himself: "I feel profound revulsion;

a human body is difficult to obtain. The Buddha used the ocean as a metaphor: a hole in a floating log is small and a blind turtle has no eyes; for it to surface once every hundred years is truly difficult to encounter."

Now my pond is small and the hole in the board is large; moreover, there are two eyes that emerge every day a hundred times, yet even they cannot find it—how much less could that blind turtle possibly find it?
Then he spoke in verse:
“The vast ocean is exceedingly great, And the hole in the floating log is even smaller;
It emerges but once in a hundred years— To encounter it is most difficult.”
My pond is now small, yet the hole in the floating log is exceedingly large;
though it repeatedly raises its head, it cannot find the hole in the log.
For a blind turtle to encounter a floating log is a most difficult thing to happen; likewise, for these two to meet is extremely rare.
To regain a human body from the evil realms is likewise difficult to encounter.
Now that I have obtained this human life, I ought not to be negligent;
for though there have been Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have never before encountered them.
Today I have received the instruction of the words of the World-Honored One of Ten Powers;
regarding the sublime Dharma spoken by the Buddha, I shall certainly practice it.
If one can cultivate it well, the salvation [thereby attained] shall be most great.
What one attains is not created by another; therefore, exert yourself with diligence.
If you fall into the eight states of adversity, how can you escape them?
Worldly karma pursues you, causing you to plummet into the evil realms.
I shall now flee and escape from the prison of the three realms of existence;
if I do not exit this prison, how can I attain liberation?
The various paths of animal rebirth endure for an exceedingly long duration across kalpas.
In the hells and among the hungry ghosts, the darkness and suffering are profound.
If I do not practice with diligence, how shall I escape these perilous and evil realms?
Without reaching the end of suffering, one cannot leave the prison of the three realms of existence;
therefore, one should diligently apply skillful means to surely escape this prison.
I now seek to go forth from the household life, so that I may certainly attain liberation.
39. Furthermore, wealth is difficult to relinquish; yet if a wise person can practice even a small act of giving, they should not give rise to thoughts of contempt.
I have heard that in the past, in the kingdom of Suvāstu, there was a king named Śatadru. Once, while out hunting, the king happened upon a stūpa and offered five coins as an offering to it.
A certain caṇḍāla, shouting "Excellent!
from afar, immediately dispatched a messenger to seize him and bring him before the king.
At that time, the king spoke to him, saying:
"Do you now mock me because you see my gift as small?
That person replied to the king:
"Grant me fearlessness first, and then I shall speak."
In the past, while I was plundering on a dangerous road as a bandit, I captured a man and forcefully clenched his hand.
I then thought to myself:
"This person must have gold coins in his fist."
I told him to open his hand, but he refused. I took up my bow and arrow to intimidate him, saying that he must release it, yet he still refused.
I drew my bow toward him; because of my greed for the treasure, I shot and killed him. Having killed him, I immediately obtained a copper coin.
One might rather spare a single coin than spare one’s own life.
Now, since Your Majesty has not been subjected to any coercion or distress, you were able to offer five coins as a gift to the Buddha’s stūpa; for this reason, I now exclaim, "Excellent!"
He then spoke in verse:
"Drawing the bow with a circle as perfect as a wheel, I was about to take his life;
Yet he would rather lose his own body and life Than be willing to pay a single coin."
I have seen such people who, when facing death, would not give up their wealth;
therefore, seeing one now who has renounced their riches,
I conceive a sense of wonder and exclaim that this is a deed most difficult to accomplish.
Seeing neither bow nor sword, nor anyone coercing the Great King,
and feeling no fear or hesitation, he opened his mind and relinquished what was difficult to give;
through arduous seeking, he finally obtained the money.
Therefore, today when I see one who renounces wealth, my heart gives rise to a sense of the unprecedented.
Having personally witnessed those who, despite extreme suffering, are unwilling to give— O Great King,
you should now know that a stingy mind is difficult to relinquish.
40. Furthermore, when one acts with careful discernment, although there may be a fault at the time, there will certainly be great benefit later on.
I have heard that in the past there was a bhikṣu who was frequently robbed by thieves. One day, he firmly closed his doors and windows; yet the thieves returned and knocked on the door, calling out.
The bhikṣu replied, "If I were to see you, I would be utterly terrified. You should insert your hand through this opening, and I shall give you what you desire."
The thief immediately thrust his hand into the window; the bhikṣu tied him to a pillar with a rope, took up a staff, opened the door, and struck him. Having struck him once, he said:
"Take refuge in the Buddha."
Out of fear, the bandits immediately followed his words and took refuge in the Buddha.
He struck them a second time and said,
"Take refuge in the Dharma."
Because the bandit feared death, he spoke again, saying, "I take refuge in the Dharma.
When struck for the third time, he spoke to him again, saying,
"I take refuge in the Saṃgha."
Out of fear at that time, the bandit said, "I take refuge in the Saṃgha.
He then thought to himself:
"How many refuges does this practitioner possess now?"
"If you have many [offenses], you will certainly not see this Jambudvīpa again; you shall surely meet your end.
At that time, the bhikṣu released him to go. Because he had been beaten, his body was in pain, and it took a long time for him to rise; he then sought to leave the household life and become a monk.
Someone asked him, "Previously you were a thief who committed various evil deeds; for what reason have you left the household life to practice the Way?
He replied to that person:
"I too observed the benefits of the Buddha-dharma before going forth as a monk.
Today, I encountered a spiritual friend who struck me three times with a staff; now only a small remnant of my life remains, yet it has not been severed."
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is truly the All-Knowing One; had he instructed his disciples in the four refuges, my life would have ended immediately.

The Buddha foresaw this matter from afar and commanded the bhikṣus to strike the bandits three times so as to prevent my death. Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke only of the three refuges and not the four; out of compassion for me, the Buddha taught the three refuges and did not teach the four.
He then spoke in verse:
"Having attained certain omniscience, Out of compassion for me,
He has thus taught the Three Refuges, And not that there is a fourth."
For the sake of those within the three realms of existence, the Three Refuges were taught;
had there been a fourth, I would have no refuge.
Out of compassion for me now, may my life and body be exhausted therein.
I beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
seeing such a thing from afar, a sense of the unprecedented arose within me, and thus I abandoned my thieving mind.
Some attain understanding through coarse matters, while others awaken through subtle ones.
The coarse awakens to coarse matters; the subtle understands subtle matters.
Because my mind was coarse, I attained awakening through coarse matters.
Since I have understood these matters, I therefore seek to leave the household life.

41. Furthermore, gain and honor disturb the practice of the Path. If one cuts off gain and honor, one should skillfully observe anger.

I have heard that in the past, there was a bhikṣu in a certain park who received offerings from rival cities and villages; those who had left the household life together with him felt envy and slandered him.
When the bhikṣu disciple heard this slander, he said to his teacher,
"The bhikṣu so-and-so has slandered the Upādhyāya.
Upon hearing these words, the Upādhyāya immediately summoned the slanderer, comforted him with kind words, and gave him a robe.
The disciples said to their teacher, "That slanderer is our enemy;
why does the Upādhyāya comfort him and give him a robe?
The teacher replied to them:
“Those who slander me have actually rendered me a service; they ought to be honored.
He then spoke in verse:
“As hail destroys the crops, if there is someone who can intercept it, [they are a benefactor].”
The landowner was greatly delighted and rewarded him with wealth and silks.
Though he slandered me as an intimate friend, he is not called an enemy;
since he warded off the hail of my gains and offerings, I ought to repay his kindness.
Hail harms but a single lifetime; gain and honor harm many lifetimes.
Hail harms only one's wealth; gain and honor destroy the path of cultivation.
A field damaged by hail will surely have some small remnant left; but one ruined by gain and honor leaves nothing behind.
Harm caused by gain and offerings utterly consumes all merit;
like Devadatta, who was struck down by the hail of gain and offerings,
because of his greedy attachment, not even a hair’s breadth of wholesome Dharma remained.
When all evils blaze most fiercely, one falls into the evil realms upon death.
Gain and honor are more violent than a raging fire, and even exceed the potency of malignant poisons,
lions, tigers, and wolves.
Having observed this, the wise would rather be harmed by those [enemies] than be harmed by gain and offerings.
The fool, craving gain and offerings, does not see their faults and evils;
gain and offerings distance one from the Noble Path, and virtuous conduct ceases and does not arise.
The Buddha has severed all fetters; the bonds of the three realms of existence are entirely released.
His merit is fully perfected, yet he still avoids gain and honor.
Roaring like a lion amidst the assembly, he utters these words:
"Let gain and offerings not come near me; I too shall remain far from them.
What person of wise mind and discernment would ever crave such gain and offerings?
Gain and honor disturb the concentrated mind; their harm is more severe than that of an enemy.
It is like being struck by a rope of hair: it cuts through the skin, tears the flesh, and destroys the bones;
only when the marrow is severed does it cease.
It severs the skin of ethical discipline, Can tear the flesh of meditative concentration,
Breaks the bones of wisdom, And extinguishes the marrow of the sublime,
virtuous mind. It is like an infant Who grasps fire, wishing to eat it.
Like a fish swallowing a hook and bait, like a bird covered by a net,
or as various beasts fall into pits and traps— all are caused by their craving for flavor.
A bhikṣu who craves gain and offerings is no different from them.
Its flavor is extremely rare, yet the affliction it causes is most profound and heavy.
Those who feign flattery and sycophancy dwell amidst gain and offerings;
they draw near to the clamor of worldly distraction—the very seeds of hindrance and suffering.
Just as with a scabies sore, scratching it only increases the itching;
likewise, arrogance and heedless desire all arise because of the pursuit of gain and sustenance.
May this person, for our sake, ward off the resentment that arises from such gain.
For this reason, I should devote my whole heart to making offerings to such a spiritual friend; how could they be called an enemy?
Because of their greed for gain and offerings, they take no pleasure in secluded and quiet places.
The mind constantly dwells upon gain and offerings, never resting day or night.
"In that place there are robes and food; such-and-such a person is my close friend;
they will surely come to invite me"—thus the mind is full of攀缘 (pān-yuán, mental attachments).
Having ruined the mind of tranquility, they take no delight in secluded places but always prefer the human world; because their fields of profit have been destroyed,
they take no pleasure in the dharma of meditative concentration, for they have abandoned that very concentration.
"He is not called a bhikṣu, nor is he called a white-robed layman.
(42) Furthermore, although both have attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), there is a distinction in their training and teaching.
I have heard that in the past, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana was instructing two disciples who were practicing meditation with single-minded devotion but had attained no realization.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked Maudgalyāyana:
"Have those two disciples attained the supreme Dharma?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“I have not yet attained it.
Śāriputra asked again:
"What teachings do you instruct?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "First, the teaching on impurity; second, the teaching on counting the breath."
"However, their minds remain stagnant and they have not yet attained awakening.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Maudgalyāyana,
"From what lineage did those two disciples come before they went forth into homelessness?"
He replied,
"One is a washerman, and the other is a goldsmith.
Then Śāriputra said to Maudgalyāyana:
"One who is a goldsmith should be taught *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), while one who is a washerman should be instructed in *aśubha-bhāvanā* (contemplation of impurity).
Maudgalyāyana taught his disciples according to this principle, and the disciples immediately applied themselves with diligence, attaining the fruit of Arhatship.
Having attained arhatship, he leaped for joy and immediately spoke this verse in praise of Śāriputra:
"The second turner of the wheel of Dharma, The great general of the Buddha’s teachings,
Among all the śrāvakas, He has attained the supreme wisdom."
Possessing the power of supreme awakening wisdom—O Śāriputra!
You have guided me toward liberation; following what I had previously practiced, you have guided me to enlightenment, and we both have swiftly attained liberation.
Moving within one’s own domain, one attains what ought to be attained;
but he who moves in another’s domain is like a fish fallen onto dry land.
I always stay by the riverbank, practicing the washing of my robes until they are pure white.
Resting the mind upon the white bones, their similar characteristics are easily understood;
without exerting great effort, they swiftly enter my consciousness.
The goldsmith constantly blows the bellows; the air that enters and exits is wind.
It is easy to enter the *ānāpāna-smṛti*;
each possesses its own superior power. Now, Śāriputra is the bridle and bit of the Buddha-dharma.
The second turning of the wheel of Dharma is that which accords with reality;
those who have attained mastery over the mind can cause both of us to well understand the path of dhyāna.
The great general among dharmas, Through his teachings, has tamed and harmonized me, Leading me to a place of peace and security; Therefore, I am filled with great joy.
(43) Furthermore, even if those whose roots of goodness have ripened were to flee and hide, the Tathāgata’s great compassion would never abandon them.

I have heard in the past that the Tathāgata is the unsurpassed, most excellent field of merit; his every movement, whether coming or going, always brings forth benefit and welfare, unlike any field found in the mundane world.

He wished to demonstrate that practicing the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) differs from worldly fields; thus, the practitioner of the field of merit went to the place where the donors and seed-sowers were located, entering the city of Śrāvastī for alms. This continued until, while still a bodhisattva, he entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food. Upon seeing his dignified bearing, the old and young, men and women, great and small within the city, all felt love and reverence in their hearts. The rest is as described in the *Buddhacarita*.

In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, sentient beings were weary of suffering, and the seeds of their roots of goodness were extremely easy to sprout. For the sake of transforming and delivering people through his manifestations, the Buddha entered the city to beg for food and spoke this verse:
"If one, with deep faith, Pays homage to the Buddha’s feet, That person, within birth and death, Shall not remain for long."
One who can practice virtue in the field of merit, making offerings as a causal condition,
will surely obtain a great retribution.
One who, with a heart of faith and reverence, places even a morsel of earth into the Buddha’s bowl, shall never be without a retribution.
When the Tathāgata entered the city manifesting his supernormal powers, all the people spoke to one another, saying,
"The Buddha has come into the city.
The rest is as described in various sūtras.

When the Buddha entered the city, it was adorned with every kind of magnificent ornamentation. Men and women, both great and small, were all stirred upon hearing that the Buddha had entered the city; they were like the great ocean when the wind stirs up the waves to produce a mighty roar—a spectacle such as this had never before occurred within the realm of Jambudvīpa.

At that time, there was a man in the city who removed filth and excrement, named Niti; his hair was long, disheveled, and soiled with grime, and the clothes he wore were entirely tattered and worn out.

If he obtained a tattered rag along the way, he used it to patch his robe, intending thereby to demonstrate the unwholesome karma of his past lives; he then took a jar of excrement upon his back, intending to carry it far away to discard it.

On the road, he beheld the Buddha and gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance; it was like beholding the great ocean. His body was adorned with a halo one fathom in width, like a mass of pure gold free from all impurity. The *kāṣāya* robe he wore was like red sandalwood, and like a jeweled pavilion, one could gaze upon him without ever being satiated.
He then spoke these verses: "His golden hue is like a flower in full bloom; His robes are like red sandalwood.
His garments and deportment are perfectly composed, Pure as a polished bronze mirror."
"Just as when the autumn moon appears, the sun dwells in the midst of the void sky, so the World-Honored One dwells amidst the great assembly, pure and majestic like the autumn moon.
At that time, sentient beings who saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, gave rise to great joy; even animals who saw the Buddha felt delight in their faculty of sight, how much more so for humans!
He then spoke in verse:
"Beholding his form, peerless in comparison, With a profound heart of supreme love and respect,
He is a fit vessel for meditative concentration, His majestic radiance doubly brilliant."
Though possessed of the poisonous mind of false views, he felt joy upon beholding the Buddha;
observing all his physical forms, he could not tire of gazing at them with every glance.
Seeing him, his heart was filled with delight, and his entire body was suffused with radiant light.
Beholding him, he becomes ever more radiant; his physical form is perfectly complete.
There is nothing in him to be censured, and his noble lineage is worthy of praise.
No one is able to find fault with him; he is a wise and virtuous man.
This seed is produced in succession; it is the jewel-adornment of the world, serving to enhance the beauty of one's physical form.
Without relying on external ornamentation, the marks and signs (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana) are loved and delighted in by all.
The manifestation of excellence always follows one’s person;
though worldly people adorn themselves with necklaces, these cannot provide constant beauty.
The Aśoka tree flourishes in full bloom, adorning the great earth.
His excellent marks do not equal those of the Buddha;
his blazingly adorned body is like a mani-armor,
embellished with every kind of jewel.
It is just as when various flowers adorn the waters of a pond;
they cannot compare to the body of the Tathāgata, for the physical form of the Sugata is resplendent with its manifest marks and signs of excellence.
When pure and free from all clouds, the moon is adorned by the many stars;
The vessel of sublime conduct is likewise beautiful, such that one gazes upon it without weariness,
As if drinking the taste of nectar, like the pure and full moon.
Beloved by all people,
possessing the majesty of perfect self-mastery, and endowed with every virtue—
who could fully praise you?
For example, within the cycle of birth and death, various performers manifest transformed forms,
yet there is nothing that can truly transform or manifest.
Though one may resemble a Buddha and produce myriad wondrous images, they do not equal the majestic marks and signs of a Buddha.
“The Buddha’s wondrous countenance and marks are peerless among gods and humans.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One’s unevenly aligned physical characteristics were exceptionally sublime and worthy of praise; all his practices were complete and his merits fully perfected. He spoke this verse in praise:
“What the Tathāgata speaks is revered by the wise.”
In his dignified deportment and every gesture, he was ultimately without fault.
The most excellent among Munis, in all matters he has never encountered, his awakened wisdom remains unshakable;
whether praised or reviled, his mind does not waver.
Because he possesses the ten powers, his manifested marks are utterly tranquil;
complete and upright, he is a mass of merit and benefit.
His gait is exceedingly dignified and graceful, and he is beloved by all people.
The meaning of his speech is profound and vast; his gaze is most discerning and precise.
His discourse is elegant and orderly; he has relinquished all things and is free from craving for food and drink.
"To summarize the essentials, there is nothing that is not lovable.

At that time, Niti, seeing that the Unsurpassed Tamer had his faculties completely stilled and composed, and was surrounded by monks whose faculties were likewise undistracted as they attended upon him, felt redoubled love and reverence. He spoke again in verse:
"All faculties are utterly tranquil, Surrounded by those who have tamed their faculties."
Clad in robes of fresh color, preceded and followed by his retinue,
the supreme leader among the Śākyas is golden-hued and unshakable;
the fourfold assembly constantly surrounds him, like crimson clouds encircling the sun.
At that time, having seen the Buddha, Niti felt self-contempt for his own foulness and impurity; carrying a jar of excrement on his back, he thought, "How can I see the Buddha?
He turned toward another path so as not to see the Buddha, his heart filled with sorrow and distress:
"In previous lives I did not create meritorious karma, but was dragged away by evil; now I undergo this suffering. I do not grieve over this lowly occupation."
"All others have obtained [the opportunity] before the Buddha, but because I now see this foul stench, I am unable to go.
For this reason, his heart was consumed with grief and distress, and he spoke these verses:
"The appearance of a Buddha in the world is extremely rare; It is difficult to encounter one."
Humans, devas, and asuras—the eight classes of beings—all surround me.
Although I have now encountered them, they cannot approach because of my foul stench;
clearly possessing evil karma, the retribution for my sins has cast me aside.
Having reflected thus, she turned from another alleyway and abandoned her pursuit to distance herself;
yet the Buddha, the World-Honored One, following with his great and impartial compassion, did not abandon her and immediately appeared standing before her at the entrance of that alley.
Having seen him, Niti was again seized with terror and thought:
"I have just now avoided the Buddha, yet now I see him once more; where shall I go to avoid him?
Overcome by fear and distress, she reproached herself, saying:
“I am extremely lacking in merit; the Buddhas are fragrant and pure, so how could I draw near to the Buddha with such extreme filth?
If I were to draw near, my transgression would become even more grave; it is my evil karma from previous lives that has brought me to such a state.”
He then spoke in verse:
"The devas, with sandalwood incense, Exquisite and wondrous māndārava flowers,
And various kinds of offerings, Bring them forth to present to the World-Honored One."
When the Buddha enters the city, scented water is sprinkled upon the ground;
gods and humans alike offer him worship, for he is truly one worthy of offerings.
Why, then, do you hold a vessel of excrement and stand before the Buddha?
He further thought to himself:
"By what means or reflection might I achieve my purpose?
Once more, he abandoned the Buddha and entered another alleyway.
The Tathāgata was again in that same street as before; when Niti saw him, his astonishment and distress redoubled, and he spoke this verse:
“A halo a fathom wide surrounds you, With flames of many colors;
All the people within the city Encircle you with palms joined.”
“Śakra holds the fly-whisk, and both humans and devas offer him worship.
Why did I previously avoid the side streets and now come along this path?
Having composed this verse, he further thought to himself:
"Now the World-Honored One is the supreme among gods and humans, while I am a base and defiled being, the lowest among the lowly; how can I now approach the World-Honored One with such foulness?"
He immediately turned aside and entered another alley. At that time, the World-Honored One was already standing there;

having seen the Buddha, he felt ashamed and retreated, whereupon his dung-pitcher struck the wall and shattered at once. The liquid filth poured out, drenching and defiling his robes. Seeing himself thus soiled, he was filled with shame and remorse, his complexion changing as he thought to himself:
"Previously, though it was foul and filthy, the pitcher still shielded it; now that the pitcher is broken, the impurity is exposed. This is truly a matter for great shame."
Deeply reviling and reproaching himself, he spoke these verses:
"Alas! How strange and wondrous it is! I am now as if heading toward death;
Foulness and stench pervade my entire body— How can I remain here?"
The Most Victorious Honored One of the Three Realms has come near me;
blocking my path ahead, there is no place for escape.
How strange! How utterly loathsome! Both inside and out, all is impure.
"Shame and great anguish are like the arrival of old age.
At that time, the great assembly all saw the World-Honored One following behind Niti. Then, a certain bhikṣu among the multitude thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata enters the city not to beg for alms at the homes of the noble and wealthy or the lowly and humble, but follows only after Niti."
"Why is this so? There must certainly be a cause for it.
He then thought to himself again:
"This matter can be understood," he said,
and then spoke this verse:
"This one must be a vessel of merit, followed by the Buddha."
Like a jewel fallen into filth, one stirs it up and seeks to retrieve it;
so the Tathāgata takes hold of the mind, making no distinction between noble and base,
nor seeking for a true lineage— thus has the Most Sublime One spoken.
Just as a physician diagnoses an illness, examining whether the patient's abdomen is hard or soft,
and administers medicine according to the ailment without regard for their lineage;
so too does the Tathāgata, with equanimity, observe the hardness or softness of the mind.
"Nor does he discriminate among castes, but bestows medicine to subdue afflictions.
At that time, Nitī encountered the World-Honored One in a narrow alley; filled with shame and shrinking back, he had no place to hide. Joining his palms toward the ground, he spoke these words:
"You can now sustain all sentient beings; I pray you open a small space to accommodate my body."
He then spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata now approaches me ever closer;
my body is exceedingly foul and filthy, so that I cannot draw near to the World-Honored One."
“Excellent! Please reveal even a small portion [of the Dharma]; I pray that you will grant me passage.

At that time, the Tathāgata, his heart suffused with great compassion, seeking the peace, happiness, benefit, and welfare of all sentient beings, approached Niti with a serene and joyful countenance. The World-Honored One comforted him with a voice as gentle as thunder, causing his body and mind to become tranquil, delighted, and happy.
The Buddha summoned Niti; having heard this, Niti looked about in all directions in bewilderment, thinking, "How can the Most Honored One of the Three Realms summon a person as lowly and base as me?"
"Could it be that someone with the same name as mine has called out to him?

The Buddha’s mind is impartial, having severed all love and hatred; the World-Honored One raised his hand toward Niti. His fingers were slender and long, his nails like red copper, and his webbed membranes between the fingers covered them; his palm was like a lotus, a hand with auspicious marks, soft, pure, and clean. Wishing to inspire in Niti a heart of courageous resolve, he spoke this verse to him:
"Because you possess the conditions for roots of goodness, I have come to your side."
Now that I have arrived here, why do you flee and hide?
You ought to remain right here; though your body is now defiled, your mind possesses the supreme and wholesome Dharma—a most excellent and wondrous fragrance.
"Now you are outside your own body; it is not fitting for you to despise yourself.
At that time, having heard the Buddha call him, Niti raised his eyes and beheld the Buddha; his heart became courageous and resolute, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, he spoke these words:

"To those who have no refuge, you act as a refuge. Toward all sentient beings, you conceive the thought of them as your own children without any [selfish] cause or condition. Your mind is impartial; you are truly a genuine savior."
"Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, converses with me, as if sprinkling nectar upon my body and mind.
He then spoke in verse:
"Even if the Great Brahma King were to engage in discourse with me..."
The honor accorded by the Lord of Devas has led him to humble himself and come to embrace me; yet,
though a Great Holy Wheel-Turning King might share a single vessel of food with me,
it is not equal to the Honored One of the Three Realms condescending to grant me a single word out of compassion.
Now that I have received your compassionate care, my joy exceeds even that;
having refined away impurities and evils, unwholesome characteristics have been extinguished, and wholesome characteristics have fully arisen.
O Sovereign One, you have delivered me across.
May I receive happiness.
Even Śakra bears me upon his head and still calls me one protected by merit;
how much more so for me, who am most base and inferior, yet have personally received the Buddha’s oral teachings?
"And yet you address me by my name; why do you not feel joy?
The Buddha said to Niti:
"Are you able to go forth from home now?"
At that time, having heard these words, Niti felt great joy in his heart and spoke this verse:
"Am one of my lowly kind Permitted to go forth into the homeless life?"
"May the World-Honored One show compassion;
if you would allow me to go forth, it would be like taking a person from hell and placing them in the heavens.
The Buddha said to Niti:
“You should not now entertain such thoughts.
He then spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata does not examine Lineage, nor noble birth or wealth;”
Observing only the karma of sentient beings— The seeds of past goodness—
Bound by all afflictions, they do not attain liberation; In birth, aging,
sickness, death, and the like, Suffering and pleasure are entirely the same for all.
How is it that only the brahmins are able to attain liberation, while others cannot?
Are not letters and sounds common to all, not just the brahmins?
Those of other castes likewise know it.
Just as one crosses at a river ferry, not only Brahmins,
but those of other castes are also able to do so.
"Are all things that must be done possible only for a brāhmaṇa and impossible for others?
You should now simply go forth out of faith in me."
In my Buddha-dharma, the compassionate mind is without partiality;
it differs from the various non-Buddhists who conceal certain teachings.
Deliverance is entirely impartial, and the Buddha-dharma never diminishes.
He teaches the Dharma without partiality, impartially revealing the true path;
for the sake of all sentient beings, he acts as the secure and correct road.
It is like a great marketplace where one purchases all manner of goods.
My Dharma market is likewise: it makes no distinction between caste, whether one is noble and wealthy or poor and lowly;
whether one is a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa, a Vaiśya or a Śūdra.
There is no one to obstruct or protect it; it is not restricted to humans or non-humans.
All come to drink from it, and my Dharma is likewise.
Even now, I do not distinguish between bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Universally for the sake of the world, you are the great physician for humans and devas.
"I do not necessarily act only for the noble, such as the selected Wise King (Bhadra-rāja) and others; I also deliver those of lowly status, such as Upāli."
I do not act solely for the sake of great and wealthy elders such as Sudatta; I also deliver the poor and destitute such as Sūrata.
I do not act solely for the sake of the one of great wisdom, Śāriputra; I also act for those of dull faculties such as Cūḍapanthaka.
I do not teach exclusively for the likes of Mahākāśyapa, who possesses few desires and is content; I also teach for the likes of Pāṇḍuka, who has many desires.
I do not teach exclusively for the likes of the venerable and long-established Elder Kāśyapa of Uruvilvā; I also teach for the likes of the youthful Sautrāyaṇīputra.
I do not preach the Dharma solely for those such as the arrogant Pāgala; I also preach it for the most wicked Aṅgulimāla, who held a sword in his hand.
I do not preach the Dharma solely for men of great wisdom; I also preach it for women of shallow understanding.
I do not provide true salvation exclusively for the assembly of those who have left the household life; I also preach the Dharma for those householders who are extremely wicked.
I do not preach the Dharma exclusively for those of few desires; I also explain the Four Noble Truths to the young sons of householders who indulge themselves in the five sensual pleasures.

I do not speak this for the sake of the Potaliputra alone, who has relinquished all affairs; I also speak it for kings such as Bimbisāra, who manage state affairs and are occupied with many worldly duties.

I do not speak exclusively for those who have already renounced alcohol; I also speak for those such as the extremely intoxicated Ugga, enabling them to attain the path of the stream-enterer (*srotāpatti*).

I do not speak exclusively for those such as Revata, who delight in the cultivation of meditative concentration, regarding the dharma of transcending birth and death; I also speak for those such as Bāṣpa, whose minds were deranged by the loss of a son.
I do not preach the Dharma exclusively for those born into families of virtuous upāsakas; I also preach it for disciples with wrong views, such as Aśvabhūti and others.
I do not preach the Dharma exclusively for the youthful Rāṣṭrapāla; I also preach it for the aged Raṅkura and others.
I do not teach the attainment of Arhatship exclusively to the veteran Bhāradvāja; I also enable the seven-year-old novice Śuddhāyana to attain Arhatship.

I do not teach this solely for the sake of answering the difficult questions and doubts of the sixteen Pāruyanas; I also speak it for the sake of those sixty villagers who are infantile, ignorant, greedy for desire, and seeking women.

I do not speak solely for those such as Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the great leaders among the bulls of debate whose eloquence is inexhaustible; I also speak for the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā of shallow wisdom, so that she may attain profound knowledge and be able to understand the questions and challenges posed by a Great Man.

I do not teach exclusively for the sake of the wealthy, the Great King, or the lady Mṛgāramātṛ and others to attain the fruits of the path; I also teach for the sake of the lowly and the servants, such as Ghoṣila and others, to attain the traces of the path.
I do not speak exclusively for virtuous wives such as Viśākhā; I also speak for courtesans such as Utpalavarṇā.
I do not speak exclusively for noble women of great eloquence such as Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī; I also speak for seven-year-old śrāmaṇerīs who are capable of subduing non-Buddhists.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Relying upon my Buddha-dharma, one should quickly go forth into homelessness;
through wisdom one attains the nectar of immortality, not by means of lineage or clan."
"The four great elements and space / Are equally present in the noble and the lowly;
/ Without wisdom one does not attain them, / For it does not depend upon birth.
At that time, Niti immediately followed the Buddha’s instruction, whereupon he left the household life and attained arhatship.
At that time, when the elders and brahmins in the city of Śrāvastī heard that Niti had obtained ordination, they all gave rise to derision, anger, and resentment, saying:
"That Niti is a base and low-born person; now that he has obtained ordination, if he comes to our assemblies, he will defile our houses, beds, and mats."
The entire country was thrown into turmoil, until the matter reached the ears of King Prasenajit.
Upon hearing this, the king spoke to his ministers, saying:

"You must no longer cause such commotion. I shall now go to the World-Honored One and petition the Tathāgata, so that he will never again permit such low-born individuals to leave the household life."

At that time, the king, accompanied by his attendants, went to the Jetavana Grove. There he saw a bhikṣu sitting upon a large rock sewing discarded rags (pāṃśukūla). Seven hundred Brahmās were at his side; some joined their palms in reverent salutation, some took up threads, and some threaded needles, as described in detail in the Sūtras.
At that time, the devas spoke these verses in praise:
"Observing his faculties to be tranquil, His deportment and majestic virtue flourishing,
Having attained the possession of the three knowledges, With sharp faculties, he is non-retrogressive."
All virtues are fully perfected; he accepts robes of discarded rags.
Seven hundred devas of majestic power have come from the Brahma palaces;
they take refuge and pay homage to the one who has crossed to the further shore.
At that time, King Prasenajit did not recognize Niti and said to him, "Go now on my behalf and inform the World-Honored One:
'King Prasenajit is currently outside the gate and wishes to come and see the Buddha.'"
When Nīti heard this, he immediately sank into the rock as if entering water, and leaping before the Buddha, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“King Prasenajit is now outside the gate and wishes to see the World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One said,
"Return by the original path and go to summon him.
Niti obeyed the command, returned by way of the rock, and called out to King Prasenajit.
At that time, King Prasenajit prostrated himself, paid his respects, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Who was that bhikṣu just now?
What great virtuous one is he, whom the devas honor and serve as his attendants, and who can enter and exit through stone without obstruction?"
He spoke in verse, asking:
“The Buddha’s wisdom is pure and unimpeded; there is nothing it does not penetrate.
That which I wish to ask has already been known by the Buddha beforehand.”
For now, let us pause for a moment; I wish to ask something.
Just now I saw a bhikṣu entering and emerging from a rock as freely as an osprey moving in and out of water, floating and sinking with complete mastery.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit, saying:
"If the bhikṣu mentioned earlier wishes to know, it is this very person whom Your Majesty suspects—the lowly and despicable Niti."
Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell to the ground; he immediately reproached himself, saying:
"I am burning myself; how could I have given rise to such contempt for one of such great virtue?"
Having witnessed this event, he attained what had never been experienced before regarding the Buddha’s Dharma; his faith doubled, and he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, speaking these verses:
"Just as Mount Sumeru is composed of various jewels, And birds and beasts that reach the mountain all turn golden— So too, having seen the Tathāgata, I have attained a mind of supreme joy."
Though I have heard this in the past, only now do I realize it through direct knowledge:
the Buddha is like Mount Sumeru, a mass of immeasurable merit.
Those who come to rely upon the Buddha are transformed into a noble lineage.
The Buddha does not regard lineage, nor wealth, nobility, or fame;
just as a physician diagnoses an illness without considering the patient's lineage,
he prescribes only the finest medicines so that their disease may be cured.
Noble and base alike share the same vital breath; all emerge from impurity.
Upon attaining the fruit of the Way, they are equal and without distinction.
All castes are the same; in realizing the fruit, there is no difference at all.

At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to increase King Prasenajit’s pure faith, taught that the four castes may be purified; if one takes spouses from among the four castes at the time of marriage, these four castes can all attain purification.
The Buddha told the Great King:

"When taking a wife or giving a daughter in marriage, one should select based on lineage; however, within this Buddha-dharma, one observes only the causes and conditions of good and evil from past lives, and does not select based on lineage;
one observes only faith and offerings, and does not observe precious treasures."
He seeks purity in the precepts, not purity of lineage;
he seeks mastery in meditative concentration, not nobility of birth;
he contemplates their wisdom, not their place of origin.
He then spoke in verse:
"Just as one extracts pure gold from within mountain rock,
Or as fire emerges when pieces of eranda wood are rubbed together."
Just as a blue lotus flower grows from within the mud, one does not regard the place of its birth, but regards only its virtuous qualities.
"If one born of a noble lineage possesses virtuous conduct, they should be honored; likewise, if one born of a lowly caste possesses virtuous conduct, they too should be honored."

All those who possess wisdom should offer worship to those of virtuous character; though their lineages may differ, their moral conduct is no different. It is just as when *eranda* wood and sandalwood both produce fire—their heat and light are indistinguishable.
The Buddha’s words are true and without error; they penetrate the depths of the heart and enable the king to attain understanding.

King Prasenajit prostrated himself before the Buddha’s feet, touching the ground with his five limbs, and paid homage, taking refuge in the Tamer of Men, the One of All-Knowledge, who is unimpeded in all meanings, possessed of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, the Bhagavat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—He who acts as an uninvited kinsman to all sentient beings and shows no partiality toward any of the four castes. This is a brief summary.
Then he spoke in verse:
“The ocean of all-encompassing wisdom, With a pure mind, has crossed to the other shore.
In this world, the Buddha alone is compassionate; His mind and will are free from defilement and evil.”
For the sake of all sentient beings, he acts as their most intimate friend;
alone he proclaims liberation, yet reveals manifold paths.
Relying on wisdom and many skillful means, he [corrects] the externalists who are mad and deluded.
"Rough and harsh ascetic practices, / Solely deluded attachment to caste.
After King Prasenajit had paid homage at the feet of the Buddha and Niti, he returned to the city of Śrāvastī.

44. Furthermore, even if one has not yet entered the vision of the truths, by the power of training in extensive learning, all Māras cannot move them; therefore, one should diligently train in inquiry.
I have heard that in the past, there was a māra who transformed himself into a bhikṣu and came to a monastic dwelling.
While a Dharma master was preaching the Dharma among the assembly, the transformed bhikṣu said:
"I have attained the path of an arhat; if you have any doubts, you may now ask them all."
Then the assembly of monks said to the Dharma Master,
"Record what has been taught.
At that time, the Dharma Master asked the manifested bhikṣu:
"How does one sever the fetters?
How does one enter meditative absorption?
Thus the transformed bhikṣu preached the Dharma in a perverted manner.
Then the Dharma Master said to the assembly of monks, "This is not an Arhat; his words must not be taken lightly.
At that moment, the transformed bhikṣu leaped into the air and performed the eighteen transformations.
At that time, the great assembly rebuked the Dharma Master, saying:
