"How can you, O Master, now claim that such a person is not an Arhat?
Although the Dharma Master was thus rebuked, by the power of his extensive learning, he still declared that he was not.
“If he is an arhat, why are his words so inverted, yet he is also able to fly?
How am I to understand this now?
He then spoke in verse:
"Regarding those who possess merit, I harbor no heart of envy or resentment;
with the stone of Abhidharma, I grind and test them to know what is right and wrong.
It is like gold that has been gilded: when it is ground, its true color does not appear."
If gold is not genuine, it is known by rubbing it with a stone.
The Buddha seals [beings] with the seal of wisdom;
those who do not correspond with that seal cannot enter the exceedingly deep City of Ambrosia, for without the seal, one may not gain entrance.
"Wishing to enter the City of Ambrosia, I wish to laugh at them.
The people asked,
"If you are not an Arhat, how can you fly?"
At that time, the Dharma Master spoke again in verse:
“Whether it be Indra, or something created by illusion,
a thorn within the Buddha-dharma— this must surely be the work of Māra.”
Then the transformed bhikṣu returned to his original form, and he felt profound joy, exclaiming:
"Ah! The Buddha-dharma is most exquisite and subtle; by relying on hearing it, one can thus definitively discern the self."
He then spoke in verse:
“Śūra, the householder, and the others, Have already attained the purity of the Dharma-eye;
They cannot be shaken— This matter is not to be considered marvelous.”
Because of my own power of wisdom, you do not now see the Truth;
your mind is firm and cannot be moved—this is truly rare.
Lacking the power of noble wisdom, I am unable to move you.
This matter is truly rare: taking refuge in the nirvāṇa of the Buddha, for his words are true, the wise are unshakable.
The Buddha, with his knowledge of all modes, spoke of observing the arhat.
There is none who can destroy it; just as the tide of the great ocean never exceeds its limit,
so too the nature of the wind remains steadfast, and such is the speech spoken by the Tathāgata.
It is entirely without change;
supreme among all treatises, it is like the light of the sun,
extinguishing all darkness.
The Arhat is supremely real; his eloquence is clear and manifest, discerned by those who possess skillful observation.
Those who lack the power of observation do not perceive such a principle.
"Truthful speech and false speech—these two are as far apart as the Buddha’s words and the treatises of outsiders; their difference is likewise so.
*Mahāvyūha-sūtra*, Fascicle Seven.
Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra, Scroll Eight.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
45 (45) Furthermore, for curing the diseases of body and mind, there is only the Buddha’s word; therefore, one should listen with diligence.

Regarding the preaching of the Dharma, I have heard that in the past there was a prince in the land of Han whose eyes were covered by a film that spread over them entirely; consequently, he fell into total darkness and could see nothing, and though treated with various remedies, his condition could not be cured.
At that time, there were merchants from the kingdom of Takṣaśilā who came to the land of Han.
The King of Han asked the merchants, "My son suffers from an eye ailment; having traveled so far, are you perhaps able to treat it?"
The merchant replied, "In a foreign land there is a bhikṣu named Ghoṣa; only he can cure him.

Upon hearing this, the king immediately made grand preparations and sent his son toward the kingdom of Takṣaśilā. Having arrived in that country, he went before the Venerable Ghoṣa and spoke these words:
"I have come from afar specifically to treat my eyes; I only pray that you will take pity on me and heal them.
At that time, the Venerable One consented to treat his eyes and made many copper bowls, which he distributed to the assembly, saying to the people:
"Should anyone shed tears upon hearing my preaching of the Dharma, place them in these bowls."
Thereupon, he preached the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* for them.
Having heard it, the assembly wept and shed tears; they caught the tears in bowls, gathered them together, and went toward the prince.
Venerable Ghoṣa then took the tears of the assembly and placed them in his right palm, and spoke this verse:
"I have now proclaimed The profound twelvefold dependent origination, Which can dispel the darkness of ignorance; All who hear it shed tears."
If these words are true, let the tears of all people be gathered—
among humans, devas, and yakṣas— together with all waters that cannot be reached,
to wash the prince’s eyes so that he may be freed from obstructions and attain clear vision.
He immediately washed [the eyes] with tears, and the cataracts were eliminated.
At that time, the Venerable Ghoṣa, having cleared the prince’s eyes so they were bright and pure by washing them with his tears, spoke this verse in order to increase the faith of the great assembly:
“The Buddha-dharma is most truly real; It can swiftly eliminate cataracts and obstructions.”
"These tears can also be dispelled, Just as the sun melts ice and snow.

When the great assembly saw this, they joined their palms in reverence, their faith redoubled; they experienced what they had never known before, and their body hairs stood on end. They then spoke these verses:
"What you have done is marvelous, Just like manifesting supernormal powers."
"What medicine cannot heal, tears can wash away and eliminate.
At that time, the bhikṣus, moved by the Dharma they heard, wept with rain-like tears. The Venerable Ghoṣa addressed the assembled multitude:
"Even for such a matter as this, it is not difficult."

Throughout billions of kalpas in the past, the Tathāgata practiced asceticism; by virtue of these merits, he has gathered this medicinal elixir of the twelve links of dependent origination, which causes those who hear it to feel such profound sorrow that tears fall from their eyes.

The Vāsuki dragon spits forth great and virulent poison; yakṣas and malevolent spirits fill the house; and the fundamental rites of suppression by the Kimpuruṣas and Tālaras—these tears can completely extinguish them all without exception; this, indeed, is difficult!
How much more so, then, this obscuration, which is like the wing of a mosquito—what difficulty could there be in eliminating it?
Even if great clouds and mists, profound darkness and gloom, or fierce winds and torrential rains were to arise, these tears would likewise be able to extinguish them.
At that time, the army of elephants in rut and the infantry, though fully equipped with armor and weapons, shed tears and retreated from the battle array.
Who, upon hearing of the Dharma cultivated and accumulated by the One of All-Knowledge, would not shed tears?
"However, these tears can ward off calamities and afflictions, with the sole exception of past karma.

At that time, having regained his sight, the prince was filled with joy and exultation; furthermore, hearing the Dharma teaching, he grew weary of birth and death, attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, and conceiving a sense of wonder, he spoke this verse:
"Who, upon hearing the Buddha’s Dharma, Would not give rise to joy?"
I have developed deep reverence and faith, listening to the teaching of the Dharma with a sincere heart.
Having heard of such rare matters with my ears, the ailment of my eyes has also been eliminated;
both the eye of wisdom and the physical eye have attained complete purity.
For treating the eyes, there is nothing superior to the Great Sage;
I now prostrate in worship to the most excellent among all physicians.
With the medicinal jewel of singular wisdom, he has opened my two eyes to purity.
Among those with hearts in this world, who would not feel reverence and faith?
If one possesses even a modicum of wisdom, why would they not give rise to faith?
Śākyamuni, the Honored One, is the compassionate father of all sentient beings.
The speech is most exquisite, gentle and delightful;
having completed the work of deliverance, one has reached the further shore.
The faculty of mind and its objects are subtle; through mental attention, they should be understood.
"Even those from the borderlands can attain awakening.

(46) Furthermore, if one attains the four kinds of indestructible confidence (*catur-avetyaprasāda*), one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever violate or harm the aforementioned objects; therefore, one should diligently cultivate the four kinds of indestructible confidence.
I have heard that in the past, there was a criminal who was to be executed. At that time, it was the turn of a *caṇḍāla* to carry out the execution.

That *caṇḍāla* was a learned lay follower (*upāsaka*) who had attained the Path of Seeing (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); he was unwilling to kill the man. The official in charge of executions became extremely enraged and said to him:
"Do you now intend to defy the king's laws?"
The upāsaka said to the executioner, "You are utterly lacking in wisdom.
Why must the King now cause me such suffering by ordering the taking of life?

Although this physical body belongs to the King and I am a caṇḍāla because of it, that which is born from the noble lineage is called the Dharma-body; it does not belong to the King and is not subject to his control."
Then he spoke these verses:
“The Honored Śākyamuni, Possessing all-encompassing wisdom,
Was able to teach and transform during his causal stage, Thereby extinguishing and eliminating all faults.”
"The law of King Yama is such that one is first taught only when the fruit ripens;
suffering is explained only when one faces it. It is easily destroyed and can also be transgressed.
At that time, the executioners, because this person had violated the king’s prohibitions, led him before the king and said:
"This candāla does not follow the king's command.
The king said to him,
"For what reason do you not follow the king's command?"
He addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
You should now give rise to faith and arouse a heart of joy."
And he spoke in verse:
"Having removed the stains of my three poisons, I have attained the cause of nirvana;
To the presence of the World-Honored One of Ten Powers, Possessor of unsurpassed great compassion,"
"Having undertaken the observance of the precepts, one does not give rise to a harmful mind even toward a mosquito or an ant; how much less so toward a human being?
At that time, the king spoke these words:
"If you do not kill me, your own life will not be preserved.
This upāsaka, possessing the majestic power of one who has realized the Truths (dṛṣṭasatya), confronted the king without hesitation and spoke these words:
"This body belongs to you, O King; you have absolute mastery over my person."
"In my opinion," he said, "even if Śakra were to command me, I would still not comply.
When the king heard these words, he became extremely enraged and ordered the executioner to kill him.

The seven brothers of that Caṇḍāla father all refused to carry out the killing. Consequently, the king killed them one by one until only two remained. When it came to the sixth, the king commanded him to kill [the prince], but he also refused; the king then killed him as well. When it came to the seventh, he again refused to kill him, so the king killed him too.
The old mother addressed the king, saying:
"Please grant me the release of the youngest, the seventh one.
The king replied:
"Now, who are these people to you?
The old woman replied,
"They are all my sons."
The king asked again,
"Are not the previous six your sons?
He replied:
"It is so," [the Buddha] replied. The King asked,
"Why are you alone the seventh son?"
At that time, the old woman spoke in verse:
"Great King, you should know: these six sons have all realized the Truth;
they are all true sons of the Buddha, and they will certainly not commit evil."
Therefore, I have no fear.
Yet even an ordinary person, when pressed by the needs of body and life,
may commit various evil deeds.
I beg the King for his life; as a sovereign ruler, you possess the power of authority—only pray, let this child live.
For even those who have committed various evils, when ordinary people face the moment of death, [their minds are transformed].
"One perceives only their present manifestation, And does not see what follows;
One who can observe the retribution of future lives Is beyond the realm of ordinary beings.
At that time, the Great King spoke these words:
"I have never heard such words from the heterodox teachers before; now you have explained cause and effect as clearly as a bright lamp.

When the Caṇḍāla spoke thus, the king conceived a resolute conviction: "This is what is called a village of noble sages, not a village of outcasts. Though he bears the name 'Caṇḍāla,' he is in truth a practitioner of austerities. He does not even spare his own life, much less his kinsmen and relatives. He guards his precepts more fiercely than he guards wealth; disregarding both body and life as well as his family, he upholds only the prohibitive precepts."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Worldly people observe one's lineage, But do not observe their inner prohibitions and precepts.
Guarding the precepts constitutes true lineage; Even if one does not guard the precepts,"
The lineage shall perish.
That person is one of pure precepts; though born a caṇḍāla, his actions are truly pure.
Although I am born of royal lineage, [my conduct is not so].
"In truth, I am a caṇḍāla.
Lacking any heart of compassion, I have most wickedly killed a worthy man; I am truly a caṇḍāla.
At that time, the Great King, together with his retinue, went to the cemetery to make offerings to the corpse, and the King spoke again in verse:
"This concealment of virtuous merit is like ashes covering a fire;
though one does not speak of it oneself, the deeds one has performed are already manifest.
Śakra constantly makes offerings to such a steadfast practitioner."
"Without sparing his own body or life, he guards his conduct of the precepts.
At that time, the king, accompanied by his ministers and several hundred billion Brahmins, proceeded on foot to the cemetery and spoke these words:
"Though this Great Being is named a Caṇḍāla, he is in truth a great ṛṣi."
As he shed tears over the accumulated corpses, the king spoke again in verse:
“The valiant upholder of the precepts, With a blade, dismembered his body;
His skeletal remains lie cast upon the ground, And mud of blood besmears his frame.”
Because of upholding the prohibitive precepts, today I relinquish this body.
With a firm mind, I do not commit evil; guarding the precepts until death, those who have attained the flavor of the Buddha-dharma—all such wise ones should act in this way.
The king spoke again in verse:
"Blinded by ignorance and defiled by the stains of craving,
Attached to the sense faculties as 'mine,' They are restless and lack stability."
Not reckoning with evil karma, but grasping only at present pleasure, one is defiled by the stains of the fetters; the wise constantly observe this.
They perceive the body and wealth as fragile and precarious, like a tree on a riverbank.
"One shall never commit evil deeds; the water of wisdom washes away the stains of the mind.
At that time, the Great King drew near to the body of the Caṇḍāla; out of reverence for the Dharma, he circumambulated the corpse three times, knelt with palms joined, and spoke this verse:
"Homage and refuge to the Dharma, which is well able to observe."
One may abandon a short life, but one does not abandon the Dharma.
Even if one were to enter a forest of fire, it is impossible for one who has seen the Truth to destroy the precepts; this is a clear proof.
This person upholds the Buddha’s words, never wavering in resolve;
though he lies amidst mud and blood, it is for the sake of guarding the Buddha’s precepts.
When this corpse is cremated by fire, it is immediately transformed into ashes and dust.
"The name of the wholesome dharma of upholding the precepts remains the same even when the world comes to an end.
For what reason was this said?
It was to demonstrate that the realization of the Way is without change.

The Buddha taught that those who have seen the Truth (dṛṣṭasatya) can never be destroyed; while the four great elements may be broken, the four kinds of indestructible purity (catur-akṣaya-viśuddhi) can never be destroyed.

(47) Furthermore, when the mind is possessed of conceit (māna), there is no evil it will not commit. Although pride makes one exalt oneself, it is called "self-humiliation" [in its ultimate effect]. Therefore, one should sever conceit.

I have heard that not long after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he converted the thousand followers of the brothers Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and his kin; their afflictions being severed, their hair and beards fell away naturally, and they followed the World-Honored One to the kingdom of Kapilavastu, as is explained in detail in the *Buddhacarita*.

King Śuddhodana had been converted and became disciplined and compliant; however, the Śākyas, relying on their noble lineage, gave rise to arrogance. The Buddha Bhagavān was such that those who beheld him never grew weary of doing so; his body was full and well-proportioned, neither fat nor thin. The Brahmins, having practiced austerities for a long time, were emaciated and frail in form; though they harbored the Way within, their outward appearance was extremely wretched, and thus they were utterly ill-suited as they followed after the Buddha’s movements.
At that time, the father-king thought to himself:
"If the Śākyas were to leave the household life to follow the Buddha, it would be most fitting.
Having had this thought, he beat the drum and proclaimed:
"Please cause one person from the Śākya clan to be sent forth to leave the household life.
They immediately obeyed the king's command and sent one person from their family to be ordained as a renunciant.
At that time, while Upāli was shaving the hair and beards of the Śākyas and others, he wept and was distressed. The Śākyas said to him:
"Why are you weeping? Upāli replied,
"Now that all these sons of the Śākya have gone forth as monks, by what means shall I live?"

When the Śākyas heard Upāli’s words, all those Śākyas who had left the household life took all the clothing, necklaces, and ornaments they were wearing and formed them into a single heap of jewels, giving it all to Upāli. They said to Upāli:
"With these various items, you shall have sufficient means to provide for yourself for the rest of your life."
Having heard these words, Upāli immediately felt weary and detached, and spoke thus:
"Now that you all have grown weary of and discarded these precious ornaments for adorning the body, why should I now take them up?"
He then spoke these verses:
"These Śākyas have cast aside all precious jewels,
As if discarding foul excrement, Along with all manner of grass and leaves."
Since he has abandoned all attachment, how could he now greedily grasp?
Even if I were to take hold of a heap of jewels, my inner mind would surely become attached;
to reckon them as "mine" is a source of great affliction.
The Śākyas have abandoned what was their affliction; if I were now to take it up, that would be a great calamity.
A dog comes to devour it; I am merely gathering what others have discarded.
What difference is there between [this] and a dog?
Just as when one is freed from the four kinds of poison, the roots of goodness are stirred within,
and one no longer clings to a heap of jewels.
"I shall now surely renounce [the world] and go to the presence of the World-Honored One, seeking the Dharma of going forth.
Having spoken this verse, Upāli further spoke in verse:
"Seeing others attain the supreme Dharma, a heart of joyful admiration first arose within me."
"May I myself likewise attain such supreme success as he has;
I now wish to go forth for myself and shall diligently apply the necessary means.
At that time, Upāli again thought to himself:
"I am now determined that I must certainly go forth into the homeless life; I shall simply seek it with diligence.

A thousand brahmins have already gone forth under the Buddha, and five hundred of the Śākya kṣatriya clan have also gone forth. While both the brahmin and kṣatriya lineages are noble, I am a śūdra of low birth and engaged in menial labor. Is it possible for me to obtain the going forth among such superior ones?"
"What power do I possess now?
How can I go forth into homelessness within this place?
He then spoke in verse:
"The Kṣatriyas are of pure lineage, and the Brāhmaṇas are highly learned;
born from wombs as precious as mani-jewels, they have all gathered here together.
I am of the Śūdra caste—how can I participate?"
Like fragments of broken iron interspersed with genuine gold, so is the Bhagavān Buddha;
I have heard that he possesses all-encompassing wisdom.
Now I shall go to him, the one who has compassion for all beings.
What should be purified and what should not be purified, what should be renounced and what should not be renounced—
none of the various followers of external paths know the place of liberation;
only those who have extinguished the fetters can know liberation.
Then Upāli, having recited these verses, went to the place where the World-Honored One was. Kneeling with his right knee on the ground and joining his palms, he spoke in verse:
"Among the four castes, Is it possible for all to go forth [into homelessness]?"
Can we attain the bliss of nirvāṇa and liberation?
O Excellent Savior, whose great compassion is universally impartial,
out of pity please grant us your hearing, so that we may attain the opportunity to go forth.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Upāli’s mind was compliant and his roots of goodness were mature and ready for conversion, raised his right hand adorned with the marks and signs of excellence and rubbed it upon Upāli’s head, saying to him:
“I grant you permission to go forth.”

The secret teachings of the non-Buddhists are not revealed to their disciples; the Tathāgata is not so, for with great compassion and impartiality, he teaches the Dharma equally without favoritism. He reveals the supreme path to them and delivers them from suffering, just as one selling goods in a marketplace does not discriminate between the noble and the lowly. The Buddha-dharma is likewise: it makes no distinction between the poor and the wealthy, nor between different castes.
He then spoke in verse:
"Who drinks from a clear stream yet remains unsatiated by their thirst?
Who holds aloft a blazing lamp yet does not dispel the darkness?"
The Dharma of the knowledge of all modes is universally shared by all beings;
who among those who practice it would not attain the supreme and wondrous meaning?
It is like eating rock honey: both the noble and the lowly alike eliminate their afflictions.
Whether Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa, within the Buddha-dharma all are universally equal;
when one attains the exhaustion of the three times, all castes are identical and without distinction.
It is like three kinds of medicine, which counteract wind, cold, and heat.
Medicine does not discriminate among castes; it can cure both the noble and the lowly.
The medicine of the Dharma is likewise: it can cure greed, anger, and delusion, removing them from all four castes without distinction between high and low.
Furthermore, just as fire burns objects, making no distinction between fine or coarse wood,
so too does the sting of venom act like fire, making no distinction between the noble and the lowly.
Just as water used for bathing removes the grime from all four castes alike, [so too does the Dharma cleanse all].
"Having reached the limit where suffering ends, one will be universally liberated from all kinds [of afflictions].

At that time, the World-Honored One—like a clear sky free of all clouds and mists—emitted a deep and far-reaching voice like the sound of thunder; like a great dragon king, like a bull king, like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, like a king of bees, like a king of men, and like celestial music, he uttered a Brahma-voice and addressed Upāli:
"Would you like to leave the household life?"
Having heard these words, Upāli felt great joy in his heart; with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying, "I wish to leave the household life.
The Buddha said to him:
“Upāli! Welcome, bhikṣu!
You shall now here cultivate the holy life well.”

Upon hearing these words, their hair and beards fell away naturally and the *kāṣāya* robes appeared upon their bodies; their deportment was perfectly composed and their faculties were tranquil and settled, just like veteran bhikṣus.
The five hundred Śākyas all received full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. The Buddha said:
"I shall now employ skillful means to eliminate the prideful minds of the Śākyas."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Śākyas:
"You all should now pay homage to the elder bhikṣus.

The elder Kauṇḍinya, the bhikṣu Abhimāra, and the others paid homage in succession; Upāli was seated at the very bottom of the assembly, while Śākyamuni Bhadrika was the foremost leader among all the Śākyas.

At that time, the Śākyas, out of reverence for the Buddha’s teaching, proceeded in order to pay homage at his feet until they reached Upāli. Upon seeing the extraordinary nature of his feet, they immediately looked up at his face; at that moment, the Śākyas were filled with great wonder and astonishment, like a mountain torrent cascading down and striking a cliff to form eddies.

They spoke these words: “We are of the Kṣatriya caste, born of the Solar Lineage, and are honored by the world. Why is it that we now pay homage to one of such lowly caste as our own servant, a member of the barber clan?”
"We shall now go before the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and fully recount these matters.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Do you also pay respect at the place where Upāli resides?
The Buddha told the Śākyas:
"Now, my clan, this Dharma is the place where pride is severed."
Then the Śākyas said to the Buddha,
"He is of the Śūdra caste.
The Buddha told them:
"All things are impermanent; their lineages are not fixed. Since impermanence is of a single flavor, so too are these lineages. What difference is there between them?
Then the Śākyas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This clan of those who shave their hair has arisen from within our solar lineage.
The Buddha told the Śākyas and others:
"The entire world is like a dream and like an illusion; what distinction can there be among lineages?"
The Śākyas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This man is our servant, while we are his masters.”
The Buddha answered Śakra, saying:
"All those in the world are slaves to affection and love; as long as they have not escaped birth and death, there is no difference between the noble and the lowly. Cast away your arrogance."
At that time, the Śākyas, exceptionally handsome and radiant like blossoming flowers, joined their palms toward the Buddha and, harboring doubts and hesitation, spoke these words:
"Will you truly require us to prostrate at the feet of Upāli?"
The Buddha told the Śākyas:
"It is not only with me; the dharma of renunciation for all Buddhas is exactly like this.

When the Śākyas had heard the Buddha’s repeated teaching on the dharma of renunciation, they stood solemnly like trees in a windless place. Their minds were filled with grief and distress, and they spoke with one voice:
"How can we contravene the Buddha's instructions?
We should follow the Buddha's teachings.
Thus spoke the wise men of former times.
"The reason the Tathāgata first ordained Upāli was to destroy the prideful minds of the Śākyas and others.

Thereupon, the Śākyas abandoned their pride and conformed to the dharma of renunciation; this was also so that future nobles who renounce the world would have a model to follow. Having uprooted the long-practiced arrogance of the Bhadras and other Śākyas, they now prostrated themselves at the feet of Upāli.
At the moment of his prostration, the great earth, its cities, mountains, forests, rivers, and oceans all shook; the devas proclaimed:
"Today, the mountain of pride of the Śākya clan has collapsed."
Then he spoke this verse:
"Alas! Having abandoned pride— Pride in lineage, physical beauty, strength, and wealth— He has followed the Buddha's teaching, Like a tree leaning with the wind."
The Kṣatriya of the Solar Lineage prostrates to Upāli;
having abandoned the mind of pride, all his faculties are tranquil and composed.
These great and eminent persons are truly without guile or hypocrisy.
Endowed with all blessings and virtues, their number is like that of the bamboo groves.
Among the renowned Brahmins, the noble Kṣatriyas,
and such illustrious and virtuous multitudes, they have entered the Dharma of the Muni.
Adorning the assembly of noble ones, like stars surrounding the moon arrayed in the sky— ah, how the Dharma flourishes!
The great ocean of the Tathāgata is filled with the water of supreme merit.
Serene and overflowing within, it is the destination of all rivers;
Of all the supreme wisdom in the world, there is none that does not turn toward the Buddha-dharma.
The multitudes of humans and devas increase therein; This is the essential path for escaping suffering.
"The Tathāgata skillfully discerns and teaches the Dharma to extinguish pride;
his assembly of disciples is of a single flavor, just as the ocean is of a single uniform taste.
For what reason was this said?
The Buddha-dharma appears in the world for the purpose of severing arrogance.

(48) Furthermore, one who has attained the vision of the Truths cannot be deceived by celestial Māras or various non-Buddhist practitioners; therefore, one should diligently apply skillful means and resolutely seek the vision of the Truths.
I have heard that in the past, the householder Śūra was extremely stingy. When Śāriputra and others visited his home, they spoke this verse:
"The evil realms are as deep as the ocean; A distracted mind is like turbid water.
Swept away by the current of stinginess, One says, 'I have nothing at all.'"
The great river of envy, filled with schools of fish and turtles of wrong views,
flows ceaselessly through such a place;
now one must uproot the root of stinginess to bring to fruition the rewards of generosity.
“The World-Honored One of Great Compassion, the fearless son of the Śākyas, sees all those submerged in suffering and distress; we ought to rescue them.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa rose early, donned his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the house of the elder Śūra to praise the virtue of giving.
At that time, because of his displeasure, the elder felt as if a spear were piercing his heart; he said to Kāśyapa,
"Have you come at my invitation,
or do you wish to beg for alms?"
Kāśyapa replied,
"I always beg for food.
The householder said to him:
"You should go for alms at the proper time.
Kāśyapa then departed.
In this manner, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the other great disciples arrived at the house one after another, but they were not received or waited upon at all.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to his house and said to Śūra:
"You should now practice the five great gifts.
Upon hearing this, Śūra was deeply distressed in mind and thought to himself:
“I am not yet able to practice even small acts of giving; why then do you tell me to perform the five great gifts?
Is there no other teaching within the Dharma of the Tathāgata?
My fellow disciples have instructed me in giving, and now the World-Honored One also instructs me in giving.”
Having had this thought, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am unable to perform even a minute and small gift, much less the five great gifts.”
The Buddha told the householder:

"Abstaining from killing is called the great gift; abstaining from stealing, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, and abstaining from drinking intoxicants—such as these are called the five great gifts."
Having heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy, and he thought to himself:
"Since these five things do not diminish by even a hair’s breadth yet earn one the name of a 'great donor,' why should I not practice them?"
Having formed this thought, he conceived a profound sense of joy, faith, and reverence toward the World-Honored One, and spoke these words:
"The Buddha is a Tamer of Men; this is truly not false. Were it not for the World-Honored One, who else could understand and speak in such a way?"
"Who would not respectfully obey him? None dare to contravene his will.
He then spoke in verse:
"In physical appearance, there is none equal to him; In talent and eloquence, he has no peer in this world."
"The World-Honored One speaks at the proper time; his Brahma-voice is exquisite and beautiful.
What he teaches is never in vain; all who hear it obtain its fruit.

Having spoken this verse, he felt a profound sense of joy toward the Buddha. He immediately entered his storehouse to take two pieces of fine cloth to offer to the Buddha, but then thought to himself that two might be too much and wished instead to give only one.
Furthermore, he thought again and, because he resented the small amount, gave him two more pieces.
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, spoke this verse:
"When giving and when quarreling, The two are said to be equal."
"The two virtues abide in neither; they are the domain of the weak and inferior man.
Whether at the time of giving or at the time of strife, the conditions for their action are identical.

At that time, having heard this verse, Śūra was filled with joy and exultation, thinking, "The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, knows my thoughts. Overcoming his stinginess, he took hold of the cotton cloth and offered it to the Buddha.

The Buddha, knowing that Śūra was filled with sincere joy, preached the Dharma according to his needs, thereby destroying the twenty billion roots of *ātman*-view and causing him to attain the stage of *srotāpanna*.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and returned to his dwelling; Śūra, having joyfully escorted the Buddha, returned to his home, his heart overflowing with celebration.
At that time, seeing Śūra filled with joy, the Māra King thought to himself:
"I shall now go to where Śūra is and destroy his virtuous mind.

Having formed this thought, he transformed himself into the body of a Buddha, complete with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and went to Śūra’s house, where he immediately spoke these verses:
“His body is like a pure mountain of gold, his circular halo most brilliantly radiant;
with sovereign power he manifests transformations, his stately gait like that of an elephant king.
He enters the Śūramgama Gate like the sun entering white clouds.”
"Those who behold him can never tire of the sight; his brilliance is like that of hundreds of thousands of suns.
At that time, the light shone upon the house of Śūla. Śūla was startled and wondered, "Who is this person?"
Then he spoke in verse:
"Like a mass of refined pure gold filling my home,
It is as if the sun has risen from the earth, Its radiance twice as bright as usual."
Having spoken this verse, he was filled with supreme joy; as if nectar had been sprinkled upon his body, he said:
"I possess great merit that the Tathāgata now enters my home once again. Although it is not rare for him to come a second time,"
"Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, constantly takes it as his vocation to deliver beings through compassion.
He then spoke a verse, saying:
“His head is like a madhuka fruit; his skin is like pure, refined gold.
Between his brows is the mark of the white tuft of hair;
his eyes are pure, long, and wide, like blossoming blue lotuses. He is tranquil, concentrated, and supremely tamed.”
Walking with fearless, slow, and measured steps, his countenance was exceptionally sublime;
a halo a full fathom wide adorned him naturally.
With courageous vigor he proclaimed: "I am now truly a Buddha."
At that time, the Māra-king, having adorned himself most elaborately, stood before Śūra and addressed him, saying:

"What I previously stated—that the five aggregates of clinging arise from the accumulation of suffering, and that the eightfold noble path is practiced to extinguish these five aggregates of clinging—this was a false teaching."
At that time, having heard these words, Śūra was filled with great doubt and wonder:
"The appearance is similar to the Buddha's, yet what is spoken is not so;
is this a dream, or is my mind deranged?"
"Listening to what he says, it is utterly full of greed and envy. What kind of evil person has manifested in the form of a Buddha? He is like a black venomous snake amidst a cluster of flowers.
I now know for certain that this is surely Māra; he is like a needle-seller who goes to the house of a master needle-maker seeking to sell needles."
"You, Pāpīyān! Now listen to what I, a son of the Buddha, proclaim.
He spoke in verse:
"One might yet cause Mount Sumeru to tremble by fanning it with a goose-wing,
but to cause the mind that perceives the Truth to waver and follow you—
such a thing can never happen."
They cannot delude the Dharma-eye; because the Buddha knows this matter, he has spoken thus.
Those who have attained the Dharma-eye cannot distinguish between the true and the false.
I have seen the Honored Muni;
having seen the one who has extinguished the fetters, I shall never follow your words.
You merely exhaust yourself in vain; you cannot delude me.
I now truly know you: you are indeed the evil Pāpīyān.
One who has seen the Four Noble Truths can never be moved.
It is like one who attempts to deceive a goldsmith by plating a coin with gold and trying to sell it as pure gold.
This matter is likewise difficult to accomplish; outwardly it manifests the appearance of gold, yet within it is actually bronze.
Used to cover a donkey, its form and color deceive the physical eye.
The words you utter reveal your falsehood.
The characteristic of wind is ever-constant; even if the light of the sun were to become dark, or the moon were to possess the quality of heat, it could not cause one to see the Truth.
Yet my mind remains unshaken.
Grasses, trees, tiles, and stones, as well as deer, birds, and wild beasts—
all these may take the form of the Buddha-image, yet they cannot move my will.
Even if all things were subject to transformation, how much less could you—
a single demonic body— shake me?
Thus he sternly rebuked Pāpīyas, like a man of great courage and strength.
When he entered the battle and struck the weak,
the Māras were immediately terrified and quickly returned to their celestial palaces;
at the dwelling place of the Lion King, even elephants arrived only to flee in haste upon encountering him.
Pāpīyān is likewise; seeing the place where those who have realized the Truths abide, none of the Māras dare to linger there.
(49) Furthermore, if one does not attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one will not attain certainty at the time of death.

I have heard that in the past, during the time of King Bāsu, there was an attendant named Tacchanaṅga who was dearly beloved by the king. Because of slanderous accusations, he was imprisoned; yet further slanders were brought against him, and the king, filled with great wrath, dispatched men to execute him.
At that time, his kinsmen all came to surround him and said to him:
"Your intelligence and insight surpass those of ordinary men; why is it that your mind is now so agitated?"
"Now that the time of death has arrived, what is the most painful thing?
Nāga replied,
"The terror of fearing death makes my mind unable to find stability."
He then spoke in verse:
"In the past, when separated from my parents, my kinsmen, and my retinue,
the grief and distress that arose were for me the ultimate among all sufferings."
At this present time of death, the suffering is such that all other sufferings are but minor;
when one reflects upon the midst of all sufferings, even the suffering of death is not great.
Not knowing the place of rebirth, the mind and body are scorched by feverish distress.
Now departing with extreme speed, one knows not where the destination lies.
Since the body has not yet left desire behind, who could fail to feel alarm and dread?
The spirit is utterly distracted and troubled, like a blind man treading a long road.
In the end, where does it go?
The mind and its intentions utterly collapse and abandon themselves, like a heap of sand scattering; there is no place where they can be restrained.
As the Buddha has taught: "The mind exists because it is driven by the mind."
I am now inverted and confused; it will be difficult for me to be born in a favorable realm.
Because my mind is autonomous, I can take any rebirth at will;
yet now my mind is restless and agitated, unable to maintain itself in stillness.
In the past, I was ignorant and shallow, Greedy for and attached to the pleasures of the five desires;
I could not contemplate my own inner body, Nor fix my mindfulness on a wholesome object.
Upon what mountain forest shall I rely? Sitting upright, I shall fix my mindfulness there.

Regarding such sublime matters as these, it is only now that I have conceived a longing for them; for he has attained the treasure-store of dhyāna, due to its peace and tranquility. I call to mind the meaning of the verses spoken by the Muni: [The three verses follow: "Even though one may live a hundred years in a forest, heedless and with senses uncontrolled, Better than that is a single day lived by one who dwells in the forest, mindful and with senses well-restrained.

Even though one may live a hundred years in negligence, heedless and with senses uncontrolled, Better than that is a single day lived by one who practices diligence, mindful and with senses well-restrained. I reflect upon the meaning of these three verses.
Acting with negligence and contrary to the Dharma, practicing what should not be done,
abandoning what is meaningful and beneficial, and becoming greedily attached to beloved objects—
just as one is about to cultivate the grounds of virtue, death suddenly arrives without one’s realizing it.
Having strayed from that level and right path, they pursue this false and perilous track;
like a broken axle suddenly halted, they sit waiting in extreme distress.
Having transgressed the Dharma of suchness, they practice matters contrary to reason.
"When death arrives for the foolish worldling, the axle breaks and they are gripped by grief and distress.
For what reason is this said?

Because they previously failed to observe correctly while forming the thought of death, they only practice meditative contemplation when facing the terrors of the end; since they have not broken the five desires, they do not know where they are going, and thus they feel regret and are struck with fear."
Then he spoke this verse:
"The wise person should fix their mindfulness and eliminate thoughts of the five desires;
one who diligently maintains the mind will have no regrets at the time of death."
When the mind and intentions are focused and singular, there are no confused or distracted thoughts;
the wise person diligently grasps the mind so that it does not scatter at the time of death.
One should be single-mindedly intent upon the object of meditation and practice until the mind reaches a state of singular focus.
At the moment of death, one will inevitably become distracted.
It is like using a grindstone to train a horse;
when it comes time for battle, it circles around instead of charging straight ahead.

One who does not practice right contemplation fails to restrain the five sense faculties; even at the time of death, their mind will be difficult to control. It is like armor and mail within a storehouse that have become worn and old; when facing an enemy on the battlefield, one's weapons and armor are shattered and ruined. Likewise, for one who has not practiced the restraint of the mind, it is the same at the end of life.
50. Furthermore, those who possess genuine merit should be honored, and the wise ought to show reverence to the virtuous.

I have heard that in the past, in the kingdom of Āvanti, there was a king named Prasenajit and a younger brother named Śūrasena; for the sake of disputing over their kingdoms, the two fought against one another.
Sūlibha threw his noose and caught Indrabhūti by the head; having caught him, he pulled it tight. Indrabhūti was struck with extreme terror and made this vow:
"If I am now released, I shall perform a Pañcavārṣika assembly within the Buddha-dharma."

When he made this vow, the noose was instantly severed; he conceived deep faith and reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, and immediately commanded a minister named Pūrṇamitra to prepare for the Pañcavārṣika festival.
At that time, the minister immediately followed the king’s command and prepared a pañcavārṣika festival, ordering people to provide additional food.

While seated at the head of the assembly, the minister saw the senior monk (sthavira) leave half of his food uneaten. After the senior monk had finished reciting the verses of blessing, the minister took this remaining food and placed it into his own bowl, then rose from his seat and departed. He did this a second and a third time.
Upon seeing this, the minister conceived a lack of faith and thought to himself,
"This bhikṣu must certainly be impure.
Having formed this thought, he reported the matter in its entirety to the king.
The king asked the great minister,
"Have you attained full confidence?
The minister replied to the king:
"I cannot have faith. Why?
Because when the Elder Bhikṣu rose from his seat after leaving half of his food behind, he must have given that food to another woman; therefore, I have conceived doubt."
Upon hearing these words, the king covered his ears with both hands and said to the ministers:
"Do not speak such words; do not now recklessly judge others."
"You lack the power of wisdom; how can you possibly judge others?
As the Buddha has said:
'If one recklessly evaluates sentient beings, one will surely bring harm upon oneself.'"
"Do not hold such perverted and false views.
He then spoke in verse:
"Through precepts, concentration, wisdom, and tranquility, One attains great learning, awakening, and insight."
This is a son of the Sugata, Concealing his virtues like fire covered by ash;
He has long dwelt in wisdom, ethical discipline, and conduct.
As the World-Honored One has taught, you should not dwell together with him.
How does one know their conduct?
It is likened to four kinds of people; only the virtuous man is truly able to discern it with skill.
Only one who has spoken as a Buddha, World-Honored One, or is equal to a Buddha may be measured as a person.
Therefore, you should not disparage the disciples of the Buddha by giving rise to arbitrary discriminatory thoughts.
For example, if a hidden treasure were covered by earth upon its surface, who would know there was a jewel beneath?
You need not depart from where you stand; you should go yourself to investigate.
"From this day forward, I shall personally provide offerings to the Saṃgha;
like a fool taking excellent medicine that turns into poison.
At that time, the Great King went in person to the midst of the Saṃgha and made offerings to the assembly of monks, serving them with his own hands.
At that time, the Elder left his food as before; having finished the ritual of blessing, he immediately took it away.
The King then followed behind the Elder and said to him, "Elder, you are advanced in years;
you may give me your alms-bowl so that I may carry it."
At that time, the Elder would not give him the bowl; though the other followed him insistently demanding the bowl, he refused to give it even as they reached the village of Caṇḍālas.
Then the Elder spoke this verse:
"I know your pure faith, Your compassion that can rescue and deliver."
Although this king was born in a degenerate age, his majestic deportment is most solemn and orderly;
even the victorious kings of antiquity could not equal him.
They do not know of my ascetic practices, but see only that he has left the household life.
Never having come or gone, nor being subject to any requital,
you are yet able to love and revere me deeply, your kindness exceeding that of a compassionate father.
Though I do not see your heart, all your faculties are serene and joyful.
The sun rises in the sky, yet it is not seen as dense clouds cover it;
though such an obscuration exists, one knows the sun has risen by the blooming of flowers.
Knowing that the King possesses profound faith—extraordinary and unprecedented—[I have come].
He was able to humble himself and bend before me, wishing to hold my almsbowl;
though possessed of honor, nobility, and prosperity, he remained free from arrogance and negligence.
While other kings enjoy sovereign power, their eyes are blinded by pride and conceit.
By committing various evil deeds, one falls headlong into many failures.
One who possesses courage and wisdom knows how to skillfully employ wealth for giving;
viewing the body as an illusion or a mirage, they know how to grasp the solid and essential Dharma.
To speak briefly, all things increase;
as you have disciplined yourself, you are supreme among those who transform others.
Follow the path practiced by the noble and excellent, and proceed in accordance with the assembly.
"I have now accepted the King's offerings; since the King has humbly requested my bowl from me, my provisions are sufficient and there is no need to take back the bowl.
At that time, the King became even more earnest and repeatedly followed his request for the bowl. The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"For what reason does the King now wish to obtain my bowl?"
He immediately entered meditative concentration and observed that the king sought the bowl because he wished to subdue his great minister;
therefore, he spoke this verse:
“An ordinary person, ignorant and dark, Desires to move Mount Sumeru.”
I shall now give him my bowl, so as to protect his mind and intentions.
Whether he should encounter blame or praise, my own mind remains entirely unchanged;
yet those who harbor distrust toward me will cause harm to many people.
Having spoken this verse, he set down his bowl and gave it to the king.
The king immediately took the bowl, just as an elephant’s trunk grasps a blue lotus, and followed the bhikṣu to the house of the caṇḍāla.
Then that bhikṣu invited the king to enter his dwelling, but the king was unwilling to enter and remained standing before the gate.

The bhikṣu’s elderly mother had previously attained the fruit of anāgāmin; she possessed the divine eye, was able to know the minds of others, and could also discern the causes and conditions of others' roots of goodness.
Then the old woman addressed the king, saying:
"O King, do not be timid; come and enter my house.
She then spoke this verse:
"You should not give rise to doubt; this is the house of a Śūdra, not the home of a Caṇḍāla. The first son has attained Arhatship;
the third is a Srotāpanna. I am the All-Knowing One."
The Buddha’s upāsikā dwells in the stage of Anāgāmin.
You need only observe her conduct of the precepts; do not inquire about her place of birth.
Take only my virtue and the Way; do not look at my family or kin.
Having finally been born into this family, his merit is most distinguished;
it is like fine, genuine gold emerging from amidst sand and stones,
or fire produced from *eranda* wood, or a lotus flower growing from the mud.
In observing a person’s attainment of the Way and its virtue, why must one concern themselves with their lineage?
Whether it be *eranda* or sandalwood, when ignited by fire they both cook food;
both achieve their purpose, and in their merit they are equal and no different.

When the king heard this verse spoken by the old woman, he exclaimed, "Alas! This is truly a great being within the Dharma. Out of the Buddha’s great compassion, he enables even a caṇḍāla to attain the state of deathlessness, making no distinction of caste. The Dharma taught by the Buddha allows even among caṇḍālas to let out the lion’s roar."
The king further reflected:
"If one honors based on lineage, one loses merit; if one honors based on merit, one should not discriminate against a caṇḍāla."
The king spoke again in verse:
"One should honor virtue alone; One should not regard the place of birth.
As the Brahmins have said by way of simile: A lotus flower grows from the mud."
The gods and the asuras wear him upon their heads with reverence;
yet when a brahmin commits a transgression, the wise all abandon him.
If he should commit an evil deed, can it be said that he is without fault?
Nevertheless, it is indeed a transgression.
How could one not accept that which possesses virtue?
Indeed, it further possesses merit.
Such a caṇḍāla, I should offer worship to;
such a caṇḍāla who practices asceticism in the mountain forests—
this one is called a sage, not a caṇḍāla.
The caṇḍāla kills the deer, and the king eats its flesh;
he also takes the arrow that was made by the other and uses it to shoot.
For this reason, I ought to act in accordance with this principle.
“If there is one of virtue among the Caṇḍālas, why would one not take them up?
Having spoken this verse, the king entered her house, knelt with palms joined, and reflected thus:
“Should I first pay homage to my mother?”
"Should one not first pay homage to the Buddha?
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has shown the Caṇḍāla this true path; he is able to show all sentient beings the secure and true path. One should first pay homage to the Buddha."
He then spoke in verse:
“Homage to the Ascetic Sage, the supreme among the Kings of Physicians!
For the sake of the Buddha, I now pay reverence to this lowly one.”
Just as by relying on Mount Sumeru, Crows and deer alike appear golden;
Having heard this from another, I now realize it through direct experience:
Relying upon the Buddha-Sumeru, Even the lowly become noble.
In the ocean of all-encompassing wisdom, with a pure mind, he has crossed to the other shore.
Only the Buddha saves the world; his compassion is equal and free from ill will.
Toward all sentient beings alike, he is able to act as their most intimate kinsman.
"One is able to distinguish and explain many kinds from a single liberation;
yet the heretics, mad and inverted, falsely differentiate various lineages.
When the Great King had spoken this verse, he paid homage and departed.
The Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra (Treatise on the Great Adornments), Scroll Eight;
The Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra (Treatise on the Great Adornments), Scroll Nine.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
51. Furthermore, because of the causes and conditions of ill will (*vyāpāda*), the Buddha is unable to provide counsel;
therefore, the wise should sever ill will.

I have heard that in the past, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were divided into two factions due to their quarrels, and because of those disputes, they spent a long time contending with one another over points of doctrine.
At that time, the World-Honored One, possessing supreme great compassion, restrained the bhikṣus with his hand marked by the wheel-sign and spoke this verse:
“Bhikṣus, do not engage in strife; Strife brings about much ruin and failure.
Competing for victory and defeat without ceasing, The succession of disputes remains unending.”
One is censured by the world, and that which is unbeneficial increases.
A bhikṣu seeking victory should distance himself from sensual desire;
having abandoned home, wife, and children, he seeks liberation with his mind.
One should follow the rules of the renunciant life; do not do what ought not to be done.
One should use the hook of wisdom to turn back the mind of arrogance, for it gives rise to strife—the very root of resentment and harm.
Relying on the dharma of renunciation, one should not give rise to what is unwholesome;
it would be like blazing fire emerging from clear, cool water.
Having donned the robes of a dyed color, one ought to cultivate wholesome dharmas.
This robe is suited for serenity; one should always contemplate self-discipline and gentleness.
Why, wearing these robes, do you stare with wide-open eyes, knitting your brows and furrowing your forehead, giving rise to thoughts of anger?
One should mindfully reflect upon one’s robes and the shaved head as the mark of one’s vocation;
having renounced everything, why engage in further strife?
With such a mark as this, one ought to sever all contention.
Then that bhikṣu joined his palms toward the Buddha and said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!
I pray that the Buddha will grant me forgiveness; those other bhikṣus have treated me with contempt.”
"How can one not retaliate?
He then spoke in verse:
"When one who is difficult to tame is met with patience, he only regards that person all the more with contempt."
When one gives rise to patience, desire for peace, and humility, the other’s anger increases all the more.
To respond to evil with further abuse is like striking a stone with an axe;
seeing such abuse directed at him, that person thinks, "I too must surely retaliate."
At that time, the World-Honored One, like a compassionate father, spoke these words:
"Those who have left the household life should diligently apply skillful means to sever anger. For even if one follows along with anger, it is utterly contrary to principle; anger has many faults."
Then he spoke this verse:
"Hatred is like that sharp blade, Severing and cutting off intimacy and affection;
Hatred can bring about the destruction Of those who follow the Dharma and conform to the Vinaya."
One who suffers from anger abandons the homeless life; it is not a place where one should dwell.
Resentment is like a butcher’s yoke; anger is indeed a source of terror.
It is a house of contempt and a seed of ugliness.
Harsh speech is the companion of [suffering], a fierce fire that burns the forest of the mind.
It is the guide to the evil realms, the gateway to strife, resentment, and harm.
It is the bed and bedding of ill repute, and the swift origin of all evils.
"Those who harbor ill will are reviled, censured, and disparaged by others; you should now contemplate such faults.
He then spoke these verses:
"Hatred is more violent than a fierce tiger, Like a malignant ulcer, difficult to touch."
A venomous snake is difficult to look upon with joy, and so it is with one who is full of anger.
One who is angry suffers even in sleep; their good reputation is ruined.
When the fire of hatred blazes intensely, one does not perceive what they themselves have done.
Nor do those committed by others enter into their reckoning; if they are in a place of jesting and laughter,
they will not be tolerated by the multitude.
Because of hatred, one enters not [into peace]; the hater is impossible to love, for such matters are extremely numerous.
Even with a hundred tongues to speak, one could never finish describing them.
I have spoken of this briefly;
it would be insufficient to discuss it in full detail. Having committed evil through anger and hatred, one suffers the fever of remorse in both body and mind.
"Therefore, those who possess wisdom should sever their competitive anger.

At that time, although the Tathāgata preached the Dharma to the bhikṣus in various ways, their anger and resentment still did not subside. Because of this, the devas and benevolent spirits all became incensed and spoke in verse:
"Just as if one were to place a maṇi jewel Into turbid water..."
The water immediately becomes clear and limpid, with no further signs of turbidity or impurity.
So it is with the Tathāgata, that jewel among men;
for the sake of the bhikṣus, he teaches various wondrous and excellent dharmas in accordance with skillful means.
These bhikṣus have minds that are turbid and not yet pure;
it would be better for them to be impure water, which a jewel’s power can make clear,
than to be such bhikṣus who, upon hearing the Dharma taught by the Buddha, [remain as they are].
Yet within your mind, it remains turbid and impure.
Just as the sun illuminates the world and dispels all darkness,
the Buddha-sun draws near to you, yet the darkness of your heart is exceedingly great.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, rebuked the bhikṣus for carrying such a heavy burden; with a heart of compassion, he further recounted the story of King Dīrghāyu.
Yet these bhikṣus knit their brows and frowned, still refusing to desist, and spoke thus:
"The Buddha is the Lord of Dharma; wait but a moment, for we shall know it ourselves."
At that time, having heard these words, the Tathāgata immediately left this place and, traveling twelve yojanas away, sat beneath a tree in the Śāla grove, reflecting thus:
"I shall now distance myself from the quarreling bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī."
At that time, there was an elephant king who, having avoided the rest of the herd, came to stand beneath a tree not far from the Buddha; with his eyes closed, he remained there, thinking to himself:
"I have escaped the herd and attained supreme purity."
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in that elephant’s mind, spoke this verse:
“The tusks of this elephant are exceedingly long; He dwells apart from the crowd, delighting in tranquility.
He delights in solitude, and I am likewise; I dwell far removed from places of strife and assembly.”
Having spoken these verses, he entered into a profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

At that time, the bhikṣus felt regret for not having accepted the Buddha’s teaching; the devas were also incensed, and all those in the land who heard of it gave rise to anger, crying out, "Shame! Shame! (chì-chì).
Then the bhikṣus said to one another:
"How may we once again behold the Buddha?
We should join our palms together and entreat the Buddha."
Then he spoke this verse:
"We have transgressed the Buddha’s teaching as proclaimed by the World-Honored One of the three realms:
that the evil fault of anger dwells within my heart."
The fierce flames of regret and remorse Burn away the forest of my mind.
How excellent, O Compassionate One! I pray you, speak for me once more.
I now make this supreme vow: I shall surely seek liberation.
"From this day forward, I would rather give up my own flesh than ever transgress the Buddha's teaching.
Knowing what the bhikṣus were thinking in their hearts, the Buddha immediately spoke these verses:
"Constrained by desire and malice, they are agitated and act contrary to the Dharma;
I should now feel compassion for them and return to rescue them from their suffering.
When the ignorant and foolish commit evil deeds, the wise should endure them with patience."
"It is like a person holding a child in their arms;
even if there are various kinds of filth within [the child's body], one cannot, because of the stench of excrement, abandon that child.
Having spoken this verse, he rose from his grass mat and intended to return to the monastery.
At that time, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others joined their palms toward the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"Alas! There is one of great compassion, The Great Sage, the True Guide.
Yet those bhikṣus there Are blinded by negligence."
Competing in anger, his mind found no rest, and he provoked the World-Honored One to vexation.
Yet the Tathāgata’s heart of great compassion remained as before, never turning away from him.
In His sorrowful pity, free from resentment or disdain, He desired only to bring him to harmony and submission.
"Just as one might tame a fierce and evil horse by striking it with a whip.
At that time, when the Tathāgata arrived at the monastery, his radiance shone brilliantly, and the bhikṣus knew that the Buddha had returned.
He immediately went out to meet him, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet in reverence, and said to the Buddha:

"Our quarrels and disputes have caused many sentient beings to give rise to hearts of anger and resentment; we have been utterly despised by the multitude. We have now all fallen into the schism of the Sangha; we only pray that the World-Honored One will once again preach the Dharma for us so that we may achieve reconciliation."
At that time, the Tathāgata taught the Dharma of the Six Points of Concordant Respect (*ṣaḍ-samānārthatā*) to the bhikṣus, causing them to regain their harmony.
For this reason, the Buddha spoke of severing ill will.
52 (52) Furthermore, one should contemplate food; the Blessed One has also spoken of the correct contemplation of food.

I have heard that in the past, for the sake of food, the Venerable Kāḷakalodāyin caused the Buddha to establish a precept. The Buddha spoke of various causes and conditions to praise the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, [encouraging] fewness of desires, contentment, and the practice of the dhūta-austerities.
The Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and praised the practice of eating a single meal, even intending to establish the precept for eating a single meal.
At that time, the community of bhikṣus remained entirely silent, like the great ocean, tranquil and without sound.
At that time, among the assembly of monks, there was a bhikṣu named Bādarī who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Do not establish this precept; I am unable to uphold it."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“In past births and deaths, this was their food and drink; within the cycle of birth and death, they underwent endless suffering, wandering until the present day.”
In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there were four creatures with a seer as the fifth.
At that time, the crow spoke these words:
"Among all sufferings, hunger and thirst are the most bitter."

At the beginning of the kalpa, when light and time first appeared in the world, there was a certain deva who, for the very first time, tasted the essence of the earth with his finger; having tasted its flavor, he then took some and ate it.
The deity at that time was none other than this very Pāṭali;
just as Pāṭali first tasted the essence of the earth back then, so it is again now.
"However, it was merely for the sake of food and drink that Pāṭali rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"
"Do not observe the practice of eating only one meal.
He then spoke this verse:
"I am now unable to maintain the World-Honored One’s precept of eating only one meal."
"If even one person were unwholesome, this precept should not have been established.
When all the bhikṣus heard these verses, they all lowered their heads; after reflecting for a long time, they spoke these words: "Alas!
Failing to see the faults and perils of solid food (kavaḷīkārāhāra), we have been subjected to such humiliation before the great assembly for the sake of solid food."
Then he spoke in verse:
“Better to eat grass with deer, Or breathe the wind like a serpent,
Than for the sake of food and drink, To act before the Buddha and the Saṅgha.”
"You have contradicted the Buddha by making such a statement. The Buddha told Pāṭali:
"I permit you to eat half of the meal at your donor's house and bring the remainder back to the monastery to eat."
At that time, Pāṭalī still refused.
At that moment, the Buddha had established the rule of eating only once a day; yet a second and a third time he made the same request to the Buddha, who still refused and maintained the rule.
Vatāli immediately departed from the Buddha; filled with intense remorse, he spoke this verse:
"I have transgressed what the Buddha taught; how could my tongue not be severed?"
How is it that the earth does not sink, yet is still able to support me?
Even rākṣasas and piśācas, malevolent nāgas and bandits—
none dare disobey my word.
Stubborn and dull-witted, one who defies the Buddha’s words would rather slit open their own belly with a blade to swallow maggots, or fill their stomach with earth—
how could they do such a thing for the sake of food?
"I have thus transgressed the teaching of the One of Ten Powers.
I now reproach myself, likening my state to that of one who is mindless.
When Pāṭali had spoken this verse, he felt shame and self-reproach; for three months, he was ashamed to see the Buddha.
As the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony drew near, he was consumed by grief day and night, becoming emaciated, haggard, and deprived of his majestic splendor.
At that time, those monks who possessed a compassionate heart felt deep pity for him and spoke these verses:
"Now these monks, are sewing, washing, and dyeing their robes."
Before long they shall disperse; do not harbor resentment later.
Now quickly approach the Buddha and pay homage at his lotus feet;
you should go to those worthy of respect and entreat them with all your might.
"You must diligently apply your effort; only then can you perform repentance.
Having heard this verse, Pāṭali choked with emotion and shed tears, then spoke another verse:
"Whatever the World-Honored One has taught, none in the world can oppose it."
Due to my own folly, I dared to disobey the Buddha’s word.
Being extremely fickle and lacking shame before the assembly,
I failed to see the laughter of later times and was loathed and despised by the multitude.
Without reflecting on this fault, you have rashly spoken these words:
"This matter is for the Saṃgha to handle; it was not my request.
Because my mind lacked stability, I suddenly uttered such speech.
When his fellow practitioners of the holy life heard this verse, they immediately wished to invite the Buddha to seek his compassion and accept their repentance. Pāṭali spoke another verse, saying:
"With my heart now full of earnest sincerity, I seek your compassion and pray for repentance.
How could I bear to look up And face the World-Honored One with such shame?"
The bhikṣus said to Bādarī:
"If the World-Honored One possessed afflictions or outflows, you might have reason to fear him;
but now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has long since severed all outflows. For what reason do you hesitate and not depart?"
Bādarī spoke again in verse:
"I suspect my own transgressions; Yet your face, free from anger, is more excellent than the pure full moon— The compassionate countenance of the Three Worlds."
I now wish to behold [the truth]; out of compassion, speak for me!
Blinded by ignorance, they do not accept the Buddha’s words;
they are like a person about to die who refuses to take medicine according to their illness.
"Having violated and lost the teaching of compassion, I now suffer remorse and distress.
His fellow practitioners of the holy life said to him:
"We shall go together to the presence of the World-Honored One; let us urge you to see the Buddha and confess your transgression before him."
Then the bhikṣus asked him again,
“Do you now truly and decisively repent?
At that time, Pāthari spoke in verse:
"If I were to prostrate to the Buddha now, I would rather let my body be shattered;
until the Buddha causes me to rise, I shall never rise.
If the Buddha speaks with me, both my body and mind will be fully satisfied."

At that time, Vattaka and the bhikkhus went to where the Buddha was. Then the Blessed One was in the midst of the great assembly, and Vattaka, standing before the Buddha, threw his whole body to the ground and spoke this verse:
"Listen to my confession of transgressions, O Tamer of Men, whose very nature is compassion."
Having transcended and harmonized with the Path,
even if one were deprived of food until the eyes sink into their sockets and the cheekbones protrude,
and one wastes away unto death— rather than endure such suffering, one would never violate the Noble Teaching.
"The Śakras, Brahmās, and supreme devas respectfully revere and uphold what has been taught;
yet because of my own ignorance, I have not followed the Buddha’s words.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands what is the proper time and what is not, as well as all forms of censure and reprimand.
The Buddha said to Bhadali:
"Suppose there were an Arhat lying amidst excrement and filth in a mire, and I were to walk upon his back.
What do you think?"
“Does that Arhat experience suffering and affliction? Pāṭali replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
Even if you were to attain the state of an Arhat, Anāgāmin, Sakṛdāgāmin, or Srotāpanna, you would never disobey my teaching.
Because you are an ordinary person, foolish and empty of anything real—like a plantain tree that has no core within—it is as explained at length in the Sūtras.”

At that time, people believed that Bhadali had attained arhatship; however, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, they realized that Bhadali was actually an ordinary person still bound by all fetters, and thus all the bhikṣus gave rise to a lack of faith.

"I have heard that he did not attain arhatship; if one from such a noble clan who has gone forth does not obtain arhatship, how could a person of low birth like Nandika, having gone forth, attain arhatship?"

If the Buddha wishes for those with outflows to exhaust them, they shall attain the exhaustion of outflows; if he does not wish for them to exhaust them, they shall not attain the exhaustion of outflows.
Knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bhikṣus, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, one will certainly be able to exhaust the outflows; if one does not cultivate them, one cannot attain the exhaustion of outflows."
If one has known and seen [the truth], one may attain the fruit of Arhatship even if born into a lowly and base family;
whereas, as with Pāṭali, who did not know and did not see, one does not attain Arhatship even if born into a superior clan.
Therefore, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma with equanimity and without partiality.
(53) Furthermore, there is nothing more extreme in its madness than sensual desire; therefore, one should diligently sever sensual desire.
I have heard that in the past, when the World-Honored One was practicing the bodhisattva path, the world was empty and no Buddhas or sages had appeared.

At that time, there was a king named Prabhāsa who, riding a well-trained elephant, went out on a tour of inspection, accompanied by a retinue of attendants, singers, dancers, and musicians, until he reached a mountainous and perilous place.

The elephant ridden by the king, seeing a female elephant from afar, was filled with a blazing lust; it trumpeted and went wild, rushing forward like a wind driving away clouds, heedless of precipices or obstacles.

At that time, the elephant trainer could not make the elephant stay by means of various hooks and goads. King Prabhāsa was greatly terrified and told his messenger that the hooks and goads were unable to restrain it, like a wicked disciple who does not follow his teacher. As the elephant departed with increasing speed, the king was seized with great alarm and distress; thinking he would surely die, he spoke this verse:
"As if seeing the void move, Swiftly shaking all directions, All things come together to converge, Seen everywhere moving like a wheel."
The great earth revolves entirely;
as if mountains were moving swiftly, all other mountains follow them,
along with the rocky ravines and the rivers within the gullies.
The king was terrified and deeply distressed; he made a vow, praying to the mountain deity to grant him safety.
His lust so intense that he was unaware of his suffering, the elephant galloped on even more swiftly.
It is like being struck by a violent wind and wounded by mountain rocks; one’s hair is all disheveled,
one is utterly covered in dust and filth, and one’s clothes are further scattered and torn asunder.
"The necklaces, bracelets, and rings have all shattered and fallen to the ground.
Then the Great King spoke to the elephant trainer, saying,
"In my current state, I fear my life will not be preserved."
He further spoke in verse:
"Exert yourself well in skillful means; restrain me and cause me to remain steady.
For I am now like one on a scale, teetering between rising and falling into the place of death."

At that time, the elephant trainer exerted all his strength with the hook and goad but could not restrain him. He sighed repeatedly, his face flushed with shame, and tears filled his eyes. Turning his face away, he avoided the king, unable to bear looking at him, and spoke again to the king:
"Great King!..."
"What plan should I now devise?
He then spoke in verse:
"I shall recite with all my might the elephant-mantra, As taught by the ancient seers."
When the power of the hook and the net is exhausted, it can no longer be restrained at all.
Like a person when the time of death approaches, even incantations and wondrous medicines cannot save them;
once the end has come, they must die, for no good medicine can provide rescue.
At that time, the great king said to the elephant trainer, "We have now fallen into this situation; what plan should we devise?
The elephant trainer replied to the king:
"There is no other way; you must simply cling to the tree.
Upon hearing these words, the king reached out his hand and clung to the tree, while the elephant immediately bolted away, pursuing the female elephant.
After the elephant had departed, the attendants finally arrived at the king’s location, and the king then walked slowly back toward the army.
At that time, the elephant trainer followed the elephant’s tracks for many days until he recovered the elephant and returned it to the army.

At that time, while the king was in the midst of the great assembly, the elephant trainer mounted the elephant and approached the king’s presence. The king, filled with anger and indignation, spoke these words:
"You previously stated that this elephant was well-trained and fit for riding; why then do you deceive me with such a mad elephant?"
The elephant trainer joined his palms and addressed the king, saying:
"This one is indeed well-tamed. If Your Majesty does not believe me, I shall now manifest the signs of an elephant's taming so that Your Majesty may know it."
At that time, the elephant trainer immediately heated iron balls and placed them before him.
Then that man told the elephant to swallow the balls.
But the king would not permit it, and said to the man:
"You say he is well-tamed; how can he be so wild and unruly?
The elephant trainer knelt with palms joined and addressed the king, saying, "Such wildness as this is not something I could have tamed."
The king said to him,
"What fault is this that you have not been able to discipline?
He then replied to the king:
“The elephant has a mind afflicted by lust; this is not something I can treat.
Great King, you should know that such a disease cannot be cured by staffs, whips, hooks, or goads; the destruction of the mind by lust is likewise beyond such remedies.”
He then spoke in verse:
“Desire is the poisonous arrow of the mind; I do not know from where it arises, nor by what cause it increases and spreads.”
"How can it be extinguished?
When the king heard that this craving could not be cured, he said to the elephant trainer,
"Is there no one who can cure this disease of craving?"
The elephant trainer replied:
"This disease of craving cannot be suppressed; it must be abandoned and not treated.
He then spoke this verse:
"One should employ various skillful means and diligently seek the dharma for severing desire;
yet, not knowing its ultimate destination, one may harbor diligence and turn back in retreat.
