Abandoning the five sensual desires, one leaves the household life to practice asceticism."
To sever the fetters of desire, one should diligently cultivate the Path.
Some indulge in the five desires, yet claim that the Path is sufficient for their own severance;
they engage in various kinds of practices, hoping thereby to distance themselves from desire.
In such places as these, one hopes to uproot the very root of desire;
yet the forest of desire is difficult to uproot.
Yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and all classes of sentient beings—
"The subtle mind is like a snare of desire, binding all sentient beings;
it causes them to revolve within the forest of existence, from which they have no means to extricate themselves.
Upon hearing that craving and desire cannot be severed, the King was deeply perplexed and spoke this verse:
"Is there no one at all who can sever and extinguish this enemy that is desire?
Is there not even a single person among gods or humans who can extinguish this craving?"
At that time, the elephant trainer replied to the king:

"I have heard from others that only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Great Teacher of the world, possesses a heart of great compassion; he regards all sentient beings as his own children. His body is like pure gold, adorned with the marks of a Great Man. He possesses spontaneous wisdom, knowing how desire arises and the causes and conditions for its cessation. He has an unimpeded mind and feels pity for all."
At that time, having heard the voice of the Buddha, the Great Man, the king immediately rose and joined his palms like a flower not yet in bloom. Before the great assembly, he made this great vow:

"By means of protecting my kingdom with the True Dharma and by the merit of relinquishing wealth and practicing charity, I pray that in the future I shall certainly attain Buddhahood and sever the affliction of craving in all sentient beings."
For what reason and by what causal conditions was this matter taught?
Because sentient beings do not know the causes and conditions of desire nor their antidotes, this sūtra was spoken.
(54) Furthermore, the Buddha observes that it takes time for them to gain faith; therefore, he does not act precipitously.
I have heard that in the past, while the Venerable Upagupta was sitting in meditation beneath a tree, the Māra Pāpīyān placed various flower garlands upon his head.
At that time, the Venerable One arose from meditative concentration; seeing the flower garlands upon his neck, he immediately entered into samādhi to observe who had performed this act.
Knowing this was the work of Māra Pāpīyān, he immediately used his supernatural power to bind three corpses to the neck of the Māra king.
At that time, the Māra king felt the corpses upon his neck and saw from afar that the Venerable One was responsible for this deed.
At that time, the Venerable One spoke these verses:
“Adorned with garlands and ornaments—these are what the bhikṣu has abandoned.
A corpse is utterly foul and putrid; those who possess desire loathe it.”
"Disciples of the Buddha, let us compete in strength; in this battle of strife, who can prevail?
I am now a disciple of the Buddha; I cast away your flower garland.
If you possess strength, remove your own corpse!"
"The waves of the great ocean flow on, and none can restrain them;
only the Iron Ring Mountains can cause the waters to turn back upon contact.

At that time, having heard these words, the Māra-king desired to remove the corpse, yet despite exhausting his supernatural powers, he could not make it go. It was as if a mosquito or an ant sought to move Sumeru, the King of Mountains; though they exerted all their strength, they could not move it.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān was unable to move the corpse and immediately flew away,
speaking this verse: "If I cannot resolve it, let other superior devas,
those possessed of majestic power and sovereignty, surely be able to resolve it as well."
At that time, the Venerable One spoke again in verse:
“Neither Śakra nor Brahmā is able to understand this;
even if one were to enter a blazing fire or be within the great ocean,”
Neither scorched nor burnt, such a corpse clings to you;
neither dried up nor decayed, it follows you wherever you go,
and none can rescue or release you from it.
And the three Heavenly Kings, including Vaisravana, up to the Brahma Heaven—
though all such devas were to exhaust their supernatural powers, none would be able to provide a remedy.
At that time, Brahmā Śakra saw that Māra had exerted all his power but was unable to turn back the corpse, and he addressed him, saying:
"Do not give rise to arrogance.
He then spoke this verse:
“The disciples of the One of Ten Powers, by means of their own supernormal powers,
now humiliate you because of your insolent provocation.
Who possesses such power as to be able to deliver you from this?”
Just as the tide of the great ocean cannot have its waves restrained,
or as if one were to use a lotus root to suspend Mount Himavat;
even if I exhausted all my supernatural powers, I could not release you.
Although I possess great power, it does not equal that of the śramaṇa.
It is like the light of a lamp or candle, which is not equal to a great mass of fire;
and though that mass of fire is bright, it is not equal to the radiance of the sun.
Having heard this verse, the Māra spoke to Brahmā, saying:
"Upon whom should I rely to be freed from this affliction?
Brahmā replied to the Māra with a verse:
"Go quickly to him, seek his compassion, and take refuge;
you who delighted in supernatural powers and fame have utterly perished and lost them all,
like a man who has fallen and must rise again by supporting himself on the ground."
Māra thought to himself:
"The disciples of the Tathāgata possess a power that even the supreme devas, such as Brahmā, cannot equal; they are thus honored and revered by all the Brahmās."
The Māra spoke in verse:
“The disciples of the Buddha are revered even by Brahmā;
how much more so the virtues of the Tathāgata—how could they ever be measured?”
Though I caused him extreme distress and turmoil, he continued to endure it out of compassion;
yet he did not bring upon me any further misfortunes or afflictions.
That he could so patiently protect and cherish me—how can this ever be adequately described?
Now for the first time I know the Buddha, The one of true and great compassion;
His essential nature is supremely merciful, Never giving rise to thoughts of enmity or hatred.
His body is like the king of golden mountains, Its radiance surpassing that of the sun.
Folly darkens my mind and causes me to act with constant agitation;
yet he is firm in his vigor and has never uttered a harsh word.
His constant compassion makes my heart feel uneasy.
At that time, Māra, the Lord of the Desire Realm, spoke these words:
"I have surveyed the three realms and found no one capable of liberating him; I must now return to take refuge in the Venerable One alone, for only then can he be freed."
Having spoken these words, he approached the Venerable One, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground at the Venerable’s feet, and spoke thus:
“O Virtuous One!
When I was beneath the Bodhi tree, even when I created a hundred kinds of afflictions to disturb the Buddha, they did not cause me any suffering.”
He then spoke in verse:
"In the village of Bārāṇasī, In the Brahmin settlement, Gautama came to beg for alms; I caused him to depart with an empty bowl."
On that very day he was unable to eat, yet he did not cast blame upon me.
Formerly I was an evil bull, as well as a venomous serpent;
with five hundred chariots I made the water turbid so that the Buddha could not drink it.
All know that these were my own deeds, yet I never uttered a harsh word.
Since what I have done is so little, you have utterly reviled and insulted me;
thus gods, humans, and asuras alike all hold me in contempt.
"You have defamed me and ruined my reputation; you have tormented me with this corpse.
At that time, the Venerable One addressed the Māra, saying:
"You are now an unwholesome and evil being; how can you, a mere śrāvaka, compare yourself to the World-Honored One?"
Then he spoke in verse:
"How can one compare a mustard seed to Mount Sumeru?
How can the faint light of a firefly be compared to the radiance of the sun?"
How can a mere handful of scant water be compared to the great ocean?
The Buddha possesses a heart of great compassion, whereas the śrāvakas lack great compassion.
By means of his great compassion, the Tathāgata pardons your manifold transgressions.
"I too shall follow the Buddha's intention, desiring to give rise to roots of goodness in you.
At that time, having heard these words, the Māra King spoke again in verse:
"Listen as I speak of the Buddha’s virtues, his merit, benefit, and magnificent splendor."
He who has severed all craving and desire,
who possesses patience and gives rise to no resentment— though I, out of folly,
have daily provoked him to anger, he regards me as a mother loves her only son.
Upagupta said to Pāpīyas: "Listen to my words.

Since you have repeatedly committed various evils against the Tathāgata, there is no way to wash them away and give rise to roots of goodness better than by recollecting the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who is most supreme."
Then he spoke in verse:
“By such causes and conditions, I know that the Buddha’s vision is far-reaching;
Never toward you has he conceived a lack of affection.”
That foremost Honored One of Wisdom, desiring to bring about faith in you,
constantly utters words of affection; when the wise develop even a slight degree of faith,
they immediately attain the bliss of Nirvana.
"The Dharma speaks of the darkness of ignorance and the faults of obscurity;
because you have now given rise to faith, these shall be washed away entirely.

At that time, the hairs on the body of Māra stood on end. Like a *pundarīka* flower, he manifested various forms of provocation; yet, just as a father still loves his son even when the son commits transgressions, his mind was more patient than the great earth and never looked upon him with reproach. He is the most excellent among sages; if one has even a slight faith in the Buddha, former faults are washed away.
Then that Māra, standing before the Venerable One, called to mind the Buddha’s virtues and prostrated at the Venerable One’s feet, saying:
"Venerable One, save me and grant me your respect; you should resolve to release the noose hanging from my neck."
"Although I have caused you distress, I pray that you will give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and remove this for me.
The Venerable One replied, "I shall make a pact with you; only then may you be released."
The Māra said:
"What is this solemn vow?
The Venerable One replied:
"From this day forward, do not trouble the bhikṣus.
Māra then replied,
"I shall no longer trouble or provoke them."
The Venerable One said:
"According to what you know, it was only after the Buddha had been gone for a hundred years that I appeared.
He then spoke this verse:
"The true salvation of the three realms—there I beheld that Dharma-body, not the golden-hued body.
You who are free from affliction have manifested for me;
show me the form and marks of a Buddha, for I now yearn for this with all my heart."
"I love the form of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Māra spoke to the Venerable One, saying:
"I too shall make a solemn vow."

"If you see my form, do not prostrate hastily; out of reverence for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), be careful not to prostrate to me, and though I manifest the appearance of a Buddha, be careful not to prostrate.
He then spoke in verse:
"Those who, with humble reverence, recollect the Buddha And offer prostrations to me..."
This would be to utterly consume me.
What power do I possess that I could receive the veneration of those free from desire?
It is like the sprout of an eranda tree, crushed by the trunk of an elephant, destroyed and rendered useless.
"If I were to accept your veneration, the matter would be exactly like this.
The Venerable replied,
"I do not take refuge [in you], nor do you owe me the fulfillment of your promise."
The Māra spoke again to the Venerable One, saying:
"Wait for me for a brief moment.
He then entered an empty forest and spoke this verse:
"First, for the sake of Subhūti, I manifested a body of blazing brilliance;
the Buddha-body is inconceivable, and I have assumed such a form.
My body manifests a blazing radiance that surpasses both the sun and the moon."
"Delighting the eyes of all people, it is as clear as drinking nectar.
The Venerable replied,
"Now act for me as you have done before, with excellence."
Māra replied,
“Yes, I shall do so now,” and he immediately removed the corpse.

At that time, the Māra entered an empty forest and manifested the form of a Buddha, like an actor on a stage; he adorned himself in various ways with the color and features of a Tathāgata, manifesting the marks of a Great Man and the eyes of one capable of producing tranquility, resembling a newly painted image.
When it was time for the manifestation, this grove was magnificently adorned, such that one could gaze upon it without ever being satiated.

A halo extending one fathom emanated, transforming into the form of a Buddha; Śāriputra attended to his right, Maudgalyāyana stood to his left, and Ānanda followed behind, holding the Buddha’s alms bowl.

The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, Subhūti, and other such great śrāvakas—numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty—attended upon the Buddha at his left and right. Appearing like a crescent moon beside the Buddha’s countenance, they proceeded toward the place where the Venerable Upagupta was.

Upon seeing the Buddha’s countenance, the Venerable was filled with supreme joy; he rose from his seat and gazed upon the Buddha’s form, exclaiming: "Alas! Wretched is impermanence, devoid of any heart of compassion. How can this King of Golden Mountains of wondrous color be thus destroyed?"
The body of the Muni was thus destroyed by impermanence.
At that time, as the Venerable One contemplated the mind, his thoughts became agitated; yet, truly beholding the Buddha’s palm like a lotus, he spoke these words:
"Alas! This magnificent and wondrous form cannot be fully described."
Then he spoke in verse:
“Your face surpasses the blooming lotus; Your eyes are like the petals of the blue lotus.
Your physical form excels a grove of flowers; Your marks and signs exceed the moon.”
Profound as the ocean, Stable as Mount Sumeru,
His majestic power surpasses the sun, His gait exceeds that of the lion king;
The blinking of his eyes is like that of a bull king, And his complexion is more exquisite than pure gold.
At that time, the Venerable One felt even greater joy and reverence; filled with great delight, his gladness increased further, and he spoke these verses:
“Ah! Pure karma, Which yields such exquisite retribution— Obtained through the conditions of past deeds, Not produced by actions performed in this present life.”
Throughout hundreds of billions of kalpas, one performs pure conduct with body and speech,
cultivating generosity, ethical discipline, patience, as well as meditative concentration and wisdom.
Resolutely practicing these right actions, one adorns oneself therewith.
Beloved by the eyes of all, pure and free from defilement;
when this form and appearance manifest, even enemies are filled with joy—
how much more so should I today not feel love and reverence?
Reflecting thus, he thought only of the Buddha and did not consider Māra; he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and paid homage.
At that moment, Māra was startled and spoke these words:
"Virtuous One, why do you violate our agreement?"
The Venerable One said:
"What vow have you made?
Māra replied:
"You previously told me not to prostrate; why do you prostrate now?
The Venerable rose from the ground and immediately spoke this verse:
"What the eyes delight to behold, I direct my mind to worship as the Buddha."
"I truly do not act out of reverence; I am merely prostrating at your feet.
At that time, the Māra King said:
"You have cast your five limbs to the ground to pay homage to me; why then do you say, 'I do not revere you'?"
The Venerable One said to Māra:
"I do not pay homage, yet you have not violated your vow; it is like a Buddha image fashioned from clay and wood, which all people and devas in the world together revere."

At that time, he did not show respect to the clay and wood, but because he wished to pay homage to the Buddha, he said, "I am paying homage to the form of the Buddha; I do not pay homage to the form of Māra.
Having heard these words, he returned to his original form, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable One, and ascended back to the heavens.
For what reason was this matter spoken?

It was because the great śrāvakas wished to cause the various donors to universally provide for the Saṃgha so that they would lack nothing, and also to ensure that the bhikṣus would hear the Dharma and practice it accordingly; for these reasons, they should preach the Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
If one wishes to praise the Buddha, one should speak thus: "Although he has severed the fetters and latent tendencies of desire, he does not perceive that [anyone] is prostrating before him.
*Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, Scroll Nine; *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, Scroll Ten.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
(55) Furthermore, if a person praises the Buddha, they will obtain great karmic rewards and be revered by all people;
for this reason, one should diligently praise and revere him with a devoted mind.

I have heard that in the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a Dharma master who preached the Dharma for the assembly. Within that great multitude, he praised Kāśyapa Buddha; by virtue of this cause and condition, at the end of his life he was reborn in heaven, where he constantly experienced happiness among gods and humans.

One hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Buddha, during the time of King Aśoka, he became a great Dharma Master who attained the fruit of Arhatship, was endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, and from whose mouth a wondrous fragrance constantly issued forth.
At that time, the Dharma Master was preaching the Dharma to the assembly not far from King Aśoka; the fragrance from his mouth reached the king’s location.
Upon smelling the fragrance, the king felt doubt and reflected thus:
"Does that bhikṣu keep some exquisite incense in his mouth?"
"The fragrance is such as this.
Having had this thought, he said to the bhikṣu,
"Open your mouth."
At that time, the bhikṣu opened his mouth, but it was entirely empty.
He spoke again, asking for water to rinse his mouth;
having rinsed his mouth, there was still a fragrance remaining.
The bhikṣu said to the king,
"For what reason do you tell me to open my mouth and rinse it?
At that time, the king replied:

"Because I smelled an aroma and a doubt arose in my mind, I had you open your mouth and rinse it; yet the aroma has become even more intense. There is only this fragrance, while the mouth itself contains nothing at all."
The king said to the bhikṣu,
“I pray that you will speak for me.
The bhikṣu smiled and immediately spoke these verses:
“O Sovereign of the Great Earth, I shall now explain this for you:
This is not agallochum incense, nor is it from flowers, leaves, or stalks;
it is not produced by the blending of various scents such as sandalwood and the like.”
A rare thought arose within me, and I spoke these words:
"Because I praised Kāśyapa in the past, I have obtained such fragrance as this.
Even though it was prepared during the time of that Buddha, it is no different from fresh incense."
"Day and night there is always fragrance, never having been interrupted.
The King said,
"Venerable Sir, how long has it been since you obtained this fragrance?"
The bhikṣu replied, “I obtained it long ago; O King, listen well now.
In the distant past there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa; at that time, through diligent and devoted cultivation, I acquired this incense.”
When the king had heard this, he was struck with wonder and asked the bhikṣu, "I have not yet understood;
I pray that you will explain it to me.
Then the bhikṣu addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!
Listen with a sincere mind!
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I was a bhikṣu who preached the Dharma; before the great assembly, I gave rise to a heart of joy and praised that Buddha."
He then spoke in verse:
“The golden body shines with brilliance; Filled with joy, I offer this praise.
By the power of this merit, In every place where I am born, I shall attain such a form.”
This body follows this karma, and it is always imbued with such a fragrance,
surpassing that of the *utpala* and the *campaka*.
As the scent fills the air, all who smell it are filled with joy.
"Like drinking the taste of ambrosia, one never tires of consuming it.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King’s body hair stood on end, and he spoke thus: "Alas!..."
"It is by praising the Buddha’s merits that one obtains this retribution.
The bhikṣu replied,
"Great King!"
"Do not say that this is the fruit [of one's actions], such that the retribution received is like this.
He further spoke in verse:
"Renown and merit, Physical strength and well-being,"
Having already attained these merits, no one treats them with contempt;
their majestic radiance is lovely and delightful, and their will is profound, vast, and expansive.
They are able to leave behind all faults and evils—all this is due to praising the Buddha.
"Such a karmic reward as this can only be described by the wise and virtuous;
once the body has been exhausted, one attains the trace of the Deathless.
At that time, the Great King again questioned the bhikṣu:
"What is the manner of praising the Buddha’s merits?
At that time, the bhikṣu answered with a verse:
"In the midst of the great assembly, I praise the Buddha’s true merits."
For this reason, his fame fills the ten directions.
As he speaks of the Buddha’s various virtuous deeds, the great assembly hears it with joy;
their countenances are all radiant and serene because they have previously praised the Buddha.
His countenance possesses majestic radiance; by preaching the Dharma, he brings an end to suffering.
What that Tathāgata has taught serves as the causal condition for those who cultivate goodness to bring about joy; thus, they obtain the retribution of happiness.
Why is he called a Buddha?
It is said that he possesses the ten powers.
All who have attained these dharmas will not be held in contempt by others.
How much more so for those who preach the Dharma,
ascending the Dharma seat to extol the virtues of the Buddha and subdue all non-Buddhists;
by virtue of praising the Buddha’s qualities, they obtain a most sublime body.
He then expounded for all people the delightful and correct Path.
By reason of this cause and condition, he is beloved by the multitude, like the full moon in autumn.
Even through the exhaustion of kalpas it would be difficult to end; even if the tongue were to wither away, one would never cease or desist.
Always maintaining such a mind, in every place of rebirth throughout successive lives, one’s speech shall be entirely eloquent and clear.
He speaks of the Buddha’s spontaneous wisdom, which increases the wisdom of all beings;
by these causes and conditions, those born thereby attain supreme wisdom.
He declares that all worlds are produced through the conditions of karma.
Having heard this, one attains all virtues, for by abandoning all evils,
one is born in a place free from faults; greed, hatred, the view of self, and the like,
are all completely consumed and dried up, like oil poured upon a red-hot iron.
In all such matters as these, where is there anything that does not please you?
With the arrows of causal conditions, I shall destroy your nets and bows;
furthermore, I am the Father of Eloquence and the Mother of Well-Spoken Thought.
At that time, having heard these verses, the Great King immediately rose, joined his palms, and spoke these words:
"What you have said is most wonderful; it perfectly accords with my own mind."
The King spoke in verse:
“Having heard this teaching, my mind is liberated; I praise the fruit of the Buddha’s meritorious virtues.
To speak of it briefly: one should always offer praise to the Buddha.”
For what reason was this matter spoken?
It is so that those who preach the Dharma may obtain great rewards; all who preach the Dharma should give rise to a joyful mind.
(56) Furthermore, if those with great merit still practice without weariness, how much more so should those without merit avoid indolence and arrogance?

I have heard that in the past, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having entered various meditative absorptions, liberations, and samādhis, wished to cause those who cultivate merit to plant wholesome seeds and obtain immeasurable blessings; therefore, at dawn, he donned the saṃghāṭī robe bestowed by the Buddha and went forth to beg for alms.
At that time, a witness spoke these verses:
"Praising that Victorious One, who is clothed in the Tathāgata’s robe,
Before the eight classes of gods and humans, the Buddha divided his seat and bade him sit."
At that time, the Buddha likewise praised Kāśyapa and spoke this verse:
“You now practice virtue well, Like the moon gradually waxing;
Like a hand moving through space, There is nothing that can obstruct you.”
Their bodies are like pure water, free from all dust and obscurations;
the Buddha constantly praises their merits before the assembly.
This shall continue until the future age when Maitreya attains Buddhahood.
He further praised him and addressed the great assembly, saying:
"This is a disciple of the Honored Muni who practices asceticism;
he possesses the twelve dhūtas and is foremost among those with few desires and contentment."
"He is the foremost, the very first; this one is named Kāśyapa.
Thus, before the eight classes of beings, including devas and humans, his merits were praised.
At that time, Śakra, seeing Kāśyapa’s dignified and composed gait, joined his palms in reverence from afar within his palace. His wife left him and asked:
“Whom do you see now that you show such reverence?
At that time, Śakra replied with a verse:
“Though dwelling amidst the fires of desire, I keep my mindfulness ever present before me.”
Though he shared a chamber with a golden-hued wife, his mind was free from attachment.
With his body established in meditative concentration, his heart and mind were also joyful;
he entered the city and its villages, desiring to go forth for alms.
"Plowing the field with wisdom, one destroys the weeds of faults and evils;
this is called a virtuous field of merit, where the fruit sown is never in vain.
At that time, Śreṇika looked up at Śakra with a heart of deep reverence and addressed him, saying:
"You, who dwell in a state of supreme nobility and heedlessness, still possess a virtuous mind and cultivate merit.
Śakra replied with a verse:
"By reason of my giving, I have attained the highest sovereignty."
Gods, humans, and asuras hold me dear and revere me;
they remember my giving day and night, and thus I have attained such a state,
like finding a great hidden treasure from which all manner of jewels overflow.
Venerable Kāśyapa went to the alleys of the poor and delighted in accepting alms from the destitute.

At that time, Śakra transformed himself into a poor old weaver, and his wife likewise transformed herself into an old woman wearing tattered rags; the couple followed one another and sat resting by the side of the road.
At that time, the Venerable One saw that the husband and wife were dressed in tattered garments and were of lowly status, and he thought to himself:
"There are none in this world more impoverished and base than these.
He then went to where they were and approached them to offer consolation.
The weaver rose quickly, took the Venerable One’s bowl, filled it with divine *sūdā* food, and offered it to him.
When the Venerable One had received this food, doubt arose within his mind, and he immediately spoke this verse:
“That man is most poor and lowly, yet his food and drink are so exquisite.”
"This matter is truly startling and suspicious; it is the height of perverse phenomena.
Having spoken this verse, he thought to himself:
"Whom should I question now?"
"You must observe for yourself.
He then spoke in verse:
"I am the seed of goodness; I sever the delusions of others."
If even the devas and humans have something they wish to do, they ought to seek clarification;
how much more so for me, who now has doubts—
how could I fail to ask another?
Having spoken this verse, he beheld Śakra with his eye of wisdom and said:
"Alas! Those who delight in cultivating merit seek supremacy through skillful means."
He then spoke in verse:
“Having renounced his noble and superior marks, he manifests the form of a poor and lowly man;
emaciated, extremely aged, and frail, he wears these tattered and worn-out robes.”
"Leaving the Vaijayanta Hall, he manifested himself dwelling by the side of the rest-path.
Having spoken this verse, the Venerable One smiled and spoke another verse:
"I wish to cause those without merit to accomplish the karmic deeds of supreme merit."
Your merit is already perfected; why then do you cause such disturbance?
By giving food to me, you shall possess the five supreme and wondrous desires.
For a long time, World-Honored One, you have severed the three evil realms for your sake.
"You do not know contentment, yet you still seek further meritorious deeds.
At that time, Śakra returned to his form as Śakra and, standing before the assembly, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable One and spoke these words:
"Venerable Kāśyapa, what have you done?"
He then spoke in verse:
"I have seen the rewards obtained from giving, And have attained all manner of supreme benefits;
Since my resources and karma have become vast, My faith has increased all the more."
"Venerable One, for what reason do you thus obstruct me?
At that time, Śakra spoke again in verse:
"When people hear it said that one should give, they are still able to practice generosity."
How much more so for me, who see the rewards of giving and clearly know them through my own realization?
Neither parents nor kinsmen can rescue or benefit one as effectively as the practice of giving,
which leads away from the suffering of birth and death.
The retribution for giving is like form and shadow; it bestows peace and happiness everywhere.
Amidst the perils of birth and death, only giving follows one along.
Amidst rain, wind, cold, and snow, only giving can bring peace and happiness.
Just as one traveling a perilous and evil road must have all provisions fully prepared,
so too can generosity serve as a secure and excellent vehicle for those who are weary;
in places of peril, evil, and banditry, generosity is indeed a virtuous companion.
Generosity removes all fears; it is the most profound among all forms of rescue.
Amidst enemies and bandits, generosity is a sharp sword.
Generosity is the most wondrous medicine, capable of curing even the most grievous illnesses.
"When walking upon uneven ground, one uses generosity as a staff.
Having spoken this verse, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, made offerings to the Venerable One and returned to his celestial palace.
For what reason and by what causal conditions is this matter taught?

It is because wise people clearly understand that giving brings merit; they wish to cause others to diligently cultivate meritorious deeds. If even Śakra, the victor among men, still cultivates merit, how much more so should worldly people practice giving?
If even the Śrāvakas are honored by Śakra, how much more so the World-Honored One?

(57) Furthermore, although one may plant but a small amount of goodness, one must certainly seek Buddhahood; seeking Buddhahood through even slight goodness is like nectar. Therefore, one should seek Buddhahood with all one's heart.

I have heard that in the past, there was a man who, through the power of certain conditions, resolved to leave the household life and seek liberation; he went to a monastic dwelling, but encountered the Buddha’s absence from the monastery due to his being engaged in teaching and transforming others.
That person thought to himself:
"Although the World-Honored One is not here, I shall go to where Śāriputra, the Great General of the Dharma, resides.
At that time, Śāriputra examined the causal conditions of that person, wondering whether, in past lives, he had possessed even a slight degree of world-weariness or had cultivated roots of goodness.

Having thus observed, he did not perceive even the slightest root of goodness; since there was none in a single body, there was likewise none throughout hundreds, thousands, or even tens of thousands of bodies.
He further observed that for one kalpa there were no roots of goodness, and even for hundreds of thousands of kalpas there were likewise no roots of goodness.
The Venerable Śāriputra said to that person:
"I shall not deliver you."
That person then went to another bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu asked him:
"To whom did you request ordination?
That person replied:
“I went to the Venerable Śāriputra, but he was unwilling to ordain me.
The bhikṣus said, “If Śāriputra was unwilling to ordain you, there must be some fault or transgression; how then could we possibly ordain you?”

Thus, he went successively to various bhikṣus, but none were willing to ordain him; it was like a patient whom a great physician would not treat, leaving no other minor physicians capable of curing him.
Since his wish was not granted, he wept before the gate of the monastery and said:
"How meager is my merit that there is no one to deliver me? Among the four castes, all may go forth into homelessness; what evil have I committed that I alone am not delivered?"
"If I do not see him, I shall surely die.
He then spoke in verse:
"Just as pure water, Is something that all may drink,"
Even outcasts (caṇḍāla) are all permitted to go forth;
yet within this Buddha-dharma, you do not accept me.
Since I am so ill-behaved and unruly, what would be the use of my living on?

Having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One, out of a heart of compassion, desired to transform them—just as a mother loves her child. Like a moving mountain of gold whose radiance eclipses the sun, he arrived at the gate of the monastic quarters and spoke this verse:
"The body of all-encompassing wisdom, Taking great compassion as its essence, The Buddha, within the triple world, Seeks those children ready for transformation."
"Just like a cow seeking her calf, your loving concern knows no rest.

At that time, the World-Honored One—pure and stainless as a flower in full bloom, his hands radiant and glorious, with palms marked by the thousand-spoked wheel and fingers joined by webbing—stroked the man's head with those wondrous hands and addressed him, saying:
"Why do you weep?"
That man, filled with grief, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I sought to leave the household life, but all the bhikṣus refused me; for this reason, I weep."
The World-Honored One asked:
"Did the bhikṣus not grant permission?
Who prevented you from being permitted to go forth?"
Then he spoke in verse:
"Who possesses all-knowledge that they would wish to fathom and predict?
The power of karma is extremely subtle; who can know its depth or shallowness?"
At that time, having heard these verses, the man addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Bhikṣu Śāriputra, the great general of the Buddha-dharma and foremost in wisdom, did not permit me to go forth."
At that time, the World-Honored One, with a voice as deep and far-reaching as thunder, comforted those people, saying:
"This is not within the reach of Śāriputra’s power of wisdom.
For immeasurable kalpas, I have performed difficult practices and asceticism to cultivate wisdom; I shall now do so for you."
Then he spoke in verse:
“O son Śāriputra, you are not omniscient, nor do you understand the nature of things;
you do not fully know the middle or the inferior.”
"That consciousness has its limits; it cannot deeply understand or realize that there is no wisdom capable of knowing the subtle retribution of karma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed that person, saying:
"I now grant you my permission; I shall allow you to go forth within the Buddha-dharma.

From among the marketplace of the Dharma, I have sought to purchase a person such as you, who possesses faith and delight; I shall transform and deliver you according to the Dharma, ensuring that no opportunity is lost."

The Buddha, with his hand marked by the auspicious wheel and possessing soft, delicate features, took the man’s arm and led him into the monastery. Before the assembly, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“For what reason did you not permit this son to go forth?”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I do not see even the slightest root of goodness in him.”
The Buddha then addressed Śāriputra:
"Do not speak such words.
He then spoke this verse:
"I observe this root of goodness, which is exceedingly subtle and minute,
like gold extracted from mountain rock or sand once it has been melted away.
Meditative concentration and wisdom are like a pair of bellows."
"By blowing with my power, I shall surely bring forth the truly exquisite gold.
This person is also like this; their slight goodness is like that gold.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra adjusted his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), bared his right shoulder, knelt on his right knee with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speaking in verse:
"Among all treatises, this is the most supreme; I pray that you will explain it to me.
It is the great illumination of wisdom that utterly extinguishes all darkness.
By how much time—whether long or short—did that person plant these roots of goodness?"
"To obtain what kind of field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) will the seed grow most swiftly?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Listen attentively now!"
I shall explain this for you.
That cause consists of the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*), which is not within the sphere of perception of a *pratyekabuddha*.

Long ago in the past, there was a poor man who entered a forest hermitage to gather firewood; when he was cornered by a tiger, out of fear he cried out, "Namo Buddhāya. By virtue of this seed, he obtained the cause for liberation.
He then spoke these verses:
"Seeing only this as the Buddha, And regarding it as subtle,
Thereby reaching the end of suffering— Such is truly excellent."
"Taking refuge in the Buddha with a sincere heart, one will surely attain ultimate liberation;
having attained such a corresponding fruit, there shall be none who can equal it.

At that time, the Bhagavān immediately ordained that man, enabling him to leave the household life. The Buddha personally instructed and transformed him, and the bhikṣu’s mind awakened as he attained the fruit of arhatship.

For this reason, by planting even a small root of goodness in the presence of the World-Honored One, one obtains immeasurable retribution; how much more so when one constructs images, stupas, and temples?
(58) Furthermore, once roots of goodness have ripened, one attains the fruit of liberation; for this reason, one ought to cultivate goodness.

I have heard that in the past, when the World-Honored One was practicing the Way as a bodhisattva, he engaged in asceticism for six years, consuming only one sesame seed and one grain of rice daily; yet he achieved nothing and gained no benefit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, through the realization of non-attainment, partook of the milk-rice gruel of a hundred flavors.
Then the five companions asked the Bodhisattva, saying:
"If even while practicing such asceticism you attained nothing, how much less could you have attained the Way by eating milk-rice?"
Having spoken these words, he immediately departed for Vārāṇasī.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had attained Buddhahood, he reflected thus:
"Which sentient beings should be the first to receive deliverance?"
He further thought:
"Only those five men have the conditions to attain the Path; they have been kind to me.
Having had this thought, he went to Vārāṇasī and approached the five men, whereupon he spoke these verses:
“With exquisite majesty and radiance, his entire body is fully adorned;
walking alone, he is endowed with all the marks of excellence; his broad chest is brilliantly manifest, and his radiant splendor is filled with majestic virtue.”
His appearance is perfectly refined and upright; his gait is like that of a great elephant king, moving with deliberate steps one by one.
His wisdom and conduct are already perfected, and profound wisdom serves as his celestial crown.
Having untied the silken bonds from his head,
the Supreme Wheel-Turning King is escorted before and behind by the devas who perform music.
Surrounded by the fourfold army, yet his majestic carriage was not like that of the Buddha as he wanders alone through the world.
With hosts of elephants, horses, and chariots, and celestial crowns of supreme subtlety, [he is surpassed].
With silk canopies covering them above,
their blessings and benefits are fully prepared; yet these do not equal the Buddha’s adornments,
which are far more sublime and surpassing than those.
His majestic virtue surpasses that of all sages; when sentient beings behold his countenance and deportment, it transcends and exceeds the radiance of the sun.
When humans, beasts, and all winged birds gaze upon the marks of the Buddha’s body, their walking and moving come to a complete halt.

At that time, those five men saw that the Buddha’s radiant appearance was fully endowed with majestic virtue, and that his perfected wisdom and merit were not as they had been before; yet, the five did not recognize him.
Then one of them spoke a verse to the other four:
“Who has emitted this wondrous radiance, Shining brightly upon the forest, mountains, and valleys?”
Just as many suns emerge, leaping up from the earth,
their nets of light and brilliance fill everywhere, shining through and reaching nowhere unpenetrated;
like a pavilion of pure gold, with a *kāṣāya* robe draped over its summit.
Furthermore, it was like molten pure gold, flowing and scattering upon the ground.
All beasts that travel on land, including the king of oxen and others,
as well as deer, antelope, pheasants, and rabbits— upon seeing the Buddha, they all came to a halt.
The grass-eaters spit it out; they gaze intently, never for a moment ceasing.
When the peacock spreads its wings, like a garland of blue lotuses, at the time of emerging from negligence, they all likewise dance with joy.
Amidst joyful entertainment, wondrous sounds emerge.
All classes of sentient beings, their minds and eyes delighting in gazing upon them, have their two faculties snatched away;
they do not realize as they go of their own accord to look.
When the Buddha travels upon the road, all who touch his feet experience joy for seven days and nights;
the Most Victorious One proceeds in accordance with the Way,
serene and free from restlessness, his body exceedingly supple.
Treading through the air without touching the ground, his walking was free from fatigue.
Then another person spoke a verse to the four men:
“When I beheld his appearance, doubt arose in my mind as well.”
"Whose majestic radiance is this, shining more brightly than the sun?
Because of the appearance of that light, the trees and forests have all turned to gold.
At that time, when the people saw that the Buddha had drawn near, they said to one another:

"This person is a youth of the Śākya clan; having abandoned his ascetic practices, he has returned to nourish his body with sensual pleasures and has come to our side after renouncing those austerities."
He then spoke in verse:
"None of us should rise; Be careful not to offer salutations.
We should merely point from afar and instruct him, Telling him to sit in that place."
When the Buddha had arrived, the people rose spontaneously without realizing it, and they spoke this verse:
“With a face like the pure full moon, Seeing him, we rose without awareness;
He is like the great ocean, Where the tide surges when the moon is full.”
We arose spontaneously, as if someone were pulling us up;
all this is through the Buddha’s majestic power, which naturally causes such a thing to occur.
It is like the banner of Śakra, which no other devas can move.
When Śakra himself arrives, he stands there spontaneously;
we are likewise: when the Buddha approaches, we rise up naturally.
It is also like pouring clarified butter onto a fire: the fire then blazes forth with great intensity.
Having beheld the Buddha’s virtues, we quickly rose up, swifter than that fire.
For countless eons, we have subdued our pride and held in high esteem our entire body toward those worthy of honor— our teachers, elders, and parents.
The devas and the people of the world, the ghosts, nāgas, yakṣas, and all others who behold the Buddha, none dare fail to pay him respectful homage.
Why should the wise have any doubt? They should discern this clearly.
"When the Buddha lifts his foot or lowers it, the earth likewise rises or sinks;
even the mountains are like light grass, all tilting and shaking upon seeing the Buddha.
At that time, those five men saw the Buddha and immediately rose, all going together to welcome him.
There were those who took up the Buddha’s bowl, prepared the seat, and fetched water for him, as well as those who washed the Buddha’s feet; they then spoke these verses:
"The five men saw the Sugata, Beholding the Buddha’s magnificent majesty, Their hearts were filled with joy, And they broke their original vow."
"Supporting their water jars on three-legged stands, they gaze intently at them for fear they might break;
all have taken the vow of silence, and even among the ten [precepts], they observe half.
When the World-Honored One heard this verse, he immediately smiled and addressed them, saying:
“You foolish men!
How can you immediately break your verbal agreement?
After the Buddha had taken his seat, they stood in respectful attendance and spoke these words:
"Venerable Gautama!
The Buddha, free from feelings of hatred or affection, spoke this verse with a mind of loving-kindness:
"Now that I have attained the Way, I am far removed from all defilements."
Do not treat this as you would ordinary things; you should instead give rise to reverence.
Just as when one fashions an image of the Buddha from clay or wood, before it has been completed, one may tread upon it or chip away at it.
Once you have attained accomplishment, pay homage with incense and flowers.
You all should likewise abandon thoughts of intimacy and friendship;
you must revere me and never give rise to contempt.
Praised, you feel no joy; reviled, you feel no anger.
Out of compassion for you now, I desire that you attain liberation, achieve the bliss of tranquility, and obtain all manner of beneficial things.
Delusion, craving, and hatred each have their own distinct characteristics;
to revile me with harsh words is like sprinkling ashes upon a wound.
Now that I abide in Bodhi, they call me Gautama.
"Although I am free from love or hatred, I should manifest an appearance of reverence;
do not speak such words again, slandering and disparaging me to others.
At that time, although those five men heard these words, they still maintained that the World-Honored One had not yet attained Bodhi, and immediately spoke this verse:
"Previously you practiced asceticism, yet you did not realize Bodhi;
you are now submerged in the mire—how can you hope to awaken to the Way?
It is like abandoning a great ship only to carry a mountain of stone upon your back."
"If one wishes to cross the river of suffering, how can this be accomplished?

At that time, the World-Honored One knew that those five men were attached to asceticism as the true path. The Buddha then taught them that because of being free from the five desires, this is the true path; and because of being free from the practice of asceticism, this too is the true path. Having removed these two extremes, he preached the Middle Way for them.
The Buddha, with compassion as his foremost quality, spoke this verse:
"Only wisdom can remove the obstacles of ignorance and folly;
therefore, one must cultivate wisdom to protect one's own life."
One who possesses life attains wisdom;
through bedding, robes, and the like, as well as food, drink, and medicinal decoctions, one sustains this physical life.
If these aforementioned things are lacking, then this body and life will perish.
One protects one's life and body by firmly upholding the precepts.
Through upholding the precepts, one attains concentration and wisdom;
yet these are not attained through the practice of asceticism, such as self-starvation or the method of fasting. One need not undergo such practices to realize the Path.
When the body perishes, life is destroyed; when life is destroyed, there is no body.
Without the precepts, there is no meditative concentration; without meditative concentration, there is no wisdom.
Therefore, one should protect life and also uphold the prohibitive precepts.
By upholding the prohibitive precepts, one then attains meditative concentration and wisdom.
Therefore, one should distance oneself from that which brings affliction and destroys the Dharma-body;
likewise, one should remain detached from the five desires and not take deep delight or attachment in them.
If one delights in and clings to sensual desires, one thereby violates the precepts and further increases craving for desire.
One may take pleasure in the practice of fasting, or subsist on grass and leaves.
Lying upon ashes and thorns, thus harming one's body and life,
yet unable to attain concentration and wisdom—
relying on such dharmas, do not sink into the mire of desire.
Nor should you afflict your body.
Regarding these two faults, one should remain in the middle, just as the moon is beloved by all.
All people mostly sink and drown; though they exhaust their bodies and minds through ascetic practices, they likewise cannot escape this affliction.
Abandoning these two extremes, one reaches nirvana by the Middle Way.

At that time, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, having understood the Buddha’s words and desiring to sever their fetters and latent tendencies, praised the upright and wholesome Dharma spoken by the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"If one employs wisdom, The bonds of delusion are naturally severed.
For these reasons and others like them, To torment the body is of no benefit."
If one can attain the traces of the Path through precept, concentration, and wisdom—
just as one who guards the body desires to extinguish all faults and evils—
one should maintain such a mind.
For this reason, one should not become attached to clothing, food and drink, or bedding;
nor should one give rise to a mind of delighting attachment toward these things.
The mass of fire and the heap of snow—you should abandon them both entirely.
Whether you are at the site of the mass of fire or dwelling on the edge of the snow, you should rest in both places;
it is not fitting to go further away.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya understood this matter accordingly. Having observed him, the Buddha praised him, saying, "Excellent!
and immediately spoke these verses:
"Regarding food, drink, medicine, And dwellings, bedding, and so forth—
Those who cherish their bodies and lives Should take these in moderation and at the proper time.
Toward these various exquisite delicacies, One should not give rise to stained attachment."
Nor is it entirely abandoned;
its essential nature is burning. When the wise employ it according to the occasion, it produces various benefits, yet they themselves are not burned by it.
At that time, having attained the wisdom of hearing, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya desired to enter the wisdom of reflection; after reflecting for a long time, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Is it not the case that abandoning food, drink, and various objects of pleasure is itself the method for cultivating the Path?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
The Buddha addressed Kauṇḍinya: "You should embody my faith."
"If you have any doubts, you may ask according to what is appropriate;
you shall cease the forest of the net of doubt, and I shall burn it with the fire of wisdom.
When Kauṇḍinya heard these words, he was exceedingly joyful, his countenance bright and serene, and he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will listen as we speak of our doubts.
He then spoke in verse:
“Having set out with revulsion, it is extremely difficult to practice asceticism;
yet having abandoned such difficult asceticism, one becomes attached to the five desires.
How can a bhikṣu, in such a state, become free from desire?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya, saying:
“By contemplating the Noble Truth of Suffering, one turns away from birth and death.
Thereupon, Kauṇḍinya rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I have not yet understood; I pray that the Buddha will explain it to me through skillful means.
How is it that one who seeks liberation contemplates the Noble Truth of Suffering?”

The Buddha observed that Kātyāyana had already attained the wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*), and that it was now the appropriate time to teach him the Dharma of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).
The Buddha then preached for him the *Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma*, addressing the bhikṣus:

"This is the Noble Truth of Suffering, which I have never heard before; I have attained right vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening regarding it," as is extensively explained in the *Dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra*.
Question: "If he preached the Dharma for Kātyāyana, why did he himself speak of the Dharma attained by the Buddha? Answer:
"It is for the purpose of manifesting the realization of the Dharma through solitary awakening without a teacher.
Question: "Why do you further say that it is a Dharma never heard before?"
He replied:

"In order to sever their doubts—having attained understanding by hearing the Dharma from Ārāḍa Kālāma, Udraka Rāmaputra, and others—and for the sake of severing such doubts, I said: 'I have never heard this before.'"
Now it is revealed that, by teaching the Middle Way through one's own power,
anyone who is able to cultivate this Middle Way can attain an understanding of the meaning of ultimate truth without hearing it from another.

The Buddha manifested the Four Noble Truths for him; Ājñātakauṇḍinya, perceiving the truths as they should be seen, followed the Middle Way and beheld the Four True Truths. Having immediately attained the fruit of the Path, he wept with joy, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke this verse:
“Like a dog suffering from a head wound, Devoured by maggots and worms, A skilled physician treats it with oil;
Yet the dog does not recognize the kindness of another.”
Instead, you bark back at the physician.
With the majestic power of wisdom, you heat and eliminate the worms of my fetters;
yet, blinded by ignorance, I did not know this was for my own benefit.
Out of great compassion, you have come of your own accord, yet I have instead provoked further offense.
Even all the devas and others should offer you worship;
O You who possess mastery over the Dharma, now hear my confession.
I previously thought that through ascetic practices, one would attain all-encompassing wisdom;
due to the blindness of ignorance, this deluded mind arose as an obscuring veil.
Now that I have heard what has been taught, I resolve to remove the film of non-wisdom.
Now for the first time I truly know that self-starvation is not the true Dharma.
The World-Honored One has shown the world the path leading toward liberation;
the doctrines of the outsiders have little meaning, being merely an adornment of various words and phrases.
The words spoken by others are beautiful and refined, yet full of guile and deceit;
they delude the world, while the ignorant bind themselves in fetters.
The speech of the Sugata is vast and expansive, illuminating all things so that nothing remains uncomprehended.
For what reason was this matter taught?
It was for the sake of the five bhikṣus, so that they might abandon the two extremes, practice the Middle Way, realize the Truths, and attain the fruit of the Path.
59 (Fifty-nine). Furthermore, sentient beings create karma and each receives its own retribution.
I have heard that in the past, there was a poor man who thought to himself:
"I shall go to a temple to seek wealth and treasures for benefit in this present life."
Having had this thought, he said to his younger brother,
"You should work diligently in the fields and manage your livelihood well, so that there is no lack or deficiency within the household."

He then took his younger brother to the field and said, "In this place you may sow sesame; in this place you may sow wheat and barley; and in this place you may sow rice as well as large and small beans."

Having indicated the place of his birth, he went to a temple of the gods and held a great assembly for the disciples of the celestial cult. He made offerings of incense and flowers, smeared the ground with fragrant mud, and worshipped day and night, seeking grace and requesting blessings, hoping for an increase in wealth and property in this present life.
At that time, the deva thought to himself:
"I shall observe whether this poor man has any karmic conditions from previous lives as the cause and condition for practicing generosity.
If there is even a slight connection, I shall employ skillful means to bring him benefit."
Observing that person, he realized there was not even the slightest cause or condition for giving; he further thought:

"Since this person lacks the necessary conditions, yet now diligently entreats me with such fervor, their toil will be in vain and of no benefit; moreover, they will surely harbor resentment toward me."
He then transformed himself into his younger brother and went toward the shrine. At that time, the elder brother said to him:
"What have you been planting?
Why have you come here?"
The transformed younger brother said,
"I also wish to come and entreat the celestial deity so that the deity may be pleased to provide for our food and clothing.
Although I do not sow the seeds, by the power of the celestial deity, the grain and wheat in the fields will naturally suffice."
The elder brother rebuked his younger brother, saying:
"How can one expect a harvest without sowing seeds in the field?
Such a thing is impossible."
He then spoke in verse:
"Within the great earth bounded by the four oceans, and in every place throughout it,
who could ever obtain fruit and grain without having sown the seed?"
At that time, the transformed younger brother questioned his elder brother, saying:
"Is there anyone in this world who does not obtain fruit because they did not plant the seed?
His elder brother replied to his younger brother:
"It is indeed so; what is not sown bears no fruit.
At that time, the celestial deity resumed his original form and spoke this verse:
"You have now declared for yourself: 'What is not sown bears no fruit.'"
If you had no cause of giving in previous lives, how could you have obtained this fruit now?
Although you undergo hardship today by fasting and making offerings to me,
you merely bring yourself needless toil and further distress me.
By what means can you bring about beneficial results in this life?
If you wish to obtain wealth and treasures, as well as wives, children, and kinsmen,
you should purify your body and speech and perform the work of giving.
If one did not plant [seeds] to obtain blessings and benefits, the sun, moon,
and constellations would not illuminate the world;
because they do illuminate the world, one should know that it is due to the conditions of karma.
Each also has its distinctions: those with much merit possess great majesty, while those with little merit have scant majesty;
all this arises from karma. Through giving, one obtains wealth.
Observing the precepts leads to rebirth in the heavens; yet if one lacks the conditions for generosity, one’s majestic power will utterly diminish.
Through concentration and wisdom, one attains liberation.
These are the rewards obtained from these three practices, as taught by the One of Ten Powers.
"All these seeds are causes; you should not disturb me.
Therefore, you should cultivate your practice in order to seek auspicious fruits.
(60) Furthermore, the seed attains its fruit not through the power of auspiciousness; therefore, one should not harbor doubts or attachments regarding auspicious signs.

I have heard that in the past, there was a bhikṣu who went to the house of a donor. At that time, the donor had already chewed a tooth-stick to rinse his mouth, applied ox-gall to his forehead, held a conch shell he intended to blow upon the crown of his head, and grasped a bilva fruit which he raised with his hands and placed upon his forehead as an act of reverence.
Having seen this, a bhikṣu asked him,
"For what reason do you perform such an act?
The donor replied:
"I am performing an auspicious rite.
The bhikṣu asked,
"What benefit or merit is there in performing an auspicious rite?"
The donor replied, "This is a great merit;
you may observe for yourself now how these so-called auspicious signs can cause those who ought to die not to die, and ensure that those who ought to be whipped or bound all obtain liberation."
The bhikṣu smiled and spoke these words:
"If such are the auspicious signs, it is most excellent!
From where have these auspicious signs come, and from what place do they emerge?"
The donor replied,
"This ox bezoar comes from within the heart and lungs of the ox.
The bhikṣu asked:

"If ox bezoar can bring about auspicious matters, why is it that those very oxen are bound with ropes, their noses pierced, and made to plow, drive, and carry loads; beaten with whips, pricked with awls, and struck in various ways; and yet they remain hungry, thirsty, and exhausted, never ceasing their labor of plowing and driving?"
The donor replied, "Indeed, this is so.
The bhikṣu asked:
“That ox possesses bezoar, yet it cannot even save itself; since it suffers in such a manner, how could it possibly bring you good fortune?
He then spoke in verse:
“The ox’s bezoar remains entirely within its heart; It cannot protect or preserve itself.”
How much more so when you grind but a small amount and smear it upon the skin of your forehead—
how could it possibly provide protection?
You should observe this well.
At that time, the donor reflected for a long while and remained silent, unable to answer.
The bhikṣu asked again:
"What is the name of this object?"
"It is as white as a ball of snow; from where does it emerge?
It is by soaking it in water and blowing upon it that the sound comes forth.
The donor replied:
"It is called a conch shell; it is born from the sea.
The bhikṣu asked:
"What you call a conch shell emerges from the ocean and is cast upon dry land; scorched by the sun and suffering for a long time, it eventually dies."
The donor replied,
"It is truly so.
The bhikṣu said:
"This is not auspicious.
He then spoke in verse:
"That insect was born together with the shell; Day and night it dwells within the shell."
When that insect dies, the conch shell cannot protect it;
how much less can it bring about auspiciousness by merely holding you for a moment?
Excellent is this matter; you should now discern it clearly.
"Why are you now thus, walking upon the path of delusion?
At that time, the Brahmin Tan-yue lowered his head and remained silent; reflecting deeply, he was unable to answer.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
“Since this donor seems intent on awakening, I shall now question him.
He addressed the donor, saying:
“What is that thing which people call a ‘joy-pill’?”
The donor replied,
"It is called the bilva fruit.
The bhikṣu said:

"The *vīraṇa* fruit is a fruit of the tree; when people gather it, they strike it with stones, causing it to fall along with the branch. Because of this fruit, both the tree and its branches and leaves are destroyed and fall away together."
"Is it so for you or not? The donor replied,
"It is indeed so."
The bhikṣu said:
"If that is so, how can you hope for good fortune by seizing her?
He then spoke this verse:
"This fruit grows dependent upon the tree; it cannot protect itself.
When someone plucks it, the branches and leaves fall away along with it.
Furthermore, it is gathered to be used as firewood, and once dried, it is used to kindle a flame."
"He cannot save himself; how then can he protect you?
At that time, the donor heard the questions in full but was unable to respond, and said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable Sir!"
"As to what you have asked above, there are truly no auspicious signs; however, I have a doubt, and I pray that you will explain it to me.
The bhikṣu replied, "I shall answer according to your questions."
Then that donor asked in verse:
"The victorious ones of antiquity Proclaimed this to be auspicious when combined;
Yet when observed in reality, There is not a single sign of auspiciousness."
How is this tradition transmitted? You have spoken perversely that this is auspicious;
by what causes and conditions is this so?
I pray that you will explain it for me.
At that time, the bhikṣu replied to that person, saying:
"All views regarding birth have causes, conditions, beginnings, and ends.
He then spoke this verse:
"In times of yore at the beginning of the eon, all were free from desire;
later, when sensual matters arose, those free from desire entered the deep forest.
Those who dwell in the forest yet delight in desire return once more toward the household."
He uttered these words:
"One who is free from desire and has no wife or children cannot be born in the heavens.
Believing this statement to be true, and because he trusted these words, [he was reborn there].
Even when seeking a wife,
they alternately adorn one another; further deceiving and deluding each other,
they consequently give rise to arrogance.
Out of a desire for adornment, he produced this auspicious writing,
whereupon people criticized and reviled him, saying:
"Why do you act like a woman and engage in such adornment?"
That person falsely claims:
"I am performing an auspicious rite; it is not for my own adornment.
The ox-gallstone, conch shells, fruits, and so forth—all these are merely ornaments."
"For this reason, auspicious matters increase and expand;
each and every causal occurrence arises entirely through the adornment of the woman.
The foolish person, with a heart of arrogance, claims that these are truly auspicious.
At that time, upon hearing these verses, the donor’s hair stood on end, and he immediately spoke in verse:
"One should associate with virtuous friends And praise those who are superior men;
Because of such superior persons, One can rightly distinguish between the good and the foul."
Therefore, one should be pliant and compliant throughout all worlds.
The Buddha’s words are entirely true; they seek neither the long nor the short, nor do they maintain victory or defeat.
All that is spoken is based on causes and conditions.
Every matter has its origin.
Meritorious karma is entirely auspicious; within evil karma there is no auspiciousness.
Whether auspicious or inauspicious, all arise from the conditions of their causes and effects.
At that time, the bhikṣu said to the donor:
"Excellent, excellent!
You are a virtuous man; you know the right path."
Then he spoke in verse:
"All worlds throughout the universe arise entirely from good and evil karma.
Good and evil lead to rebirth in the five realms; karma sustains the lives of all beings."
Karmic conditions create the sun and moon: the fifteenth day of the waxing moon and the fifteenth day of the waning moon.
Though evil karma may be subtle, it is called the beginning of the dark fortnight; virtuous karma is called the bright fortnight.
Because of karma it is called the "White Moon," and because of the differentiation of karma,
there is thus black and white.
Even that which is unwholesome becomes auspicious, just like Mount Sumeru.
Both black and white are golden; for those who have performed no meritorious deeds,
auspicious signs become inauspicious, just as all waters, whether good or bad,
are of a salty taste in the great ocean.
All arise from the conditions of karma; therefore,
the wise should all abandon evil deeds and diligently cultivate wholesome ones, just like those who till the fields.
If one places [a seed] upon an auspicious field,
yet obtains a fruiting reward without having sown the seed, this is what is called "auspicious.
For what reason is this said?
One should always diligently listen to the Dharma; by listening to the Dharma, one can eliminate ignorance and the mind will be able to discern between all that is wholesome and unwholesome.
*Mahālaṃkāra-śāstra*, Volume Ten; *Mahālaṃkāra-śāstra*, Volume Eleven.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.

(61) (61) Furthermore, if even a person of little wisdom gives rise to a virtuous mind upon seeing the Buddha’s marks and signs of excellence, how much more so would a person of great virtue and wisdom not give rise to a virtuous mind?

I have heard that in the past, when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to observe the ninety-day summer retreat. He gathered a herd of cows near the Buddha’s vihāra and had them milked to provide milk as an offering for the Buddha.
At that time, there were a thousand brahmins who, out of greed for cow’s milk, traveled and stayed together with cowherds.

When these cowherds heard the brahmins reciting the supreme Vedas, they mastered them all and understood their distinctions well. Among them, some brahmins had only the empty name but no actual knowledge; others were well-versed in incantations but did not understand the Vedas, while others understood the Vedas but did not know the incantations.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had completed his summer retreat of four months, during the period of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, the King commanded the cowherds:
"There is no need for milk now; let your cows roam at will among the water and grass."
He further commanded him, saying:
"When you depart, you must go to take leave of the Buddha; if the Buddha preaches the Dharma, you should listen attentively.
At that time, the cowherd thought to himself:
"Is the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, omniscient,
or is he not? Having had this thought,
he went toward the Jeta Grove to the place where the World-Honored One was.

At that time, the World-Honored One was seated beneath a tree surrounded by a great assembly. Knowing that the cowherd had arrived in the forest, he immediately emitted rays of light from the pores of his body for the cowherd’s sake. The radiance shone so brightly that it eclipsed the woods and fields; it was like a mass of molten gold, or like clarified butter being poured into a fire. The cowherds gazed upon it without weariness, conceiving a sense of its rarity and difficulty to behold, and they said to one another:
"This radiance is like *campaka* flowers filling the entire forest; what kind of light is this?"
He then spoke in verse:
"This grove is most majestic and beautiful, yet its radiance has suddenly changed from its usual state.
Could it be that the celestial Jewel Grove has been transplanted to this garden?"
Resplendent like a golden pavilion, it is also like the banner of the Lord of Devas;
its brilliance surpasses lightning, and its blazing heat exceeds that of clarified butter fire.
Could it be that the Sun or Moon Deva Kings have descended to roam within this grove?

When the cowherd had spoken this verse, he proceeded toward the Jeta Grove to the place where the World-Honored One was. There he beheld the Buddha’s halo, like a hundred thousand suns, and his thirty-two marks of a Great Man, resplendent and clearly manifest. Each of them felt joy and conceived a sense of the extraordinary, and they each offered praise.
Then he spoke in verse:
“The body of the Prince of the Śākya clan Is upright, majestic, and exceedingly wondrous;
His radiant splendor is most intense and blazing, Beholding which, joy and delight arise.”
Body and mind are both blissful; how excellent is this tranquil detachment!
Serene and free from fear, I shall briefly describe its physical marks.
Well-praised as the knowledge of all modes, it is proclaimed throughout the world.
True and not false, all declare this to be the Buddha.
There is none who does not praise the Buddha;
remembering and holding it in mind, one speaks thus with the mouth as well—summarizing its essential meaning.
It cannot be fully explained in detail.
Among this Śākya clan, he is a sun; his name accords with his true nature, and his physical form likewise accords with his name.
Vividly manifesting, like a multitude of jewels arranged to adorn themselves;
with a halo extending a full fathom, like a mountain of pure gold.
It can steal away the eyes of all people; they gaze upon it with delight and cannot bear to leave it—such is that which is beloved by all.
Like a person crying out loudly, their mouth utters these words:
The one who possesses all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñā) is the world-transcending wisdom; it must reside within this very [mind].
What kind of virtuous wisdom could there be that does not perceive such wisdom?
Knowing that this wondrous vessel of a body is truly capable of receiving [the teaching],
and having never before seen such an image through skillful artistry or upon a canvas,
one will ultimately never again give rise to doubt, claiming that he is not omniscient.
With such wondrous physical form, his merit must surely be complete.
Possessing this exquisite appearance to such an extent, he will never be devoid of virtue.
One should seek certain understanding; one should not merely follow the sound of his voice.
At that time, the cowherds spoke these words:
"We should apply ourselves with resolute understanding.
They further thought thus:
"Now, what wisdom or power do we cowherds possess that we should use it to reach a definitive conclusion?
We too can certainly understand and know; how might we come to know?
They spoke again:

"Although we ourselves herd cattle and can distinguish their characteristics, he was born in the royal palace and has studied all forms of wisdom and technical skills; one should not expect him to know the methods of herding cattle."
"I shall now question him about the art of cowherding; he will surely not know it.
He then spoke in verse:
"The Vedas and the arts of archery, The medical sciences and the sacrificial rites,"
The treatise on astronomy and phonology, the fundamental treatise on literary composition,
the treatise establishing the ancestral sacrifices— the source and basis of all treatises—
and the treatise on eloquence and skillful rhetoric, as well as the treatise on the mastery of licentiousness.
Discourses on seeking wealth and profit, discourses on pure lineage,
discourses on all phenomena, and discourses on the ten types of names;
discourses on calculation and accounting, and discourses on go and board games.
Treatises on calligraphy, treatises on music and performance;
treatises on the methods of blowing conches and singing, treatises on the methods of dancing and laughing;
treatises on deception, wrestling, and formal decorum, as well as treatises on gestures and flower garlands.
He has thoroughly mastered all such treatises as these.
He is skilled in massage to relieve fatigue, expert in appraising the value of mani jewels,
proficient in the methods for treating silks and fabrics, and knowledgeable in dyes, waxes, and seals.
He was skilled with mechanical devices and animal glues, and his mastery of archery involved the strategic application of union and separation.
Furthermore, he was adept at cutting and carving to produce various images;
in literature, calligraphy, and painting, there was nothing to which he did not attain complete proficiency.
Furthermore, he was well able to know how to blend fragrances and fashion flower garlands;
he was skilled in the methods of interpreting dreams, skilled in the cries of flying birds,
skilled in discerning the marks of men and women, and skilled in the training of elephants and horses.
Furthermore, he was skilled in the sound of the drum and the method of beating it;
he was skilled in the art of warfare and skilled in non-warfare;
he was skilled in the methods of training horses and wielding spears, and skilled in the methods of leaping and vaulting.
He was well-versed in the art of swift movement and well-versed in the art of crossing over;
regarding all such dharmas, there was nothing he did not master.
"All these superior forms of wisdom and skillful arts were thoroughly mastered by the Prince; if one knows that these are what he studied, it is not considered extraordinary."
"If one knows even this shallow and mundane method of cattle-herding learned by common folk, one should know that he is truly an omniscient one.
Thereupon, the cowherd asked the Buddha:
"By the accomplishment of how many factors in the art of cattle-herding are cattle made to increase?"
The Buddha told him: "If eleven qualities are perfected, the herd of oxen will increase and not diminish.

These are: not knowing the color; not knowing the physical marks; not knowing how to rise early and groom them; not knowing how to cover their wounds; not knowing how to produce smoke; not knowing the great road-methods; not knowing the oxen’s joyful methods of coming and going well; not knowing the places for crossing over; not knowing good pastures; not being skilled in the method of milking while leaving a remainder; and not being skilled in managing the master’s theft."
"If one does not skillfully understand such dharmas as these, they are not said to be 'understanding the method of tending cattle';
if one knows this dharma, they are said to be 'skillfully understanding. " When the cowherds heard these words, they were all filled with joy and said:
"Even we elder cowherds do not know this; how could people like us possibly know these eleven dharmas?"
"Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses all-encompassing wisdom.

The cowherds, having conceived faith and understanding, sought to leave the household life to follow the Buddha. The Buddha then taught them that there are eleven dharmas which a bhikṣu should study, as explained in detail in the Sūtras.
62 (Sixty-second). Furthermore, such great beings do not seek offerings or honor; they seek only to uphold and practice [the Dharma].

I have heard that in the past, when the Tathāgata had completed his ninety-day summer retreat at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove near Śrāvastī and wished to depart, Sudatta immediately entreated the World-Honored One to remain there.
