At that time, the Tathāgata did not accept her invitation; the laywomen (upāsikās), including Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā and others, also requested the Buddha, but the Tathāgata did not grant their request.

The upāsakas of Śrāvastī, along with the long-standing elder ministers and counselors, also entreated the Buddha; King Kapphiṇa and his brothers, as well as Prince Jeta and King Prasenajit, likewise entreated the Buddha, but at that time the World-Honored One did not grant their requests to any of them.
At that time, Sudatta, having failed to achieve his wish because the Buddha did not grant it, returned home and wept in grief and distress.

When the Tathāgata was formerly a bodhisattva, he visited Uruvilvā Kāśyapa; when the latter’s disciples parted from the Buddha, they felt great anguish and suffering—how much more so would Sudatta, who had seen the True Dharma and had long served the Buddha as a lay follower, not be grieved and distressed at parting from the World-Honored One?

As explained in detail in the *Mūlapravṛtti*, at that time there was a maidservant of Sudatta named Puṣpikā. She came from outside carrying water and entered where Sudatta was; she set the water she had carried into a large vessel, and while she was still pouring it out, she saw the elder weeping with grief.
She set down her jar on the ground and said to the elder, "For what reason are you weeping?"
Then the householder Sudatta replied to the maidservant, saying:

"The World-Honored One wishes to travel to other regions; the various great householders, kings, and ministers have each made requests for him to stay, yet he is unwilling to remain in any of them. This is why I weep."
The maidservant said to the elder,
"Could you not invite the Buddha to remain in the country?
The elder replied:

"We have exhorted him with all our might, and all the people within the city, including the eminent Brahmins, have likewise exhorted him; yet he accepted none of it. Although the kings and great ministers exhorted the Tathāgata, they were utterly exhausted and unable to make him remain."
"The True Savior of the world now intends to depart; because of our longing for him, we are filled with grief and find no joy.
The elder said to Pūliya, "It is not only I who experience sorrow and suffering; the people of Śrāvastī are all likewise unhappy."
Then he spoke in verse:
“The people within the city of Śrāvastī, Both old and young, men and women alike,
All give rise to grief and distress, Just like at the time of a lunar eclipse.”
"Everyone is filled with anxiety and fear; we should all join together in making this request.
At that time, having heard these verses, Puṇyālaṅkāra’s countenance brightened and his heart was filled with joy.
He said to the elder, "You should feel glad and not give way to distress; I am able to request the Buddha to remain in our kingdom."
Then Sudatta spoke to the maidservant, saying:
"The king and all these people entreated the Tathāgata, yet they could not make him stay; now you yourself say:
'I am able to invite the Buddha to remain in the kingdom.'"
"I do not believe your words.
Then Puṣkarasārin replied,
"I am certainly capable of it now."
At that time, upon hearing what Pūliya had said, Sudatta’s heart leaped with joy, and he immediately asked the maidservant,
"What power do you possess? Pūliya replied:
"I have no further power; the World-Honored One himself possesses the heart of great compassion.
He then spoke in verse:
"Abiding in reliance upon the knowledge of all modes, His compassion is like a mother’s thought for her calf."
Seeking out those to be transformed, his mind never grows weary;
Sentient beings dwell in the depths of existence, and the Tathāgata constantly desires to pull them out.
It is like a mother who has lost her calf; she seeks it until she finds it, and only then does she rest.
I grasp the robe of great compassion; it will surely cause him to return.
The Buddha does not take into account lineage, wealth, nobility, or physical beauty;
nor does he consider riches, sensual charms, or whether one is good or evil. He observes only the presence of superior faith.
Seeing those sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured,
I shall compassionately rescue them.
If I now remain as a Buddha here, all the people within the kingdom will be filled with joy.
At that time, Puḷinā was carrying water; her clothes were still wet and had not yet dried when she went with her companions to the Jetavana.

At that moment, the king of that country and the great assembly were all at the Jetavana. Then the great assembly opened a path for Puḷinā to reach the Buddha’s presence. Her original roots of goodness all blossomed forth, and she addressed the Buddha in a loud voice, speaking these verses:
“The king and his ministers, The kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas...”
Of all the most eminent beings, there are none who do not make offerings to the Buddha.
Now my heart aspires to joy, and I likewise wish to make offerings;
I now pray to the Buddha, O World-Honored One, may you deign to listen.
Although you know that these superior beings have entreated the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata of great compassion ought to accept my request.
The World-Honored One’s mind is impartial; it is entirely without distinction between high and low.
From those most base and lowly, up to the exalted Śakra,
I have fallen into the ocean of poverty, amidst waves of manifold sufferings;
submerged without end, I constantly hear the sounds of distress.
World-Honored One, you should take pity on us and rescue those who are impoverished, wicked, and withered.
Now, with deep reverence and faith, I address the most steadfast and supreme among the assembly;
may your great compassion bear witness to this.
Within all worlds, he knows and perceives everything;
there is nothing he does not understand. Only the Buddha possesses the complete eye;
there is nothing he does not know.
Now that I have no offerings to present, I invite the Buddha and the assembly of monks; I possess only faith, acceptance, and understanding.
This body is not my own; it belongs to another and is not independent.
Unable to follow the Buddha myself, I only pray that you will accept my invitation.
If the Buddha were to depart far away, my heart would be like one intoxicated with madness.

Since I have already made offerings to his physical body (rūpakāya), if the Buddha were to remain here, I would be able to revere the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). As for that which the Buddha has taught:
I am fully able to receive and practice [your teachings].
How excellent! I pray that you remain and swiftly grant me your instructions; toward the noble and the lowly alike, there shall be no distinction.
You are the solid core among all sentient beings, shared by the entire world.
An unbidden friend, with webbed fingers that cover his hands,
adorned with the wheel-mark upon his palms—
he who causes all to tremble yet comforts them with his hand— who possesses such supreme great compassion?
The fame of your compassion fills the world; it is all the sound of true salvation.
As for the Six Teachers who claim omniscience, you have already subdued them.
Who else can, before this great assembly, let out the fearless lion’s roar?
Whose fame pervades the three realms, causing all who walk and stand to tremble?
Who is known throughout the world as being entirely without fault?
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able; how excellent! We pray that you will be gracious and joyful.
With a mind of refuge in the Triple Gem, like a calf longing for its mother,
for the sake of all sentient beings, you have performed the most difficult ascetic practices.
Having come here despite such exhaustion, you now proclaim the Eightfold Noble Path.
"Revealing the path of ambrosia, you, O Hero among Men, are worthy to be a vessel.
At that time, Piliyakkha’s roots of merit had already ripened; the Buddha Bhagavā, emitting a Brahma-like voice, addressed Piliyakkha with this verse:
"Since you possess such skillful means, you were able to cause me to return and dwell here."
With the hook of your words, you are able to restrain all dragon-elephants.
You possess a firm resolve and a most expansive discernment;
with a mind of diligent application, you entreat me to remain.
How could I now possibly refuse your request?
If I had merely observed your heart from afar, I should still have come to you;
how much more so now that I see your very person—how could I abandon you and depart?
It is not for wealth or profit, nor for nobility or fame,
but because of your steadfast mind that I shall dwell here long.
Observing your pure mind, it is like that of a noble and excellent horse.
Who would not mount and travel about upon a saddle and crupper so finely adorned?
For the sake of many beings, I have become a cause for their liberation;
therefore, I have renounced the household life, unbound by gain or honor.
Just as a great elephant is bound with a tethering rope, so too are gains and offerings; they cannot restrain me.
When I was originally dwelling in the womb, amidst that dark obscurity,
If he still thinks of benefiting sentient beings, how much more so now that he has attained perfect enlightenment?
Having accumulated immeasurable ascetic practices, he remains ever self-dried and withered.
It is not for the sake of all sentient beings that I should enter nirvana.
Desiring to deliver sentient beings, I therefore remain in this world.
For the sake of all beings, I cast myself from cliffs and enter into fire;
for the purpose of transforming them, I do not avoid any suffering or affliction.
Nor did I decline the weariness;
for the sake of fulfilling Pūrṇika’s wish, I returned once more to dwell there. Pūrṇika, you should know:
I have now fulfilled your vow. For I act for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Carrying this mass of poisonous snakes, I dwell for the sake of Puṇya.
The sentient beings of Śrāvastī all conceived a sense of wonder and each uttered these words:
He does not accept the words of kings, nor does he act for the sake of great ministers;
he does not act for the sake of the people of the kingdom or cities, nor does he act for the sake of women with their soft and subtle speech.
Because the Buddha is a teacher who perceives this virtuous mind, he immediately remains still.
All those who walk and stay know that the Buddha acts for the sake of *puṇya*;
therefore, he remains still, not for the sake of any gain or offerings.
Regarding fame, profit, and wealth,
for the sake of those to be transformed, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
he constantly observes all sentient beings.
"For the sake of sentient beings, one should act when it is appropriate to act, and stop immediately when it is appropriate to stop.
(63) Furthermore, in upholding the precepts, one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever violate them.
I have heard that in the past, there was a bhikṣu who went on his almsround in succession and stood outside the door of a pearl-drilling workshop.

At that time, the pearl master was drilling a *maṇi* gem for the king; the color of the bhikṣu’s robe reflected upon the gem, making it appear deep red. The pearl master then entered his house to fetch food for the bhikṣu.
At that time, there was a goose that saw the pearl; its red color and shape resembled meat, so it immediately swallowed it.
The jeweler brought food to offer to the bhikṣu and soon searched for the pearl, but could not find where it was; this pearl was of great value and belonged to the king.
At that time, the jeweler’s family, being impoverished after losing the king’s precious jewel, spoke to the bhikṣu with an agitated mind, saying:
"Return our jewel to us!
Then the bhikṣu reflected thus:
"This jewel has been swallowed by the goose; if I tell that man, he will surely kill the goose to retrieve it.
Now that the time for my own suffering has arrived, what plan can I devise to escape this calamity?"
He then spoke in verse:
"I now protect another's life, My own body suffers pain and distress;
There is no other expedient means, Save for my life to take his place."
If I were to tell that person that it was swallowed by a goose,
he might not believe me and would further endanger its life.
By what means can I act so that both myself and the creature may be fully saved?
Furthermore, "Did you not harm those geese?"—
this statement is also untenable; even if one's own person remains free from fault,
one should not utter a falsehood.
I have heard that Brahmins may tell lies for the sake of their lives;
I have heard the ancient sages say: "It would be better to sacrifice one's own body and life than ever to commit a falsehood."
The Buddha taught that even if a wicked person were to have their body cut and sliced with a saw,
they would never destroy the Dharma despite undergoing such agony.
One should not even tell a lie for the sake of saving one's own life.
It is better to sacrifice one’s body and life with a mind that guards the precepts than to speak falsely.
If I were to utter a lie, my fellow practitioners of the holy life would censure me for breaking the precepts;
such censure and disparagement are light.
It still burns my heart.
For this reason, one should not violate the prohibitions and precepts, lest one now enter into great suffering.
I should now train myself, just as a swan drinks milk from water.
Just as one can drain the milk from a vessel and leave only the water behind, so too shall I now do:
I shall cast away evil and take up what is good.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "When the wise associate with the foolish,"
Although we share the same circumstances, I shall never follow that evil;
for a good person can abandon evil just as a swan drinks milk from water.
Now I sacrifice my own body and life for the sake of this swan’s life.
"By reason of my cause for guarding the precepts, I shall thereby accomplish the path to liberation.
At that time, having heard this verse, the pearl-driller said to the bhikṣu:
"Give me back my pearls! If they are not returned to me, you shall suffer in vain; I will never let you off."
The bhikṣu replied,
"Who took your pearl?
and stood there in silence.
The jeweler said, "There is no one else here; who has stolen this jewel?
At that moment, the jeweler immediately closed the door and spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"Today you must hold fast for yourself.
The bhikṣu immediately looked in the four directions, but found no one upon whom he could rely; like a deer caught in a trap, not knowing where to go, the bhikṣu was likewise without rescue.
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately composed his body and adjusted his robes with dignity. The man spoke to the bhikṣu again, saying:
"Are you now intending to fight with me?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"I am not fighting with you; I am fighting against the thieves that are the fetters (saṃyojana). Why is this so?"
"Lest our physical forms be exposed at the time of being beaten,
we bhikṣus, even when suffering great hardship, always use our robes to cover and protect ourselves so as not to reveal our bodies at the moment of death."
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke again in verse:
“The World-Honored One is endowed with a sense of shame and dread;
I now follow and learn from him, until the end of my life, never shall I expose my body.”
Then that jeweler said to the bhikṣu,
"Is there anyone who does not begrudge their own body or life?
The bhikṣu replied:

"In the Dharma of my renunciation, I have always protected my body and life until liberation; though I have encountered perilous difficulties, I have preserved my life. Now I shall resolutely cast off this body, so that the assembly of renunciants may praise my name."
He then spoke in verse:
"When I relinquish my body and life, Falling to the ground like dry firewood,
May people proclaim my excellence, Saying that for the sake of the geese, I was able to sacrifice my body."
It will likewise cause future generations to give rise to sorrow, suffering, and distress; therefore,
those who hear this should abandon such a body, exert themselves with diligence,
practice the true Path, and steadfastly uphold all the prohibitions and precepts.
"If there are those who would cause others to break the precepts, may they instead take delight in upholding them.
At that time, the jeweler said to the bhikṣu, "What you have just said is deceitful and untrue; do you wish to cause others to proclaim your own fine reputation?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"Do you think there is any falsehood in my wearing these dyed robes now?
Why do you say I am appearing beautiful?"
"It is not out of flattery or self-delight that I do this, nor do I wish for others to praise my name; I desire only that the World-Honored One know my sincere heart.
He then spoke in verse:
"Disciple of the Great Sage, For the sake of upholding the prohibitive precepts..."
Having renounced that which is most difficult to renounce— his very life—
he causes all people of the world to conceive a sense of wonder toward those who have gone forth;
though such a thought has not yet arisen, it will certainly arise in the future.
Then the jeweler seized and bound the bhikṣu, beating him with a staff and asking him,
"Where is the jewel?
Return my jewel to me!"
The bhikṣu replied, “I did not obtain the jewel.
The jeweler wept and felt remorse in his heart; moreover, because of the king’s jewel, he was further afflicted by suffering, and he immediately spoke this verse:
"Alas for this poverty! I know well the nature of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, yet I give rise to a heart of regret; alas for this poverty!
It is because of poverty that one commits evil."
Then the pearl-driller immediately wept and prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣu, saying to him:
"Grant me joy and give me back my pearls; do not burn yourself, nor trouble me."
The bhikṣu replied,
"I truly did not take it.
The jeweler spoke again:
"This bhikṣu is extremely stubborn; even while undergoing such suffering and distress, he still says he has not received [the pearl].
At that time, because he was driven by poverty and desperation, the jeweler had no other recourse but to beat him again in anger.
At that time, the bhikṣu was bound by both hands and his neck; looking in the four directions, he knew not to whom he could appeal and would surely die in vain.
Then the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"The suffering endured in birth and death should all be like this; one ought to remain firm in resolve and never violate the precepts."
If one were to violate the precepts, the retribution for the sins of hell would exceed the suffering experienced now.
He then spoke these verses:
"One should keep in mind the Omniscient One, Whose very essence is Great Compassion."
This is my honored teacher.
You should also remember the words of Pūrṇaka:
"In the forest, the Seer of Endurance had his hands and feet cut off."
Even if their ears and noses were cut off, they would not give rise to a mind of anger.
A bhikṣu should remember what is taught in the Sūtras,
where the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
Regarding the limbs, hands, feet, and so forth, one should not give rise to evil thoughts;
rather, one should single-mindedly recollect the Buddha, keep in mind the life of renunciation,
and remember all the prohibitive precepts.
Through lust and theft, they have sacrificed their bodies and lives;
such instances are beyond counting. As sheep, deer, and the six domestic animals, they have surrendered their bodies in incalculable numbers, suffering in vain at those times.
Better than being born with broken precepts and falsely seeking self-protection—
which ultimately ends in destruction— is it not better to uphold the precepts for the sake of others,
thereby protecting their lives and bodies, and relinquishing this perilous and fragile frame?
Seeking liberation for one's life, though both may sacrifice their bodies and lives, some possess merit while others have nothing to gain.
The wise protect their bodies and lives; thus they achieve renown and possess merit.
"The fool abandons body and life, / Perishing in vain with nothing gained.
Then that bhikṣu said to the pearl-driller:
"Do not abandon your compassionate heart; it is truly a great suffering!"
At that time, the pearl-driller wept and lamented in distress, speaking in verse:
"Though I struck you and caused you great suffering, I recall the King’s reprimand for my pearls; he intends to punish you even more severely."
Now that you have abandoned this suffering, may you likewise cause me to leave behind evil.
You are one who has left the household life; you ought to sever greedy desire.
It is fitting that you abandon this heart of craving and give me back my jewel.
The bhikṣu smiled and spoke in verse:
"Though I possess a mind of desire, I shall ultimately not take this jewel;
you should listen to what I say."
Admired by the wise, they likewise cherish the prohibitive precepts and the dharma of liberation.
The path to the nectar of immortality is like a *maṇi* jewel for you.
In truth, I have no heart for gain or profit;
begging for alms is my vocation, and dwelling beneath trees is sufficient for me.
"For what reason would you commit theft?
You should examine this well.
The pearl-stringer said to the bhikṣu:
"What is the use of so much talk?
he said, and proceeded to bind him even tighter and beat him twice as hard, strangling him with a rope until blood flowed from his ears, eyes, mouth, and nose.
At that moment, the goose came to drink the blood; the pearl merchant, filled with rage, struck the goose and killed it.
The bhikṣu asked,
"Is this goose alive or dead?
The pearl merchant replied:
"What is the use of asking whether this goose is now dead or alive?
At that time, the bhikṣu went to where the goose was; seeing that the goose was already dead, he wept and was filled with sorrow.
He then spoke this verse:
"I have endured all manner of suffering and affliction, hoping only that this goose might live;
yet while my own life has not yet ended, the goose has died before me.
I hoped to protect your life, and for this purpose I have undergone such extreme hardship."
"For what reason did you die first?
My karmic fruition has not yet been realized.
The pearl-driller asked the bhikṣu:
“Gander, what kinship do you have with me that you are so distressed?
The bhikṣu replied,
“Because my wish has not been fulfilled, I am unhappy.”
"I previously formed the intention to save the life of this goose; now that the goose has died, my vow remains unfulfilled.
The jeweler asked, "What vow do you wish to make?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"When the Buddha was a bodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings he cut off his hands and feet, not sparing even his own body or life.
I wish to emulate him."
Then he spoke in verse:
"In a former life, the Bodhisattva sacrificed his own body to ransom a pigeon;
I too formed this intention, wishing to give up my life to save a goose."
"I have attained a most excellent state of mind, desiring to save the life of this goose;
because you have killed the goose, my heart's aspiration remains unfulfilled.
The jeweler asked:
“I do not yet understand what you have said; you should explain to me in detail the reason for it.
At that time, the bhikṣu replied with a verse:
“I am wearing robes of crimson hue, Which, reflecting upon the pearl, resemble the color of flesh.”
Thinking this goose was meat, he immediately swallowed it.
I endured this suffering for the sake of protecting that goose;
though I was pressed by extreme anguish, I hoped only that its life might be preserved.
Toward all beings in the world, the Buddha regards them as his own children;
even toward those who possess no merit at all, the Buddha gives rise to compassion.
Gautama is my teacher—how could he harm living creatures?
"I am his disciple; how could I possibly cause him harm?
When the pearl merchant heard these verses, he immediately opened the goose's belly and recovered the pearl.
He then raised his voice in lamentation and said to the bhikṣu, "By protecting the life of this goose and sparing no thought for your own body, you have caused me to commit this unrighteous act."
He then spoke in verse:
“You concealed your meritorious deeds, Like covering fire with ashes;
Because of my own folly, I have burned and tormented myself for hundreds of lifetimes.”
Your physical marks are most perfectly suited to your Buddhahood;
yet, due to my own ignorance, I was unable to observe them well,
being consumed by the fire of delusion.
"Please listen briefly to my confession:
like one who has stumbled and fallen, supported by the ground, may I rise once more; wait until I have obtained a small offering.
Then that jeweler, with hands joined in *añjali* toward the bhikṣu, spoke these verses again:
“Homage to those of pure conduct; homage to those who firmly uphold the precepts.
Having encountered such extreme suffering and hardship, they do not commit acts of violation or deficiency.
Had they not met with such evil, upholding the precepts would not be so rare.”
One must encounter such suffering; yet for one who is able to maintain the prohibitive precepts, this is indeed called difficult.
To undergo suffering in the body of a goose while not transgressing the prohibitive precepts—this is truly a rare occurrence.
At that time, having completed his confession, the pearl-driller immediately sent the bhikṣu back to his dwelling.

Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty.

(64) Furthermore, the Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear. In the past, when the Tathāgata was a bodhisattva, he did not spare his own body or life in his quest for the Dharma; therefore, one should listen to the Dharma with a diligent mind.

In the past, I heard the parable of the pigeon: there was a teacher of false views who expounded perverted teachings to Śakra Devānām Indra. That non-Buddhist teacher lacked true wisdom, yet he claimed for himself omniscience, asserting that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not exist.
At that time, having heard these words, Śakra was displeased in his heart and gave rise to extreme sorrow.
Then Śakra, seeing those in the world who practiced asceticism, went to all their locations to seek out one possessed of omniscience, as stated in a verse from the *Śakrapraśna Sūtra*:
“I now desire to seek it, yet I cannot attain fulfillment.”
Day and night harboring doubts, I could not distinguish right from wrong.
Since long ago, I have constantly contemplated and sought extensively;
not knowing where the Great True Savior now resides, I ask: where is he?
Viśvakarman addressed Śakra, saying:

"One should not grieve while dwelling in the heavens. In the world, there is a king of Kuśinagara named Śibi who diligently practices austerities in pursuit of *samyak-saṃbodhi*. When a wise person observes him, they see that this king will surely attain Buddhahood before long; you should go to attend upon him."
Śakra replied: "Is that which he has performed not unshakable?
He then spoke this verse:
"Just as when fish give birth, though the offspring are many, those that survive are few;
and just as with the mango fruit, it is difficult to distinguish between the ripe and the unripe—so too it is with Bodhisattvas:
those who resolve their minds [upon enlightenment] are exceedingly numerous."
Those who achieve success are extremely few;
if one performs difficult austerities without falling back, it can be said that they will certainly attain it.
Those who wish to know a bodhisattva must hold their resolve with firm steadfastness.
Viśvakarman said:
"We shall now go to test him; if he truly does not move, we shall perform offerings.
At that time, Śakra, desiring to observe the Bodhisattva’s mind, transformed himself into a hawk and spoke to Viśvakarman:
"Transform yourself into a pigeon.
Thereupon Viśvakarman immediately transformed himself into a pigeon, with a body like azure-green and eyes like red pearls, and went to where Śakra was.
At that time, Śakra, giving rise to a heart of compassion, said to Viśvakarman:
"How can we cause provocation and offense toward the Bodhisattva, inflicting suffering and distress upon King Śibi?"

Although one undergoes suffering as if refining fine jewels to test and recognize their authenticity—just as the method for testing jewels involves cutting, breaking, burning, and hammering them before their true nature is finally known.

At that time, a transformed dove, pursued by a hawk, appeared terrified and came before the great assembly to enter beneath the armpit of King Śibi. Its color was a greenish-blue like the leaf of a lotus flower, its radiance brilliant like a rainbow amidst black clouds, and its beak was white and magnificent. All the people conceived a sense of wonder and immediately spoke this verse:
"With a heart of true compassion, All sentient beings trust in you;
Just as when the sun is hidden by darkness, A bird seeks refuge in its own nest."
The transformed hawk spoke these words:
"I pray that Your Majesty restore my food.
At that time, having heard the hawk's speech and seeing that the pigeon was filled with extreme terror, the Great King immediately spoke this verse:
“Because this pigeon fears the hawk, it has come to me, fluttering in flight;
though it cannot speak with its mouth, it weeps in terror with tears filling its eyes.
Therefore, at this moment, I ought to provide it with protection.”
At that time, in order to comfort the pigeon, the Great King spoke again in verse:
"Do not give rise to fear; I shall never let you die.
As long as my own body remains, I will surely save you."
Not only do I protect and rescue you, but I also protect all sentient beings.
For the sake of all, I act as a laborer;
like one hired by the people of a state, I receive one-sixth of their produce.
"I am now, for all [beings], like a hired laborer;
I must provide protection so that no suffering or calamity befalls them.
At that time, the hawk spoke again to the king:
"Great King!
Please release this pigeon; it is my food.
The king replied to the hawk:
"I have long since attained loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and I ought to protect and rescue all sentient beings.
The hawk asked the king,
"In what way have you attained it for so long?"
At that time, the Great King spoke in verse:
"When I first resolved upon Bodhi, I immediately took up the protection of all sentient beings alike,
bringing forth a heart of compassion toward them all."
The hawk replied in verse:
“If these words are true, you should quickly return my dove to me;
if I die of hunger, you will surely abandon your heart of compassion.”
Having heard this, the king immediately reflected:
"As I am now situated in such extreme difficulty, how shall I deliberate so as to reach a reasoned conclusion?
Having formed this thought, he replied to the hawk:
“Is there any other meat that might save your life?
The hawk replied to the king,
“Only fresh flesh and blood can sustain my life.”
At that time, the Great King thought to himself,
"What means should I employ?
and immediately spoke this verse:
"I shall always practice mindful protection for all sentient beings;
such warm flesh and blood cannot be obtained without killing.
Having formed this thought, he realized: "Only the flesh of my own body can save them, and this is extremely easy."
He further spoke in verse:
“Even by cutting the flesh from my own body to give it to that hawk,
and even unto the sacrifice of my own life, I shall protect this terrified life.”
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Great King addressed the hawk, saying:
"Will you be able to survive by eating my flesh?
The hawk replied:
"It may be so. I pray that Your Majesty will weigh the flesh of your own body against the pigeon; once it has been made equal, you may give it to me, and only then shall I eat.
When the Great King heard these words, his heart was filled with joy, and he immediately said to his attendants, "Quickly fetch the scales!"
"By sacrificing my own flesh to ransom this pigeon's life, today is truly a day of great auspiciousness for me.
Why is it a day of auspiciousness?
He then spoke in verse:
"This abode of old age and sickness is precarious, fragile, and exceedingly foul;
for the sake of the Dharma, I must long ago have abandoned this base and filthy flesh.
Then the king’s attendant, following his command, brought forth the scales.

At that time, although the Great King saw the scale approaching, he showed no sign of distress. He immediately exposed his thigh, which was white, smooth, and lustrous like a *tāla* leaf. He called to an attendant and spoke this verse:
"Take now a sharp blade And cut away the flesh from my thigh;
Simply follow my words And do not give rise to thoughts of doubt or fear."
Without performing difficult austerities, one cannot attain omniscience;
the Knower of All Aspects is the most supreme in the three realms.
Awakening cannot ultimately be obtained through easy means.
"Therefore, I must now act with the utmost firmness.
At that time, the attendant’s eyes were filled with tears of grief; he joined his palms together and spoke these words:

"I pray you, have pity on me and forgive my inability to do this. I am constantly supported by Your Majesty and serve at your command; how could I bear to take a knife and cut the flesh from Your Majesty's thigh?"
He then spoke in verse:
"The King is my savior; if I were to cut the King's flesh, my body and this sword should both instantly fall away."

At that time, the Great King took the knife in his own hand and was about to cut the flesh from his thigh; though the prime minister and high officials wailed and pleaded with him in protest, they could not make him desist, nor could the people within the city, despite their various exhortations, cause him to stop cutting the flesh from his thigh.
Those who were near him also turned back, unable to bear the sight; the brahmins each covered their eyes, unable to look upon him, while the palace ladies raised their voices in mournful wailing.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, in the midst of the void, each said to one another:
"Such a thing is truly unprecedented."

At that time, the Great King’s body was tender and weak; having grown up in the royal palace, he had never before experienced suffering. His entire body was racked with agony, and he fell into a state of fainting and exhaustion. Composing himself, he spoke these verses:
"Alas, O mind, you should remain firm! Such a minor suffering as this— why do you become so bewildered and faint?"
Bound and oppressed by hundreds of thousands of sufferings, Without refuge and without protection,
With no one to provide nurture, None have attained any autonomy.
Since you alone possess the mind [to do so], You should act as their savior.
"Why do you not reproach yourself, yet instead give rise to thoughts of suffering?
Śakra Devānām-indra thought to himself:
"The deeds of this Great King are most grievous; can his mind remain steadfast?"
He then wished to test him and spoke these words:
"The pain you now suffer is extremely difficult to endure; why do you not stop? Why do you allow yourself such torment?"
"You need not do this now with your feet; release the pigeon and let it go.
The Bodhisattva smiled and replied to him, saying:
"I shall never violate my vow and resolve out of pain. Even if there were pain exceeding this, I would never have a thought of retreat."
"Present minor suffering cannot even serve as a metaphor for that of the hells; therefore, one should resolve to generate redoubled compassion for those beings who are afflicted by suffering.
Having formed this thought, he spoke these verses:
"My present bodily pain is but a fraction, Yet my mind is exceedingly vast."
Those of small wisdom and weak resolve suffer the agonies of hell;
such suffering is long-lasting and vast, without bound or shore—
how can it be endured?
"Therefore, one should swiftly and urgently seek awakening,
so as to rescue and liberate oneself from such various sufferings.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again thought to himself:
"The Great King has not yet suffered greatly because of what he has done; however, there are those whose suffering and distress are far more severe than this—would their minds be moved?
I shall now put him to the test.
Having thought thus, he remained silent and said nothing.

Then the great king placed the flesh he had cut from himself on one end of the scale and the pigeon’s body on the other end; the pigeon’s body became heavier. He then cut both thighs and further flesh from his own body and placed them on the scale, yet it was still lighter than the pigeon.
At that time, the great king was deeply struck with doubt and wonder, asking, "For what reason has this come to pass?
He then prepared to mount the scale with his entire body.
Thereupon, the hawk asked:
"Why have you risen? Is it because you wish to repent?
The Great King replied, "I do not wish to repent;
rather, I desire to place my entire body upon the scale to save the life of this pigeon."

At that time, when the Great King was about to ascend the scale, his countenance was serene and joyful; those close to him on the left and right could not bear to look at him, and they even drove away other people so that they would not witness the sight.
Then the king said, "Look as much as you wish.
At that time, the great king had his flesh cut away until it was exhausted; his bones and joints were interlaced like a painted image being destroyed by rain, difficult to discern.
At that time, the Great King made this proclamation:

"I now relinquish my body not for the sake of wealth or treasure, nor for sensual pleasures, nor for wife and children, nor even for my kinsmen and retinue; rather, I seek all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) in order to rescue and deliver all sentient beings."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, nāgas,
and ghost-spirits— all classes of sentient beings."
May all who behold my body be established in non-retrogression.
For the sake of craving wisdom, I have painfully and cruelly cut this body;
those who wish to seek the seed of knowledge should firmly maintain a heart of compassion.
"If it is not firm and solid, then this shall abandon enlightenment.

At that time, the Great King, disregarding his own body and life, immediately ascended the scale. Then the great earth shook in six ways, like blades of grass trembling with the waves; the gods in the sky marveled at this unprecedented event, crying out:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Truly, his name is one of diligence, for his resolve is firm and steadfast.
He then spoke in verse:
"For the sake of protecting that life, I have cut the flesh from my own body."
"Purely virtuous and harboring compassion, holding fast to his resolve without wavering—
among all devas and humans, everyone conceives a sense of wonder.
At that time, the transformed hawk sighed:
"How marvelous!
His mind is firm and solid; he will soon attain Buddhahood, and all sentient beings will finally have someone to rely upon.
Viśvakarman then restored his original form before the Great King and spoke to him:
“Restore his body, and we shall now together provide him with offerings.
For this Bodhisattva’s resolve and strength are as firm as Mount Sumeru situated in the great ocean, never wavering; the mind of this Bodhisattva is likewise.”
Then he spoke these verses:
"We should make offerings to those who are courageous and diligent;
now we shall together rouse ourselves, praising them so that their virtue may increase."
Whatever obstacles or sufferings there may be, we should together prevent them;
by acting as companions to one another, our practice shall remain firm for a long time.
Abiding on the ground of great compassion, [we shall cultivate] the tree of all-encompassing wisdom.
"When the sprout first seeks to appear, the wise should protect it.
Viśvakarman said to Śakra Devānām Indra:

"Now that Your Majesty possesses compassion for the essential nature of all sentient beings, you should cause their bodies to be restored as they were before; may the wisdom-mind of all sentient beings remain unshakable."
At that time, Śakra asked the king:
"In sacrificing this body for the sake of a single pigeon, do you feel no grief or distress?
Then the Great King replied in verse:
"This body shall be abandoned, like that wood or stone;
it will eventually be discarded for birds and beasts, burned by fire, or rot in the earth.
Yet with this useless body, one seeks great benefit."
One should be filled with supreme joy, never harboring a heart of sorrow or regret.
What person of wisdom, having traded this fragile and precarious body for the steadfast Dharma, would not feel exultation?
At that time, Śakra addressed the Great King, saying:
"These words are difficult to believe; moreover, such a matter as this has never occurred before. Who could be trusted?"
The Great King replied:
“I know my own mind. If there were a great seer in the world capable of discerning it, he would surely know that my mind is truly without any change or deviation.”
Śakra said, "Speak the truth. Thereupon,
the Great King made this vow:
"If my mind is now free from regret, may this body be restored to its former state.
At that time, the Great King, observing the places where he had cut his own flesh, spoke these verses:
"When I cut the flesh from my body, my mind took no account of suffering or joy."
Without anger and without sorrow, there is no lack of joy in my heart.
If this matter is indeed true, may my body return to its former state;
may I swiftly accomplish the path to Bodhi and rescue sentient beings from their suffering.
Having spoken this verse,
the flesh of the Great King’s body that had been cut returned to its former state, and he immediately spoke another verse:
“The mountains and the great earth— All of them trembled.”
The trees and the great ocean surged and subsided without ceasing,
like those struck with terror, trembling and finding no peace.
The devas played music, and fragrant flowers rained down from the sky.
The various sounds of bells and drums, All resonate together at once;
The celestial and human music, All break into song.
All sentient beings are stirred, And even the great ocean utters sound.
The heavens rained down fine powdered incense, filling all the paths;
flowers in the void descended at varying speeds,
while the celestial maidens of the sky scattered blossoms until they covered the ground.
Various kinds of colored silks, garments adorned with gold and jewels,
fell from the heavens like rain; the celestial robes, with their many threads and fringes,
produced sounds as they brushed against one another.
Precious vessels emerge spontaneously, adorning the dwellings, while sounds issue forth naturally.
In all directions there are no clouds or obscurations; on every side, all is clear and bright.
A gentle breeze wafts the fragrance; the river flows silently and still.
The yakṣas thirst for the Dharma, their joy and reverence redoubled;
before long he shall attain perfect enlightenment, as they sing and offer praise.
With hearts filled with supreme joy, the most excellent gandharvas sang praises and played music;
with beautiful voices and harmonious tones, they uttered these words of praise: "Before long, you shall attain Buddhahood."
"Having crossed the ocean of vows, you have swiftly reached the auspicious place;
since your fruit and aspirations are now fulfilled, remember me and deliver me.
Then Śakra, together with Viśvakarman, having made offerings to the Bodhisattva, returned to his celestial palace.
65 (6.5) Furthermore, one should associate with virtuous friends; by associating with virtuous friends, the burning afflictions (*saṃyojana*) can be extinguished.

I have heard that in the past, King Subhira had a prince named Sāraṇa. When the king passed away, Prince Sāraṇa was unwilling to succeed him; he relinquished the throne to his younger brother and went to Kātyāyana to seek ordination.
Having gone forth, he followed the Venerable Kātyāyana to the kingdom of Prasenajit and took up residence in a forest there.
King Prasenajit, accompanied by his court ladies, went to that forest to rest and sleep beneath the trees.

When that venerable Sāraṇa had returned from his almsround and was sitting in meditation beneath a tree, the palace women, who were fond of flowers and fruit, went into the grove and searched everywhere for them.

The bhikṣu Srona had left the household life in his prime and was exceedingly handsome. At that time, when the palace women saw that the bhikṣu was both young and robust and possessed such extraordinary features, they conceived a sense of wonder and remarked:
"In the Buddha-dharma, there is even a person such as this who has gone forth to study the Path."
He then sat down at the edge of the perimeter.
When King Pāyāsi awoke from his sleep, he looked about for the palace women and his attendants; they had all dispersed in every direction, and he could not find them.
The king immediately sought out his location and pursued him; seeing the palace ladies surrounding the bhikṣu, seated and listening to his preaching of the Dharma, he spoke this verse:
“Though she wears fresh white robes, She is not as eloquent as you in speech;
Surrounded by a thousand women as she sits, They love and revere her appearance.”
At that time, out of anger and resentment, the king said to the bhikṣu,
"Have you attained arhatship?
He replied:
"No. "Have you attained the stage of Anāgāmin?
He replied:
"No. "Have you attained the stage of Srotāpanna?
He replied:
"No. "Have you attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, up to the fourth dhyāna?
He replied:
"It is not permitted.
When the king heard these words, he became extremely incensed and said to the Venerable One, "You are not one who has transcended desire;
for what reason do you sit together with this palace lady?"
He immediately commanded his attendants to seize this bhikṣu, strip off his robes leaving only his undergarments, and beat the bhikṣu with a staff of thorny spikes.
At that time, the palace women wept and said to the king, “That venerable one has committed no offense; why do you beat him to such an extent?”
Upon hearing these words, the king’s rage and indignation redoubled, and he beat him excessively.

At that time, the Venerable One was formerly a prince; his body being delicate, he had never experienced such suffering, and blood flowed from his entire frame. When the palace ladies saw this, there was none among them who did not weep.

Not long after the Venerable Sāraṇa had received these instructions regarding the beating, he fell to the ground in a swoon. After a long while he regained consciousness; his body was covered in wounds as if from the bites of dogs, resembling a man who has been swallowed by a great serpent and entered its mouth—a situation truly difficult to escape, and even if he were to emerge from its mouth, it would be difficult for him to survive.

Saraṇa’s escape from that peril was likewise; with eyes wide in terror and fearing further blows, his entire body was covered in blood and he could not even put on his clothes. He fled clutching his garment, looking back in all directions, still dreading that someone might come again to seize him.
Having witnessed this event, a fellow practitioner of the holy life (sabrahmacārin) spoke these verses:
"Who is it that, lacking a heart of compassion, Beats and destroys this bhikṣu?
How can one give rise to thoughts of martial prowess In a place where one has gone forth from the household life?"
How can you be so utterly merciless, Giving rise to such a cruel and harmful intent?
To inflict harm upon one who has done no wrong Is truly the act of an irrational person.
Having left the household life and renounced glory and wealth, He is solitary and without power.
"Carrying only his robes and bowl, he kept no superfluous possessions.
What kind of cruel and harmful person is this, who beats him so?
His fellow students supported him by the hand and led him to the Venerable Kātyāyana. Seeing Sona weeping aloud, they felt a sense of revulsion and spoke these verses:
"Just like that jambu fruit, mottled with red, white, and blue,
and with patches of dark red where blood flows out in every place—
who has taken your body and caused it to become such a color?"
At that time, the bhikṣu Sāraṇa pointed to the places on his body where blood was flowing and spoke this verse to the Venerable One:
"Just as I am without protection, living alone as a beggar, I have examined myself and found no fault;
yet, because of my humble appearance, I have been beaten."
Bāhudantī, self-indulgent, a noble lord of the land,
gave rise to a violent and licentious mind; with an evil whip like pouring fire,
he used it to burn and destroy my body.
"Since I have committed no fault or evil, you have come unprovoked to strike and beat me, causing such injury as this.
Knowing that Sarana’s mind was filled with resentment and anger, the Venerable Kātyāyana addressed him, saying:
"The Dharma of those who have left the household life does not consist in protecting one's own body, but in extinguishing the suffering of the mind."
He then spoke in verse:
"Since your body is already beset by suffering and distress, why do you give rise to resentment?
Do not whip yourself with the lash of anger; do not let your deranged mind wound itself."
Saraṇa felt deep anguish in his heart, and signs of anger manifested externally; like a dragon fighting who spits out its tongue and emits light, or like thunder and lightning, he spoke this verse:
“O Upādhyāya, you should know: Anger and pride burn my heart, Just as fire breaks out within the hollow Of a withered, dried-up tree.”
Having left the home life to practice the holy life for all this time,
I now, just as I am today, wish to return to my home.
One who is weak, inferior, and timid cannot even endure such suffering.
How could I possibly endure such great suffering?
I now wish to return home and reclaim the royal throne;
I shall assemble a host of elephant troops that will cover the earth in black.
The fire of hatred blazes intensely, day and night without rest,
like a great and fierce conflagration that consumes mountains and wilds;
even a glowworm is scorched within it, and so it is with Pāṭaliputra.

Having spoken this verse, he immediately gave his three robes to his fellow practitioners of the holy life (sabrahmacārin). With tears and a choked voice, he prostrated at the feet of his preceptor (upādhyāya) and took leave to return home, further speaking in verse:
“Preceptor, please listen to me: I repent to purge my transgressions.
I shall now certainly go home; My mind has no desire or joy [for the path].”
"Within the Dharma of renunciation, one cannot extinguish this enmity.
At that time, his preceptor—who was foremost in skillfully discerning the meaning of the Sūtras and foremost in eloquence and delight in preaching—addressed him, saying:
"You should not do such a thing now."
Why is this? This body is not firm;
it will inevitably perish and be extinguished. Therefore, you should not now disregard the Buddha-dharma for the sake of the body; rather, you should contemplate its impermanence and impurity.
Then he spoke these verses:
"This body is impure; from its nine apertures, filth flows constantly.
Foul and loathsome beyond measure, it is truly a vessel of manifold sufferings."
This body is utterly base and vile, a gathering place for sores and ulcers;
when it is even slightly touched, it gives rise to great suffering and distress.
That your mind is deludedly attached to this is most certainly contrary to the principles of wisdom.
One should abandon inferior aspirations; you should now remember and uphold this verse spoken by the Tathāgata.
One who is able to exercise self-restraint is like one using a leather thong and bridle.
Restraining the evil horse is called the "good vehicle"; failing to restrain it is called "heedlessness.
Dwelling at home is called "imprisonment"; leaving the home life is "liberation from bonds."
Having already attained liberation, why do you return to seek shackles and fetters, remaining in a place of firm bondage and confinement?
Anger is an internal enemy; do not follow after anger, lest you be restrained by it.
I praise those who are learned, the kings among sages;
you should follow their words. Now, remember what you have heard and do not pursue anger.
Regarding the body and its limbs,
that which the Buddha has proclaimed for Pūrṇa and others— you should keep in mind such words as "the much-heard."
You should recall, Śāriputra, what was said regarding the five things that do not cause affliction.
You should carefully examine the eight worldly dharmas;
you ought to deeply weigh the faults and evils of anger.
One should examine oneself: "Does my mind accord with the outward signs of one who has gone forth, or does it not?
Having lived by begging from others, how can I consume the offerings of the faithful?"
Why does one give rise to such intense anger?
When another’s food is within one’s own belly, how can anger arise?
Is it for the sake of consuming what was given in faith?
One should not give rise to anger; for one who speaks of practicing the Dharma and serves as a model for the assembly,
to give rise to anger is what ought not to be done.
Yet if one utters evil words from the mouth, one will be censured and rebuked by the wise;
therefore, one should not do so.
One should instead fulfill three matters and remain disciplined and compliant as a bhikṣu.
Practicing patience without giving rise to anger, Resolutely upholding the prohibitive precepts,
Speaking truthful words and not uttering falsehoods— One who skillfully cultivates patience should not give way to resentment.
One of the śramaṇa class should not utter harsh words; he should wear gentle and soft robes.
What is unbecoming for one who has left the household life is to give vent to anger and speak coarse, evil speech—like a seer sitting in dhyāna who draws a sword and places it upon his lap.
The robes and vessels of a bhikṣu differ in every way from those of the laity;
yet if his anger is the same as that of a white-robed householder, this is something he ought not to do.
If his coarse speech is the same as that of worldly people, how can he be called a bhikṣu?
Having shaved one's hair and removed ornaments, one humbles oneself to practice begging for food;
yet while manifesting such humble signs, one does not sever arrogance.
If one wishes to diminish arrogance, one should discard the defiled and evil mind.
Quickly seek liberation; the body is like a target:
where there is a target, arrows strike it; where there is a body, manifold sufferings assail it;
where there is no body, there is no suffering.
Drums were beaten at its side; a man coming from afar, utterly exhausted and wishing for sleep, reached the gate only to find the drums beating.
There was no rest to be found, and this man could not sleep.
Feeling anger toward the one who beats the drum,
he later reflects upon its root; realizing that this root is simply the drum and not the fault of the people at all,
he immediately rises and chops the drum to pieces.
Only then can one sleep in peace.
For the sake of happiness one has gone forth from home; yet mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and poisonous plants can all sting and bite a person.
One should always be diligent and energetic, distancing oneself from this body; do not dwell in it with long-lasting attachment.
One should perceive its fundamental nature as a mere collection of aggregates and elements;
by destroying the suffering of these aggregates and elements, one rests in the peaceful sleep of Nirvana.
When the preceptor had spoken this verse, he said to him:
"At this time, you ought to abandon your mind of anger, resentment, and malice. Even if you wish to harm others, you should listen to what I have to say."
All the worlds are already afflicted and distressed; how can you now wish to harm and afflict sentient beings?
All sentient beings are subject to the King of Death; myself, you, and even that king shall soon die. For what reason do you now wish to kill your enemy?
All that has life must return to death; why then do you seek to harm them?
Birth is inevitably followed by death, of this there is no doubt or difficulty, just as the rising sun must inevitably set. Since their very nature is death, why inflict further injury upon them?
What benefit or happiness do you derive from harming them?
You are called one who upholds the precepts, yet you wish to bring ruin upon others; in future lives, you will surely receive heavy retribution and undergo immeasurable suffering.
This retribution is likewise; why must you further inflict harm?

That king reviled you, and you gave rise to great anger. The dharma of anger brings great suffering in the present and will yield bitter retribution in future lives. You should first subdue your own anger; why then do you seek to injure him?
If one gives rise to anger for even a single moment, it afflicts both body and mind. I shall now explain this teaching to you; listen to this analogy.
It is like one who holds a finger on fire, intending to burn another; before he can harm the other, he himself suffers the pain.

Hatred is likewise: desiring to harm others, one undergoes bitter suffering oneself; with the body like dry firewood and hatred like fire, before one can burn another, one's own self is already scorched.
"Even if he merely gives rise to a mind of anger wishing to harm him, whether he succeeds or not, the act of self-harm will certainly be accomplished.

At that time, Sāraṇa listened silently to the essential Dharma taught by the Upādhyāya; his fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life all felt great joy and said to one another, "Having heard the essential Dharma taught by the Upādhyāya, he will certainly not abandon the Path."
Sarana, harboring an unbearable resentment, spoke in a loud voice:
"Even a mindless person could not endure such a thing; how much less could I, who possess a mind, bear it?"
Saraṇa spoke in verse:
“Lightning flashes through the void, Like a golden whip;
though the void is insentient, It still produces the sound of thunder.”
"I am now a prince; in this I am no different from him.
How could I possibly endure this and not retaliate?
Having spoken this verse, he addressed his preceptor, saying:
"What you have said is indeed true.
However, my mind is now as hard as stone, so that not even a drop of water can enter it; seeing my skin torn and blood flowing outside, I immediately gave rise to thoughts of anger and arrogance."

I have not made a request, nor am I his slave, nor his hired laborer, nor his subject; I have not committed robbery, nor have I caused others to fall into ruin, nor have I incited strife against the king—for what fault have I been subjected to such humiliation?

Dwelling upon the royal throne, he considers himself powerful; yet now we are destitute commoners, each with our own lot. While I sit in the empty forest begging for alms, he has wantonly inflicted harm and injury upon me.
I shall cause those like me to never dare to harm him; I shall take my revenge so that he may not sleep in peace.
I am a virtuous person who has been unjustly insulted; I shall now inflict suffering upon him so that after this day passes, no more wicked and violent persons will dare to commit such evil.
Having spoken these words, he knelt before the preceptor and said:
"Please grant me leave to relinquish the precepts.
At that moment, his fellow teacher and all his co-students and fellow practitioners of the holy life raised their voices and wept aloud.
"Why do you now abandon the Buddha-dharma?
Some grasped his hand, some embraced him, and some prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground to pay him homage, saying to him:
"Be careful not to abandon the Buddha-dharma now!"
Then he spoke in verse:
"Why do you depart alone from among the assembly,
retreating from the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts?"
Why do you commit such evil, saying that the Buddha is not your teacher?
When a bhikṣu comes to your home, why are you without shame or remorse?
Having vowed to uphold [the precepts] for as long as life lasts, how can you lack loyalty and faith?
Yet you wish to abandon the holy life?
Having long practiced the mendicant’s way, you now put on armor and grasp weapons,
intending to enter the ranks of battle.
Having abandoned the dharma of a śramaṇa and not remembering the patience of the Rishi,
though his hands and feet were severed, he alone was truly one who has gone forth;
are you not also one who has gone forth?
"He alone knows the Dharma; do you not know the Dharma?
Even so, you should give rise to a heart of compassion. Maintain your resolve with steadfastness and do not let your mind be distracted.
Why have you now lost your composure because of these blows?"
The Venerable Kaccāyana said to the group:
"His mind is already concentrated; you all depart, and I shall treat him for you.
After the bhikṣus had left, the Venerable Kaccāyana stroked Masaraṇa’s head and spoke these words:
“Are you certain you will go?
He replied, “Preceptor!”
"I must certainly depart now.
Kātyāyana said, "Stay here for one night; you may go tomorrow. Do not hastily abandon the precepts."
He replied, "So be it.

I shall now follow my preceptor’s final word; tonight I shall stay with my preceptor, and tomorrow I will renounce the precepts and return home to take up the royal throne and contend with Prasenajit."

At the feet of his preceptor, he spread out grass as a mat and stayed there for the night. Then, by means of his supernormal power, Kātyāyana caused him to fall into a deep sleep and dreamed that he returned to his native land, renounced the precepts, went home, and occupied the royal throne; he then assembled the fourfold army and marched toward Pāṭaliputra.
At that time, Vāsavadatta also assembled the fourfold army and engaged them in battle. Sālaṇa’s forces were completely defeated; Sālaṇa was captured, bound, and taken away.
Vāsavadatta said, "This man is wicked; he should be executed."
A garland of karaṃvīra flowers was tied around his neck; the executioner made a terrible sound as he led him, surrounded by a multitude of guards bearing weapons, to the cemetery.
On the way, he saw Kātyāyana carrying his robes and bowl into the city to beg for alms, weeping and shedding tears as he spoke this verse to his preceptor:
"Disregarding the instructions of my teacher, My body is turbid with anger and affliction;
Now, having gone beneath the tree, I shall bring ruin to the Buddha-dharma."
I am now heading toward death, surrounded on all sides by many blades;
like a deer caught within a trap, so too am I now.
I can no longer see Jambudvīpa; this is the last time I behold my preceptor.
"Though you harbor an evil heart, it is still like a cow that thinks only of its calf.
At that time, the executioner held a sword as blue as a lotus and said to him:
"This sword shall cut you down; even if you have a preceptor, what can he possibly do for you?"
Seeking compassion from his preceptor, he raised his voice and wept aloud,
saying, "I now take refuge in my preceptor.
Startled and terrified, he immediately rose from sleep and prostrated at the feet of his preceptor.
"I pray that the Upādhyāya will understand my words, which were spoken out of distress.

He said, "I was originally foolish and wished to abandon the Buddha's prohibitions; please grant me permission to leave the household life. I harbor no resentment, nor do I seek the king. Why is this so?"
The flavor of sensual pleasure is meager, while its suffering and afflictions are manifold; I have fully realized the faults and evils of resentment and malice.

Now I desire only to attain the Dharma of liberation. I have no fixed resolve and am a fickle being who fails to observe things well; I do not engage in conversation with the wise and have become a vessel for the reproaches of all sentient beings.

I only pray that the Upādhyāya will ordain me as a renunciant; when I am beset by suffering and affliction, may you manifest the aspect of compassion, for within my pain and distress, the Upādhyāya has shown me mercy.
Kātyāyana said, "You have not abandoned the path; I merely manifested this dream through my supernormal powers.
Yet he still did not believe him.
The Upādhyāya extended his right arm, emitting light, and said to him:
"If you do not abandon the path, observe your own marks yourself.
Sarana rejoiced and spoke these words:
“Ah, how excellent is my spiritual friend!
By means of skillful expedients, you have opened my understanding; my transgressions have been sustained by your dream.
What the Buddha said—that a spiritual friend is the entirety of the holy life—is indeed true.”
"Who could attain liberation without relying on a spiritual friend?
Only the deluded do not rely on virtuous friends; how then could they ever attain liberation?
Venerable Kātyāyana has extracted the poisonous drug of ill-will from Śroṇāparāntaka, extinguishing it without remainder. Therefore, those who possess wisdom should draw near to spiritual friends.
The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra, Fascicle Twelve;
The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra, Fascicle Thirteen.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.

(66) Furthermore, the merit of making offerings to a Buddha stūpa is exceedingly great; therefore, one should diligently make offerings with a devoted mind. I once heard that King Prasenajit went to the place where the Buddha was staying and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. He smelled a wondrous fragrance, more exquisite than celestial incense; having smelled this scent, he looked in all four directions but could not discern its source.
He then addressed the World-Honored One: “Whose fragrance is this?”
The Buddha said to the king,
"Do you now wish to know the source of this fragrance?
The king immediately replied:
“Indeed, we wish to hear it.
At that time, the World-Honored One pointed to the ground with his finger, and immediately a bone appeared, like red sandalwood and five zhang in length. The Tathāgata said to the king:
“The fragrance you have smelled comes from this bone.”
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying,
"By what causes and conditions does this fragrance of bone arise?
The Buddha told the king:
"Listen well and attentively!
the Buddha said.
"In the past there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa; that World-Honored One, having completed his work of transformation, entered into parinirvāṇa."

At that time, there was a king named Kāśyapa who took the Buddha’s relics and constructed a stupa made of the seven precious substances, two yojanas in height and breadth. He further issued a decree throughout the kingdom:
"Those who possess flowers shall not use them for any other purpose; all must be brought to offer as worship to that stupa."

At that time, there was a son of a householder in that country who had an affair with a courtesan; his mind was so preoccupied with matters of desire that he could not part from them. Seeing that all the flowers were in the Buddha-stūpa, he became blinded by lust and entered the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha to steal a flower and give it to the courtesan.

At that time, the son of the elder, realizing the Buddha’s merit, felt remorse for having committed this unrighteous act driven by lust; his carnal desire subsided. When the next day arrived, he felt a sense of revulsion and thought to himself:
"I have done what is unwholesome, stealing flowers from the Buddha to give to that courtesan."

Immediately, he was consumed by the fever of remorse, and sores broke out all over his body; at first like mustard seeds, they subsequently grew until there was no space left uncovered. He then spoke this verse:
“I have now committed unwholesome deeds, Transgressing the teachings of all Buddhas.
Having abandoned shame and remorse, I am thus devoid of a respectful heart.”
One who violates the words of the Sugata is not a disciple of the Buddha.
While all the people dare not disobey the king’s commands,
I alone have transgressed both the national laws and the teachings of faith.
I am now devoid of shame; truly, I am like those beasts and birds.
Among all fields of merit, none is more supreme than the stupa of the World-Honored One;
yet, because of my folly, I committed the base act of stealing flowers.
Why does this arm not fall away at once?
And why does this great earth not sink down,
yet remains able to support me?
Burning away all wholesome deeds, deluded by desire,
they enter into the thicket of darkness.
Now I am a servant of desire, failing to perceive its karmic retribution.
“Stealing flowers to adorn oneself, one shall long endure the sufferings of hell.
As he felt a redoubled sense of regret and remorse, his body became increasingly parched and withered.
At that moment, the sores that had appeared upon the man’s body immediately burst open, becoming exceedingly foul and putrid.

At that time, the man’s parents and brothers all came to attend to him and administered cooling medicines to treat his illness, but the disease grew even more severe. They summoned a skilled physician to re-examine him, who said:
"It is necessary to apply ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*) to the body; only then can he be cured."
At that time, his parents immediately purchased precious ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*) and used it to anoint the boy’s body, yet the pain only increased and did not subside.
Then, weeping and filled with alarm, the man said to his parents:
"Your efforts have been in vain; for this illness of my son arises from the mind, not from a physical ailment."
The father said to his son,
"What is this sickness of the mind?
The son then replied to his father with a verse:
“‘My base and vulgar conduct is shameful; it should not have been told to my father.
Yet now, constrained by illness, I have cast aside all sense of shame.’”
Having stolen flowers from a noble stūpa and given them to a courtesan, he committed this evil deed;
yet later, he attained a heart of remorse.
By day he wished to be scorched by the sun, and by night he attained a mind of awakening.
If one is granted the opportunity for repentance, it is like being doused with cold water.
My body and mind are now burning hot; later, I shall suffer the torments of hell, just as fire blazes from within a rotten tree.
I am now likewise thus, with the fire of the mind flaring from within.
Cold water, *uśīra* root, blue lotuses strung with pearls,
*kośātaki*, *mālatī*, and various types of *candana*— [These cannot extinguish it.]
If one applies such things as these to the exterior of the body, one will ultimately be unable to achieve recovery.
Since the fever of anxiety arises from within, one ought to apply [remedy] to the mind; what benefit would there be in merely applying it to the body?
"Take me to the stupa and provide offerings for me;
this illness will surely be cured.
Then they together lifted his bed and went to the site of the Buddha’s stupa.
His body grew increasingly feverish, and his breath was on the verge of ceasing.

At that time, his parents, brothers, and kinsmen brought him to the site on a bed; the man focused his mind solely on the *samyak-saṃbodhi* of Kāśyapa Tathāgata, his eyes filled with tears, and with the *candana* incense he held, he approached the stūpa in sorrow and spoke this verse:
“O Great Compassionate One, savior from suffering and distress, You who always proclaim all manner of virtuous deeds...”
Deluded by desire, blind and seeing nothing,
I committed various transgressions and evils against those who provide true salvation.
Though the stupa was like Mount Sumeru, I, out of ignorance, violated it.
One acquires an evil reputation in the present life, And in the future birth falls into the evil realms.
Failing to contemplate the virtues of the Buddha, One now undergoes this evil retribution;
Having already obtained these manifest fruits, One will surely suffer further torment hereafter.
The Enlightened One, with his eye of wisdom, has left suffering behind and eliminated all desires;
I now harbor grief and sorrow, and with a sincere heart take refuge in the Buddha.
For all the transgressions and afflictions I have committed, may you please deliver and rescue me.
"Just as a person who has stumbled and fallen Rises up by relying on the ground.
At that time, his parents and all his kinsmen praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
That you are now able to offer such praise is because only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can eliminate your illness.
He then spoke in verse:
"You should now, in the presence of the Buddha, give rise to a mind of faith and understanding;
only the great merit of the Buddha can deliver you."
"Just as when one enters the great ocean, though the ship is wrecked and wealth and treasures lost, if the body does not sink, one may yet recover the riches again.

At that time, the son of the elder and his kinsmen, having seen that his body was covered in festering wounds, putrid and foul-smelling, became weary of birth and death; they immediately used flowers, incense, unguents, and powdered perfumes to make offerings at the stupa of Kāśyapa Buddha, and further used ox-head sandalwood to paint the Buddha’s body.
As his bodily sores gradually healed, he felt a heart of joy, and the affliction of heat was completely cured.
At that time, the elder’s son, having received this manifest retribution, gave rise to a heart of joy; knowing that his transgressions were extinguished, he immediately spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata, the All-Knowing One, Is liberated from all fetters and latent tendencies.”
Kāśyapa, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is able to deliver all sentient beings.
The Buddha is the father of all sentient beings; for the sake of all worlds, he acts as a friend who does not need to be asked.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can possess such a heart of compassion.
Having now committed great transgressions and evils before the Buddha, I pray that you will grant me the opportunity to repent.
I make this vow within my heart: listen but to what I say.
Driven by desire, I have lost my composure and committed various evils.
May you cause me to be free from craving and from the enemies that are the fetters and afflictions.
With the faculties untamed, like a refractory horse, do not commit evil deeds; always attain the state of quiescence.
By offering gośīrṣa sandalwood to the Buddha’s stūpa, [one attains such merit].
"May you always possess this fragrance in your body, and never fall into the various evil realms.

Subsequently, that son of the elder passed away and was reborn among the devas or among human beings; his body was always fragrant, and all his limbs and joints were endowed with the marks and signs of excellence. His parents gave him the name "Fragrant Body" (Gandhagātra).
At that time, Gandhāṅga grew weary of the aggregates and the realms, sought and attained the path of a pratyekabuddha through renunciation;
these bones are those from which the fragrance of a pratyekabuddha’s remains issues forth.
Therefore, all people should make offerings to the stūpa to obtain great merit.

(67) Furthermore, those who previously possessed roots of goodness and were destined for liberation may fall back into hell due to causes and conditions such as not hearing the Dharma; for this reason, one should listen to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
I have heard in the past that Śrīgupta, a disciple of Pūraṇa, was the husband of Śuddhikā’s elder sister; at that time, Śuddhikā’s father was formerly a disciple of the Nirgranthas.

Although all sentient beings habitually follow the teachings of their respective teachers, Jyotiṣka, having received the transformative grace of the Buddha, and his father likewise having gained faith as disciples of the Buddha, no longer sought instruction from the followers of the six heretical masters.
At that time, in order to convert her brother-in-law Śrigupta, Śuddhika went to him repeatedly and said to him:
"The Buddha Bhagavat is omniscient."
Her brother-in-law said,
"Pūraṇa is also omniscient. Because they were disputing over omniscience,
they subsequently engaged in debate together.
Jyotiṣka said to Śrīgupta: "I shall now demonstrate to you that I possess all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
You, Pūraṇa, do not possess all-knowledge; with his meager wisdom, he deceives and deludes the people of the world, claiming to have knowledge when in truth he is not all-knowing."
"By merely conjecturing based on appearances, one can only possibly know minor matters; how, then, could this be called 'all-encompassing wisdom' (sarvajñatā)?
He then spoke in verse:
"Just as one born blind, Who takes rock crystal for an eye,"
Deceiving small children and others, he claims, "I have eyes.
Yet he himself had no eyes before; now he claims, "I have eyes.
These words are not to be trusted; they are fit only for deceiving the foolish.
Able to explain the treatises on causal characteristics, they employ skillful means to falsely manifest their own excellence;
because of such appearances, they delude the multitude.
Though their outward appearance suggests they have attained these states, what is it that they actually know?
Śrigupta said to Jyotiṣka:
"You have been deluded by the magical arts of Gautama; Pūraṇa is omniscient, yet you do not recognize this and instead give rise to slander."
"Pūraṇa is fully able to understand all matters of the three periods of time regarding walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
Jotika said: "I shall now demonstrate to you how Pūraṇa is not omniscient."
He immediately invited Pūraṇa to accompany him to his home.
At that time, Pūraṇa thought to himself:
"As for Jyotiṣka, his father was formerly my disciple; having previously served Gautama and come to know its faults, he has now returned to me—this is my merit."
Having formed this thought, he consented to accept the invitation.
On the following day, Pūraṇa, leading several hundred thousand followers and surrounded by five hundred disciples, went to the house of Jyotiṣka.
Having arrived at his home, Pūraṇa smiled; Śrīgupta asked Pūraṇa, "For what reason did the Blessed One smile?"
Pūraṇa said: "I saw from afar that on the banks of the Nammadā River, a monkey had fallen into the water; that is why I laughed."
Śrīgupta addressed him again, saying: "The Blessed One possesses the pure divine eye;
from within this city, you saw from afar a monkey falling into the water on the Narmadā River a thousand *li* away."
Then that non-Buddhist teacher, leading his disciples, entered the house of Jyotiṣka and immediately took his seat.
Once the assembly was settled, Jyotiṣka covered the rice with the soup and presented it to Pūraṇa.
Pūraṇa said, "This rice has no soup; how can it be eaten?"
Jyotiṣka then stirred the rice and soup together and said to Śrīgupta,
"If even your teacher cannot see that there is soup beneath the rice in his bowl, how could he possibly know from afar that a monkey has fallen into a river a thousand li away?"
The evidence of these matters makes it clear that he does not possess omniscience; rather, he merely craves fame for the sake of gain and offerings.
Alas for sentient beings! Having already deluded himself, he proceeds to teach others as well.
He then spoke in verse:
“Your teacher Pūraṇa, Deluded and possessed of perverted views,
Has lost the lamp of wisdom And dwells in the darkness of ignorance.”
Deluded by self-love, the foolish revere one another;
