yet among the Śākyas, there is one most excellent, endowed with the thirty-two marks.
He alone is the All-Knowing One; there is no other who is supreme.
At that time, because of his shame and remorse, Pūraṇa did not eat his fill and departed with his head bowed.
Śrīgupta was then sorrowful and unhappy; as a teacher and disciple, he wished for his pupil to excel even though he possessed such shortcomings and ugliness.
Śrīgupta went to Pūraṇa and said to him: "Do not be distressed!

Although Jyotiṣka has now brought disgrace upon the Blessed One, it is not yet enough to be ashamed that he has returned home. If I were to invite Jyotiṣka’s teacher to my house, he would only be able to enter, but never leave."

Having spoken these words, he went to the Jeta Grove to invite the World-Honored One. His heart was truly crooked and deceitful, yet he feigned reverence; with palms joined in *añjali* toward the World-Honored One, he spoke this verse:
"I shall prepare a modest offering tomorrow; I pray you will deign to visit my home.
O Supreme Vessel within the Three Realms, I pray you will not cast me aside."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Śrīgupta harbored a mind of deceit while feigning outward respect,
spoke these verses: "Harboring two conflicting schemes within the heart, While manifesting outwardly a semblance of intimacy,
gentleness, and goodness— Just as when a fish dwells in water, The water must inevitably be stirred."
It is like the making of a necklace: copper within and gold painted on the outside;
once the wise have examined it, they immediately know it is not true gold.
When the mind harbors what is crooked, the outward appearance will surely be different.
If even that which is mindless can be known, how much more so that which possesses a mind?
One who observes the marks and signs of pure golden color will immediately know it to be real;
yet if copper were coated with gold, one who discerns well would know it is not genuine.

At that time, the World-Honored One, deeply knowing that Śrigupta harbored deceit and hypocrisy in his heart, yet out of great compassion and pity, and further observing that the roots of merit from his offerings were nearing ripeness, the World-Honored One immediately accepted his invitation in silence.
At that time, Śrīgupta thought to himself:
"If he is truly omniscient, why does he not know my mind and accept my invitation?
He then spoke this verse:
"How can one possess omniscience without practicing asceticism,
yet delighting in worldly pleasures?
If they cannot know my mind, how can they be called omniscient?"
Alas! The fools of this world do not recognize their own faults and shortcomings, but instead give rise to perceptions of merit.
Lacking true wisdom, they falsely praise his virtues;
deluded and attached to the fan of the physical marks and signs, they extol him throughout the world.

When Śrīgupta had spoken this verse, he immediately returned to his home and prepared the offerings. He placed lethal poison throughout the meal, and inside the middle gate, he dug a large, deep pit, filling it with *gadhara* charcoal so that no smoke or flame remained; he then covered the top with ash and earth, and further covered it with grass.
Then the wife asked her husband,
"What task have you undertaken that you have exerted yourself so greatly?
Her husband replied:
"I am now doing this because I wish to harm my enemy.
His wife asked, "Who is this enemy?"
Śrīgupta then spoke in verse:
"Delighting in and clinging to various pleasures, Fearing matters of suffering and affliction,
Without practicing any ascetic austerities, Yet wishing to seek liberation— How can this be?"
"Delighting in sweet delicacies, yet also valiantly practicing eloquent discourse—
this son of the Śākya clan is my great enemy.
Then Śrīgupta’s wife joined her palms and said to her husband:
"You should abandon this angry mind. In the past, I saw such a Great Man, the Buddha, at my younger brother’s house; why then do you harbor resentment?
He then spoke in verse:
"That Sage is able to endure, having severed all signs of aversion and hatred."
Furthermore, having extinguished pride and arrogance, and having abandoned strife and contention—who among those who harbor enmity toward him could be considered a kinsman?
Behold his marks of a Great Man; he possesses no heart of anger or malice.
He constantly utters gentle sounds, first speaking kind words of consolation;
his nose is round and straight, without any depressions or crookedness;
he gazes directly ahead without looking back, nor does he glance to the left or right.
Their speech is neither coarse nor harsh; they avoid abusive words and double-tongued talk.
With a serene countenance and free from angry expression, they are likewise not violent or cruel.
Their words do not cause injury or offense, nor do they bring about grief or distress.
Why do you pointlessly give rise to poisonous thoughts of hatred toward him?
His face is like the full moon of autumn; his eyes are like blooming blue lotuses.
His gait is like that of the lion king; his arms extend past his knees.
Your body is like a mountain of pure gold;
you have encountered such an enemy that the evil realms are entirely emptied.
Had it not been for this enemy, the world would be filled with the greatest sufferings of the three evil paths.
Śrīgupta thought to himself:
"Because he was my own younger brother, he has developed a partisan bias toward me; I must now protect him, for if I do not, he might leak my words to others."
Having formed this thought, he immediately confined his wife in a deep chamber.
He then sent a messenger to summon the Nirgranthas, saying:
"Come now, for I shall rid you of your enemies; I have prepared a pit of fire and poisoned rice."
"These Nirgranthas, having scorched their bodies with the five heats, were all blackened like charred ashes; they gathered together and went to the place where Śrīgupta resided."

Śrīgupta’s residence was adorned and pure white, as bright and clean as a *koṭṭhaka* tree. When the Nirgranthas arrived at his house and stood upon the upper terrace, they were like a flock of crows; or rather, like *kroñca* birds and black bees swarming around a *koṭṭhaka* tree, leaping about with joy.

The Nirgrantha sons were just the same, and they spoke thus: "We shall now watch how the śramaṇa Gautama is being scorched; if he is not consumed by the fire, the poisoned rice will surely suffice to harm him, and he will certainly die."
Having spoken these words, he smiled with joy.
Then Śrīgupta immediately dispatched a man to go to the Buddha’s dwelling and say to him:
"The time has come; the meal is prepared."
Having ascended the high tower, he deliberated on this matter together with Pūraṇa.
At that time, the deity residing in Śrīgupta’s house wept in sorrowful lamentation, saying:
"The Tathāgata, the Hero of the World, the Honored One of the Triple Realm, the Buddha Bhagavān!"
Why do you harbor such an evil mind, wishing to destroy and harm me?
For me, there is now no path to survival at all. Why is this so?

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, who is unsurpassed in the three realms, has passed away here; yet his ill repute spreads and pervades the world, and all the gods mock me, saying, "This is an evil man."
"How shall I sustain my life?

When the Tathāgata was formerly a bodhisattva, he did not begrudge his wealth, body, hands, or feet; he performed such deeds out of compassion. How much more so now, when he would surely cherish his own body?"
"How could I possibly give rise to a mind of malice or rebellion toward such a person?
Therefore, I must certainly sacrifice my life.

Furthermore, in the present world, for the sake of sentient beings, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, practiced austerities for six years, consuming only one sesame seed and one grain of rice per day, until his body was emaciated and his flesh and bones were withered away."
He then spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata practiced austerities, Emaciating himself for six years;
He performed such difficult and painful deeds For the sake of all sentient beings.”
"How could one who possesses such compassion wish to inflict harm?
The person sent by him went to the Bamboo Grove and said,
"World-Honored One!..."
"The meal is prepared; please know that it is time.
At that time, the World-Honored One, his heart permeated by great compassion and desiring to benefit all sentient beings, waved his hand and said:
"Alas, you foolish commoners!"

You should now perceive the Truth; having made offerings to the Buddhas in past lives, the roots of goodness that lead to liberation have already matured. Why, then, do you dispatch such a messenger to perform such a perverse act?
"A pit of fire and poisoned rice await me!
Why do you commit such an extremely evil deed as to summon me here?
This act you have done is utterly unreasonable."
He then spoke in verse:
"In days of yore, for six years I practiced austerities;
for the sake of all sentient beings, I performed these various difficult deeds."
How is it that these sentient beings now wish to inflict harm and injury upon me?
Alas! How utterly foolish and blind are they, lacking the eye of wisdom, to commit such unrighteous acts and recklessly seek to cause me distress and harm.
I regard all sentient beings as surpassing even my own compassionate parents;
how could they harbor thoughts of malice toward me?
Today the time has come, for this is the constant law of all Buddhas.
For the sake of providing true relief to sentient beings, like a physician wishing to save the sick,
even when subjected to various forms of abuse and insults, I still give rise to a mind of patience;
I am now like that physician, going to that household.
For what reason did he go there?
Driven by great compassion.
Like a person afflicted with a demonic illness, his mind and thoughts were no longer under his own control.
Furthermore, one should not revile or curse the mantra-reciter;
nor, for the sake of treating a disease caused by a spirit, should one blame the patient.
The spirit of affliction dwells within the mind; out of ignorance, one fails to discern this.
"Seeking to inflict harm and injury upon me;
I am now likewise doing so, merely to expel the demons of affliction—I should not reproach that person.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, manifesting an air of displeasure, and spoke again in verse:
"Ānanda, bring the robes; Rāhula, take the bowl.
Nanda, you too must go—quickly summon the bhikṣus.
You must not delay any longer; you should proceed with all haste."
That Śrīgupta now urgently awaits my conversion.
Dwelling within this body of a venomous serpent, for the sake of delivering sentient beings,
I now harbor this enemy in order to benefit those beings.
At that time, the Tathāgata emerged from among the forest trees, like the sun shining forth as clouds disperse.

Then, the deity of that grove, seeing with her divine eye the fire pit and the meal of poisoned rice prepared within Śrīgupta’s house, wept and shed tears. Out of reverence and love for the Buddha, she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, gazed up at his venerable countenance, and spoke this verse:
“His mind harbors cruelty, And he possesses no heart for benefit.”
I pray that the Buddha need not go, but turn back toward the Bamboo Grove.
A World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter; he appears but once in the course of vast eons.
Although the Buddha does not cherish his own body, it is for the sake of delivering all sentient beings.
Such a supreme and wondrous body as this should be diligently protected.
Those who have not yet attained liberation should be enabled to cross over;
to those who fear, grant fearlessness; and to those who are weary, grant rest.
May those who have no refuge find a place of refuge.
To speak briefly, there are immeasurable benefits.
We only pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will not go to that house.
"May you serve as a place of refuge for the devas and asuras.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the reason, asked the celestial deity intentionally:
"For what reason should you not go to the place where Śrīgupta resides?"
At that time, a certain deva spoke this verse:
"Śrīgupta’s house has a great, deep fire-pit,
Filled with blazing flames, Deceitfully covered over its surface."
The Buddha further spoke in verse:
"The fires of greed and delusion are exceedingly difficult to extinguish;
with the water of wisdom, I have doused them, eliminating them without remainder."
How much less could the fires of the world harm me?
Even if the fierce fires of hell were to blaze up and fill the entire world,
burning heaven and earth for seven days until the whole world was melted away—
"Such a fierce fire as this cannot harm me.
How could the fire of Śrīgupta ever be able to wound or destroy me?
Then another deva spoke these words:
"If fire cannot burn the Tathāgata, what then shall we do with this meal of poisoned rice?
Now Śrīgupta has defiled his mind with the poison of false views; with this poisonous and malevolent heart, he intends to harm and destroy you by mixing poison into the rice."

Furthermore, harboring deceit and hypocrisy, he manifested a gentle appearance and came to invite the World-Honored One; yet in his inner heart, he truly harbors malice and rebellion. We only pray that the World-Honored One need not go there.
The Buddha told the deva:

"I have applied the Agada medicine of compassion to my body and mind; the poison of craving is the most difficult to eliminate, yet I have long since uprooted its very source—how then could worldly poisons affect me?"
"Do not grieve!
At that time, the Tathāgata emerged from the Bamboo Grove and proceeded toward the city gate. Then, seeing the Buddha advancing directly forward, the deity of that grove spoke these words:

"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, will likely not return again to this Bamboo Grove; the Buddha is now heading toward the direction of liberation. Just as the rising sun must head toward the west without its gaze ever turning away, I fear that at a later time I shall no longer behold the Buddha."

If the fire does not burn him, he will certainly be harmed by the poisoned rice; because of various causes and conditions, it is difficult to see him again, yet those with merit are able to see him. He utters the lion’s roar in the great assembly, crushing the arguments of others; only those with merit can hear him further, and those with blessings and profit receive his prostrations at his feet.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his faculties serene and composed like a moving jeweled pavilion, was followed by all the bhikṣus, just as the bright moon is surrounded by a multitude of stars; he proceeded to the home of Śrīgupta.
At that time, Śrīgupta’s house spirit raised its voice and wished to weep, crying out, "Alas! How strange!
The Buddha has come here, yet this Śrīgupta now prepares a pit of fire and poisoned rice, intending to harm the Buddha."
At that time, the deity of the house, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, spoke these verses:
“When I had not yet beheld the Buddha, I prayed for the Great Compassionate One to come to my home.
Now that I have seen the Buddha arrive at my home, My heart finds no joy.”
The reason for my lack of joy is that there exists what is contrary to the Dharma.
His body is adorned with the marks and signs of excellence; one can gaze upon him without ever being satiated.
Such a Great Man as this shall now become a heap of ashes.
Recalling this matter, my very body seems to dissolve.
Who, upon seeing such a thing, would not be afflicted with grief?
Even if one were extremely wicked and fierce, a fool who harms others—
Even if one were to behold the body of the Tathāgata, one could not bear to give rise to an evil thought, much less wish to inflict harm.
When the moon enters the mouth of Rāhu, all people in the world feel resentment and distress; how excellent it is that you have returned home!
A fire pit seven fathoms deep, filled with blazing flames—
may you not enter this place; protect yourself and protect me,
and protect the host as well, along with all other beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the deity of the house, saying:
"Swords, poison, water, and fire cannot harm one who possesses a compassionate heart.
He then spoke these verses:
"I protect all sentient beings, regarding them as my only child;
even if they should wish to harm me, I still give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
When the fires of affliction blaze fiercely, I shield and protect them so that they may escape evil."
"For this reason, who could possibly burn me with fire?
The Buddha told the deity of the house:

"You should now cast off your fear. I shall now roar the lion’s roar to eliminate the obstacles of the non-Buddhists; just as Rāhu swallows the sun and moon, I am now certainly not to be harmed by Śrīgupta."
"If you cannot even eliminate these, how can you possibly subdue Māra?
Having thus comforted the house spirit, he immediately entered the dwelling.
When the non-Buddhists saw the Buddha enter the house, they were filled with great joy and said to one another:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has now entered the outer gate and has further reached the middle gate.
The Buddha, with his fearless majestic radiance and moistening grace, entered directly without hesitation and approached the third gate, drawing closer to the pit of fire.

At that time, while in an empty room, the woman heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had arrived at the place where the fire was covered. Her mind became frantic with agitation, and she thought to herself:
"The Tathāgata has now reached the fire pit; if his feet touch the grass, the fire will surely blaze up fiercely. Alas! How strange and terrible!"
He then spoke in verse:
"Now one shall sink into the smoke; With a cough, eyes raining tears, When the fire blazes and burns the robes, One should shake them off and discard them."
Seeing this, he cried out for rescue; writhing and tossing about, he was utterly consumed.
His majestic radiance was then extinguished and dissolved.
His physical form was completely incinerated, and his hair fell away, scorched and fallen.
The broad forehead with its white tuft of hair is now utterly extinguished, like a crane upon a flower consumed by fire.
His face is like the pure, full moon; when sentient beings behold his eyes, they are filled with wonder.
Just as delicious nectar, once fallen into a mass of flaming fire,
looks in all four directions in terror and alarm, so too the fierce fire, devoid of compassion,
will surely burn it until it is completely consumed.
All who behold you are without fail delighted;
the marks of a Great Man are brilliantly manifest, exquisite and most extraordinary.
Such a form as this is now shriveled and scorched by fire.
Like a golden brocade robe, rolled up and folded in one place,
gradually fading away like the moon at its waning;
the Buddha’s body is most subtle and wondrous, bringing joy to the body and mind of all who behold it.
“The Tathāgata is most extraordinary; there is no one in the world who can equal him.

At that time, as the World-Honored One entered the third gate and drew near to the fire pit, the various Nirgranthas on the upper story of the multi-storied pavilion saw the Tathāgata approaching the fire pit ever closer. Their hearts were filled with leaping joy, like a flock of crows perched upon a tree in a cemetery, looking toward the flesh of a corpse, desiring to devour it.
The various Nirgranthas on the upper stories of the multi-storied pavilion did likewise.
At that time, Pūraṇa felt great joy in his heart and spoke this verse:
“You have skillfully performed this illusory art, Turning the entire world about.”
"Having today sunk into the pit of fire, can you still perform illusions?
Furthermore, another Nirgrantha spoke these words:
"With one foot already treading upon it, how could you not sink and fall?"
"Is it that my eyes do not perceive clearly, or is this a dream or an illusion?

At that time, the World-Honored One stepped upon the fire pit with his feet marked by the wheel-sign; immediately, the fire pit was transformed into a cool, refreshing pool, filled with lotus flowers whose leaves were in full bloom, vivid and lustrous, covering the entire surface of the water. Among those lotuses, some were in full flower while others were still unopened.
Having witnessed this event, Śrīgupta said to Pūraṇa:
"You previously wished to compete with the Buddha regarding omniscience; you should now abandon these words."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Excellent! You should have faith and understanding; you must eliminate the mind of anger and abandon thoughts of resentment."
An unprecedented majesty: fierce flames were transformed into water;
the earth was entirely changed into fish; the various embers within the pits all became black bees; furthermore, within the waters of the pond,
He manifested many lotus flowers, each complete with a thousand petals,
spread throughout the pond; their filaments were most brilliant and flourishing like blossoms blooming in autumn,
and their hundred petals were exceedingly soft.
Adorned and filled with this pond, cranes dwell within its waters,
all emitting harmonious and elegant cries; kalaviṅka birds and others likewise sport therein,
flapping their wings as they sprinkle one another with spray.
“Bees surround the Buddha, producing wondrous sounds;
ruddy sheldrakes follow one another, again enjoying themselves with sovereign ease.
At that time, Pūraṇa said to Śrīgupta:
"Do not now allow yourself to be deluded by the illusory arts of Gautama.
Śrīgupta, having conceived deep reverence and faith toward the Tathāgata, said to Pūraṇa:
"Is this an illusion?"
He replied, "It is indeed so; this was produced by illusion. Śrīgupta said:
"Are you omniscient? He replied,
"I am an omniscient person."
Śrīgupta spoke to him again:
"If you are indeed the All-Knowing One, listen to what I have to say.
He then spoke these verses:
"If you were omniscient, you should also know this illusion;
why then do you not perform such illusory transformations?
If you do not know illusion, you are not omniscient."
At that time, Pūraṇa was reduced to silence and his arguments were exhausted, so he could offer no further reply. The Nirgranthas said to Śrīgupta:
"Do not speak such words!"
"Why is this? Because Pūraṇa is truly omniscient and is able to manifest everything.
Śrīgupta then said to the Nirgranthas:
"Do you still claim that this Pūraṇa is omniscient?
'Pūraṇa' means 'full'; because he has filled the hells with the commission of all manner of evils, he is named Pūraṇa."
"Do you all, in this regard, conceive the notion of 'omniscience' toward Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who is full of evil paths?
Śrīgupta replied to them again:
"Can one not give rise to the notion of 'knowledge of all modes' toward the Blessed One, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is able to bring peace and liberation among the Śākyas?"
He then spoke in verse:
"Only after I have rebuked you will you depart; you are truly heartless people.
If you possessed any sense of heart, even if you were as hard as a diamond,"
Seeing such a rare occurrence, one should still give rise to faith and reverence.
To behold the Tathāgata directly before one’s eyes— an event never before experienced—
and yet fail to give rise to a mind of faith, is the height of folly.
At that time, the Nirgranthas immediately dispersed and fled in all directions, just as a master of incantations scatters ghosts, or as the rising sun naturally dispels all darkness.
When Śrīgupta saw the Nirgranthas fleeing in this manner, it was exactly like that.
Then he spoke in verse:
“With eyes wide with terror, they hurriedly looked about; in frantic alarm, they sought to flee together.
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they were all struck with fear and scattered in every direction.”
The Nirgranthas now retreat and scatter, like the defeated army of Māra;
their bodies are covered in dust and grime, as if still wearing heavy armor and weapons.
At that time, the various Nirgranthas rushed forward with extreme speed.
Just as that wild ox, stung by gadflies in the forest,
wallows in the mud with his body, running wildly without stopping;
yet like dark clouds that hang low, they naturally disperse when blown by the wind.
When the Nirgranthas had thus dispersed and fled, Śrīgupta felt ashamed and remorseful, and he thought to himself:
"Who will take me to see the World-Honored One?"
She further thought to herself:
"Sister Cūḍāpanthaka has already seen the Buddha; I shall now go together with her to the place where the World-Honored One is.
Having had this thought, she went immediately to the door of the room where her sister-in-law was confined, knocked on the door, called out to her, and spoke this verse:
“Excellent! You are truly a supreme vessel for the sublime Dharma;
because you possess wisdom, you have drawn near to and served the World-Honored One.
It was only due to my own wrong views that you attended upon the Nirgranthas.”
"Come out quickly now; let us together make an offering to the Buddha.
When the elder sister Śrīghuṣā heard this verse, she immediately reflected:
"Śrīgupta has come to deceive me by feigning an intent to harm the Buddha."
Weeping and distressed, he spoke this verse:
"You know of my grief and affliction, Yet you have come here to mock me.
How shall I now go To see the Tathāgata?"
"When the Nirgranthas assemble, they are like a swarm of locusts;
the blazing fire of their false views shall extinguish the lamp of the Śākya clan.
Śrīgupta said to his wife:
"Do you not know the Buddha's supernatural power?
Why do you now speak such words?
He then spoke in verse:
"How could all the fires in the world burn the Buddha?
Who can burn a vajra?
Who can lift up the great earth?"
Behold the Honored One of Ten Powers, who has crushed all the heterodox teachers;
at the four sides of the fire pit, lotus flowers have all blossomed,
and like a swan dwelling amidst the blooms, the Buddha is surrounded by the petals of the flowers.
At that time, having heard these verses, his wife saw from afar the World-Honored One within the lotus flower; leaping for joy, she spoke these words:
"The Buddha has not been burned!"
Śrīgupta choked with sobs and, shedding tears, spoke this verse:
“The World-Honored One possesses a vajra body, Nothing can burn it;
yet because of my proximity to Pūraṇa, I am now myself consumed by fire.”
"Just as when a small amount of damp firewood is placed close to a stack of dry firewood,
both burn together with a fierce blaze when set alight by fire.

At that time, the wife quickly emerged from the upper story, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, gazed up at his venerable countenance, and spoke this verse:
"Those who behold your majestic countenance are all inspired with faith and reverence in this world;
by virtue of my present merit, I have now been able to hear your voice.
Your face is like the pure, full moon; I have now beheld it."
Because I now possess merit, I am able once again to behold the World-Honored One,
whose body is adorned with the marks and signs of excellence. Even if I were to witness his passing into extinction,
the resulting ill repute would fill the world and burn our bodies to ashes.
At that time, his wife prepared the offerings and invited the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the assembly of bhikṣus to take their seats; she then said to her husband:
"Noble son!..."
"You may come forward and prostrate at the Buddha's feet.
Śrīgupta, with tears filling his eyes, spoke this verse:
"I have now prepared a pit of fire, intending to harm the life of the World-Honored One."
"With what face could we possibly meet again now?
At that time, his wife said to her husband, "Noble son, you should cast away your doubts;
the Buddha, the Blessed One, harbors no resentment whatsoever."
He then spoke in verse:
"Just as a hand in the air has no place of contact or obstruction, so too are the dharmas of all Buddhas;
regarding all dharmas, the Buddha [is likewise unimpeded]."
Untainted and unattached, he is free from the eight worldly concerns,
like a lotus in the water.
Blinded by a mind of malice, he sought to harm the Buddha out of desire.
They used a mechanical device to roll a great stone down from the sky;
it could not harm the Buddha.
These two were indeed sons of the Tathāgata; regarding these two individuals, the Buddha—
With an impartial mind free from hatred and love, I regard enemies and kin as no different than my left and right eyes.
My compassion exceeds that for an only son; never, in your presence, shall I—
"And yet you harbor a heart of hatred. Therefore, you should not fear.

At that time, Śrīgupta, out of shame and remorse, bowed his body and followed [his wife’s words]. His lips became parched and withered; he felt deep humiliation and shame. His gait became faltering and slow, as if about to sink into the earth. His entire body trembled, his mind was utterly cowed and terrified, and he prostrated himself on the ground, wailing and weeping in grief, speaking these verses:
"Better to embrace a blazing fire, And even a venomous serpent, Than to draw near an evil friend.
If bitten by a venomous serpent, One may rely upon a skilled physician; But for the bite of an evil friend, There is no remedy at all."
I hope to be freed from poison and harm;

I pray that you will again look upon me with compassion. Having committed grave transgressions and evils, I only pray that you will deign to regard me with pity and now grant me the opportunity to repent.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with a serene and joyful countenance, addressed Śrīgupta, saying:
"Noble son! Do not be distressed or afraid."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Arise, arise! I am without anger; I have long since abandoned the mind that distinguishes between enemy and kin.
If one anoints my right side with sandalwood paste and cuts my left side with a sharp blade,"
"Between these two people, his mind is equal and without distinction.
Just as I am now, it is not a rare thing that he has severed the fetters and possesses a mind free from increase or decrease."
In the past, when I was a white elephant, though struck by a venomous sting, I still covered the hunter with my two hind legs to protect him from harm;
again, when I took the form of a tortoise, though my limbs and joints were severed and dismembered by men, I gave rise to no thought of anger;
furthermore, when I took the form of a bear, I felt compassion for a man in distress, even though that distressed man pointed out the hunter’s location to me, yet I gave rise to no thought of anger.
When I was a seer, my hands, feet, ears, and nose were all cut off and mutilated, yet I did not give rise to even a hair’s breadth of anger.

In the past, when I was the Brahmin Sarvāstida and had my neck severed, I felt no resentment; how much less so today, when I have severed all fetters—could I possibly harbor a heart of aversion toward you?
"Just as empty space does not receive dust or grime, and just as a lotus flower is not defiled by water, so too is it with me who am detached from the eight worldly concerns.
Then Śrīgupta joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"If you would deign to show compassion, please wait but a moment and we shall prepare food for you.
The Buddha said to Śrīgupta,
"Did you not send a messenger to inform me that the time for my meal had arrived?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
I originally did send someone to invite the Buddha in order to do him harm."
The Buddha said to Śrīgupta:
"I have indeed severed all that is unprofitable; what is it that you now do which is not beneficial?
He then spoke this verse:
"What I have now done out of folly is something that butchers and hunters do not do.
Beyond this evil deed, I have placed poison within food;
though it cannot harm another, it will surely bring destruction upon myself."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Śrigupta,
"The gift you now offer is indeed appropriate for this moment.
Śrigupta replied:
“World-Honored One!
The food I offer is entirely poisoned.
The World-Honored One then spoke in verse:
"When the Dragon King Vasuki was at the height of his rage,
even such fierce venom could not harm me.
Now that I cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, how could I possibly cry out for medicine?"
"By means of the fruit of my great compassion, I shall now manifest it for you.
At that time, Śrigupta took the poisoned rice and went before the Buddha; weeping and wailing with tears, he spoke this verse:
"I now bring this poisoned rice to you, O treasury of merit."
My mind was exceedingly wicked, marked by the sign of poisoned rice.
The Buddha, having extinguished the three poisons, used his supernormal powers to remove the poison from the rice;
eating it enabled me to attain an unshakable mind.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Wait until the *saṃghabhedaka* has been announced, and only then may you eat.
He then spoke this verse:
"Standing before the Elder, once the *saṃghabhedaka* has been recited, all poisons will naturally be eliminated; you may now eat as much as you wish.
When the *saṃghabhedaka* was finished, the Buddha and the assembly of monks all partook of the food and drink.
At that time, Śrīgupta looked up and down and thought to himself:
"Is there anyone in this assembly who has been struck by poison?
Seeing that all the monks were entirely safe and sound and had not been affected by the poison, his faith and respect redoubled, and he felt profound joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"The time has come for Śrīgupta to receive faith, reverence, and the conditions [for liberation]. What should I do?
I shall extinguish the fire of his afflictions and remove the poison of his false views."

The Buddha, as was appropriate, taught him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. Upon hearing the Dharma, he attained faith and understanding, severed the fetters of the truths to be seen (*satyadarśana-heya*), removed the poison of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and extinguished the fires of all the fetters.
At that time, Śrigupta, having attained the vision of the truths, spoke this verse:
"I have crossed over the ocean of folly And of false views."
They have no fear of the evil realms;
having encountered the Buddha, they obtain great illumination. As if wishing to enter a great conflagration, they instead find a cool and refreshing pool.
Alas! The purity of the Dharma cannot be fully and extensively explained;
I shall now speak of it only in brief.
One who obtains the food of the Deathless should avoid losing their wealth through strife and contention.
On the contrary, one obtains great benefit.
Therefore, by drawing near to the Buddha, the wisdom-eye of sentient beings opens, and they are able to behold the True Path.
*Mahāvyūha-śāstra-sūtra*, Fascicle Thirteen.
The Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra (Treatise on the Great Ornament), Fascicle Fourteen.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
68 (Sixty-eight): Furthermore, the appearance of a Buddha in the world is most rare; even though she was a woman burdened by heavy fetters and afflictions, she has nonetheless attained liberation.

I have heard that in the past, when the Buddha’s maternal aunt, the Bhikṣuṇī Gautamī, was about to enter nirvāṇa, she desired to adorn herself with various ornaments so as to appear most excellent and sublime.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, he sneezed amidst the great multitude. Hearing the sound of the Buddha’s sneeze, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, out of her love for him as a foster-father to her own son, spoke these words:
"Long-lived World-Honored One!"
This sound spread further and further, even reaching the Brahma Heaven.
The Buddha said to Gautamī:
"This is not the method for offering respectful prayers to the Buddha."
He then spoke these verses:
"One should apply oneself with diligent vigor, To subdue this mind of mine;
Diligently cultivate the firm and solid Dharma, And practice asceticism with perseverance."
"Seeing the assembly of śrāvakas all gathered together in harmony,
when paying homage to the Buddha, one should make such a vow.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī had this thought:

"To say that the harmony of the assembly of śrāvakas is called 'paying homage to the Buddha' is not yet sufficient for the World-Honored One to cause the assembly of śrāvakas to remain in harmony; it is because He does not wish to see them separated.
For this reason, I do not wish to see the Buddha enter nirvana."
"Since there has not yet been any among the World-Honored One’s assembly of śrāvakas who has fallen away, for this reason I ought to enter parinirvāṇa first.
At that time, the yakṣiṇī of the bhikṣuṇī monastery, knowing that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was about to enter parinirvāṇa, wept with such grief that her tears fell upon the robes of the bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī observed this deity and wondered by what cause or condition tears were falling onto her robe.
Upon investigation, she knew that Gautamī was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs all went to the place where the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was.
Then Mahāprajāpatī said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"This casket of four great venomous snakes is difficult to dwell in for long; therefore, I now wish to enter parinirvāṇa."
"This deity possesses a gentle heart; for this reason, he sheds tears upon your robe.
The five hundred bhikṣuṇīs said, "We have all left the home life at the same time; do not enter parinirvāṇa before us."
Then he spoke in verse:
"We have gone forth together, Both having abandoned the darkness of ignorance;
We shall now go together To the city of Nirvana, secure and peaceful."
Amidst the multitude suffering from birth and death, dwelling within the dense forest of existence,
how can you go alone toward the path of ambrosia?
How is it that you all have now attained complete nirvana?
"If you wish for nirvana, I too shall go with you.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, rose from her seat and left her place; she then took leave of the deity residing in the dwelling:
"I now depart for the last time, bidding farewell to this house."
The deva asked,
"Where do you wish to go?
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī said:

"I shall go to that place which is without aging or death, without illness or suffering, and free from both love and hatred, where there is also no sorrow of separation from the beloved; I desire to proceed to the state of Nirvana."
At that moment, the ordinary bhikṣuṇīs cried out:
"Alas, how strange!

In a single kṣaṇa, the bhikṣuṇī saṃghārāma has become entirely empty, like stars falling from the sky vanishing in the four directions. The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has departed together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, just as the Gaṅgā River flows into the great ocean along with five hundred tributary rivers."
At that time, the upāsikās prostrated at the feet of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, saying:
"We pray that you will have compassion for us and not abandon us.
The bhikṣuṇīs then comforted the upāsikās, saying:
"You are not in a time for sorrow now.
He then spoke these verses:
"We have already understood suffering, And severed the fetters of its origin."
By practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, one attains the realization of the Truth of Cessation;
having completed what was to be done, you should not grieve or suffer.
As long as the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples is not lacking and the Dharma-treasure of the Muni remains, [there is no cause for sorrow].
While the World-Honored One remains in the world, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
As for the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya and those such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya—
such stainless persons, none have yet fallen away.
I desire to enter parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda Samatha and Ānanda— while such as these remain in the world, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
The Muni has attained peace; the community of bhikṣus is in harmony.
The wings of the non-Buddhists have been shattered, and those of the false paths have likewise retreated and dispersed.
This single most excellent lineage shall not be severed; now I enter parinirvāṇa.
This is precisely the time of full maturity;
now that fulfillment has been attained, for what reason do you all weep and shed tears?
Before this voice has ceased, I shall proceed to the abode of liberation;
now is precisely the time for it.
If you all hold me in mind, you should diligently protect the Dharma.
To cause the Dharma to endure for a long time is to keep me in mind.
Therefore, you should be diligent; you must strive to protect the True Dharma.
Out of compassion, the Buddha permitted women to go forth.
"You all should guard the precepts so that people do not revile you;
even in future lives, do not allow yourselves to be reviled as women.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs comforted the other bhikṣuṇīs and the upāsikās.

Then five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, like flowering trees in bloom, approached the place where the Buddha was. They adjusted their upper robes (uttarāsaṅga), prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and spoke these verses:
“I am now the mother of the Buddha; The Tathāgata is my father.
I was born from the stream of the Dharma; I nurtured his physical body with my milk.”
The Buddha nourished my Dharma-body; I nursed the World-Honored One.
To quench thirst for but a moment, the Buddha has now nourished me with the milk of the Dharma.
Thus, I am forever free from hunger and thirst, having eternally severed all craving and attachment.
I have now spoken briefly; though I nourished you with my milk, my debt of gratitude is immense.
I vow that all women shall obtain sons like the Buddha—just as Rāma and Añjana did.
Vasu and the other Mothers dwell within the ocean of existence,
cycling through saṃsāra without end or beginning; yet by virtue of my connection to my son,
I have attained deliverance from the sea of birth and death.
Renowned as the consort of the Lord of Men, the mother of the One Possessing All-Knowledge—
this name is ungraspable, yet I have now attained it.
Whether my aspirations were great or small, they have all been fulfilled.
Now that you wish to enter parinirvāṇa, I inform the Buddha so that he may know.
Your feet are like lotus petals, with the marks of the wheels all brilliantly manifest;
I pray that for my sake, at the very end, you will grant me the honor of prostrating at your feet.
With my final act of reverence, I prostrate with deep faith;
I bow to the Bhagavān, whose body is like a mass of pure gold.
I pray that you open your uttarāsaṅga and reveal your form so that I may behold you.
"Behold well the body of the Tathāgata; I now proceed toward nirvāṇa.
At that time, the body of the Tathāgata, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, opened his upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having beheld the Buddha’s body, prostrated at his feet and said:
"World-Honored One,
I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
The Buddha said to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“If you desire nirvāṇa, I shall grant your wish.
The Saṅgha will not be diminished; it will be like the moon at the end of its cycle, gradually setting until nothing remains.”
"The disciples shall go first; I shall go last.
It is like merchants on a journey: while the merchants are on the road, the caravan leader follows behind.
Then, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs circumambulated the Buddha, the World-Honored One, just as they would circumambulate Mount Sumeru.

Having circumambulated the Buddha, they stood before the Tathāgata; gazing upon his venerable countenance, they could never look enough, and hearing the sound of the Dharma, they likewise found no satiety.

Having attained fulfillment and obtained the flavor of the Dharma, Nanda, Rāhula, Ānanda, and Samantabhadra prostrated themselves to seek forgiveness from all the assembly of noble ones, who remained as unshakable as mountains, dwelling in tranquil silence.

Only Ānanda, Rāhula, and Sāmāvatī remained; though Ānanda’s fetters were not yet exhausted, because his heart was compassionate and submissive, he could not restrain his grief. Like a tree in a windless place, he joined his palms and shed tears.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said to the Venerable One:
"Venerable Ānanda, you have heard much and realized the Truths; why then do you now act like an ordinary person?
The Tathāgata has always taught that all affectionate attachments end in separation."
He spoke again to the Venerable One, saying:
"You did not request the Buddha, the World-Honored One, on my behalf!
How then shall I now obtain this Dharma?"
And he spoke in verse:
"Because of your request, we have been able to go forth;
you are now truly not in vain, for all have obtained the true fruit of retribution."
None of the teachers of the various non-Buddhist paths have ever attained this state;
yet within a woman’s body, one can obtain the trace of the nectar of immortality.
By relying on the Buddha as a virtuous friend, it is for this reason that it has now been attained.
"You shall guard the treasury of the Buddha-dharma; you must protect and uphold it most excellently.
Today is the last time that I shall see you.
I am now entering parinirvāṇa, proceeding there by way of the Path."
When the Buddha sneezed amidst the assembly, I then cried out, "May you live long!
The Buddha said that this was not a respectful salutation; the matter is as explained above.
The Buddha likewise protects the Saṃgha, desiring that it never suffer decline or diminution.
I, too, do not seek to take pleasure, but enter the state of liberation.
When the great wind of impermanence arrives, it blows upon the śrāvaka-tree,
uprooting it so that it falls to the ground.
It can scatter Mount Sumeru; the Tathāgata-sun dispels the darkness of ignorance.
The supreme and wondrous path of Nirvāṇa is the Dharma taught by the One of Ten Powers.
The golden radiance of the Dharma shines forth, shattering the treatises of heterodox paths;
as the sunlight shines everywhere with full brilliance, so too does the Buddha’s virtue.
Now that this wondrous time has arrived, I therefore desire to relinquish my body.
At that time, having heard these verses, Ānanda immediately wiped away his tears and spoke again in verse:
“Now your resolve is great; I shall no longer harbor anxious thoughts.”
Just as in a deep forest there are many sufferings from thorns,
or as a female elephant runs away, leaving the forest and its afflictions behind—
so too are you now, running away from all the worlds.
What is now to be lamented are pride and folly,
the fires of all evil fetters, which burn within the three realms of existence.
You have already attained nirvana, yet I still harbor doubts regarding the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
"Just as a great mass of fire, when its flames are exhausted, the fire is extinguished.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī joined her palms toward the Buddha, gazed up at his venerable countenance, and praised him with a verse:
"Homage and refuge to the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Great World-Honored One."
One who speaks words of truth and reality, who speaks words of meaning and Dharma;
who speaks words of benefit that are not in vain, who can speak words of true quiescence;
who speaks words regarding the non-self and the self, yet transcends all speech.
One who possesses the perfectly fulfilled eye, Who shows and guides toward the sublime path for those yet to come,
And who is further able to constantly contemplate The true nature of all phenomena, acts as a great illuminator.
He who can dispel all darkness and extinguish anger and strife;
who kindles the torches and lamps of the Dharma court to illuminate all beings;
who can bestow the light of many lamps and further grant those who follow the light.
The Great Man who tames others, who has returned to the Teacher of Great Liberation;
he who is endowed with the ten powers and possesses the four fearlessnesses;
who has attained non-retrogression and whose preaching of the Dharma is never in vain.
One who will certainly benefit all sentient beings,
Who utters the lion’s roar among the Śākyas, Firm and solid in diligence,
And a supreme practitioner of wondrous diligence, Is one who can fully embody great compassion.
One who cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas—
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, Maheśvara, King Yama, Varuṇa,
and those with mastery over wealth— [is such a one].
Thus these superior persons and others joined their palms and praised the Buddha together:

“In harmony, you have relinquished the exquisite and profound; fearlessly, you manifest the supreme truth. You are able to provide guidance through various teachings, being well-versed in the cries of all flying birds. Your fame fills the void; you emerged from the lineage of great kings such as Mūrdhaja, Utpalaka, and Bharata. Like the sun and moon, the Tathāgata is venerated by devas, humans, and asuras. Having attained the seven factors of enlightenment, you have dispelled the darkness of ignorance, and you are further able to establish the supreme banner of the Triple Gem.”

The Tathāgata’s countenance is like the summit of a mountain of gold, its radiance shining brilliantly; he is the Supreme Man, named Lotus, the Utpala among men, and the Puṇḍarīka among men, who is able to sever greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all fetters of existence and the four bonds.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has forever severed all sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, negligence, arrogance, contention, anger, self-conceit, and the like.

Deceit, gambling, rivalry for victory, and the cheating of others; mutual litigation, resentment, and separation—all such evil habits and latent tendencies have been completely severed without remainder, unlike the externalist teachers who keep their secret teachings hidden behind closed fists.

They topple the banner of pride and erect the supreme banner of the Dharma; they are able to turn the wheel of the Dharma, causing the oceans of tears, milk, and blood to dry up entirely, and they attain an ocean of meditative concentration that is deep, boundless, and limitless.
He is able to relinquish all internal and external wealth and possessions without any sense of attachment or regret, maintaining a mind of equanimity toward both enemies and kin.
The Buddha’s body is subtle and wondrous, like a mass of molten gold; his tongue is broad and long, like a lotus petal, free from all impurity and perfectly pure and bright.
His abdomen is level and full, and his navel curls to the right like a fragrant casket.
His halo extends one fathom, as brilliant as lightning and like pure gold.

Clad in the armor of diligence and protected by meditative concentration, he uses the arrows of wisdom to pierce even a hundredth part of a hair’s breadth, hitting every mark. He destroys the hosts of Māra’s army with courage and fearlessness; he is a great dragon among men, a true savior for humanity.

The bases of power of meditative concentration are immeasurable, boundless, and formless; they proclaim and distinguish the Eightfold Noble Path, severing the perceptions of craving, hatred, and harm. Their vows are firm and their resolve dwells in peace, never wavering or frivolous—like the udumbara flower, they are exceedingly difficult to encounter.

The merit of the Tathāgata exceeds that of the great earth and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of motes of dust; by means of the Eightfold Noble Path, he washes away the fetters and afflictions, rescues all sentient beings, and leads them across the river of birth and death to the other shore, where he can point out the way and the place.
Adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics as if by colorful painting,
he wields the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter all the heterodox arguments of external paths and is able to reveal the sublime method for liberation and nirvana.

Having attained mastery over the Dharma, they are unattached to the world; they are able to teach the remedies for the sense bases and all afflictions, and having attained supreme eloquence, they are skillfully able to discern all phenomena.
He weeds out the matters of flattery, falsehood, and delusive confusion; through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, he reaches the far shore.

Honored by the seer Asita, his fame resounds throughout the ten directions, and dwelling in his final body, he has awakened himself and enlightened sentient beings. He is a treasury of merit, a Sumeru of merit, and a great ocean of merit, possessing immeasurable renown and immeasurable eloquence, knowing gratitude and repaying kindness.

Having finished praising the Buddha, she prostrated before him and withdrew; taking the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs with her, she entered a secluded place, relinquished her life-force, and sat cross-legged for half a [watch].
Then the laywoman arrived last at the bhikṣuṇī’s quarters; she prostrated at the bhikṣuṇī’s feet and wailed aloud, immediately speaking in verse:
“We have committed many transgressions; O one of profound wisdom, hear our confession.
We shall never again be able to behold one another.”
Because the bhikṣuṇī Prajāpatī was free from desire, her mind was courageous and resolute; she raised her hand, touched the upāsikās, and said to them:
"You should not pursue a heart of attachment; for all gatherings born of affection must inevitably end in separation."
Then he spoke in verse:
“The Buddha has said that for those who gather, There will inevitably be separation;
All conditioned phenomena Are entirely impermanent.”
The fire of impermanence blazes fiercely, consuming and extinguishing the three realms of existence.
Those who love me are exceedingly many, and those whom I love are not few;
yet now I am able to relinquish them all—such attachments as these.
In the dark realm of birth and death, amidst the perilous obstacles of saṃsāra,
relatives cherish one another; yet through evil views they are estranged,
and impermanence, devoid of compassion, causes them to be broken apart and separated.
If there were no parting from those one loves, one need not seek liberation;
yet as affectionate bonds grow ever more intimate and deep through mutual attachment,
they will inevitably end in separation.
"For this reason, the wise who seek liberation have no lingering attachment whatsoever.

At that time, having praised *nirvāṇa* through various causes and conditions, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī remained silent; she took her leave of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and entered *nirvāṇa*, truly not failing to act according to her words.

The bhikṣuṇīs, fixing their mindfulness before them, entered the first dhyāna; proceeding in this manner through the stages until they reached the attainment of cessation, they contemplated [the meditative states] both in forward and reverse order, manifested various supernormal powers, and then spoke these verses:
"Standing upon the earth, I reach out my hand to touch the sun and moon.
I transform my body so that it vanishes, And leap forth into the midst of space."
From one body he becomes many bodies; from many bodies he becomes one body.
His body emits a great radiance that can shake the great earth.
He enters the earth as if entering water; he enters the water as if walking upon dry land.
"From their bodies they emit great radiance, and furthermore, they pour down heavy rain; by means of their divine power of *ṛddhi*, they are able to manifest such deeds.

The remaining five hundred bhikṣuṇīs likewise manifested these great supernormal transformations. To manifest the power of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-dharma, they all displayed their spiritual powers, leaping into the air like collapsing clouds and pouring down heavy rain. They were also like torches in a courtyard scattered in all directions by the wind in mid-air: water issued from the upper part of their bodies while fire issued from the lower, and fire issued from the upper part of their bodies while water issued from the lower. Then, they spoke these verses:
Each emits a thousand flames of light, surrounding and adorning themselves;
from their bodies, flames of fire issue forth while great rains pour down below.
The void is filled with flowers, like the branches of the campaka tree.
A multitude of flowers accumulated upon the water,
causing all the donors to give rise to a heart of joy;
like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted, he entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

At that time, Brahmā Śikhin, leading the assembly of Brahmās; Śakra Devānām Indra, leading the devas of the six desire realms; and the great celestial deities, as well as the most eminent nāgas and yakṣas, came to where the Buddha was. They all joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"The Tathāgata, having severed the fetters of craving, shall now pass into the world; what, then, do you wish us to do?
This is the final act of personal care from the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Tathāgata, according to what was appropriate for each, gave instructions to them all.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Proclaim to those far and near that all who wish to make offerings to the Mother of the Buddha should assemble here.
Then the Venerable Ānanda raised his voice in a mournful wail and spoke these words:

"All who are disciples of the Buddha, regardless of distance, must listen to my words and comply with the Buddha's teaching; all of you, assemble here to hear the Buddha’s instruction. He nourished me from infancy until my final body now enters parinirvāṇa, like a lamp extinguished when its oil is exhausted."
All those with faith who know them to be disciples should quickly assemble to make offerings to the body of the Mother of Buddhas.

Among gods and humans, there is no female form capable of nourishing the body of a Buddha; there is no one else like her who can thus sustain a Buddha. Therefore, all bhikṣus should assemble here without exception.

At that time, monks from near and far in the four directions brought ox-head sandalwood and traveled through the air like a king of geese or cranes; like the sun entering a cloud and illuminating the sky, the bhikṣuṇīs filled the air, their appearance being just like his.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings supported the four legs of Mahāprajāpatī’s bed, while Śakra, Brahmā, and others likewise held the beds of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs. At that moment, banners and streamers were erected upon each of the beds; celestial māndārava flowers formed a floral canopy over the bhikṣuṇīs, covering them like a meditation cave. These banners and streamers stood tall, filling the entire earth, while celestial silken pennants and canopies filled the air in a thousand varieties of color and form. The heavens rained down flower garlands and powdered incense; the smoke from the incense rose like clouds, pervading the void, and the sounds of celestial music resounded everywhere.

The Buddha followed behind, surrounded by Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Nanda, Rāhula, Aniruddha, Ānanda, and others, as well as Brahmā and the various devas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, devas, nāgas, and yakṣas.

At that time, the World-Honored One, like a moving mountain of gold, stood before the seat of the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī; the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs were seated in order behind her. The entire great earth was adorned and embellished with a splendor never seen before, just as the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī had herself performed the adornment.

When Mahāprajāpatī entered nirvana, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Lord of Dharma, was present and had assembled the assembly of noble ones; yet at the time of the Buddha’s own nirvana, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others were no longer there, for the Buddha’s body was already gone and Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and all the rest had likewise passed away.
For this reason, none of her adornments could equal those of Mahāprajāpatī. This couch was placed in a spacious location;

various fragrant woods were piled up to serve as a pyre, upon which the corpses of these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs and others were laid. It was covered over with various kinds of sandalwood and miscellaneous incenses, including ox-head sandalwood, and further drenched with a great quantity of fragrant oils.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, seeing that the bhikṣuṇīs had already lit the fire, wept with grief and distress, and spoke these verses:
"In this very sequence, the Tathāgata too will not remain long;
he is about to enter into parinirvāṇa."
A single great tree remains alone, its branches and leaves scorched by flames;
it cannot endure for long.
Having spread the Dharma throughout the three realms, the Honored One of the Three Realms has entered parinirvāṇa.
There is not a single thought-moment of Dharma remaining.
Having gathered it over immeasurable eons, this supreme honey of the Dharma was obtained; the bees of the śrāvakas flocked together to consume it.
Now that the Buddha has entered nirvāṇa, who shall provide the honey of the Dharma?
Before long, the Dharma will be extinguished; images and stūpas will all vanish.
When even those who paint images no longer exist, how much less those who wear the Dharma robes?
All those who have not yet abandoned desire weep and are overcome with extreme anguish.
"The one who has detached from desire contemplates the Dharma;
once the cremation by fire is complete, his bones are collected to erect a stūpa, so that sentient beings may make offerings.
At that time, some people had doubts: "Who should erect the stūpa and perform the offerings?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to sever doubts, declared that there are three kinds of persons for whom one should erect stupas and offer worship.
What are these three?
They are the Buddha, the Arhat whose outflows are exhausted, and the Wheel-Turning Sage King; these are called the three kinds.
69 (Sixty-nine) Furthermore, by recollecting the virtues of the Saṃgha and skillfully observing them, one may even give up one’s body and life while still maintaining a virtuous mind.
I have heard that in the past, when Śākyamuni was a bodhisattva, he manifested as a six-tusked white elephant.
At that time, the king’s consort harbored resentment toward the elephant and immediately posted a reward, dispatching men to point out the elephant’s location and instructing them to take its tusks.

The dispatched men went to the place where the elephant resided and saw a six-tusked white elephant, resembling Airāvaṇa, who had separated himself from his herd and was dwelling alone with a female elephant.
Then he spoke these verses:
"In a great pond filled with clear water, Where lotuses and blue utpala flowers bloom—
In such a place as this, One may behold the dragon-elephant."
The *kucīna* white flowers, in shape like milk or snow,
are all the same color, white; they are just like the Great White Mountain,
yet possessing feet and able to move.
Its color is like that of the moon; six tusks emerge from its mouth, shining with great majesty like a cluster of white lotuses.
When viewed closely, those ivory tusks are like white lotus roots.
At that time, the hunter, clad in saffron robes and carrying a bow and arrows under his arm, moved slowly behind a tree toward the location of the elephant.
When the female elephant saw the hunter with the bow and arrows tucked beneath his arm, she said to the elephant king,
"He intends to harm you."
The elephant king asked,
"What kind of clothing does he who carries a bow and arrows wear?
The female elephant replied:
"His body is clad in the kāṣāya," the elephant king said.
"When one is clothed in the kāṣāya, what is there to fear?"
Then he spoke these verses:
“Such a banner-sign does not harm external things;
Within, it possesses a heart of compassion, Constantly rescuing and protecting all beings.”
Therefore, those who dwell with such a person should not give rise to fear.
Those who see them obtain peace and security; they attain tranquility and supreme excellence.
Like the moon, which possesses coolness, they never change into heat.
At that time, having heard these verses, the female elephant was no longer startled or suspicious.
Then the hunter entered the dense forest to watch for his opportunity, and immediately struck the elephant king with a poisoned arrow.
Then the female elephant said to the elephant king:
"You claim that those who wear the *kāṣāya* must possess compassion; why then do you now perform such an act?
At that time, the elephant king spoke this verse:
"This is the garment of liberation, yet produced by a mind of affliction;
it is far removed from compassion. None of this is the fault of the clothing.
Just as when copper is coated with gold, one only knows of the impurity after smelting and refining."
Deceiving all ordinary people, the foolish take it to be real;
the wise discern well that this is gold-plated copper,
and because of their evil hearts and bows and arrows, they have thus harmed me.
"The *kāṣāya* is the garment of sublime tranquility; yet those with evil minds wear it.
If one observes with wisdom, the *kāṣāya* is always worn well.
At that time, the female elephant was filled with intense anger and spoke to the elephant king, saying:
"What you say is excellent!
I cannot endure it; I will not follow your words.
I wish to seize that person and have his limbs severed."
The Bodhisattva Elephant King said to the female elephant:
"When the mind is not disciplined regarding the fetters (saṃyojana), it is just like this. Do not harbor anger and speak such words; you should not give rise to wrath toward him."
He then spoke in verse:
"Just as when a ghost enters a person's mind, That foolish and mad man reviles the physician;
Yet the physician treats the ghost, And does not reproach the suffering patient."
The fetters and latent tendencies are like ghosts;
because they are shrouded by ignorance, they give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion. One should simply eliminate these afflictions;
why need one blame that person?
His fame pervades the three realms;
through mindfulness, concentration, diligence, and vigor, he has extinguished all defilements of flattery and deceit.
With the sharp point of wisdom, he has severed and cut off those various fetters.
"I shall surely cause it to dry up completely, burning it away until nothing remains.
In the future, I shall certainly bring about its total destruction through suffering and distress.
When the Bodhisattva, the Elephant King, spoke this verse, the female elephant remained silent.
At that time, all the elephants of the herd gathered together, and the Bodhisattva, the elephant king, thought to himself:
"Will these elephants cause harm to those people?"
Having had this thought, he went to where the hunter was and said to him:
"Come beneath my belly; I shall protect you.
If those elephants should attempt to harm you, I will immediately drive them all away."
He said to the hunter,
"Whatever you require, take it now as you please.
When the hunter heard these words, he thought to himself:
"I am now devoid of a compassionate heart; I am not like that elephant," he said, weeping and wailing.
The Elephant King asked him:
"Why do you weep?
The hunter replied,
"I weep because of my distress."
The elephant king said, "I called you to my belly because I feared that other elephants might harm you; it was not my body that was pressing upon you?
He replied:
"No, it was not my body being crushed.
He spoke again, saying,
"Was it not this female elephant who uttered harsh words to provoke you, causing you to weep?"
He replied:
"No harsh words have come to trouble me; it is because of my present great compassion and virtue.

Although I harmed you with the poisonous arrows of an evil mind, you instead used a heart of loving-kindness to frighten the other elephants away so that they would not harm you, and you sheltered me beneath your belly."
"This matter has distressed my heart, and it is out of fear that I weep.
He then spoke in verse:
"With a poisoned arrow today, I have wounded the body of the elephant king."
By means of your compassionate virtue, you have wounded my heart.
While a wound inflicted by a malicious mind may be healed, the injury now done to your virtue leaves a scar upon my foolish mind that is difficult to recover from.
Your virtue is like the great ocean; who could ever speak of it until its end?
You comfort and compassionately protect all. Were I to speak of it, though my form is that of a human, I would possess no virtue of kindness or benevolence at all.
This empty corpse exists; it is more wretched than a beast.
Though its appearance resembles that of a human, it commits evils worse than those of an animal.
Although you have received the body of a beast, in terms of the Way and virtue, you are the most eminent among men.
"Though his form is not that of a human, his virtue and wisdom are truly human.
The Bodhisattva, King of Elephants, asked the hunter:
"Answer me quickly!"
"For what purpose have you come to shoot me?
The hunter replied, "I have been dispatched by the king to take a small portion from your body; it was not my own will that led me to harm you."
The elephant king replied,
"Take whatever you require now, quickly.
At that time, the elephant king spoke this verse:
"If you have anything you require, stretch out your hands and receive it quickly.
All those who have resolved upon the Bodhisattva path have no stinginess whatsoever;
whatever you may need, I shall surely relinquish and give it all to you."
If you need teeth, I shall give you teeth; pull them out and take them as you please.
For the sake of providing relief and rescue, I have assumed this form;
I shall relinquish everything I possess—take whatever you require according to your will.
For those who seek their own benefit, one can swiftly reach nirvāṇa;
but for the sake of all sentient beings, one takes birth within the three realms of existence.
For the sake of all-encompassing wisdom, compassion and rescue serve as the cause.
The hunter, filled with shame, spoke these words:
"I have been sent by the king to come and take your tusks.
The elephant king replied:
"Take whichever you wish according to your own intent; do not harbor doubts or difficulties.
The hunter replied, "I truly cannot pull out your tusks."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Your heart of loving-kindness is overflowing; I fear that compassionate father.
If he were to pull out your tooth, my hand would surely fall off."
Then the elephant king said to the hunter, "If you are afraid, I shall pull it out for you.

Having spoken these words, he coiled his trunk around the tusk; as its root was extremely deep, it took a long time before he could extract it. At that moment, the elephant king’s blood flowed profusely, and he immediately spoke this verse:
“From the place where the tusk was extracted, blood flowed down from his shoulder;
the elephant king of supreme merit had it as white as the *padma*,
*kumuda*, and other such flowers, which accumulated into a great mass.”
At that time, those clusters of flowers were as white as the body of an elephant king,
resembling a great mountain of rock with white snow covering its summit;
they were like the peak of a high mountain from which vermilion-red liquid flows downward.
At that time, the elephant king, though trembling with the pain of his suffering, continued to comfort himself.
Then a certain deva spoke this verse:
"Let the mind dwell firm and at peace; Do not be distressed by folly."
One should contemplate the masses suffering from affliction:
how may they be rescued and delivered? The entire world is subject to death; you should act as their savior.
You must maintain a firm and steadfast resolve, and never give rise to a mind of sorrow or distress.
Devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas,
and yakṣas filled the void of space, extolling what had never been before.
The celestial beings spoke these words:
"From of old, this has been most rare; you are able to perform such difficult and painful deeds.
Enduring suffering in the present, your inner mind is directed toward Bodhi;
seeking the most supreme fruit, you never have an intention to retreat."
Furthermore, another celestial deity spoke to that deity, saying:
"Such a bodhisattva shall never regress.
He then spoke this verse:
"Knowing the pain of having your tusks pulled out, I grieve for you in hell.
Having thus had his tusks extracted, the elephant king remained silent.
At that time, the hunter thought to himself:
"If he plants his tusks in the ground, will he not regret it?
Why does he not give them to me?"
The Elephant King, perceiving his thoughts, comforted him with words and spoke this verse:
"Your tusks are like kumuda lilies, And resemble the roots of white lotuses;
I bestow all six of my tusks upon you— The most excellent among all tusks."
May my gift bring you peace and happiness;
may it gradually cause your suffering to subside,
so that I may gain respectful faith in you.
I am an extremely evil person; I have killed, stolen, committed adultery, and deceived you, possessing every kind of falsehood and unwholesome quality.
You may commit all manner of evils; let your mind of malice be the bow and your sharp arrows be your intent.
I have forgotten all else and remember nothing, save that I recall respecting the *kāṣāya*;
upon seeing it, my heart feels reverence and faith.
Whether it be pure or impure, I am now its donor.
"Only when you are fully endowed with purity and wait for me to cultivate my mind so that the karmic fruit may become vast shall I bestow it upon you.
At that time, the elephant king spoke to the hunter, saying:
"This *kāṣāya* robe is the banner of detachment; I regard it with a heart of reverence and respect.
With his trunk, he lifted the tusk and handed it to the hunter, then spoke this verse:
"I now speak these words of truth: A poisoned arrow has pierced my body;..."
Without the slightest trace of resentment, I shall not inflict any evil retribution upon you.
By virtue of these truthful words, may you swiftly realize Bodhi and deliver all sentient beings from such various sufferings and afflictions.
Having spoken this verse, he immediately offered his tusks to the hunter. For what reason was this analogy cited?

Throughout countless hundreds of thousands of past lives, he constantly practiced such difficult acts of giving. He originally made a vow desiring to fulfill the fruit of that aspiration: to cause all sentient beings in the realms of existence to escape their suffering and attain the fundamental Way; and to enable people to understand, so that they might maintain purity themselves and give rise to faith and reverence. It is for this reason that this analogy was cited.
70. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not spare his own body or life for the sake of all sentient beings.
I have heard that in the past, within the Snowy Mountains, there were two deer kings, each leading a herd of five hundred deer, grazing upon the mountain grasses.
At that time, there was a king in the city of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta. The king then went into the Snowy Mountains and dispatched men to set up an encampment, surrounding those Snowy Mountains.
At that time, all the deer fell into the enclosure; there was no refuge and no way to escape, such that not even a single deer could be saved.
Then the Deer King appeared, his coat variegated like an inlay of various jewels.
"What skillful means can I employ to enable these deer to escape this peril?
He further thought:
"There is no other recourse; I must go directly to the king."
Having formed this thought, he went directly to the king's presence.
When the king saw him, he commanded his attendants:
"Be careful not to harm him; let him come as he pleases."
Then that deer king, having arrived at the king’s presence, spoke these words:
“Great King!
Do not take pleasure in killing the herds of deer for sport; do not do such a thing.”
"I pray that Your Majesty will have compassion and release these deer, not allowing them to be harmed.
The king said to the deer king,
"I require the meat of deer for food."
The deer king replied, "If Your Majesty requires meat, I shall present one deer daily.

If Your Majesty were to slaughter them all at once, the meat would surely rot before it could be consumed; by taking one deer each day, the deer population will increase daily, and Your Majesty will never lack for meat."
The king immediately agreed.
Then the Bodhisattva Deer King said to the other deer king, Devadatta:
"I shall now provide one deer daily for the king's meal with you. Today I shall send one deer, and tomorrow you shall send one."
They made a mutual agreement and alternately sent deer for a long time.
Later, on one occasion, a doe belonging to Devadatta, the deer king, became pregnant and was about to give birth. She approached Devadatta, seeking his compassion and pleading for her life, saying:
"I do not dare refuse death now; I must wait until I have given birth before I can be provided for the kitchen."
At that time, the deer king would not listen to his words:
"Go now; who else shall take your place?
and he became filled with anger.
At that time, having been rebuked with anger, the female deer thought to herself:
"That Deer King is exceedingly compassionate; I shall go to him and entreat him to spare my child's life."
Having formed this thought, he went to where the Bodhisattva was, knelt on his right knee before the Deer King, and related all that had occurred to him, speaking these verses to the Deer King:
"I am now without protection; I pray only that you deliver me.
There are many other beings, yet I alone am now terrified and oppressed."
I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and pity, and deliver me from this suffering and distress;
I have nothing else to rely upon, and thus I come to take refuge in you alone.
You always delight in benefiting others and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
"If I were to die now, both our lives would not be preserved.
I pray that you will save my fetus, so that one life may be made whole.
Having heard this verse, the Bodhisattva Deer King asked the other deer:
"Did you go to speak to your king on your own behalf?
The doe replied, "I went to him, but he would not listen to my words;
instead, he only scolded me in anger, saying, 'Who can take your place?'"
He then spoke in verse:
"Seeing him rebuke you with anger, he has no heart of compassion or rescue;
seeing him command you to go there quickly—who is there to take your place?"
"I now take refuge in you, whose very essence is compassion;
therefore, please grant that I may escape with my life.
The Bodhisattva deer king spoke thus to the other deer:
"Do not be distressed; go as you please, while I reflect upon this myself.
Having heard this, the deer leaped for joy and returned to his original herd.
The Bodhisattva deer king then reflected thus:
"If I am sent away while other deer remain, I should say:
'I ought not to go; why do you send me away?
Having formed this thought, his mind was immediately awakened, and he spoke this verse:
"I shall now go in person to that king's kitchen;
regarding all sentient beings, I vow that I must surely save them.
If I were to use my own body to trade for the lives of mosquitoes and ants,"
