One who can act in this manner still possesses great benefit.
The reason for maintaining this body is precisely for the sake of rescue and relief;
were one to save even a single life, one would cast away the body as if it were mere grass or chaff.
Having spoken this verse, he immediately gathered all the deer under his care and said, "For whatever deficiencies I have committed against you, please accept my repentance."
"I wish to abandon you so that I may take your life in place of another's and go to the royal kitchen.
When the deer heard these words, they were all filled with grief and longing, and spoke thus:
"We pray that Your Majesty do not go; let us go in your stead."
The Deer King replied, "I have made a vow that I must go in person; if I were to send you, it would surely cause you distress, whereas now I am joyful and feel no displeasure."
He then spoke in verse:
"Without abandoning desire, one casts off the body, And will inevitably have a place of rebirth.
Now, for the sake of saving them, I cast off my body; this must surely be far superior."
I now know that this body must inevitably perish;
for the sake of saving and compassionating others, I shall now relinquish it as the Dharma.
Since this serves as a cause for attaining the Dharma, why should I not rejoice?
At that time, the deer offered various admonitions and parables, yet they became utterly exhausted without being able to cause him to cease his intent.

Then the Deer King went to the royal kitchen; the entire herd of deer, including the herd of Devadatta, followed the Deer King toward Pāṭaliputra. Once they had emerged from the forest, he took leave of the herd of deer, sending them back to their dwelling, and proceeded alone to the royal kitchen.

At that time, the kitchen superintendent, who had previously seen the deer king, immediately recognized him and went to inform the king, saying that the deer king had come to the kitchen of his own accord.
Upon hearing these words, the king came out in person to where the deer king was.
The king said to him,
"Are your deer exhausted?
Why have you come here of your own accord?"
The deer king replied, "Because of Your Majesty’s protection, the number of deer has doubled.
The reason I have come is that there is a pregnant doe; I wish to sacrifice my own life in her stead so that she may go to the royal kitchen."
Then he spoke in verse:
“If one desires to seek something, It is insufficient to satisfy the heart;
If I am capable of accomplishing it by my own power, And yet do not do so, [it would be a failure].”
In what way is this different from wood?
Once this foul and impure body is cast aside, it will naturally decay and perish of its own accord,
having performed not even a hair’s breadth of good.
"This body must inevitably perish; by relinquishing it, another shall obtain its wholeness, and I shall thereby attain great benefit.
When King Brahmadatta heard these words, the hairs on his body stood on end, and he immediately spoke this verse:
"I am a deer in human form; you are a man in the form of a deer."
One endowed with merit is called a human; one who is cruel and evil is a beast.
Alas, those who possess wisdom! Alas, those who possess courage!
Alas, those capable of compassion! May they rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
By manifesting such a form as this, you have already instructed me.
Now return to your home, along with the other deer and your herd;
do not harbor thoughts of fear.
"I now make this vow: from this day forth, I shall never again eat the flesh of any deer.
At that time, the Deer King addressed the king, saying:
"If Your Majesty will show compassion, you should go in person to where that herd of deer is, and comfort them with your own hands by granting them fearlessness."
Upon hearing these words, the king went to the forest in person; arriving at the place where the herd of deer resided, he granted them fearlessness and spoke this verse:
"All you herds of deer within my kingdom, I shall protect you with steadfast resolve; Be careful not to give way to fear."
These woods and groves of mine, along with all the springs and ponds, I now bestow entirely upon the deer; henceforth, no killing shall be permitted.
For this reason, this forest is named the Deer Park of Bestowal.
The Mahāyāna-uttaratantra-śāstra (The Treatise on the Great Vehicle), Fascicle Ten;
The Mahāyāna-uttaratantra-śāstra, Fascicle Fifteen.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
(71) Furthermore, one who is skillfully discerning—even regarding vast territories where all things are fully provided—recognizes their suffering and distress, and thus abandons them and departs.

I have heard that in the past, when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva, he served as a great king. To those who came as poor beggars seeking anything they desired, he gave everything; he provided protection for those in distress and, out of a desire to benefit all sentient beings, occupied the royal throne with wisdom and courageous vigor.

At that time, the king of a neighboring country led his armies to engage in battle. Then the Bodhisattva King reflected thus: "One who clings to the pleasures of the five desires cannot discipline the mind;

the six sense faculties are difficult to satisfy, and since the requisites for their gratification are so numerous, one must further manage and protect them, which leads to strife over these very things. I vow to abandon such matters and not engage in conflict; instead, I should further cultivate and gather the supreme dharmas that accompany me."
Then he spoke these verses:
"When examining well, the wise should exercise discernment;
if one acts without reflection, regret will come too late."
"By observing right and wrong, one will certainly know where they lie.
He further spoke in verse:
"Desire is like grasping a torch of grass, And it is also like a mass of raw meat."
Attachment to desire inevitably leads to injury and ruin, bringing harm to both worlds.
The wise should swiftly abandon it—kingdoms, possessions, and all such things;
for such possessions must ultimately be relinquished.
It is better to undergo many sufferings now, rather than endure such long-lasting suffering in future lives.
One should be capable of subduing those [afflictions] and realize the fruit of clear evidence in the present.
Though one’s reputation may be praised as good, one will later suffer harm.
Even if you know yourself to be capable, you should wish to protect others;
for if you do not protect them, you will surely harm yourself in the end.
Having had this thought, he fled into the forest. There, an old brāhmaṇa who had lost his way arrived at that woodland, and the Bodhisattva asked him:
"For what reason have you come to this forest?"
The brāhmaṇa said,
"I wish to see the king.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Why have you come to see the King?
The brāhmaṇa replied, "I am currently impoverished and burdened with many debts; hearing that the King is fond of giving alms, I have come to beg for the purpose of repaying them."
“Having been far removed from poverty and suffering, we have nowhere else to turn; we look only to the King’s grace for our salvation.
The Bodhisattva said, “Go back all of you. Since there is no king here, to whom can you offer your sincere devotion?”
Upon hearing these words, the brahmin fell to the ground in a faint.
When the Bodhisattva saw this, he was deeply moved by compassion; having formed this thought, he spoke this verse:
"For the sake of protecting others, I have completely renounced that which is so difficult to give up."
"Now that I have renounced [all else], with what shall I give?
For the sake of this person, I shall now sacrifice my own body and life.
Having spoken this verse, he immediately assisted the brahmin to his feet and addressed him, saying:
"Do not grieve or be afraid!
I shall cause you to obtain wealth and profit.
When the brahmin heard these words, his heart was filled with joy. The Bodhisattva immediately made a rope out of grass; having finished making it, he gave it to the brahmin.
"I am the one who gives all things.
And he spoke this verse:
"As long as that king has not obtained me, his mind will never find peace."
"You should take this rope and bind me by the elbow,
then lead me to that king's presence; let the king be pleased,
and he shall bestow upon you precious jewels, gold, silver, and all manner of wealth."
You shall attain great wealth, and that king will likewise rejoice.
All who are born must die; life inevitably comes to its end.
For the sake of rescuing others from peril and distress, one may even lose one's own body and life.
"The wise die for this sake; it is called an ornament.
When the brahmin heard these words, he was filled with great joy and immediately bound the Bodhisattva with a rope, leading him away to the king.
Having seen him, the king spoke these verses to the brahmin:
"Who is this person? His majestic radiance is so exceedingly brilliant, Like the sun illuminating the world."
His countenance is exceedingly majestic; all who behold him are filled with joy.
One possessed of such merit should be the lord of the great earth;
why then is he now seized and constrained, suffering such hardship and distress?
As I sit upon this lion throne, I feel extreme shame and disgrace;
it is he who should occupy the royal seat, not one such as I.
Since I am unsubdued and unruly, I ought not to remain on this throne.
When the brahmin had heard this verse, he said to the great king,
"This is your enemy.
The king asked the brahmin:
"Who bound this man?
The brahmin replied,
"It was indeed I who bound him."
The King said:
"This man should not have been bound by you; you have spoken falsely.
He then spoke this verse:
"He is like a great, rutting elephant, his physical strength exceedingly powerful;
you are now emaciated and weak, and furthermore lack the force of an army—
how can you possibly bind him?"
"This matter cannot be trusted.
You should speak the truth; do not utter false words.
At that time, the brahmin related the preceding events in detail and spoke in verse:
"Seeing me lose hope, that person bound himself;
he bound himself out of compassion, desiring to rescue me.
Such a noble being has his fame spread throughout the ten directions."
Just as when a courtyard torch is lit, it shines universally upon all things;
so too, when the torch blazes fiercely, it can extinguish the ignorance of the unwholesome and foolish person until nothing remains.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King immediately rose in alarm, joined his palms, and said:
"Excellent, excellent!
Truly a virtuous man!"
"You have performed such deeds for the sake of saving others.
He then spoke in verse:
"The one called the Great King Is named Rāja."
Benefiting the world, for this reason you are named Rāja.
You should now become king and protect the great earth;
I pray that you will now listen to me as I confess all my transgressions.
I am indeed but a childish fool, impulsive and lacking in wisdom;
you may return to be king, while I shall abandon this kingdom and depart.
You are able to bring all sentient beings to a state of peace and happiness.
"If other men were to become kings, they would oppress and afflict all the world.
Having thus established that king, he returned to his own dwelling.
(72) Furthermore, one should perform meritorious deeds of purification and provide offerings; therefore, one ought to diligently cultivate meritorious deeds.

I have heard that in the past, there was a king of Śrāvastī named Udayana; the people of his entire kingdom collectively established a Buddhist assembly, and a certain woman peered at the World-Honored One from within a window.
At that time, the king, seeing that the woman was of such exquisite beauty, immediately untied his pearl necklace and dispatched an attendant minister to deliver it to her.
Thereupon, the king’s attendants said to him:
"That woman is already a wife within our kingdom; if Your Majesty desires her, you should simply go and summon her yourself—why trouble yourself by giving her this necklace?"
People will surely laugh at this as a strange thing.
Upon hearing these words, the king covered his ears with his hands and spoke thus:
“Alas, what great evil!”
"How could such words have reached my ears?
He then spoke this verse:
"By this oath, I swear: If I harbor any other thought,"
Though this has caused me great suffering, I did not become stained by attachment;
I gave the jewel to that woman so that she might hear my intention.
Karma is the sovereign lord; thus says the one who teaches the most excellent karma.
This is created without a sovereign creator; it is fashioned solely by karma.
The mind acts as the sovereign; virtuous karma is praised by the Buddha.
Such wondrous forms have no other sovereign or self.
It is solely through wholesome karma that this was made; I should revere wholesome karma and distance myself from unwholesome karma.
The fruit of retribution is manifest now, as if I were threading it upon a string of jewels.
Adorned with various precious jewels, with a *tāḍaṅka* suspended upon his brow and pearl strings white as snow—this is due to my past merits;
it is not for the sake of attachment to sensual desires. If one knows the nature of wholesome and unwholesome karma, [one will understand this].
How could one further be attached to form?
Even from afar one does not gaze upon it, much less harbor defiled attachment.
Rather than succumbing to unrighteous greed, one would sooner enter a mass of fire.
One should not engage in wicked or depraved deeds.
If one possesses attachment, whether in this life or in future lives, one will suffer immeasurable and extreme pain.

(73) Furthermore, if there is wholesome karma, by the natural power of that karma one receives a favorable retribution; even with the supporting power of a king’s faction, it does not equal the good retribution obtained through the power of karma. Therefore, one ought to cultivate wholesome karma.
I have heard that in the past, while King Udayana was sleeping during the day, there were two chamberlains—one at his head and one at his feet—who held fans and whisks and engaged in this discussion:
"By what means are we currently being thought of by the king?"
One claimed it was by his own karmic power, while the other claimed it was by the power of the king; for these reasons, they served the king.
At that time, those two men frequently listened to the Dharma and understood its discourses, so they spoke this verse:
"Just as when a bull crosses a river, The leader goes straight and the followers go straight as well."
"When a king of men establishes the True Dharma, his followers do likewise.
At that time, because the two men were competing for the point of their argument, their voices grew louder; one of them said:
"I live by relying upon the King."
The second replied,
"I rely on the power of karma.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately awoke from his sleep and asked him:
"Why do you raise your voice?

The king again heard those two disputing over principle; although he already knew their views clearly, he had not yet severed his own *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of self). His heart was displeased that they were supporting their own side, so he addressed the one who claimed the power of karma and spoke this verse in question:
"Residing within my kingdom, You claim for yourself the power of karma."
"I shall now test you to see by whose power this is.
Having spoken this verse, he went to the lady's quarters and said to her:
"I shall now send someone to come to you; you must adorn yourself like the consort of Śakra, the Lord of the Gods."
He replied,
"I shall obey the King's command!
Then the King gave grape juice to those who lived under his patronage and sent it to the Queen.
Having dismissed him, he reflected:
"Since you are called 'Karmic Power,' you ought now to repent for speaking such words.
Not long after he had this thought, Karmic Power arrived before the king, dressed in fine garments.
When the king saw this, he was greatly astonished and immediately spoke this verse:
"Did I, through my own error, Give him the dregs of the drink?"
Is it by the power of that person's karma that they have forcibly snatched this away?
Or could it be because of a close intimacy with them that they sent someone to take it?
Or perhaps it was the lady’s anger that caused her to seize this and give it to them?
"Could it be that I am deluded and have given [this] to him?
Or could it be that he has deluded me and caused me to become confused?
Having spoken this verse, he questioned that person, saying:
“Good man, speak the truth to me! It was because I relied upon your karmic power that I did not dismiss you;
how else could you have obtained it? That person replied to the king, “I obtained it through the power of karma.”
He then related the facts of the matter in detail to the King, saying:
"After this man had set out on his mission, he suddenly began to bleed from the nose; he gave me this gruel to deliver to the Queen, and upon arriving at her side, I obtained these garments."
Having heard this, the king immediately spoke in verse:
“Karmic retribution is like a shadow or an echo, and it is also like that magnificent array.
That which he said regarding the power of one’s own karma— these words are indeed not false.”
By the power of listening to the Dharma, one’s speech accords with reason;
as for those who speak of the power of karma, these words are surely proven true.
I am heavily burdened by my own faults, while he prevails by relying on the power of karma.
The Buddha has said that the power of karma is strong; these words are truly authentic.
The Buddha is the skillful charioteer, and the power of karma is excellent, for it can destroy even the might of a king.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, likewise speak of the power of karma.
You now rely on the power of karma to adorn your own body, thereby severing my power.
74 (74) Furthermore, even if one harbors enmity toward a wise person, they can still bring benefit; therefore, even if one is at odds with them, one should always remain close to a wise person.
I have heard that in the past, there was a brahmin in the kingdom of Mathurā who was clever and wise, yet did not believe in the Buddha-dharma and did not associate with the bhikṣus.
Having previously had a dispute with other brahmins, out of anger he went to the monastery and spoke falsely, saying:
"A certain brahmin will provide various offerings at his home tomorrow and shall hold a great assembly to invite the bhikṣus."

Wishing to ensure that the bhikṣus would arrive at his house the following morning without receiving food or drink, and so that the man’s ill repute would spread throughout the world, he instructed the bhikṣus:
"At dawn tomorrow, go to his house and say to the gatekeeper:
'The master of this house has invited us for a meal; you may go and inform him.'"
Then the gatekeeper went inside and informed the master:
"There are several bhikṣus outside the gate now, saying they have come to visit because you, sir, invited them.
Having heard this, the master reflected thus:
"For what cause and condition has such a thing occurred?
He further thought: "That brahmin is my enemy; therefore, he has done this."
"Although it is now midday, this city is extremely vast; let me send someone to procure provisions to provide for the bhikṣus.
Having had this thought, he immediately dispatched a person to summon the bhikṣus into his house to take their seats, where he prepared various kinds of food to offer them as alms.
When the bhikṣu has finished eating, he says to the donor:
"Please sit for a moment; it is the dharma of bhikṣus that after a meal one should preach the Dharma to the donor. Although you may not have faith, such is the way of the Buddha's Dharma."
Then the host immediately took a small seat and sat before the Elder.

For him, he preached on the discourse of giving, the discourse of morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven; he explained that sensual desires are impure and that transcendence from the world is true happiness, even proceeding to teach the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
This brahmin, having already planted various roots of merit in the past, perceived the Four Noble Truths while still seated and attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. He then spoke this verse:
"Alas! The power of delusion Is able to destroy right view.
The fool does not discern; He perceives treasure as non-treasure."
I have now attained victory, having discerned the Three Jewels;
the true jewels are mine: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha.
Having perceived them with clear vision, I shall close the gates to the three evil realms.
That which Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas could not obtain, I have now fully attained.
Thus I am named Brahmā; now I shall proceed toward that state.
The immortal elixir of liberation—I have now finally attained it, the supreme Dharma of the Brahmins.
Today is truly the full moon; today I have finally attained it.
The most excellent and wondrous Veda-dharma transcends all other Vedas;
I am now truly this great field of merit for offerings.
"I shall diligently perform great sacrifices, yet I am unable to properly distinguish between those worthy of sacrifice and those unworthy of sacrifice.
From this day forward, I shall make offerings to the God among Gods,
the Tathāgata."
To speak briefly, today at last I have gained the benefit of attaining the fruit of human birth.
From this day forward, I shall follow the teachings of the Buddha and never again seek refuge in other devas.
The Dharma that I now study accords with and leads toward the Right Path;
through this Dharma and its conformity, I shall surely attain its fruit.
I now take refuge and pay homage to the root of world-weariness cultivated in past lives.
Having practiced the Dharma and its applications, I have now attained their fruits and benefits.
By drawing near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), the benefits of the Dharma are spontaneously accomplished;
had I not drawn near to those disciples of Great Compassion, [these would not have been so].
They shall forever fall into wrong views and transmigrate through the three evil realms.
If there were no Brahmins who acted as my enemies,
I likewise would not have been able to draw near to such a noble assembly.
Because of his anger and resentment, he enabled me to attain this Dharma;
though outwardly appearing to be an evil friend, he was in truth a spiritual benefactor,
whose kindness exceeded that of my parents and all my kinsmen.
Because of this brahmin, the monks have come to my home;
like a downpour of sweet rain, the seeds of virtue have all been made to sprout.
The rain of Dharma is most nourishing, sprinkling the dust and grime from my heart.
Since the dust of affliction no longer arises, one is able to perceive the True Dharma.
Therefore, it is said in the world that "wealth is obtained through an enemy.
Reflecting upon this great benefit he had gained, he immediately received the Three Refuges.
To that brahmin, he prepared a great variety of delicacies.
(75) Furthermore, if a person gives wealth as an offering with sincerity, they will obtain wealth and merit like a flower; knowing this to be so, one should give with a devoted heart.
I have heard that in the past, a husband and wife from the land of Kaśmīra were lying together upon a grass mat. As dawn was about to break, a wholesome thought arose in them, and they reflected:

"In this country there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people who all cultivate merit and make offerings to the Saṃgha. We, however, are poor; having encountered this island of jewels, if we do not take even a small amount of treasure with us into the next world, our misfortune and suffering will be endless. Since we currently lack merit, our future suffering will be long."
Having had this thought, he sighed with grief and lamented; as he wept piteously, his tears fell upon his wife.
At that time, the wife immediately asked her husband, "For what reason are you so unhappy?"
He then spoke in verse:
"Why are you so deeply distressed?
Why do you sigh again and again, with tears raining down to drench my arms, as if pouring water upon them?"
At that time, her husband replied with a verse:
"I possess not even the slightest merit To carry into the next world;
Having reflected upon this matter, For this reason, I lament for myself."
In this world there is a fertile field of merit, yet I possess no seeds of goodness;
whether in this life or in future lives, the suffering of hunger and destitution is beyond reckoning.
Having failed to sow seeds in previous lives, I am now utterly impoverished in this world.
"If you do not act now, there will likewise be no fruit in the future.
At that time, having heard these verses, the wife said to her husband:
"Do not be sorrowful or anxious."
"I belong to you; you have sovereign power over my person. If you sell my body, you may obtain wealth sufficient to fulfill your heart's desire.
At that time, when her husband heard these words from his wife, joy arose in his heart and his countenance became serene;
he said to his wife, "Without you, I cannot live."
He then spoke in verse:
"My body and your body are like those ruddy sheldrakes;
let us sell our bodies together, and with the wealth obtained, cultivate merit."
At that time, the husband and wife went to the house of the elder and spoke these words:

"Please lend us some gold. If we cannot repay it after one month, the two of us shall become your slaves. After one month, we will certainly be unable to repay the gold; let us divide ourselves as slaves so that during this month we may provide offerings to the community of bhikṣus."
At that time, the elder immediately gave him gold. Having received the gold, they said to one another, "We should provide offerings to the community of monks at the monastery of Revata."
The wife asked her husband,
"On what day will it be?
He replied:
“On the fifteenth day.
He asked again:
“Why is it the fifteenth day?”
At that time, her husband replied with a verse:
"On the fifteenth day of the month, the celestial kings such as Kuvera and others traverse the world; this is what the Buddha has taught."
"Desiring to let humans and devas know, for this reason it is on the fifteenth day.

At that time, the husband and wife exerted themselves in their preparations until the thirteenth day; when all the food provisions were ready, they sent them to the monastery and addressed the administrator, saying:
"We pray only that the Venerable One..."
"On the fifteenth day, please ensure that none of the members of the Sangha go outside; I wish to extend my invitation to you.
The administrator replied, "So be it."
On the fourteenth day, the husband and wife stayed overnight at the monastery; encouraging one another, they spoke these verses:
"Exhort your own self: Be careful not to shrink from fatigue.
Now that you have attained this freedom, You ought to exert yourself to the utmost."
"Later, being directed by others, one's actions will lack autonomy;
one will undergo manifold toil and hardship without gaining even a hair’s breadth of benefit.
Having spoken this verse, the husband and wife did not sleep for even a moment throughout the night. By dawn, all the prepared delicacies were ready, and the husband said to his wife:
“Excellent, we! What was to be done has been accomplished, and our hearts’ desires are fulfilled.
By selling this one body on such an auspicious day as this, we shall always enjoy abundance throughout hundreds of thousands of future lives.”
At that time, a ruler of a small kingdom prepared food and drink and came to the monastery, saying:
"I pray that the various monks will accept my offerings."
The administrator said, "We monks have already accepted another invitation; let us seek another day.
Then that minor king earnestly entreated him, saying:
"I am now pressed by many affairs; I pray you accept my invitation.
At that time, the monks remained silent and offered no reply.
Then the sovereign spoke to the husband and wife, saying:
"I shall now strike the *gandī* myself; you must pay me the price for the food you have prepared.
When the husband and wife heard these words, they prostrated themselves before the king with their five limbs touching the ground and addressed him, saying:

"We, your subjects, are destitute and possess nothing. We sold our own bodies to provide these offerings; having spent the night preparing them, we have completed the arrangements. Today alone do we have the freedom to offer them ourselves. If by tomorrow we are driven into service by others and lose our autonomy, we pray that Your Majesty will show us compassion and not deprive us of this day."
He then spoke in verse:
"Like a pair of mandarin ducks, husband and wife, the preparations have now been completed;
I pray you will surely remember me, for tomorrow I shall belong to another."
"Each of us has employed different strategies, and there is no further opportunity to cultivate merit.
Thus, we have sold our own bodies for the sake of practicing virtue.
When the king heard this account in full, he praised them, saying, "Excellent! and spoke these verses:
“You have well understood the Buddha’s teaching and clearly comprehend cause and effect;
you are able to use this deceptive body to exchange it for a firm wealth of life.
Do not harbor fear; I grant you leave to fulfill whatever you wish.”
"Out of compassion for you, I shall repay your price with wealth;
though you now afflict your own bodies, in the end you will obtain great profit and happiness.

When the lord of the land had spoken this verse, he permitted the husband and wife to make offerings to the assembly of monks. He immediately used his own wealth to pay their debt to others and provided the couple with capital to manage their own livelihoods, so that they might enjoy these rewards in the present without any lack.
76 (Seventy-six) Furthermore, upholding the precepts with a sincere heart yields visible retribution even unto the end of one's life.
I have heard that in the past, in the city of Natabhatika, there were two lay brothers who both observed the five precepts.

At that time, his younger brother suddenly suffered from pain in his ribs and his vital breath was on the verge of ceasing. A physician examined him and prescribed freshly slaughtered dog meat along with wine, saying that his ailment would surely be cured.
The patient said:

"As for the dog meat, it may be purchased from the market for me to eat; however, regarding the matter of drinking wine, I would rather sacrifice my life than ever violate the precept by consuming alcohol."
Seeing his younger brother in extreme distress, the elder brother bought wine and said to him,
"Relinquish your precepts and drink this wine to cure your illness.
The younger brother replied to his brother:
"Though I am gravely ill, I vow to sacrifice my body and life; I shall never violate the precepts by drinking this wine.
He then spoke in verse:
"How strange! As my life draws to its end, You would destroy the jeweled necklace of my precepts."
Adorn the body with the precepts; there will be no need for elaborate funeral rites.
Since a human body is so difficult to obtain, and encountering the precepts is even more difficult, I vow to sacrifice hundreds of thousands of lives rather than violate the prohibitions.
Only after immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas does one encounter the precepts;
within the world of Jambudvīpa, a human body is extremely difficult to obtain,
and though one may obtain a human body, encountering the True Dharma is twice as difficult.
At times one encounters the treasure of the Dharma, yet the foolish do not know how to take it;
even for those who are well able to discern it, this matter is likewise difficult.
Now that the jewel of the precepts has come into my hands, why would you wish to seize it back?
"He is indeed one whom we hate and loathe; he is not one with whom I am intimate.
Having heard this verse, the elder brother replied to his younger brother:
"Because he is my relative, I shall not cause him to be ruined."
The younger brother said to his elder brother,
"This is not out of affection, but rather because it is ruined.
He then spoke this verse:
"I desire to proceed toward the superior state, yet you destroy my precepts and cause me to fall;
since you have harmed me in such a way, how can you be called a loved one?
While I am diligently practicing the roots of virtue, you seek to plunder them."
"Among the five precepts one upholds, the precept against alcohol is the most important.
Now you wish to forcibly harm me; you cannot be called a kinsman.
The elder brother asked the younger brother:
"How is it that alcohol is the root of the precepts?
The younger brother then replied to his elder brother with a verse:
"If, regarding the prohibitive precepts, one does not guard and uphold them with a wholehearted mind,"
This would be to violate great compassion;
I do not even dare to touch it. For this reason, I know that alcohol is the cause for the evil realms.
The evil retribution of alcohol—only a Buddha can discern it;
who else could measure it?
Of the three types of unwholesome karma, alcohol alone is the root.
They fall once more into evil conduct;
because of the cause and condition of alcohol, they subsequently destroy the remaining four precepts.
This is called the category of evil conduct, and it is also termed the "five great transgressions."
This is also the fivefold fearlessness:
by not drinking [intoxicants], one closes off the evil realms; one is able to attain a mind of faith and joy;
and by removing stinginess, one is able to relinquish wealth.
I am entirely without any other thought than that one can obtain immeasurable benefit;
how could I wish to violate [the precepts]?
Rather than giving up hundreds of thousands of lives, I shall not violate the Buddha's teaching.
I would rather let my body wither away than ever drink this wine.
Even if one were to commit a transgression against the precepts and live for a hundred or a thousand years,
it would not equal the merit of guarding the prohibitions, even if one’s life were to end at that very moment.
Even when I was certain that it would cure me, I still did not drink;
how much more so now, when I do not know for certain whether it will cure me or not?
Having formed this resolute mind, my heart gave rise to great joy.
One immediately attains the vision of the True Dharma, and that which was troubling is instantly eliminated.

(77) Furthermore, if one has faith in the Buddha’s words, regarding all external treatises as being like the speech of infants, fools, or the insane, one should therefore diligently study the Buddha’s teachings and discourses.
I have heard that in the past there was a kingdom named Śākala, whose king was named Rudhāmadha; that king went frequently to the monastery to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, as the Dharma Master was speaking on the faults of alcohol, King Nanda challenged the Dharma Master seated on the high throne, saying:
"If giving alcohol to others results in madness and delusion, then why is it that those who drink much themselves do not receive such retribution of madness and delusion?"
At that time, the Dharma Master pointed toward the non-Buddhists. When the king saw this, he exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
Then some non-Buddhists deliberated among themselves, saying, "That speaker of the Dharma has no knowledge or insight;
he merely points empty space. The king, for his part, does not understand the Dharma Master at all, yet he vainly exclaims 'Excellent!'"
Unable to provide an explanation for this question, he thought:
"Yet there are among this assembly great and wise individuals; why do they not answer the King?
He then spoke in verse:
"The Dharma Master possesses keen eloquence and is well able to answer this meaning;
however, out of compassion for you all, he has guarded and withheld it from speaking.
The non-Buddhists said:
"For the sake of this Dharma Master, you have perversely attempted to explain the principles.
The King said,
"The understanding I possess has yet another dimension."
At that time, the king said to the Dharma Master,
"The meaning you have just explained may now be set forth in detail.
The Dharma Master replied:

"The reason I refer to them as 'non-Buddhists' (tīrthika) is that these various non-Buddhists each give rise to divergent views and possess inverted minds; for this reason, they are called deluded and insane people."
He then spoke in verse:
"It is not necessary for a ghost to enter one's body to be called a madman;
rather, it is one with a mind of wrong views, like a yakṣa, who is said to be mad."
The faults of the insane and deluded do not know how to understand their own affairs;
you who possess such madness have been described by the One of All-Knowledge.
You contradict the words of the One of All-Knowledge and follow after false views.
Having personally witnessed these supernatural transformations, he has been humiliated by that Great Sage.
Having transgressed the bounds of his prohibitions, he was already driven to madness beforehand;
how then can I explain to you the hundreds of thousands of causes for such insanity?
Why do you speak with such discrimination?
You throw yourself into abysses and rush into fires; you cast yourself down from high peaks and abandon the precepts of giving.
Chasing after delusions, you are perverse and insane; you do not cultivate the practice of the Right Path.
Madly deluded, falling from a cliff into fire; selling salt, destroying pure conduct.
Drinking and touching the waters of the Ganges—this is called establishing right practice.
What is the causal significance of losing purity and attaining the right?
The seller of meat is a gathering of manifold evils; There are three kinds of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
Apart from these three kinds of transformations, there are further miraculous powers.
There are only these twelve factors (*dharma*); Apart from these, there is no separate self (*ātman*).
I have witnessed the supernatural transformations of seers and gods, and further observed thirteen such phenomena.
Such instances of madness number in the hundreds;
I have seen them cast themselves into abysses and fires, or hurl themselves from the heights of mountain peaks.
To desire birth in heaven for this reason is merely a false view;
it is not the cause for birth in heaven.
Observing the precepts, practicing generosity, and skillfully disciplining the mind—these are the causes for birth in heaven.
The River of Touch removes all evils, yet selling salt involves great evil;
the River of Touch possesses great goodness. What is the meaning of this, that they are designated as "good" and "evil"?
One immediately falls into the loss of the Dharma; even by grasping a blade, one loses the Dharma.
If one further sells meat—thirty-six *jin* of it—one brings ruin upon the status of a Brahmin.
All these are termed the loss of the Dharma; seeing a fly tasting honey, both constitute faults.
Deceiving others with a scale does not constitute theft, yet selling meat constitutes taking life.
Both sheep and rice possess life; eating rice does not constitute killing.
Since both sheep and rice should be eaten, why do you eat rice but not eat sheep?
One who ultimately fails to be reborn in heaven, yet falls from a cliff or throws himself into deep waters while claiming he will be reborn there;
one who says he has committed a sin by killing, yet feeds and nourishes his own body— why does such a person fail to obtain merit?
Observing that you do not accord with reason, all of this is the inversion of ignorance;
for these causes and conditions, I call you all "mad.
This is precisely ignorance, the defining mark of a rākṣasa.
Therefore it is said of you: "You have accomplished the dharma of madness.
This is the cause and effect of drinking alcohol;
hatred is the cause of delusion, and through hatred one becomes dark and turbid.
It can cause one’s complexion to change;
anger is the cause of emaciation and darkening, while drinking alcohol makes the complexion turbid—
both of these can lead to emaciation.
You yourself previously drank liquor and also taught others to drink it, saying there was no retribution for such acts;
therefore, in the present life, you have already obtained the body of a hungry ghost.
Such is the "flower-retribution" [the immediate result] you have already received.
"The karmic retribution will follow later.
When the brahmins heard these words, many of the non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika) immediately went forth into homelessness.
(78) Furthermore, one who skillfully distinguishes the merit of reverence does not base it upon lineage or clan.
I have heard that in the past, there were two princes from the city of Puṣpapura who fled and sought refuge in the kingdom of Mālava.
At that time, there was a domestic official in that country named Vararuci, who served as a minister to the king of the neighboring state and personally distributed food to the assembly of monks.
After the community of monks had finished eating, he sent someone to collect the remnants of the food from the grass and take them to the palace;
there, he would first pay homage to the food before eating it himself, and then distribute what remained to those he held dear.
"By eating that leftover food, one can destroy my afflictions.
Therefore, he first took it and ate it, then gave some to the two princes.
After the princes had eaten it, because their minds felt revulsion and contempt, they went outside and immediately vomited it up, saying these words:
"The monastics are of various and mixed castes; we now eat their leftovers.
Having eaten them, we must vomit them up and discard them, and only then can our transgression be removed.
When the employer heard this, he spoke as follows:
"These two infants are utterly ignorant.
He then spoke this verse:
"Those who obtain this leftover food, The wise eliminate their faults and afflictions."
They give rise to doubt, derision, and aversion; such people are called infantile fools.
In the Buddha-dharma, one contemplates food; this is entirely absent among the non-Buddhists.
When a śramaṇa contemplates food, he is able to eliminate the obstacles of affliction.
"The Muni has touched this leftover food; it should be worn upon the head with reverence.
Having taken hold of the remains of the meal, one should wash them with water to remove the fault.
Subsequently, the employer did not give him any more leftover food.
At that time, those around him asked,
"For what reason do you not divide the food and give it to the two princes?
He then spoke this verse:
"Because he lacks understanding, and because he relies on his own lineage to claim that what remains from a śramaṇa’s meal is impure,
he does not give rise to a heart of joy; for this reason, I do not give it to him."
One who does not know the lineage of a śramaṇa should not eat his food;
one who does not know my own lineage should not eat my food.
Śramaṇas are born everywhere; they do not belong to my clan.
I am not equal to the śramaṇas, nor do they eat my food.
They say I have no lineage and no seniority;
like a horse without a breed, so too is the eunuch.
The inner attendants come from all quarters, having no fixed direction or place;
they behold only my wealth and status, not my lineage.
Because they see only wealth and status, they consume the remnants of my food.
One who does not eat the food of a śramaṇa is called an infant fool.
A śramaṇa whose mind is self-mastered and who possesses the seven kinds of wealth—
yet who does not eat the food of a śramaṇa and instead eats what remains of mine— [is truly a śramaṇa].
Just as one who has leaped over half a well cannot see where he stands, so too,
seeing that I possess power and am held in the king’s thoughts,
he then ate the remnants of my food.
The Prince, son of King Śuddhodana, has come from such a lineage;
could he not surpass me?
He is peerless and without equal; it is not his caste that I take into account.
One who possesses only virtuous conduct is also called lowly;
one who is endowed with both precepts and wisdom is called noble.
When the two princes heard these words, they spoke thus:
"You who show us the right path are our father; from this day forward, we shall respectfully receive your instruction."
He then spoke in verse:
"You now speak of lineage, Which is most certainly not in accordance with the Dharma.
Since conduct has no fixed nature, And understanding has no fixed direction."
One who understands speech and discourse correctly is not said to speak of extremes;
one who understands as you do belongs to a noble lineage.
(79) Furthermore, if you wish to observe and know the Buddha’s supernormal transformations, visit the various stūpas and temples and make offerings to the Buddha’s stūpas.

I have heard that in the past, in the kingdom of Āliṃcavīka, there was a stūpa for the hair and nail relics of the Buddha at its city gate; nearby stood a nyagrodha tree, and beside it was a well of water.
Then the brahmin addressed the king, saying:

"If you see that stūpa while traveling, it will be the grave of a śramaṇa and will destroy your merit and virtue. Since Your Majesty is the sovereign ruler of this great earth, you ought to remove this stūpa."
At that time, because the king believed the words of the brahmins, he immediately issued an order to his ministers:
"Quickly remove this stupa; do not let it be seen again when I go out tomorrow."
At that time, the city deity and all the people wept with grief.
Then the upāsikās prepared offerings, and those who lit lamps spoke these words: "This is our final offering."
There was an upāsaka who embraced the stūpa and wept bitterly, immediately speaking in verse:
"I now embrace you for the last time, The base and foot of your stūpa;
As if Mount Sumeru were falling over, Today it is all shattered and wounded."
The stūpa of the World-Honored One of Ten Powers has now fallen into ruin.
If I have committed any transgressions, please grant me leave to repent;
for sentient beings shall no longer behold the deeds performed by the Buddha.
At that time, the upāsakas spoke thus:
"We should now return home; we cannot bear to look upon others destroying this stūpa."
Then the king later sent his own men with spades, intending to remove it. When they arrived at the site, both the stupa and the tree had completely vanished. He then spoke this verse:
"Alas, how truly strange! The entire city lets out a great cry, Like the surging waves of the ocean;
Yet the stupa of the One of Ten Powers is nowhere to be seen."
"The *nyagrodha* tree and the well—no one knows where they are!
The brahmins and others felt deep shame and wonder in their hearts.
Upon hearing this, the king conceived a sense of rare wonder.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"Who has taken this stūpa away?
He immediately went to the site of the stūpa, but could not discover its whereabouts.
At that time, the king dispatched more than a thousand men, riding elephants and galloping horses, to search in all four directions.
There was an old woman by the roadside who, seeing those people coming and going with great haste, immediately asked them:
"Why are you acting in such a manner?"
The people replied,
“We are searching for the tree of the stūpa.
The old woman said:
"I witnessed a rare event upon the road: a stūpa and a nyagrodha tree were flying through the air; I do not recall seeing a well.
I saw many people wearing celestial crowns upon their heads, with flower garlands hanging down and their bodies adorned with various blossoms, carrying the stūpa away."
"I felt a sense of wonder when I saw him depart.
He pointed out the direction he had gone, and upon hearing this, the people reported the full details of the matter back to the king.
Hearing this, the king was filled with joy and spoke this verse:
“That stūpa flew away of its own accord; did it go toward the heavens?
Now my heart is filled with faith and reverence, and I feel the utmost great joy;
if I were to destroy this stūpa, I would surely fall into hell.”

At that time, the king immediately made grand offerings at the site of that stūpa; this stūpa is now called "The Self-Transferred," and it, along with the tree and the well, stands thirty *li* away from the city of Vigaya.
80. Furthermore, the Buddha-stūpa possesses great majestic power; therefore, one ought to make offerings to the Buddha-stūpa.

I have heard that in the past, in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, there was a stūpa-temple which King Prasenajit set on fire and burned down. The Buddha then established a single pillar there, yet it decayed and fell away again.
At that time, there was a king of that country named Kuṣadhvaja. A certain bhikṣu requested of the king:
"I now require timber for the construction of a stūpa; I pray that Your Majesty will grant me permission to take it. Should there be large trees, may Your Majesty not begrudge them."
The king then spoke to them, saying, "With the exception of all the trees within my palace, you may take every other tree.

Having received the king's command, the bhikṣus searched everywhere. By the side of a certain village there was a large pond with a great tree upon it called a śirīṣa tree; it was protected by a nāga, and because a wicked nāga resided nearby, no one dared to touch it.
That tree was extremely large; if anyone were to take its branches or leaves, the dragon would kill them. For this reason, no one dared to approach it.
Someone said: "There is a great tree over there."
Then the bhikṣu immediately took those people, carrying axes and tools, intending to go and cut them down.
At that time, another person said to the bhikṣu:
"This nāga is extremely malevolent."
The bhikṣu said:
"I perform the work of the Buddha; I do not fear the evil nāgas.
At that time, there was a brahmin who served [the Buddha] and spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"That dragon is extremely malevolent; if you cut down this tree, it will cause much injury. Do not hack this tree to pieces.
The brāhmaṇa then spoke a verse:
"Do you not hear of that thief, who acted for a moment out of stinginess and greed?"
One should always protect oneself in all circumstances; do not allow yourself to be harmed for the sake of this tree.
The bhikṣu spoke again in verse:
“Because of you, the venomous dragon, You have given rise to arrogance yourself;
I rely upon the Dragon among Men, And by depending on him, I too am high.”
Observing that your strength is superior, I have thus gained the advantage to let all people see it.
Out of reverence for the Buddha, I shall now sacrifice my body and life.
"You have become a dragon king; give rise to thoughts of great reverence.
The Buddha is gentle, disciplined, and tranquil, as well as the King among this assembly;
I now likewise revere the Tathāgata, the Bhagavān."
"Who is able to subdue the venomous dragon and become his disciple?
At that time, the bhikṣus and the brāhmaṇas vied with one another over their respective doctrines and subsequently fell into dispute.
At that time, the bhikṣu cut down the tree, yet there were no signs of clouds, thunder, or other miraculous portents.
When the brahmin witnessed this event, he spoke these verses:
"If one had previously taken its branches and leaves, Clouds would have risen and thunderbolts struck."
"You are subdued by a spell; death has arrived for you in the next world.
When the brahmin had spoken this verse, he immediately fell asleep and dreamed that a venomous dragon spoke this verse to him:
"Do not give rise to anger; this is called present worship."
"It is not that I wish to slight or disparage you;
I myself would carry this stūpa upon my own body, let alone use a tree as a pillar for it—how could I fail to cherish and protect it?
As for the stūpa of the World-Honored One, the One of Ten Powers, how shall I protect it?"
The trees in this grove grow of their own accord for the sake of the Buddha’s stūpa;
since these trees grow spontaneously in this way, how could one feel attachment or regret for them?
There is yet another cause and condition which I shall now explain—listen well.
I too lack the power; the Naga King Takṣaka has come himself to take this tree—how could I possibly protect it?
So too the Naga King Elāpattra and Vaiśravaṇa.
Having come here in person, what power do I possess that I could resist those of such majestic virtue— the devas, nāgas, and others?
Whether the Tathāgata remains in the world or has passed into parinirvāṇa, [his power is the same].
Those who construct stupas and temples— these two are equal and no different.
All those who have attained the Way— humans, devas, and yakṣas—
their fame pervades the ten directions, peerless throughout the world.
"Because of such renown, bells of precious jewels are suspended from the stupa's crossbeams;
their sound is most harmonious and elegant, heard and known by all far and near.
Upon hearing these verses, the brahmin awoke from his sleep and immediately went forth into homelessness.

81. Furthermore, I have heard that in the past there was an old woman who was traveling along a road carrying a jar of ghee on her back. Seeing an *āmalaka* tree, she ate its fruit; having eaten it, she became thirsty and immediately went to a well to beg for water to drink.

Then the water-drawer immediately gave him water; because of the power of the *āmalaka* fruit he had previously eaten, he thought the water was as sweet and delicious as rock honey (*śarkarā*), and said to the man:
"I will exchange my jar of ghee for your jar of water."
At that time, the water-carrier followed her words and gave her a jar of water. Having received it, the old woman carried it back home.
Once she arrived at her house, the heat from the mango she had previously eaten had already subsided; she took the water and drank it, finding only the taste of water and no other flavor.
He immediately gathered his kinsmen and had them all taste it;
they all said, "This water has the smell of rotting, decayed rope-juice and mud; it is utterly foul and loathsome. Why have you brought this here now?"
Having heard these words, he took some himself to taste it and felt deep regret, thinking:
"For what reason have I traded this fine ghee for this foul-smelling water?"

"All ordinary beings and common folk are likewise; because they are foolish and lack wisdom, they trade the future vessel of the cream of merit for the foul and filthy vessels of the four inversions, regarding them as excellent."
Later, realizing that it was not genuine, he felt deep regret and remorse, exclaiming: "Alas! Why did I trade the jar of merit-essence for this perverse, foul, and filthy water?"
And he spoke in verse: "Alas!
What have I done? With pure conduct of the three karmas, I have bartered them for attachment to the various realms of existence."
It is like exchanging pure, fine ghee for foul, stinking water;
or like eating an *āmalaka* fruit with an inverted tongue that fails to perceive its flavor, whereby one mistakes foul water for nectar (*amṛta*).

82. Furthermore, I have heard that in the past there was once a householder’s wife who, having been rebuked by her mother-in-law, fled into a forest intending to commit suicide. Being unable to find a means to do so, she immediately climbed a tree to hide herself; beneath the tree was a pond, and her reflection appeared in the water.
At that time, there was a maidservant carrying a jar to fetch water; seeing her own reflection in the water, she thought it was someone else and spoke these words:
"My face is so handsome and well-proportioned; why then am I carrying this jar for another to fetch water?"
He immediately smashed the jar and returned home, saying to his master:
"My facial features are so handsome; why do you make me carry jars to fetch water?"
At that time, the mistress of the house said, "This slave girl must be possessed by a malevolent spirit; that is why she acts this way.
She gave her another jar and sent her to the pond to fetch water, yet she saw her own reflection again and once more smashed the jar.
At that time, the elder’s wife was atop the tree; having witnessed this event, she immediately smiled.

Seeing her shadow smile, the maidservant suddenly realized what was happening. She looked up and saw a woman on the tree smiling, dressed in the garments of a beautiful woman rather than her own; only then did she feel shame.
For what reason was this analogy spoken?

It was for the sake of the masses who are deluded by inverted views; it is like the fragrance of *campaka* oil used to anoint the hair on the crown of the head, which the deluded do not understand, thinking, "This fragrance issues from my own crown."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Even when unguents are applied to the body, And used to perfume one's robes, necklaces, and ornaments, The deluded mind is just like this:
It imagines that [the fragrance] issues forth from its own body."
"Just as that ugly maidservant, seeing her reflection, thought it was herself.
(83) Furthermore, when a cat gives birth to kittens, they grow gradually from small to large.
The kitten asked its mother, "What should we eat?"
The mother replied to her son, "A person taught you yourself.
At night, she went to another house and hid among the jars and vessels; someone who saw her then made a mutual agreement and gave her instructions:
"The ghee, milk, meat, and other delicacies are well-covered; lift up the chick so that the cat does not eat it.
The cat immediately understood: "The chicken, ghee, milk, and curd are all my food."
For what reason is this analogy spoken?
The Buddha has attained the path of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, is fully endowed with the ten powers, and his vows are fulfilled; with a heart of great compassion, he delivers and uplifts many beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"By what Dharma should I transform and deliver them?
Great Compassion replied:

"The mental activities of all sentient beings are manifested; observing their afflictions with the knowledge of others' minds, one sees that all such formations as greed, hatred, and delusion have increased throughout the long night, perpetually sustained by the notions of permanence, pleasure, self, and purity."
To speak in such a manner cannot increase the realization of the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Therefore, having understood this matter, the Tathāgata teaches the remedies for various inversions for the sake of sentient beings.
The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is subtle and profound, difficult to understand and difficult to enter; it is called the exposition of the Path.
How can one possibly expound such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings?
Having observed and known that sentient beings possess inverted views and perceptions, he preaches the essentials of the Dharma to them according to their needs.

Sentient beings themselves have various types of conduct; therefore, one knows that the Tathāgata teaches remedial dharmas to destroy these inversions, just as one covers meat with ghee and milk for the sake of a cat.

84. Furthermore, I have heard that in the past there was a kingdom where a stone pillar had been erected that was exceedingly tall. Having removed the ladder, the rungs, the ropes, and the cables, they placed a craftsman at the very top of the pillar.
For what reason?
Should he remain alive, he might erect stone pillars elsewhere that would surpass these.
Then, during that night, the kinsmen and relatives of that stonemason gathered around the pillar and said to him:
"How can you possibly descend now?
At that time, the stone mason, possessing many skillful means, immediately untied the threads of his garment and let two strands of thread hang down to the base of the pillar.

The kinsmen immediately tied a coarse thread to the hem of his garment; the artisan pulled it up until it reached the top, where he grasped the coarse thread and said to his relatives, "You all should now tie on even smaller, coarser ropes."
Those kinsmen followed his instructions accordingly; thus it was passed along until finally a thick, heavy rope was obtained.
At that time, the stonemason descended by following the rope.

The stone pillar is a metaphor for birth and death; the rungs and crossbars of the ladder are metaphors for the dharmas already extinguished by past Buddhas; "kinsmen" is a metaphor for the assembly of śrāvakas; "clothing and threads" is a metaphor for the concentration and wisdom of past Buddhas; and "tearing the clothing" is a metaphor for contemplating the past flavors and other such dharmas of desire.

The thread descending from above is a metaphor for faith; the attachment of coarse thread is a metaphor for drawing near to virtuous friends and attaining extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). The fine cord represents the thread of extensive learning, upon which is suspended the thread of ethical discipline (*śīla*); the thread of ethical discipline suspends the thread of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the thread of meditative concentration suspends the rope of wisdom (*prajñā*). By means of these, the coarse rope becomes firm and secure.
The "bindings" are a metaphor for being bound to birth and death; "descending from above" is a metaphor for descending from the pillar of birth and death.
"With faith as the thread, Much learning and the observance of precepts are like its coarse strands; Virtue and concentration are the small cords."
"Take wisdom as the coarse rope, and pull down the pillar of birth and death.

(85) Furthermore, I have heard that in the past, there was a kingdom where the royal lineage was on the verge of extinction. At that time, there was a member of the royal family who had previously entered the mountains and forests to study the Way and seek immortality. They forcibly brought him back and established him as king. He then demanded clothing and food from the person assigned to prepare his bedding.
Then the person in charge of spreading the bedding addressed the king, saying:
"Each of us has our own specific duties; Your Majesty should not now expect me to attend to every single request. I know only the matter of spreading the bedding;
as for bathing, clothing, and food, these are all handled by others and are not my responsibility."

By this analogy, one may understand that all karmas are like the attendants who prepare bedding for a king, each having their own specific charge; karma is likewise, with each instance being distinct from the others.

Physical beauty, freedom from illness, wealth, and desirable objects, as well as wisdom and other such karmic results, are each distinct; some karma results in freedom from illness, while some karma can result in physical beauty, strength, and vigor. For example, it was like that seer who requested various items from the person preparing his bedding, yet in the end, he could not obtain them at all.
If one is born into a noble lineage, it does not necessarily entail wealth; for the retributions of various karmas differ from one another, and one does not obtain diverse fruits from a single karma.
If one performs the karma of physical beauty, one will obtain a handsome appearance and strength; as for wealth, it must be sought from other karmic causes.
Therefore, the wise should cultivate various kinds of pure karma to obtain various kinds of retribution:
"Freedom from illness, physical beauty, noble lineage, and wisdom—each has its own distinct cause.
Just as that King of Rishis [requested] one who was fully equipped to prepare his bedding."

86. Furthermore, I have heard that in the past there was a king who maintained many excellent horses. When another neighboring king came to engage him in battle, he retreated immediately upon learning that this king possessed such fine steeds.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"I previously raised these horses intending to confront a hostile nation; now that they have all retreated and dispersed, what is the use of keeping them?
I shall employ these horses to provide labor for men, so that the horses will not suffer harm and men will benefit."
Having had this thought, he immediately issued an order to his officials to distribute the various herds of horses among the people for constant use as grinding stones over many years.

Later, when a neighboring country again invaded his borders, he ordered that the horses be taken to fight against them; however, because they had been used for grinding, the horses moved in circles and refused to advance, remaining obstinate even when whipped with sticks.
Sentient beings are likewise; if they attain liberation, it must be through the mind, meaning that after experiencing the five desires, they subsequently attain liberation.
Once the enemy of death has arrived, if the mind remains attached to the pleasures of the five desires, one cannot advance directly to obtain the fruit of liberation.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Wisdom should properly discipline the mind, Do not allow it to become attached to the five desires.
Because the mind was not disciplined from the start, One gives rise to craving and longing at the moment of death."
If the mind is neither disciplined nor compliant, how can it attain tranquility?
The mind constantly indulges in the five desires; deluded and distracted, it cannot awaken.
If the mind is neither disciplined nor compliant, how can it attain tranquility?
"The mind is constantly addicted to the five desires, Deluded and wild, unable to awaken;
Like a horse untrained for battle, It turns away when facing the enemy.
(87) Furthermore, it was once heard that there was a king who fell ill, and none of the physicians in the kingdom were able to cure him.
At that time, there was a skilled physician who came from afar to treat the king's illness until it was cured. The king was greatly delighted and thought to himself:
"I have now obtained the power of this physician; I must reward him handsomely."

Having formed this thought, he secretly dispatched his attendants to bring a great quantity of wealth and goods to the physician’s residence. There they constructed a house and provided all necessities for living, including people, fields, houses, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, slaves, servants, and laborers; there was no asset whatsoever that was not fully prepared.
Once the preparations were complete, the king dispatched the physician back to his home.
At that time, the distant physician saw that the king had sent no one ahead from his presence and was returning empty-handed; he felt profound resentment.
As he was about to arrive home, he encountered on the road oxen, sheep, elephants, and horses that he had never seen before.
When asked whose they were, they all replied, "They belong to that physician; they are that physician's oxen and horses."

Having finally arrived home, he saw that his house was magnificent and magnificently adorned with beds, curtains, woolen rugs, carpets, gold and silver vessels, and his wife’s various necklaces and garments.
When the physician saw it, he was struck with great amazement, as if it were a celestial palace.
He asked his wife,
"How did you obtain such a magnificent thing?"
The wife replied to her husband,
"How can you not know?
Because you cured the illness of that king, they have come to repay your kindness."
Upon hearing this, he was filled with profound joy and thought to himself:
"The King possesses supreme virtue; his knowledge of gratitude and his repayment of kindness exceed my original expectations."
"Due to my own short-sightedness, when I first arrived, I harbored resentment because I had attained nothing.
Using this as an analogy, the essential meaning shall now be explained.

The physician is a metaphor for all wholesome karmas; the king has no metaphor for that which has not yet yielded its present retribution, as there is nothing to be obtained in the body. Just as that physician, initially seeing no object, thought there was nothing to be obtained and felt resentment in his heart, so too does one who cultivates goodness in this present life, seeing no immediate reward, feel resentment in their heart, thinking, "I have gained nothing."
Having arrived at home, it is as if one has cast off the body and is heading toward the next world.
Seeing herds of oxen, sheep, elephants, and horses is like reaching the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Upon seeing various auspicious signs, she then thinks:
"Because I have cultivated wholesome deeds, I see these favorable rewards; I shall surely be reborn in heaven."

Having reached the heavens, as one who has arrived at home and beholds various signs of prosperity, he then conceives a heart of reverence toward the king, recognizing him as one who repays his kindness—the donor and patron.

Having been born in the heavens, they finally realize that such is the retribution for generosity and ethical discipline; only then do they understand that the Buddha’s words are truthful and not false, and that by cultivating even a small amount of wholesome karma, one obtains immeasurable retribution.
Then he spoke in verse:
"When giving while the reward is not yet seen, The mind harbors doubt and regret, thinking:
'It is merely a weary toil, In the end, nothing at all is gained.'"
"Once one has attained birth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one first beholds auspicious signs;
it is like a physician who, having reached his home, only then gives rise to great joy.

(88) Furthermore, it was heard that there were two women who both obtained mango fruits (*āmraphala*). One woman ate them without leaving the seeds behind, while the other woman ate the fruit and left the seeds.
As for those who remain behind, having perceived the excellence of that fruit, they sow seeds in fertile soil and irrigate them at the proper time, thereby obtaining a great harvest of fine fruit.
In the same way, worldly people establish the roots of virtue and extensively cultivate wholesome deeds, subsequently reaping their karmic rewards.

One who eats the seeds together with the food is likewise like a person who does not recognize the nature of wholesome karma; failing to cultivate it until the end, they obtain nothing at all and only then give rise to regret.
Thus he spoke in verse:
"Just like one who obtains fruit to eat, Yet fails to preserve any of the seeds,"
Later, seeing others eating the fruit, he then gave rise to regret;
it was just like that woman who, having planted seeds and obtained fruit,
felt great joy once again.

Furthermore, it has been heard that in the past there was a bhikṣu named Sumeru, who was skilled at joking and laughter; he entertained a certain king with boisterous merriment, pleasing him to the point of satisfaction.
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately requested land from him, wishing to establish a monastic dwelling (saṃghārāma). The king said to the bhikṣu:
"You may run as fast as you can without resting until you reach the furthest limit; all that ground shall be granted to you."

At that time, the bhikṣu adjusted his robes and immediately ran with great speed; though he became exhausted, because of his greed for the ground, he still did not stop. Later, as his exhaustion reached its peak and he could no longer move forward, he lay upon the ground and crawled along by twisting and turning.
In a short while, he again grew weary and threw a staff back toward him to drive him away, saying:
"As far as this staff reaches shall be my territory.
Having already explained the parable, I shall now explain its corresponding meaning.
Just as Mount Sumeru does not cease its efforts despite exhaustion for the sake of supporting the earth, so too is the Buddha; desiring to rescue and deliver all sentient beings, he reflects thus:
"How may I cause all sentient beings to obtain the happiness of humans and devas, as well as liberation?"

"Just as Mount Sumeru moves without ceasing, so too is the Buddha Bhagavān; for the sake of people such as Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and Aṅgulimāla, he brings them all to subdual. Whenever there are sentient beings who may be transformed and delivered, the Tathāgata immediately goes to transform and deliver them."

Just as Mount Sumeru, having become exhausted, lies upon the ground and rolls about, so too did the Buddha; having already undergone the weariness of delivering all sentient beings, he lay down with his body leaning against the twin *śāla* trees, breathing heavily. Like a *kāśika* tree whose roots have been severed and has fallen entirely, he remained with his body reclining between the twin trees; yet even then, he did not abandon the mind of diligence, continuing to deliver the Mallas of Kuśinagara and Subhadra.

Just as Sumeru cast away his staff to obtain the earth, so too did the Buddha; at the time of entering *nirvāṇa*, for the sake of saving sentient beings, he shattered his body into relics totaling eight *hu* and four *dou*. These benefit sentient beings such that, although the shattered relics are as minute as mustard seeds, wherever they go, the offerings people bestow upon them are no different from those given to the Buddha himself, enabling sentient beings to attain *nirvāṇa*.
Then he spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata himself has delivered Uruvilvā and his others,
along with their retinues and followers, as well as Ugra and Aṅgulimāla."
By the power of his vigor and dhyāna-pāramitā, even at the final moment when reclining on his right side,
he still delivered the Mallas and others such as Subhadra.
Out of a desire to provide salvation, he distributed his various śarīras.
"Until the extinction of the bequeathed Dharma, all these are offerings to me.
Just as that Sumeru, he cast his staff far away.

(90) Furthermore, I have heard that in the past, in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, there was a village called Balavattī. There lived a merchant named Siṃhala who built a saṃghārāma, which still exists today.

Cengqiebatuo was formerly the son of a wealthy elder; his household had long been affluent, but later, due to decline and depletion, he fell into poverty. His kinsmen and relatives all treated him with contempt and no longer regarded him as a human being. Carrying a heart full of grief and distress, he abandoned his home and departed, joining a group of companions who traveled to the Great Qin country, where they acquired vast wealth and treasures before returning to their own land.
When his kinsmen and relatives heard of this matter, they each prepared food, drink, incense, flowers, and music, and went out along the road to welcome him.

At that time, Cengqiebatuo (Saṃghāṭa) was dressed in humble attire and walked at the head of the group; because he had previously been poor and of low status, and because his age had increased since he acquired wealth, none of the welcoming relatives recognized him, and they asked:
"Where is Saṃghāṭa?"
He immediately said,
"It is still behind us.
When they reached the company of travelers, he asked them again:
"Where is Kātyāyana? His companions replied,
"The one who went on ahead is that very person."
At that time, his kinsmen went to where he was and said to him, "You are Kātyāyana; why do you tell us that you are behind?"
Cengqiebatuo said to his kinsmen, "Cengqiebatuo is not this person here;
he is among the companions, riding upon a donkey laden with pack-animals."

Why is this so? Since I arrived here, my kinsmen have treated me with contempt and would not speak to me at all; only upon hearing that I possessed wealth and treasures did they come to welcome me. For this reason, I was made to carry the load at the rear.
The kinsmen said, "What are you saying? We do not understand your words.
Keng-kia-p'o-t'a immediately replied to them:

"When I was poor, I spoke with you all, yet I received no response. Now that you see I possess much wealth and treasure, you have prepared these offerings to come and welcome me; you have come for the sake of my riches, not for my person."

The one who offers this analogy does so to illustrate that the World-Honored One is like Gābhaṭa, who was called "one who has acquired wealth" when his local clansmen and kinsmen prepared offerings to welcome him home. The Buddha is likewise; having attained Buddhahood, humans, devas, ghosts, spirits, and various dragon kings all come to make offerings. It is not that they are making offerings to me, but rather that they are making offerings to the merit of having become a Buddha.
"When I had not yet attained the Way and possessed no merit, all sentient beings would not even speak with me, much less offer me worship.

Therefore, you should know that it is the merit of the offering itself, not the act of worshipping me, that matters; for through such observation, even if one were to receive extensive offerings from all the devas and humans, there would be neither increase nor decrease."
“Humans, devas, asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas,
and all such multitudes likewise made extensive offerings;
yet the Buddha felt no joy of mind, because he observes with perfect equanimity.”
This offering is for all merits; it is not for the sake of making an offering to me.
Just as when one says "Gavāṭa," it indicates his entire retinue, so too is the analogy for saying that one is "behind oneself."
The Mahāvyūha-sūtra, Scroll Fifteen.
